Example: ID3 on the weather data

The 14 days have 9 times “Yes” and 5 times “No”, so H(\mathbb{T}) = -\frac{9}{14} \log_2 \frac{9}{14} - \frac{5}{14} \log_2 \frac{5}{14} = 0.940 bits.

Splitting by Windy gives 8 days with False (6 Yes, 2 No, entropy 0.811) and 6 days with True (3 Yes, 3 No, entropy 1). The gain is 0.940 - \frac{8}{14} \cdot 0.811 - \frac{6}{14} \cdot 1 = 0.048. The same computation for the other features gives 0.247 for Outlook, 0.152 for Humidity, and 0.029 for Temperature. Outlook becomes the root.

The four overcast days are all “Yes”, so that branch ends in a leaf. The five sunny days (2 Yes, 3 No) have the entropy 0.971; within them, Humidity separates the labels perfectly, with a gain of 0.971, while Temperature reaches 0.571 and Windy 0.020. The five rainy days (3 Yes, 2 No) are separated perfectly by Windy. The learned tree has three tests and gives the rules: if overcast, then Yes; if sunny and humid, then No; if sunny and normal humidity, then Yes; if rainy and windy, then No; if rainy and not windy, then Yes. Temperature is never used.

Since ID3 chooses the feature with the maximum gain, the base of the logarithm does not matter: another base scales all gains by the same factor. If a value v does not occur in a subset, the branch for it receives the most common label of its parent node.

hierarchy.lvl2: Continuous Features and the Gain Ratio
Continuous Features and the Gain Ratio

records.content:
Quinlan’s C4.5 algorithm (1993) extends ID3 in several ways and became one of the most widely used classifiers; a survey of data mining algorithms in 2008 ranked it first. Two extensions matter most.

Continuous features are split with a threshold. C4.5 sorts the training examples by the feature value and considers a threshold between each pair of neighbors with different labels, typically at the midpoint. Each candidate is scored with the information gain of the resulting binary split. Unlike a discrete feature, a continuous feature may be tested again further down the tree, with a different threshold.

Example: Splitting a continuous temperature

Six days have the temperatures 40, 48, 60, 72, 80, 90 and the labels No, No, Yes, Yes, Yes, No, with an entropy of 1 bit. The label changes between 48 and 60 and between 80 and 90, so the candidate thresholds are 54 and 85. The split at 54 separates two “No” days from four days with three “Yes” and gains 0.459 bits; the split at 85 separates five days with three “Yes” from one “No” day and gains 0.191. C4.5 chooses the threshold 54.

The gain ratio corrects a bias of the information gain toward features with many values. A feature such as a date has a different value on every day, splits the training set into subsets of one example each, and reaches the maximum gain, although it is useless for new days. C4.5 divides the gain by the split information, the entropy of the subset sizes, which is large for features that split into many small subsets:

Key Formula: Gain RatioGR(\mathbb{T}, x_j) = \frac{IG(\mathbb{T}, x_j)}{SI(\mathbb{T}, x_j)}, \qquad SI(\mathbb{T}, x_j) = -\sum_{v \in \mathbb{V}_j} \frac{|\mathbb{T}_{j,v}|}{|\mathbb{T}|} \log_2 \frac{|\mathbb{T}_{j,v}|}{|\mathbb{T}|}

The gain ratio rates the information a split gains about the labels relative to the information needed to describe the split itself.

For the weather data, Outlook splits the 14 days into subsets of 5, 4, and 5, so SI = 1.577 and GR = 0.247/1.577 = 0.156. Humidity splits into 7 and 7, so SI = 1 and GR = 0.152. Outlook remains the best choice, but by a much smaller margin. A split in which one subset contains almost all examples has a split information close to zero and an inflated gain ratio, so C4.5 considers only features whose information gain is at least average, for example above the mean or the median gain of all features, and chooses the best gain ratio among them. The CART algorithm by Breiman and colleagues uses a different impurity measure, the Gini index 1 - \sum_i P(y_i)^2, and builds binary trees; it is the basis of most current tree libraries.

A tree that grows until every leaf is pure fits the training data perfectly, including its noise and its exceptions, and generalizes poorly. Two kinds of pruning counter this. Pre-pruning stops the growth early: a node becomes a leaf if it holds too few examples or if the best split gains too little. Post-pruning grows the full tree first and then simplifies it with a validation set, as described in 

Training and Model Selection. It visits the inner nodes, tentatively replaces the subtree below a node by a leaf with the most common label, and keeps the replacement if the accuracy on the validation set does not drop. It repeats this until no replacement helps.

C4.5 can also prune the rules instead of the tree. It removes conditions from each rule as long as the accuracy improves. The rules are then no longer mutually exclusive, so C4.5 sorts them by their accuracy and applies the first rule that matches.

Real training data also needs preparation before a tree is grown. Examples without a label are removed, outliers eliminated, and missing feature values predicted or treated as a value of their own. Identical feature vectors with conflicting labels are collapsed into one entry with the most frequent label, keeping their count so that the entropies remain correct. Features that cannot help, such as a date or an identifier, are removed. Most of this work is specific to the domain: a good tree depends more on a small set of informative, weakly correlated features than on the learning algorithm.

A single tree is unstable. A small change in the training data can change the feature chosen at the root and thereby the whole tree, so trees have a high variance in the sense of 

Over- and Underfitting. Ensembles average many trees to reduce this variance.

A random forest (Breiman 2001) trains hundreds of trees, each on a bootstrap sample of the training set, drawn with replacement, and each split considers only a random subset of the features. The randomness makes the trees differ, and their majority vote is far more accurate and stable than any single tree.

Gradient boosting (Friedman 2001) builds the ensemble one small tree at a time. Each new tree h_m is fitted to what the current ensemble F_{m-1} still gets wrong, and it is added with a small learning rate \nu:

Key Formula: Gradient BoostingF_m(\mathbf{x}) = F_{m-1}(\mathbf{x}) + \nu\, h_m(\mathbf{x}), \qquad h_m \approx -\frac{∂ L(y, F)}{∂ F}\Big|_{F = F_{m-1}}

Each tree fits the negative gradient of the loss with respect to the current predictions. For the squared error L = \frac{1}{2}(y - F)^2, the negative gradient is the residual y - F_{m-1}(\mathbf{x}), the difference between the target and the current prediction. Each tree is trained on these residuals, not on the targets, and its output is a correction that is added to the prediction of the ensemble.

Example: Boosting stumps on eight points

Eight examples have the features x = 1, \dots, 8 and the targets 1.0, 1.5, 1.2, 3.8, 4.1, 3.9, 6.2, 5.8. The ensemble starts with the mean, F_0 = 3.44, with a mean squared error of 3.587. Each round fits a stump, a tree with a single split, to the residuals y_i - F_{m-1}(x_i) and adds it with \nu = 0.5. The leaves of a stump therefore hold corrections, not predictions: a negative value lowers the prediction.

The first residuals are -2.44, -1.94, -2.24 for x = 1, 2, 3, whose targets lie below the mean, and 0.36, 0.66, 0.46, 2.76, 2.36 for x = 4 to 8. The split at x < 3.5 separates them best. Each leaf takes the mean residual of its side, -2.20 and 1.32, because the mean minimizes the squared error within a leaf. With \nu = 0.5, the prediction drops from 3.44 to 2.34 for the first three points and rises to 4.10 for the others, and the error falls to 1.401. The second stump splits the new residuals at x < 6.5 with -0.63 and 1.90, and the error drops to 0.497. The third splits at x < 3.5 again and reaches 0.220. After ten rounds, the error is 0.017: ten stumps of one split each together approximate the step-shaped targets closely.

The learning rate keeps each tree from correcting too much at once, and the number of trees and their depth are hyperparameters chosen on validation data. With other losses, the trees fit other gradients: the logistic loss for classification, or the pairwise ranking gradients of LambdaMART for the learning-to-rank models of 

Learning to Rank. Libraries such as XGBoost and LightGBM implement gradient boosting efficiently, and on tabular data with mixed feature types, gradient-boosted trees often outperform neural networks.

hierarchy.lvl1: Linear Classifiers: Logistic Regression and Support Vector Machines
Linear Classifiers: Logistic Regression and Support Vector Machines

records.content:
Where this is used

 trains a logistic regression on frozen image embeddings, a linear probe, and 

 classifies HOG descriptors with a support vector machine. 

Automated Feature Extraction names decision trees and support vector machines as the standard classifiers of the two decades before deep learning. 

Evaluating Text Classifiers evaluates multi-class classifiers one class against the rest, the same decomposition that turns binary classifiers into multi-class ones below.

A linear classifier decides by the sign of a weighted sum, \mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x} + b: examples on one side of the hyperplane \mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x} + b = 0 belong to one class, examples on the other side to the other. The perceptron of 

From Perceptrons to Multilayer Networks is the simplest linear classifier, and it accepts any hyperplane that separates the training data. This section describes two methods that choose the hyperplane more carefully. Logistic regression turns the weighted sum into a probability and fits it with the cross-entropy loss. The support vector machine chooses the hyperplane with the largest distance to the nearest examples, and with the kernel trick, it separates classes that no hyperplane in the original space can separate.

hierarchy.lvl1: Linear Classifiers: Logistic Regression and Support Vector Machines
Linear Classifiers: Logistic Regression and Support Vector Machines

records.content:
Logistic regression models the probability of the positive class with the sigmoid of the weighted sum, the function of a single neuron in 

From Perceptrons to Multilayer Networks:

Key Formula: Logistic RegressionP(y = 1 ∣ \mathbf{x}) = \sigma(\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x} + b) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x} + b)}}, \qquad \frac{∂ J}{∂ \mathbf{w}} = \bigl(\sigma(\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x} + b) - y\bigr)\, \mathbf{x}

The weighted sum is the log-odds of the positive class, \log \frac{p}{1 - p} = \mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x} + b. With the cross-entropy loss J = -y \log p - (1 - y) \log (1 - p), the gradient is the prediction minus the target, times the input.

The gradient has the same form as the gradient of the softmax with the cross-entropy loss in 

Cross-Entropy: with two classes, the softmax reduces to the sigmoid. The loss is convex in \mathbf{w} and b, so gradient descent finds the global minimum, but there is no closed-form solution. The interpretation of the weights is simple: increasing a feature by one unit multiplies the odds of the positive class by e^{w_j}.

Example: Passing an exam

Eight students studied 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 3.5, and 4 hours, and the labels say whether they passed: 0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 1, 1, 1. At the start, with w = b = 0, every prediction is 0.5. The gradient averaged over the eight students is ∂ J / ∂ w = -0.438 and ∂ J / ∂ b = 0: more weight on the hours lowers the loss.

Gradient descent converges to w = 2.565 and b = -5.770. The decision boundary, where p = 0.5, lies at 5.770 / 2.565 = 2.25 hours. A student with 2 hours passes with probability 0.35, a student with 3 hours with probability 0.87. Each additional hour multiplies the odds of passing by e^{2.565} = 13.

With K classes, the sigmoid becomes the softmax of 

Softmax, and the model computes one weighted sum per class: softmax regression, a network with a single layer. The linear probe of 

 is such a model on top of fixed embeddings. Like all linear models, logistic regression overfits when there are many features and few examples, which the L2 penalty of 

Training Deep Networks prevents.

Logistic regression and Naive Bayes (

Naive Bayes) solve the same task in two different ways. Naive Bayes is generative: it models how each class produces its features and derives the decision from Bayes’ rule. Logistic regression is discriminative: it models the decision boundary directly and makes no assumption about how the features are distributed. Ng and Jordan (2002) showed that Naive Bayes reaches its best accuracy with fewer training examples, while logistic regression is more accurate when many examples are available.

hierarchy.lvl1: Linear Classifiers: Logistic Regression and Support Vector Machines
Linear Classifiers: Logistic Regression and Support Vector Machines

records.content:
When the classes are linearly separable, infinitely many hyperplanes separate them. 

Figure 1 contrasts two of them. The perceptron stops at the first one it finds. The support vector machine (SVM), developed by Vapnik and colleagues in the 1990s, chooses the hyperplane with the largest margin, the distance to the nearest training examples on either side. A large margin leaves the most room for new examples that lie a little closer to the other class than the training examples did.



Figure 1:Decision boundaries of the perceptron (left), one of many separating lines, and of the support vector machine (right), the line with the largest margin.

We label the classes y_i = +1 and y_i = -1 and scale \mathbf{w} and b so that the nearest examples satisfy y_i(\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x}_i + b) = 1. The margin then has the width 2 / \lVert \mathbf{w} \rVert, and maximizing it means minimizing \lVert \mathbf{w} \rVert while every example lies on the correct side, outside the margin. Real data is rarely separable, so the soft-margin SVM allows violations and penalizes them with the hinge loss:

Key Formula: Soft-Margin Support Vector Machine\min_{\mathbf{w}, b} \; \frac{1}{2} \lVert \mathbf{w} \rVert^2 + C \sum_{i=1}^{N} \max\bigl(0,\; 1 - y_i (\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x}_i + b)\bigr)

The first term widens the margin, the second penalizes examples that lie inside the margin or on the wrong side. The hyperparameter C sets the trade-off: a large C tolerates few violations, a small C prefers a wide margin.

The examples that lie on the margin or violate it are the support vectors. Only they determine the solution: moving or removing any other example does not change the hyperplane. Unlike the perceptron rule, the SVM solves a convex optimization problem with a single optimum.

Example: The maximum margin for six points

Three examples of the class -1 lie at (1,1), (2,1), (1,2), three of the class +1 at (4,3), (3,4), (4,4). The SVM finds \mathbf{w} = (0.5, 0.5) and b = -2.5, so the decision boundary is the line x_1 + x_2 = 5. For (2,1), \mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x} + b = 1.5 - 2.5 = -1, and for (4,3), it is 3.5 - 2.5 = 1: these two, together with (1,2) and (3,4), lie exactly on the margin and are the support vectors. The margin is 2 / \lVert \mathbf{w} \rVert = 2 / 0.707 = 2.83 wide. The points (1,1) and (4,4) lie farther away; moving them outward would not change the solution.

hierarchy.lvl1: Linear Classifiers: Logistic Regression and Support Vector Machines
Linear Classifiers: Logistic Regression and Support Vector Machines

records.content:
A linear classifier cannot separate classes that are not linearly separable, such as the XOR of 

From Perceptrons to Multilayer Networks. The remedy is to map the examples into a higher-dimensional space with a nonlinear function \phi, in which a hyperplane separates them. For XOR with the inputs coded as \pm 1, the product x_1 x_2 is enough: it is +1 when both inputs agree and -1 when they differ, so a single threshold on this new feature separates the classes.

The mapped space can be very large. The SVM, however, needs the examples only in dot products \phi(\mathbf{x})^\top \phi(\mathbf{x}'), both for training and for classifying, when the optimization is written in its dual form. A kernel K(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}') computes this dot product directly from the original vectors, without ever computing \phi. This is the kernel trick.

Example: A polynomial kernel

For two-dimensional vectors, the kernel K(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}') = (1 + \mathbf{x}^\top \mathbf{x}')^2 equals the dot product in a six-dimensional space with \phi(\mathbf{x}) = (1, \sqrt{2}\, x_1, \sqrt{2}\, x_2, x_1^2, x_2^2, \sqrt{2}\, x_1 x_2). For \mathbf{x} = (1, 2) and \mathbf{x}' = (3, 1), the kernel gives (1 + 3 + 2)^2 = 36. The explicit dot product gives 1 + 2 \cdot 3 + 2 \cdot 2 + 1 \cdot 9 + 4 \cdot 1 + 2 \cdot 6 = 36 as well. The mapped space contains the product x_1 x_2, so an SVM with this kernel separates XOR.

The Gaussian kernel K(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}') = \exp(-\gamma \lVert \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}' \rVert^2) corresponds to a mapping into a space with infinitely many dimensions and can separate almost any training set; its width \gamma and the penalty C are tuned on validation data. The kernel trick is powerful, but choosing a good kernel is a design decision made by a human, much like choosing hand-crafted features, and training an SVM costs between quadratic and cubic time in the number of examples. For very large datasets, linear models and neural networks, which learn their features, took over.

records.content:
The perceptron and the SVM separate two classes. Two strategies combine binary classifiers into a classifier for K classes. One-vs-rest trains K classifiers, each separating one class from all others, and predicts the class whose classifier gives the highest score. One-vs-one trains K(K-1)/2 classifiers, one per pair of classes, and predicts the class that wins the most pairwise decisions; with 10 classes, this means 45 classifiers, each trained on the examples of two classes only. Logistic regression extends naturally to many classes with the softmax and needs neither strategy.

Where this is used

Approximate Nearest-Neighbor Search builds the codebooks of product quantization with k-means, and 

Losses and Performance Measures lists the measures that judge clusters without labels. Naive Bayes in 

Naive Bayes can model a continuous feature with a mixture of Gaussians, whose parameters the expectation maximization of this section estimates. Classical speech recognizers quantize acoustic feature vectors with k-means before an HMM models them.

Clustering is unsupervised learning: the algorithm observes data without targets and finds groups of similar items. The result is a finite set of clusters and a rule that assigns new items to one of them, or to several with different weights. In multimedia retrieval, clustering serves four purposes. Feature quantization reduces a multi-dimensional feature to a small number of discrete values, much like a histogram approximates a distribution. Vector compression maps groups of dimensions to a few bits, as product quantization does for vector search. Cluster analysis extracts groups from a collection and infers labels for them. Image segmentation groups the pixels of an image into regions that belong together: clustering first quantizes the colors, and morphological operators then build coherent regions. This section describes k-means, expectation maximization with Gaussian mixtures, and how to choose the number of clusters.

k-means goes back to the 1950s, when Lloyd developed it at Bell Labs to quantize signals for transmission; MacQueen gave it its name in 1967, and it became one of the most popular methods for cluster analysis. It represents each of K clusters by its centroid, the mean of the cluster’s items, and assigns each item to the cluster with the nearest centroid. The centroids divide the space into Voronoi cells, which define the shapes of the clusters.

For N items \mathbf{x}_1, \dots, \mathbf{x}_N in d dimensions, k-means looks for a partition into K sets \mathbb{S}_1, \dots, \mathbb{S}_K that makes the clusters as compact as possible:

Key Formula: Within-Cluster Sum of Squares\text{WCSS} = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \sum_{\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{S}_k} \lVert \mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_k \rVert_2^2, \qquad \boldsymbol{\mu}_k = \frac{1}{|\mathbb{S}_k|} \sum_{\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{S}_k} \mathbf{x}

The sum of the squared distances between the items and the centroids of their clusters. k-means minimizes it: small values mean tight clusters around their centroids.

Finding the partition with the smallest WCSS is NP-hard, but Lloyd’s algorithm finds a local optimum with a simple iteration:

Choose K initial centroids.

Assign each item to the cluster of its nearest centroid; if several centroids are equally near, choose one at random.

Compute the new centroids as the means of the items in each cluster.

Repeat steps 2 and 3 until the assignments no longer change.

Neither step can increase the WCSS. Step 2 moves each item to its nearest centroid, and step 3 places each centroid at the point that minimizes the squared distances to its items. The algorithm therefore converges, usually in a few iterations, but the local optimum depends on the initial centroids.

Example: k-means on six numbers

The items are 1, 2, 4, 7, 8, 12, and we start with K = 2 and the poor initial centroids 1 and 2. In the first iteration, only the item 1 is nearest to the centroid 1; all others go to the centroid 2. The new centroids are 1 and 6.6, with a WCSS of 59.2. In the second iteration, the item 2 joins the first cluster, and the centroids become 1.5 and 7.75 (WCSS 33.25). In the third, the item 4 moves as well: the clusters \{1, 2, 4\} and \{7, 8, 12\} have the centroids 2.33 and 9 and a WCSS of 18.67. The fourth iteration changes nothing, and the algorithm stops. For comparison, a single cluster has a WCSS of 85.3.

The result depends on the start, and three strategies are common. Random points picks K random items as centroids, which spreads the centroids across the data. Random partition assigns every item to a random cluster and computes the centroids of these clusters, which places them close together near the center of the data. k-means++ (Arthur and Vassilvitskii 2007) chooses the first centroid at random and each further one among the remaining items with a probability proportional to the squared distance to the nearest centroid chosen so far. Distant items are therefore likely to become centroids. The seeding costs more, but it leads to much smaller final errors and faster convergence, and it is the default in most libraries. Running k-means several times with different starts and keeping the result with the smallest WCSS further reduces the risk of a poor local optimum.

k-means makes a hard assignment: each item belongs to exactly one cluster. A Gaussian mixture model makes a soft assignment instead. It assumes that the data comes from K Gaussian distributions \mathcal{N}(\mu_k, \sigma_k^2), each representing one cluster, and that an item comes from cluster k with the prior probability w_k, where \sum_k w_k = 1. 

Figure 1 shows two Gaussians and their mixture. With enough components, a mixture can approximate any distribution, which is why Gaussian mixtures also serve as density estimators (

Tasks and Experience).



Figure 1:Two Gaussian distributions (left) and the mixture they form (right).

Estimating the parameters would be easy if we knew which cluster each item came from: the mean and the variance of each cluster would follow from its items, and the prior from its share of the items. Conversely, if we knew the parameters, Bayes’ rule would give the probability that an item comes from each cluster. Expectation maximization (EM) alternates between the two. It starts with initial parameters and repeats two steps. The E-step computes for every item x_i and cluster k the responsibility \gamma_{i,k}, the probability that the cluster produced the item, from the current parameters:

Key Formula: E-Step of a Gaussian Mixture\gamma_{i,k} = \frac{w_k\, f(x_i; \mu_k, \sigma_k^2)}{\sum_{l=1}^{K} w_l\, f(x_i; \mu_l, \sigma_l^2)}, \qquad f(x; \mu, \sigma^2) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}\, e^{-\frac{(x - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}}

The responsibility of a cluster for an item is the prior of the cluster times its density at the item, normalized over all clusters. The responsibilities of each item sum to 1.

The M-step re-estimates the parameters from the responsibilities, with each item counted in each cluster with the weight \gamma_{i,k}:\mu_k = \frac{\sum_i \gamma_{i,k}\, x_i}{\sum_i \gamma_{i,k}}, \qquad \sigma_k^2 = \frac{\sum_i \gamma_{i,k}\, (x_i - \mu_k)^2}{\sum_i \gamma_{i,k}}, \qquad w_k = \frac{1}{N} \sum_i \gamma_{i,k}

The two steps repeat until the parameters stop changing. Each iteration increases the likelihood of the data under the mixture, or leaves it unchanged, so EM converges, but like k-means only to a local optimum. At the end, each item can be assigned to its most responsible cluster, k^* = \operatorname{argmax}_k \gamma_{i,k}.

Example: EM on six numbers

The items are 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 6.0, 6.5, 7.5, and we start with the means \mu_1 = 2 and \mu_2 = 5, the variances \sigma_1^2 = \sigma_2^2 = 1, and equal priors. The log-likelihood of the data under these parameters is -15.03.

The E-step gives the item 2.0 a responsibility of 0.989 for the first cluster: its density under \mathcal{N}(2, 1) is far larger than under \mathcal{N}(5, 1). The items 1.0 and 1.5 belong to the first cluster with 0.999 and 0.998, and the three large items to the second with more than 0.999. The M-step moves the means to 1.499 and 6.645, shrinks the variances to 0.171 and 0.494, and keeps the priors near 0.5. The log-likelihood rises to -8.61. After the second iteration, the parameters reach their final values, \mu = (1.5, 6.667), \sigma^2 = (0.167, 0.389), and w = (0.5, 0.5), with a log-likelihood of -8.57.

In d dimensions, each cluster becomes a multivariate Gaussian \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_k, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k) with a covariance matrix, and the M-step computes \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k as the responsibility-weighted average of (\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_k)(\mathbf{x}_i - \boldsymbol{\mu}_k)^\top. The clusters can then be elongated and tilted ellipsoids instead of the spheres of k-means.

The name comes from the general form of the algorithm. The cluster memberships are latent variables: they are not observed, and the likelihood of the data is a sum over all their possible values, which has no closed-form maximum. EM instead maximizes the expected log-likelihood of the data together with the latent variables, where the expectation uses the distribution of the latent variables given the data and the current parameters (the E-step), and the maximization over the parameters has a closed-form solution (the M-step). Dempster, Laird, and Rubin (1977) showed that this never decreases the likelihood itself.

k-means is a special case of EM. With hard responsibilities, \gamma_{i,k} = 1 for the nearest centroid and 0 otherwise, equal priors, and identical spherical covariances, the E-step becomes the assignment step and the M-step the centroid update. Gaussian mixtures with a common variance that shrinks toward zero turn into k-means in the limit.

The number of clusters K is not known in advance, and it controls the capacity of the model like the polynomial degree of 

Over- and Underfitting. With K = 1, all items form one cluster, the extreme of underfitting. With K = N, every item is its own cluster with a WCSS of zero, the extreme of overfitting. Without labels, there is no validation accuracy, so we need measures that rate the clusters themselves: their compactness and their separation.

The elbow method plots the sum of squared errors, the WCSS for k-means, against K, as in 

Figure 2. The error always falls with growing K, but beyond a certain point it falls much more slowly: adding clusters then splits real groups instead of separating them. This point, the elbow, is a good choice for K. To find it automatically, we can compute the curve for K from 2 to an upper bound and pick the point farthest from the straight line between the first and the last point of the curve. Alternatively, we increase K step by step and stop when the distance of the curve point to the corner (2, 0) starts to grow, which needs fewer runs. Both methods need the two axes normalized, for example by min-max scaling. For Gaussian mixtures, the squared Mahalanobis distance (\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_k)^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k^{-1} (\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_k) takes the place of the squared Euclidean distance.



Figure 2:The elbow method: the sum of squared errors as a function of the number of clusters K, with the elbow point where the curve levels out.

The silhouette score (Rousseeuw 1987) rates each item by how much closer it is to its own cluster than to the next one. With a_i the mean distance of item i to the other items of its cluster and b_i the mean distance to the items of the nearest other cluster, the silhouette of the item iss_i = \frac{b_i - a_i}{\max(a_i, b_i)}

It lies between -1 and 1: values near 1 mean that the item sits well inside its cluster, values near 0 that it lies between two clusters, and negative values that it is probably in the wrong cluster. An item that forms a cluster of its own gets s_i = 0. The mean silhouette over all items rates the clustering, and the K with the highest mean is a good choice.

Example: Silhouettes for two and three clusters

For the k-means result \{1, 2, 4\} and \{7, 8, 12\} above, the item 1 has a = (1 + 3)/2 = 2 and b = (6 + 7 + 11)/3 = 8, so s = (8 - 2)/8 = 0.75. The item 4 lies closer to the other cluster and gets only 0.50, the item 7 only 0.36. The mean silhouette is 0.58. Splitting off the item 12 as a third cluster lowers the WCSS from 18.7 to 5.2, but the mean silhouette drops to 0.54. The items 7 and 8 gain, since their cluster is now tight (0.79 and 0.75), but the single item 12 gets a silhouette of 0, and the item 4 falls to 0.29, because the new cluster \{7, 8\} lies only 3.5 away on average. The silhouette prefers two clusters.

Other measures exist: the Davies-Bouldin index compares the spread within clusters with the distance between their centroids, and with reference labels, the adjusted Rand index compares a clustering with a known partition (

Losses and Performance Measures). No measure is right for every purpose: for vector compression, more clusters always mean less error, and K follows from the memory budget instead.

Where this is used

Query Understanding tags the words of a query with their parts of speech, where a hidden Markov model learns the tag transitions from an annotated corpus and the Viterbi algorithm of this section decodes the most likely tag sequence. Classical speech recognizers model each phoneme with a hidden Markov model, the pipeline that 

Transcription summarizes and 

Speech Recognition with HMMs describes in detail.

Sequential data arises whenever observations unfold over time: words in a sentence, acoustic frames in speech, nucleotides in DNA. Often the process that generates the data has a state that we cannot observe directly. A speech recognizer measures acoustic features, not the phonemes that produced them; a part-of-speech tagger sees words, not their grammatical roles. A hidden Markov model (HMM) describes such a process with a sequence of hidden states that follows a Markov chain and emits one observation per step. This section defines the model and the three algorithms that make it practical: the forward algorithm, Viterbi decoding, and Baum-Welch training.

hierarchy.lvl2: From Markov Chains to Hidden States
From Markov Chains to Hidden States

records.content:
A Markov chain describes a sequence of states X_1, X_2, \dots, X_T in which the next state depends only on the current one, the Markov assumption:P(X_t ∣ X_{t-1}, \dots, X_1) = P(X_t ∣ X_{t-1})

A weather model with the states sunny, cloudy, and rainy, and the probabilities of moving from one to another, is a Markov chain. It is adequate when we can see the states. Many systems provide only indirect evidence. In a hidden Markov model, the state sequence evolves as a Markov chain, and each state emits an observable symbol according to its own probability distribution. The observations are noisy reflections of the hidden states. An HMM consists of

a finite set of hidden states 1, \dots, N,

a set of observable symbols, or a density for continuous observations,

the transition probabilities a_{ij} = P(X_t = j ∣ X_{t-1} = i),

the emission probabilities b_j(o) = P(O_t = o ∣ X_t = j),

and the initial distribution \pi_i = P(X_1 = i).

For a state sequence x_1, \dots, x_T and an observation sequence o_1, \dots, o_T, the joint probability factors into the initial, transition, and emission terms:P(x_1, \dots, x_T, o_1, \dots, o_T) = \pi_{x_1}\, b_{x_1}(o_1) \prod_{t=2}^{T} a_{x_{t-1} x_t}\, b_{x_t}(o_t)

The factorization expresses two assumptions: the states follow the Markov property, and each observation depends only on the state at its own time step. In speech recognition, the states can stand for parts of phonemes, and each emits acoustic feature vectors from a mixture of Gaussians (

Clustering).

We use a small model as the running example. A friend lives far away and spends every day walking, shopping, or cleaning, depending on the weather, which we cannot observe. The hidden states are Rainy and Sunny, with the initial probabilities 0.6 and 0.4. Rainy days are followed by rainy days with probability 0.7, sunny days by sunny days with 0.6. On a rainy day, the friend walks with probability 0.1, shops with 0.4, and cleans with 0.5; on a sunny day, the probabilities are 0.6, 0.3, and 0.1. On three days, the friend reports walk, shop, clean.

Working with an HMM involves three problems. Evaluation computes the probability of an observation sequence, which measures how well a model explains the data and lets us choose the best of several models, for example one per word. Decoding finds the most likely sequence of hidden states, such as the phonemes or the part-of-speech tags. Learning estimates the parameters from data.

The probability of the observations is the sum of the joint probability over all state sequences. With N states and T steps, there are N^T sequences, far too many to enumerate. The Markov property allows a recursion instead. The forward variable \alpha_t(j) is the probability of the first t observations together with the state j at time t. It is computed from the forward variables of the previous step, because the state at time t depends only on the state at time t - 1:

Key Formula: Forward Algorithm\alpha_1(j) = \pi_j\, b_j(o_1), \qquad \alpha_t(j) = b_j(o_t) \sum_{i=1}^{N} \alpha_{t-1}(i)\, a_{ij}, \qquad P(o_1, \dots, o_T) = \sum_{j=1}^{N} \alpha_T(j)

Each step sums over all ways to reach state j from the previous step and multiplies with the probability that j emits the current observation. The cost is N^2 per step, N^2 T in total, instead of N^T.

Example: How likely is walk, shop, clean?

On the first day, \alpha_1 = (0.6 \cdot 0.1, \; 0.4 \cdot 0.6) = (0.06, 0.24) for Rainy and Sunny. On the second day, the friend went shopping: \alpha_2(\text{Rainy}) = (0.06 \cdot 0.7 + 0.24 \cdot 0.4) \cdot 0.4 = 0.0552 and \alpha_2(\text{Sunny}) = (0.06 \cdot 0.3 + 0.24 \cdot 0.6) \cdot 0.3 = 0.0486. On the third day, the friend cleaned: \alpha_3 = (0.0290, \; 0.0046).

The probability of the observations is 0.0290 + 0.0046 = 0.0336. Summing the joint probabilities of all 2^3 = 8 state sequences gives the same value, but the recursion needs only N^2 = 4 transition products per step instead of enumerating the sequences, and the advantage grows exponentially with the length.

A backward variable \beta_t(i), the probability of the remaining observations after time t given the state i at time t, is computed in the same way from the end of the sequence. Together, \alpha_t(i)\, \beta_t(i) / P(o_1, \dots, o_T) gives the probability of being in state i at time t, which the training below needs.

Decoding looks for the single most likely state sequence. The Viterbi algorithm uses the same recursion as the forward algorithm with a maximum instead of a sum. This is dynamic programming: the best path to a state at time t consists of the best path to some state at time t - 1 plus one transition, so we only need to keep the best path to each state.

Key Formula: Viterbi Recursion\delta_1(j) = \pi_j\, b_j(o_1), \qquad \delta_t(j) = b_j(o_t) \max_{i} \bigl(\delta_{t-1}(i)\, a_{ij}\bigr), \qquad \psi_t(j) = \operatorname{argmax}_{i} \bigl(\delta_{t-1}(i)\, a_{ij}\bigr)

\delta_t(j) is the probability of the best state sequence that ends in state j at time t, and the backpointer \psi_t(j) records its previous state. After the last step, the algorithm picks the state with the largest \delta_T and follows the backpointers to recover the whole sequence.

Example: The most likely weather

The first day gives \delta_1 = (0.06, 0.24). For a rainy second day, the best predecessor is Sunny, since 0.24 \cdot 0.4 = 0.096 exceeds 0.06 \cdot 0.7 = 0.042, so \delta_2(\text{Rainy}) = 0.096 \cdot 0.4 = 0.0384. For a sunny second day, the best predecessor is Sunny as well: \delta_2(\text{Sunny}) = 0.24 \cdot 0.6 \cdot 0.3 = 0.0432. For the third day, Rainy is best reached from Rainy, \delta_3(\text{Rainy}) = 0.0384 \cdot 0.7 \cdot 0.5 = 0.01344, and Sunny from Sunny, \delta_3(\text{Sunny}) = 0.0432 \cdot 0.6 \cdot 0.1 = 0.0026.

The best final state is Rainy with 0.01344. Its backpointer leads to Rainy on the second day, whose backpointer leads to Sunny on the first: the most likely weather was sunny, rainy, rainy. On the second day alone, Sunny had the larger \delta; the best overall path still goes through Rainy, because only Rainy explains the cleaning on the third day well. This is why Viterbi keeps one path per state and decides only at the end.

With labeled data, where every observation sequence comes with its state sequence, as in a part-of-speech corpus, the parameters are relative frequencies: count the transitions and emissions and normalize them, with smoothing (

Naive Bayes) for the counts that are zero.

Without state labels, the Baum-Welch algorithm estimates the parameters with the expectation maximization of 

Clustering. Its E-step uses the forward and backward variables to compute the expected number of times each state is visited and each transition and emission is used. Its M-step sets the parameters to these expected counts, normalized. Each iteration increases the likelihood of the observations. Viterbi training is a simpler alternative that updates the parameters from the single best state sequence instead of the expected counts, a hard assignment like k-means; it is faster but more prone to poor local optima. Both depend on a good initialization, because the likelihood has many local optima.

The forward variables and the Viterbi probabilities are products of many probabilities and fall below the smallest representable number after a few hundred steps, which is a short utterance in speech recognition. Viterbi runs in log space, where products become sums and the maximum is unaffected. The forward algorithm needs a sum of probabilities, which in log space becomes \log \sum_i e^{l_i}, computed stably by factoring out the largest term; alternatively, the forward variables are rescaled to sum to 1 at every step and the scaling factors are accumulated in log space.

Hidden Markov models were the standard for speech recognition for three decades, and they have been used for part-of-speech tagging, for gene prediction, where hidden states stand for coding and non-coding regions of DNA, and for the segmentation of sensor data into the phases of an activity. Several extensions relax their assumptions. Higher-order models let a state depend on several previous states, hierarchical HMMs nest models at several levels of abstraction, for example phonemes inside words, and discriminative models such as conditional random fields train for the accuracy of the labels instead of the likelihood of the observations. On large datasets, the neural sequence models of 

Recurrent Networks and transformers have replaced HMMs in most applications, but HMMs remain useful where the model must be small, trained on little data, or interpretable.

Naive Bayes applies Bayes’ rule with the assumption that the features are independent given the class. The decision sums the log prior and the log likelihoods of the features, learning reduces to counting, and Laplace smoothing keeps unseen values from vetoing a class. Its decisions are often right even though its probabilities are too extreme.

A decision tree classifies with a sequence of tests on single features. ID3 chooses the test with the largest information gain, C4.5 adds thresholds for continuous features and the gain ratio against features with many values, and pruning on a validation set keeps the tree from overfitting.

Single trees have a high variance. Random forests average many randomized trees; gradient boosting adds small trees one at a time, each fitted to the negative gradient of the loss (for the squared error, the residuals of the current ensemble) and added as a correction, and is among the most accurate methods for tabular data, including the learning-to-rank models of web search.

Logistic regression models the log-odds as a linear function and is trained with the cross-entropy loss; its gradient is the prediction minus the target, times the input. It is the discriminative counterpart of Naive Bayes.

The support vector machine chooses the hyperplane with the largest margin; only the support vectors determine it, and the soft margin trades width against violations with the hyperparameter C. The kernel trick computes dot products in a high-dimensional feature space without ever constructing it.

k-means minimizes the within-cluster sum of squares with Lloyd’s algorithm and finds a local optimum that depends on the initialization; k-means++ chooses good starting centroids. Expectation maximization fits Gaussian mixtures with soft assignments, and k-means is its hard-assignment special case.

The number of clusters is a capacity parameter: the elbow method and the silhouette score choose it without labels.

A hidden Markov model describes a sequence of hidden states that follows a Markov chain and emits one observation per step. The forward algorithm computes the probability of the observations, the Viterbi algorithm the most likely state sequence, both in N^2 T time, and Baum-Welch learns the parameters with expectation maximization.

Key Formula: Naive Bayes Decision Rulek^* = \operatorname{argmax}_k \; \Bigl( \log P(C_k) + \sum_{j=1}^{M} \log P(x_j ∣ C_k) \Bigr)

The class with the largest sum of log prior and log likelihoods of the observed features wins.

Key Formula: Information GainIG(\mathbb{T}, x_j) = H(\mathbb{T}) - \sum_{v \in \mathbb{V}_j} \frac{|\mathbb{T}_{j,v}|}{|\mathbb{T}|}\, H(\mathbb{T}_{j,v})

The reduction of the label entropy when the training set is split by the values of a feature.

Key Formula: Viterbi Recursion\delta_t(j) = b_j(o_t) \max_{i} \bigl(\delta_{t-1}(i)\, a_{ij}\bigr)

The probability of the best state sequence that ends in state j at time t; backpointers recover the sequence.

Most of the models in the second half of this book are neural networks: the encoders that turn text into embeddings, the convolutional networks that describe images, and the classifiers that label sounds. The chapters use these networks as tools and explain what they compute, but not how they learn. This chapter covers the mechanics: how a network computes its output, how backpropagation trains it, why deep networks were hard to train for a long time, and which architectures made convolutional networks succeed.

Where this is used

Automated Feature Extraction lists the milestones of neural image classification; 

CNN Architectures describes the architectures behind them.

 uses pretrained convolutional networks as feature extractors and relies on convolution, pooling, and training as described here.

Word Embeddings trains a shallow network with a softmax output, and 

Transformer Embeddings builds on layers, residual connections, and normalization.

Prerequisites

Losses, gradient descent, and the gradient of the cross-entropy loss: 

Losses and Performance Measures.

Over- and underfitting, which regularization addresses: 

Over- and Underfitting.

From Perceptrons to Multilayer Networks follows the history of the field and explains why a single layer of perceptrons is not enough. 

Backpropagation and Gradient Descent derives backpropagation on a small network with all numbers worked out. 

Training Deep Networks explains vanishing and exploding gradients and the activation functions, initializations, normalization layers, regularization methods, and optimizers that made deep networks trainable. 

Convolutional Networks introduces convolution, strides, padding, and pooling, and 

CNN Architectures walks through the architectures built from them, from Rowley’s face detector and LeNet to ResNet and the Vision Transformer. 

Recurrent Networks covers networks for sequences, from recurrent networks and LSTM cells to attention.

Where this is used

Every network in this book is built from the neuron defined in this section. Word2vec in 

Word Embeddings is a network with one hidden layer, the transformer layers of 

Transformer Embeddings contain fully connected feed-forward networks between their attention layers, and the convolutional networks of 

 end in fully connected layers that compute the class scores. 

Automated Feature Extraction lists the milestones of neural image classification that the history below explains.

A neural network computes its output with many simple units, the neurons, each of which forms a weighted sum of its inputs and passes it through a nonlinear function. This section follows the idea from its beginnings to the multilayer network. We start with a short history, because the setbacks of the field explain many design decisions of today’s networks. Then we look at the perceptron, the first trainable neuron, and at the reason why one layer of perceptrons is not enough. The section ends with the multilayer network and a small example network that 

Backpropagation and Gradient Descent trains.

hierarchy.lvl2: Three Waves of Neural Network Research
Three Waves of Neural Network Research

records.content:
Figure 1 shows the milestones of the first decades. The first wave began with a model of the biological neuron. McCulloch and Pitts described in 1943 a neuron as a threshold unit that fires when the weighted sum of its inputs exceeds a threshold. In 1958, Rosenblatt turned this unit into the perceptron, a neuron that learns its weights from examples, and built it in hardware. Several perceptrons could work in parallel, but each connected the inputs directly to an output. In 1969, Minsky and Papert showed that such a single layer cannot compute even simple functions such as the exclusive or (XOR), which the next subsection explains. Interest in neural networks declined for more than a decade.



Figure 1:Milestones of neural network research from 1943 to 2006.

The second wave came in the 1980s with networks that have hidden layers between input and output, and with an algorithm to train them. Rumelhart, Hinton, and Williams popularized backpropagation in 1986; the underlying method of computing derivatives backward through a chain of functions had appeared earlier, in work by Linnainmaa (1970) and Werbos (1974). The revival produced convolutional networks, recurrent networks, and belief networks, many of the concepts of modern deep learning. Yet deeper networks were unstable and slow to train, for reasons that 

Training Deep Networks explains, and computers were too slow for large networks. From the early 1990s until the early 2010s, support vector machines with well-chosen kernels matched or beat neural networks on most benchmarks.

Convolutional networks existed long before they won. LeNet read handwritten digits in the 1990s, but for almost two decades it was not clear whether convolutional networks would scale from small digit images to large collections of realistic photos. Early networks also depended on many hand-designed steps and solved one task only, as the face detector in 

CNN Architectures shows. The 

TensorFlow Playground trains small fully connected networks in the browser and makes the limits of the early multilayer networks tangible.

The third wave started in the mid-2000s. A research program of the Canadian Institute for Advanced Research, led by Hinton, kept the field alive when funding was scarce. In 2006, Hinton, Osindero, and Teh showed how to train deep belief networks layer by layer, and the field adopted the name deep learning. At the same time, graphics processors became fast and programmable. They compute the matrix products of a network in parallel and trained networks in days instead of weeks. 

Figure 2 shows how the energy efficiency of these processors grew over the following decade. In 2012, a network trained by the Google Brain project on 16,000 processor cores learned to detect cats in YouTube frames without any labels. In the same year, AlexNet won the ImageNet challenge with a large margin and showed for the first time that features learned from data beat features designed by hand on a large benchmark. 

Figure 3 shows the jump on object detection benchmarks that followed.



Figure 2:Energy efficiency of NVIDIA graphics processors from 2011 to 2021 in GFLOPs per watt, on a logarithmic scale.



Figure 3:Object detection results on standard benchmarks from 2007 to 2018, with the turning point of 2012.

The transformer of 2017, which 

Transformer Embeddings explains, replaced recurrent networks for text and later reached images and audio as well. It is the architecture behind today’s large language models. In 2024, Hopfield and Hinton received the Nobel Prize in Physics for their foundational work on neural networks.

The perceptron is a binary classifier. It maps an input vector \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^K to the output 1 or 0 with a weight vector \mathbf{w} \in \mathbb{R}^K and a bias b:f(\mathbf{x}) = \phi_{\text{step}}(\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x} + b), \qquad \phi_{\text{step}}(s) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } s > 0 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}

The equation \mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x} + b = 0 describes a hyperplane, a line in two dimensions, and the perceptron outputs 1 on one side and 0 on the other. 

Figure 4 shows the general configuration: L perceptrons share the K inputs, and each has its own weights w_{k,l} and bias b_l, so that the layer computes L binary outputs o_l at once.



Figure 4:A layer of L perceptrons with K inputs, weights w_{k,l}, biases b_l, and the binary step function.

Rosenblatt’s learning rule adjusts the weights only when the perceptron makes a mistake. For each training example \mathbf{x} with target t \in \{0, 1\}, the perceptron computes its output o and then updates its parameters.

Key Formula: Perceptron Learning Rule\mathbf{w} \leftarrow \mathbf{w} + \alpha\,(t - o)\,\mathbf{x}, \qquad b \leftarrow b + \alpha\,(t - o)

If the output is correct, t - o = 0 and nothing changes. If the output is 0 but should be 1, the weights move toward the example; if it is 1 but should be 0, they move away from it. The learning rate \alpha > 0 sets the step size.

Example: A perceptron learns AND

The four examples (0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1) have the targets 0, 0, 0, 1 of the logical AND. We start with \mathbf{w} = (0, 0), b = 0, and \alpha = 1, and present the examples in this order in every epoch.

In the first epoch, the first three examples give \mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x} + b = 0, so the output is 0 and correct. For (1,1), the output 0 is wrong, and the rule adds the example: \mathbf{w} = (1, 1), b = 1. In the second epoch, this perceptron now answers 1 for (0,0), because 0 + 0 + 1 > 0, and the rule subtracts: b = 0. Corrections continue in both directions, ten in total. In the sixth epoch, no example is misclassified anymore, and the perceptron has converged to \mathbf{w} = (2, 1) and b = -2.

The line 2x_1 + x_2 = 2 separates (1,1), where 2 + 1 - 2 = 1 > 0, from the other three examples. For (1,0), the sum is exactly 0, so the output is 0: the example lies on the line, which the strict inequality of the step function still classifies correctly.

The rule does not minimize an objective function. It is a heuristic that stops as soon as all examples are classified correctly. If a separating hyperplane exists, that is, if the data is linearly separable, the rule finds one after a finite number of corrections. It finds one of many possible hyperplanes, and which one depends on the order of the examples. If no separating hyperplane exists, the rule never stops correcting.

The exclusive or is the classic counterexample. XOR outputs 1 for (0,1) and (1,0) and 0 for (0,0) and (1,1). No line separates the two pairs, because the points of each pair lie on opposite corners of the unit square. A single perceptron therefore cannot compute XOR, and neither can any single layer of perceptrons, since each output is a perceptron of its own.

Figure 5 compares the perceptron with the support vector machine on a separable problem. The perceptron accepts any separating line, while the support vector machine chooses the one with the largest distance to the nearest examples of both classes. 

Linear Classifiers: Logistic Regression and Support Vector Machines describes the support vector machine, the kernel trick that lets it separate data that is not linearly separable, and how binary classifiers combine into multi-class classifiers.



Figure 5:Decision boundaries of the perceptron (left), which accepts any of many separating lines, and of the support vector machine (right), which chooses the one with the largest margin.

A multilayer network differs from a layer of perceptrons in four ways. It has hidden layers between the input and the output layer. Its neurons use smooth activation functions instead of the step function, so their outputs are real numbers. It is trained by minimizing an objective function, the loss of 

Losses and Performance Measures. And it uses backpropagation to compute how the loss depends on every weight, which 

Backpropagation and Gradient Descent derives.

Figure 6 shows the model of a single neuron. It receives the inputs a_k, multiplies each with a weight w_k, adds a bias b, and applies the activation function \phi to the sum s.

Key Formula: Neurons = \sum_{k} w_k\, a_k + b, \qquad y = \phi(s), \qquad \phi(s) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-s}}

A neuron computes a weighted sum of its inputs and passes it through a nonlinear activation function. The sigmoid shown here, also called the logistic function, maps any sum to a value between 0 and 1; 

Training Deep Networks introduces the activation functions that replaced it.



Figure 6:A neuron with inputs a_k, weights w_k, bias b, summation, and the sigmoid activation function.

Hidden layers make XOR easy. A hidden neuron can compute any function that one perceptron can, so the hidden layer can compute two linearly separable functions, and the output neuron can combine them. To keep the numbers simple, we use the step function \phi_{\text{step}} of the perceptron as the activation instead of the sigmoid. One hidden neuron computes OR, h_1 = \phi_{\text{step}}(x_1 + x_2 - 0.5), and another computes AND, h_2 = \phi_{\text{step}}(x_1 + x_2 - 1.5). The output neuron fires when the first fires and the second does not, o = \phi_{\text{step}}(h_1 - h_2 - 0.5):

The sigmoid gives the same result if all weights and biases are multiplied by 10. The sums then lie about 5 or more away from 0, where the sigmoid is close to a step: \phi(5) = 0.993 and \phi(-5) = 0.007, and the network outputs 0.007, 0.992, 0.992, and 0.007 for the four inputs.

The hidden layer transforms the inputs into a new representation, (h_1, h_2), in which the two classes are linearly separable. This is the general role of hidden layers: each layer computes a representation in which the next layer’s task is easier. The weights above were chosen by hand. The point of a multilayer network is to learn them, and the perceptron rule cannot do this, because it needs a target for every neuron, and hidden neurons have none.

Figure 7 shows the small network that 

Backpropagation and Gradient Descent trains. It has two inputs x_1, x_2, two hidden neurons h_1, h_2, and two outputs o_1, o_2. Following the figure, all hidden neurons share the bias b_1 and all output neurons the bias b_2; a bias is a weight from an extra neuron whose state is always 1. The weights w_1 to w_8 connect each layer to the next, with no connections within a layer and no cycles. The nodes J_1 and J_2 measure the error of each output against its target, and J is their sum.



Figure 7:A network with two inputs, two hidden neurons, two outputs, shared biases b_1 and b_2, and the error nodes J_1, J_2, and J.

The network computes its output in a forward pass: it feeds the example into the input layer and computes one layer after the other. All neurons of a layer can be computed at the same time.h_1 = \phi(w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2 + b_1), \qquad h_2 = \phi(w_3 x_1 + w_4 x_2 + b_1)o_1 = \phi(w_5 h_1 + w_6 h_2 + b_2), \qquad o_2 = \phi(w_7 h_1 + w_8 h_2 + b_2)

Example: Forward pass through the small network

The example is \mathbf{x} = (1.0, 0.5) with the targets \mathbf{t} = (1, 0). The weights start at w_1 = 0.2, w_2 = -0.4, w_3 = 0.5, w_4 = 0.1, b_1 = 0.1 for the hidden layer and w_5 = 0.3, w_6 = -0.2, w_7 = 0.6, w_8 = 0.4, b_2 = -0.1 for the output layer.

The hidden layer computes s_{h_1} = 0.2 \cdot 1.0 - 0.4 \cdot 0.5 + 0.1 = 0.1 and s_{h_2} = 0.5 \cdot 1.0 + 0.1 \cdot 0.5 + 0.1 = 0.65, so h_1 = \phi(0.1) = 0.525 and h_2 = \phi(0.65) = 0.657. The output layer computes s_{o_1} = 0.3 \cdot 0.525 - 0.2 \cdot 0.657 - 0.1 = -0.074 and s_{o_2} = 0.6 \cdot 0.525 + 0.4 \cdot 0.657 - 0.1 = 0.478, so o_1 = 0.482 and o_2 = 0.617.

Both outputs are far from their targets 1 and 0. With the squared error of 

Backpropagation and Gradient Descent, the loss is J = \frac{1}{2}(1 - 0.482)^2 + \frac{1}{2}(0 - 0.617)^2 = 0.325.

In matrix notation, a layer computes \mathbf{h} = \phi(\mathbf{W} \mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}), with the activation function applied to each component. A deep network stacks many such layers; 

Figure 8 shows a network with three weight layers. Networks of this kind are called multilayer perceptrons or fully connected networks, although their neurons are no longer perceptrons.



Figure 8:A multilayer perceptron with an input layer, two hidden layers, and an output layer; each layer has a bias node fixed at 1.

How powerful are such networks? The universal approximation theorem states that a network with a single hidden layer and enough neurons can approximate any continuous function on a bounded region as closely as desired (Cybenko 1989, Hornik 1991). The theorem says nothing about how many neurons are needed or how to find their weights. In practice, deep networks with many smaller layers learn more efficiently than shallow networks with one huge layer, because each layer can build on the representation of the previous one.

Where this is used

Every network in this book is trained with the method of this section: the word embeddings of 

Word Embeddings, the transformer encoders of 

Transformer Embeddings, the image networks of 

, and the contrastive models of 

Multimodal Transformers. 

Losses and Performance Measures introduces gradient descent and derives the gradient of the cross-entropy loss with respect to the logits; this section continues from there to the gradients of all weights of a network.

The forward pass in 

From Perceptrons to Multilayer Networks left the small network with outputs o_1 = 0.482 and o_2 = 0.617 for the targets 1 and 0, a loss of J = 0.325. Training must change the ten parameters w_1, \dots, w_8, b_1, b_2 so that the loss falls. Gradient descent knows how to do this once it has the gradient, the vector of all ten partial derivatives ∂ J / ∂ w. This section shows how to compute it: first by applying the chain rule to the small network, then with backpropagation, which organizes the same computation so that it scales to networks with billions of parameters. It ends with the softmax output and the cross-entropy loss that classification networks use instead of sigmoid outputs and the squared error.

For a training example \mathbf{x} with targets \mathbf{t} and network outputs \mathbf{o}, we use the squared error as the loss of one example, with a factor \frac{1}{2} that cancels when we differentiate:J(\mathbf{x}; \mathbf{w}) = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{l} (t_l - o_l)^2

Here \mathbf{w} stands for all weights and biases of the network. The loss over the training set \mathbb{T} is the average, J(\mathbf{w}) = \frac{1}{|\mathbb{T}|} \sum_{\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{T}} J(\mathbf{x}; \mathbf{w}), which is half the mean squared error of 

Losses and Performance Measures. For classification, the cross-entropy loss of that section takes the place of the squared error; the method below works for any differentiable loss.

A network is too large and the training set too big to solve \nabla J(\mathbf{w}) = \mathbf{0} directly. Gradient descent instead starts with small random weights and repeats the step \mathbf{w} \leftarrow \mathbf{w} - \eta\, \nabla J(\mathbf{w}) with the learning rate \eta, until the loss stops falling or a maximum number of steps is reached. It finds a local minimum, and it can be slow: near a minimum the gradient becomes small, and in long, narrow valleys of the loss the steps zigzag from one side to the other.

Computing the gradient over the whole training set before every step is expensive. Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) estimates it from a small random subset, a mini-batch of typically 32 to a few thousand examples. In each epoch, the training set is shuffled and divided into mini-batches, and the weights are updated once per mini-batch. The estimate is noisy, but many cheap steps make more progress than a few exact ones, and the noise helps to leave shallow local minima.

Momentum reduces the zigzag. It keeps a running update \Delta that accumulates a fraction \gamma of the previous updates, so that steps in a consistent direction add up while steps that change their direction cancel.

Key Formula: Stochastic Gradient Descent with Momentum\Delta \leftarrow \gamma\, \Delta + \frac{\eta}{|\mathbb{B}|} \sum_{\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{B}} \nabla J(\mathbf{x}; \mathbf{w}), \qquad \mathbf{w} \leftarrow \mathbf{w} - \Delta

For each mini-batch \mathbb{B}, the update combines the average gradient of the batch with a fraction \gamma of the previous update. With \gamma = 0, this is plain stochastic gradient descent.

A common schedule starts with \gamma = 0.5 and raises it to 0.9 or higher once training has stabilized (Sutskever et al., see 

Further Reading). 

Training Deep Networks describes optimizers that also adapt the learning rate for each parameter. All of them need the same input: the gradient of the loss of one example with respect to every weight.

hierarchy.lvl2: The Chain Rule on a Graph
The Chain Rule on a Graph

records.content:
The loss is a composition of many functions: sums, activation functions, and the squared error. Its derivatives follow from the chain rule. For z = f(y) with y = g(x), the derivative of z with respect to x is the product of the two local derivatives:\frac{dz}{dx} = \frac{dz}{dy} \cdot \frac{dy}{dx} = f'(y) \cdot g'(x)

Figure 1 draws the composition as a computational graph. The forward pass computes y from x and z from y. The backward pass starts at the end with \frac{dz}{dz} = 1, multiplies by f'(y) to obtain \frac{dz}{dy}, and multiplies by g'(x) to obtain \frac{dz}{dx}. The backward pass needs the intermediate value y from the forward pass, so the forward pass must keep it.



Figure 1:Forward pass (top) and backward pass (bottom) through the composition z = f(g(x)): the backward pass multiplies the local derivatives from right to left.

When a value feeds into several functions, its derivative collects the contributions of all paths. For z = f(y, w) with y = g(x) and w = h(x), the multivariable chain rule gives\frac{dz}{dx} = \frac{∂ z}{∂ y} \cdot \frac{dy}{dx} + \frac{∂ z}{∂ w} \cdot \frac{dw}{dx}

In the graph of 

Figure 2, the backward pass follows both branches back to x and adds what arrives. These two rules are all that backpropagation needs: multiply along a path, add where paths meet.



Figure 2:Forward and backward pass through z = f(g(x), h(x)): the derivatives arriving at x through both branches are added.

We start with the weight w_5, which connects h_1 to o_1. It affects only o_1, so only the first term of the loss depends on it. The chain runs from the loss through o_1 and the sum s_{o_1} = w_5 h_1 + w_6 h_2 + b_2 to w_5:\frac{∂ J}{∂ w_5} = \frac{∂ J}{∂ o_1} \cdot \frac{∂ o_1}{∂ s_{o_1}} \cdot \frac{∂ s_{o_1}}{∂ w_5} = (o_1 - t_1) \cdot o_1 (1 - o_1) \cdot h_1

The first factor is the derivative of \frac{1}{2}(t_1 - o_1)^2 with respect to o_1. The second is the derivative of the sigmoid, which has the convenient form \phi'(s) = \phi(s)\,(1 - \phi(s)) and can be computed from the neuron’s output alone. The third is the input that w_5 multiplies.

The first two factors are the same for every weight that enters o_1. We give their product a name, the delta of the neuron: \delta_{o_1} = ∂ J / ∂ s_{o_1} = (o_1 - t_1)\, o_1 (1 - o_1). Then ∂ J / ∂ w_5 = \delta_{o_1} h_1 and ∂ J / ∂ w_6 = \delta_{o_1} h_2, and in the same way ∂ J / ∂ w_7 = \delta_{o_2} h_1 and ∂ J / ∂ w_8 = \delta_{o_2} h_2. The shared bias b_2 enters both outputs, so its derivative collects both paths: ∂ J / ∂ b_2 = \delta_{o_1} + \delta_{o_2}.

The weight w_1 lies one layer deeper. It enters h_1, and h_1 feeds both outputs, so two paths lead from the loss to w_1:\frac{∂ J}{∂ w_1} = \bigl(\delta_{o_1} w_5 + \delta_{o_2} w_7\bigr) \cdot h_1 (1 - h_1) \cdot x_1 = \delta_{h_1} x_1

The bracket collects what flows back to h_1 from both outputs, each delta weighted with the weight on its connection. Multiplied with the derivative of h_1’s sigmoid, it gives the delta of the hidden neuron, \delta_{h_1}. Every hidden delta is computed from the deltas of the layer above, which is why the method runs backward. The pattern is the same for every layer.

Key Formula: Backpropagation\delta_l = \phi'(s_l)\, \frac{∂ J}{∂ o_l} \;\;\text{(output layer)}, \qquad \delta_k = \phi'(s_k) \sum_{l} w_{k,l}\, \delta_l \;\;\text{(hidden layers)}, \qquad \frac{∂ J}{∂ w_{j,k}} = a_j\, \delta_k

The delta of a neuron is the derivative of the loss with respect to its sum. Output deltas come from the loss, hidden deltas from the deltas of the next layer, weighted with the connecting weights. The gradient of a weight is the input it multiplies times the delta of the neuron it feeds.

Example: One training step of the small network

The forward pass of 

From Perceptrons to Multilayer Networks gave h_1 = 0.525, h_2 = 0.657, o_1 = 0.482, o_2 = 0.617 for \mathbf{x} = (1.0, 0.5) and \mathbf{t} = (1, 0).

The output deltas are \delta_{o_1} = (0.482 - 1) \cdot 0.482 \cdot 0.518 = -0.129 and \delta_{o_2} = (0.617 - 0) \cdot 0.617 \cdot 0.383 = 0.146. The negative delta says that o_1 is too small, the positive one that o_2 is too large. The hidden deltas follow from them: \delta_{h_1} = (-0.129 \cdot 0.3 + 0.146 \cdot 0.6) \cdot 0.525 \cdot 0.475 = 0.0121 and \delta_{h_2} = (-0.129 \cdot (-0.2) + 0.146 \cdot 0.4) \cdot 0.657 \cdot 0.343 = 0.0190.

Each gradient is an input times a delta:
