A numerical check confirms the table: changing a parameter by \pm 10^{-6}, computing the loss twice, and dividing the difference by 2 \cdot 10^{-6} gives the same values to ten decimal places.

One gradient descent step with \eta = 0.5 moves every parameter against its gradient, for example w_5 = 0.3 - 0.5 \cdot (-0.0680) = 0.334 and w_7 = 0.6 - 0.5 \cdot 0.0766 = 0.562. The new outputs are o_1 = 0.491 and o_2 = 0.602, and the loss drops from 0.325 to 0.311. Repeating the step on this one example gives J = 0.212 after 10 steps, J = 0.011 after 100 steps with \mathbf{o} = (0.899, 0.104), and J = 0.0006 after 1,000 steps with \mathbf{o} = (0.976, 0.024).

The gradients of the first layer are much smaller than those of the second: the largest is 0.031, against 0.096 in the output layer. Each step back through a sigmoid multiplies by \phi'(s) \le \frac{1}{4}. In a network with many layers this shrinkage compounds, a problem that 

Training Deep Networks takes up.

The sign of the output delta

The derivative of \frac{1}{2}(t - o)^2 with respect to o is o - t, not t - o. Some texts write the delta with t - o and then add the update instead of subtracting it; both conventions are correct on their own. Mixing them, a delta with t - o and the update \mathbf{w} - \eta \nabla J, makes the network climb the loss instead of descending it. A numerical check of a few gradients, as in the example above, catches this and most other mistakes in a hand-written backward pass.

For a network of any size, we number the layers from the input layer L_0 to the output layer L_N, as in 

Figure 8. Layer L_i has M_i neurons with the states o_{i,1}, \dots, o_{i,M_i}, and an extra state o_{i,0} = 1 carries the bias. The weight w_{i,k,l} connects neuron l of layer L_{i-1} with neuron k of layer L_i, so that w_{i,k,0} is the bias of neuron k. One training step for an example \mathbf{x} with target \mathbf{t} runs as follows.

Forward pass. Set o_{0,k} = x_k. For each layer i = 1, \dots, N, compute s_{i,k} = \sum_{l} w_{i,k,l}\, o_{i-1,l} and o_{i,k} = \phi(s_{i,k}) for all neurons, and keep these values. Compute the loss J from \mathbf{o}_N and \mathbf{t}.

Output deltas. Compute \delta_{N,k} = \phi'(s_{N,k})\, ∂ J / ∂ o_{N,k}; for the sigmoid and the squared error, \delta_{N,k} = o_{N,k}(1 - o_{N,k})(o_{N,k} - t_k).

Backward pass. For each layer i = N - 1, \dots, 1, compute \delta_{i,k} = \phi'(s_{i,k}) \sum_{l} w_{i+1,l,k}\, \delta_{i+1,l}.

Gradients. Compute ∂ J / ∂ w_{i,k,l} = o_{i-1,l}\, \delta_{i,k} for all weights.

Update. Change all weights with the optimizer, for example SGD with momentum, after all deltas are computed.

The order of the last steps matters. Step 3 for layer i uses the weights of layer i + 1, so updating these weights while the backward pass is still running would compute the deltas with wrong weights. 

Figure 3 shows steps 3 to 5 for one hidden layer.



Figure 3:Forward pass (top) and backward pass (bottom) for a hidden layer of sigmoid neurons: the delta collects the deltas of the next layer, weighted with the connecting weights v_{l,m}, and drives the momentum update of the weights.

A bias shared by several neurons, like b_1 and b_2 in the small network, receives the sum of the deltas of all neurons that use it. 

Figure 4 shows the graph: the bias fans out to K neurons in the forward pass, and their deltas add up on the way back. Convolutional layers in 

Convolutional Networks use this mechanism on a large scale, since one kernel is shared by every position of an image.



Figure 4:A bias shared by K neurons: its gradient is the sum of the deltas of all neurons that use it.

In matrix notation, the backward pass of a fully connected layer is a single product, \boldsymbol{\delta}_i = \phi'(\mathbf{s}_i) ⊙ \mathbf{W}_{i+1}^\top \boldsymbol{\delta}_{i+1}, where ⊙ multiplies component by component. The backward pass therefore costs about as much as the forward pass, independent of the number of weights: computing each of the millions of partial derivatives separately, as we did for w_1 above, would repeat the same products over and over. Deep learning libraries do not ask us to write the backward pass at all. They record the operations of the forward pass as a computational graph and apply the two rules of the chain-rule section automatically, which is called automatic differentiation.

The small network has one sigmoid output per class and the squared error as its loss. Classification networks are usually built differently, and the reason lies in the backward pass. A classifier must finally name one class, a hard assignment that keeps the largest output. Its accuracy changes only when the winning class flips, so its gradient is zero almost everywhere, and gradient descent receives no signal from it (

Losses and Performance Measures). Training therefore uses a soft assignment: a probability for each class that changes smoothly with the weights. The hard decision follows at prediction time, by picking the most probable class.

The softmax turns the sums s_l of the K output neurons, which 

Softmax calls logits, into such probabilities, and the cross-entropy measures how much probability the correct class receives:o_l = \frac{e^{s_l}}{\sum_{j=1}^{K} e^{s_j}}, \qquad J = -\sum_{l=1}^{K} t_l \log o_l = -\log o_c

The exponential makes every output positive, the division makes the outputs sum to 1, and the order of the sums is preserved. Unlike independent sigmoids, the outputs compete: raising one probability lowers the others. With a one-hot target, where t_c = 1 for the correct class c and all other targets are 0, the loss is the negative log probability of the correct class. It is 0 when the network gives that class the probability 1, and it grows without bound as the probability approaches 0.

Key Formula: Output Delta for Softmax and Cross-Entropy\delta_l = \frac{∂ J}{∂ s_l} = o_l - t_l

The delta of each output neuron is its predicted probability minus its target. 

Cross-Entropy derives it; the backward pass then continues exactly as above.

Three properties make this pairing the standard choice for classification.

The delta is simple. No derivative of the activation function appears. The delta has the same form as the gradient of a linear output with the squared error and of the logistic regression in 

Linear Classifiers: Logistic Regression and Support Vector Machines: prediction minus target.

The delta does not vanish when the network is confidently wrong. With a sigmoid output and the squared error, the factor o(1 - o) multiplies the error. An output of 0.99 for a target of 0 gives the delta 0.99 \cdot 0.99 \cdot 0.01 = 0.0098, almost no signal for the worst kind of mistake. With the softmax and the cross-entropy, the delta is 0.99, a hundred times larger.

The computation is numerically stable. The exponential overflows for large sums, in single precision above 88.7. Implementations therefore subtract the largest sum from all sums first, which does not change the probabilities, and compute the logarithm directly as \log o_l = s_l - \log \sum_j e^{s_j}, without forming tiny probabilities. Libraries combine the softmax and the cross-entropy into one function that receives the sums, not the probabilities, as the warning in 

Cross-Entropy explains.

Example: The small network with a softmax output

The output sums of the small network are s_{o_1} = -0.074 and s_{o_2} = 0.478. The softmax turns them into o_1 = 0.365 and o_2 = 0.635, which sum to 1, unlike the two sigmoid outputs 0.482 and 0.617. Subtracting the larger sum first gives the shifted sums -0.552 and 0 and the same probabilities. For the target \mathbf{t} = (1, 0), the cross-entropy is -\log 0.365 = 1.007, and the output deltas are 0.365 - 1 = -0.635 and 0.635 - 0 = 0.635. They are about five times larger than the deltas -0.129 and 0.146 of the squared error, mainly because the factor o(1 - o) \le \frac{1}{4} is gone.

Where this is used

Automated Feature Extraction names ReLU activations, dropout, data augmentation, and better optimizers such as Adam as the improvements that made deep networks trainable; this section explains each of them. The transformer layers of 

Transformer Embeddings combine residual connections with layer normalization, and the fine-tuning in 

 relies on the regularization methods described here.

Backpropagation computes the gradient of any network, but for a long time, networks with more than a few layers did not train well. Adding layers did not improve the results, and larger networks became unstable. This section explains why and describes the techniques that solved the problem: activation functions that keep gradients alive, an initialization that keeps signals at a stable scale, normalization layers, regularization against overfitting, and optimizers that adapt their step sizes. Together, they turned neural networks into deep learning.

The example in 

Backpropagation and Gradient Descent already showed the problem: the gradients of the first layer were about three times smaller than those of the second. Every step back through a sigmoid neuron multiplies the delta with \phi'(s) = \phi(s)(1 - \phi(s)), and 

Figure 1 shows that this derivative is at most \frac{1}{4}, reached at s = 0, and close to zero for large positive or negative sums.



Figure 1:The derivative of the sigmoid function: at most \frac{1}{4} at s = 0, and close to zero for |s| > 5.

With weights below 1 in absolute value, a delta that travels back through n sigmoid layers is multiplied by at most (\frac{1}{4})^n, so it shrinks by a factor of at least 4^n: to at most 6 \cdot 10^{-2} of its size for two layers, 

10-3 for five, and 

10-6 for ten. The first layers of a deep network then receive almost no gradient and learn extremely slowly, even when their weights are far from good values. This is the vanishing gradient problem.

The opposite happens with large weights. If the products of weights and derivatives along the backward path exceed 1, the deltas grow exponentially with the depth. The updates become huge, the weights grow, and the next gradients are even larger, until the computation overflows. This is the exploding gradient problem. Both effects grow with the number of layers, which is why the second wave of neural network research stalled at shallow networks. Recurrent networks, which apply the same weights at every time step, suffer even more; 

Recurrent Networks returns to them.

The rectified linear unit (ReLU), \phi(s) = \max(0, s), replaced the sigmoid in deep networks. Its derivative is 1 for positive sums and 0 for negative ones, so a delta passes back through an active neuron unchanged instead of shrinking by a factor of at least 4. ReLU is also cheap to compute, and its outputs are exactly zero for about half of the neurons, which makes the representation sparse.

The zero derivative for negative sums has a drawback. A neuron whose sum is negative for every training example never receives a gradient and stops learning; such neurons are called dead. The leaky ReLU keeps a small slope for negative sums, \phi(s) = 0.01\, s for s < 0, so that its derivative never becomes zero and a dead neuron can recover. The parametric ReLU learns the slope \alpha for negative sums as a parameter of the network. 

Figure 2 compares ReLU and leaky ReLU.



Figure 2:ReLU (left), zero for negative inputs, and leaky ReLU (right), with a small slope for negative inputs.

ReLU and leaky ReLU have a kink at zero, where the derivative jumps. The exponential linear unit (ELU) is smooth for negative sums and approaches -\alpha there, which 

Figure 3 shows together with its derivative:\phi(s) = \begin{cases} s & \text{if } s \ge 0 \\ \alpha\,(e^{s} - 1) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}, \qquad \phi'(s) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } s \ge 0 \\ \alpha\, e^{s} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}



Figure 3:The exponential linear unit with \alpha = 1 (left) and its derivative (right).

Transformers such as BERT and GPT use the Gaussian error linear unit (GELU), \phi(s) = s \cdot \Phi(s), where \Phi is the cumulative distribution function of the standard normal distribution. It behaves like ReLU for large positive and negative sums and is smooth around zero. Without any nonlinear activation, a deep network would collapse to a single linear map, since a product of matrices is again a matrix.

The output layer is an exception. Classification networks end with a softmax that turns the logits into probabilities, trained with the cross-entropy loss; 

Losses and Performance Measures explains both.

The initial weights decide whether signals survive the forward pass. In a layer with n inputs and weights drawn with standard deviation \sigma, the variance of each sum is about n \sigma^2 times the variance of the inputs. If n\sigma^2 is below 1, activations shrink from layer to layer; if it is above 1, they grow. Gradients behave the same way in the backward pass. He initialization draws the weights of a ReLU layer with \sigma = \sqrt{2/n}, where the factor 2 compensates for the half of the neurons that ReLU sets to zero. For sigmoid and tanh layers, Glorot initialization (also called Xavier initialization) uses \sigma = \sqrt{2/(n_{\text{in}} + n_{\text{out}})}.

Example: Twenty ReLU layers with three initializations

A network of 20 fully connected ReLU layers with 512 neurons each processes 1,000 random inputs with standard deviation 1. We measure the standard deviation of the activations after the first, fifth, tenth, and twentieth layer:

With \sigma = 0.01, n\sigma^2/2 = 0.026, and the signal vanishes; with \sigma = 0.1, the factor is 2.56, and the signal explodes. He initialization keeps it at the same scale through all twenty layers.

Even with a good initialization, the distribution of a layer’s inputs changes during training, because the layers before it change their weights. Batch normalization stabilizes these distributions. For each feature, it computes the mean \mu_{\mathbb{B}} and the variance \sigma_{\mathbb{B}}^2 over the current mini-batch, normalizes the value, and then scales and shifts it with two learned parameters \gamma and \beta:\hat{x} = \frac{x - \mu_{\mathbb{B}}}{\sqrt{\sigma_{\mathbb{B}}^2 + \varepsilon}}, \qquad y = \gamma\, \hat{x} + \beta

The small constant \varepsilon avoids a division by zero. The learned scale and shift let the network undo the normalization where that helps. During training, the layer also keeps running averages of the means and variances; at inference, it uses these averages, so that the output for an example does not depend on the other examples in its batch. Batch normalization needs mini-batches large enough for reliable estimates, which is difficult for tasks with high-resolution inputs such as object detection, where only a few images fit into memory at once.

Layer normalization computes the mean and the variance over the features of a single example instead of over the batch. It needs no batch statistics, behaves identically in training and inference, and works for sequences of any length. Transformers and recurrent networks use it. Group normalization divides the features into groups and normalizes each group separately, a middle ground that works well for convolutional networks with small batches. Weight standardization normalizes the weights of each layer instead of the activations and is often combined with group normalization. In practice, convolutional networks for image classification mostly use batch normalization, and transformers layer normalization.

A deep network with millions of parameters can memorize its training data, the overfitting of 

Over- and Underfitting. 

Figure 4 shows the typical signs on a validation set: an almost perfect training accuracy, a much lower validation accuracy, and a gap that grows during training, sometimes with a phase in which the validation accuracy falls again. With regularization, a gap remains, but the validation accuracy follows the training accuracy much more closely. Making the network smaller is rarely the best remedy, because small networks cannot learn complex tasks. Regularization keeps the large network and constrains how it learns.



Figure 4:Training and validation accuracy over the epochs without regularization (left), with a growing gap, and with regularization (right).

More training data is the most effective regularizer. Data augmentation creates new examples from existing ones without new labels: for images, small rotations and crops, changes of brightness, added noise, or blur. The augmented examples also make the model robust against these small changes. Language models obtain their data through self-supervised learning, described in 

Self-Supervised Learning: they learn to predict masked or next tokens in text collections of trillions of tokens. For a fixed computing budget, Hoffmann and colleagues found that a language model is best trained on about 20 tokens per parameter, so a model with one billion parameters needs about 20 billion tokens. A pretrained model can then be fine-tuned for a task with much less labeled data.

Early stopping monitors the loss on the validation set during training and keeps the weights of the epoch with the lowest validation loss, before the network starts to fit the noise of the training data.

Weight penalties add a term to the loss that grows with the size of the weights. L2 regularization adds the sum of the squared weights; the biases are not penalized:

Key Formula: L2 Regularization and Weight DecayJ_{\text{reg}}(\mathbf{w}) = J(\mathbf{w}) + \frac{\lambda}{2\,|\mathbb{T}|} \sum_{i} w_i^2, \qquad w_i \leftarrow \left(1 - \frac{\eta \lambda}{|\mathbb{T}|}\right) w_i - \eta\, \frac{∂ J}{∂ w_i}

The penalty shrinks every weight by a constant factor in each step, unless the gradient of the loss pushes it back. The regularization parameter \lambda > 0 is a hyperparameter, chosen on the validation set.

With \eta = 0.1, \lambda = 5, and |\mathbb{T}| = 50{,}000 examples, the factor is 1 - 10^{-5}: each step removes a hundred-thousandth of every weight, and a weight that the data does not support decays toward zero over many steps. For this reason, L2 regularization is also called weight decay. L1 regularization adds the absolute values \frac{\lambda}{|\mathbb{T}|} \sum_i |w_i| instead. It subtracts a constant amount in each step instead of a fraction and drives many weights to exactly zero.

Dropout changes the network during training (

Figure 5). In each training step, every neuron of a layer is kept with probability p and dropped with probability 1 - p; a dropped neuron outputs 0 and does not pass back any gradient, so its weights receive no update in that step. Each step therefore trains a different thinned network, and a neuron cannot rely on the presence of specific other neurons. At inference, all neurons are active; to keep the expected input of the next layer the same as in training, their outgoing weights are multiplied by p. Libraries usually apply the equivalent inverted dropout, which divides the kept outputs by p during training and leaves the network unchanged at inference. Dropout can be seen as training many networks that share their weights and averaging them for the prediction.



Figure 5:A fully connected network (a) and the same network during one training step with dropout (b), where the crossed-out neurons are dropped.

Plain SGD uses one learning rate for all parameters and all steps. The learning rate can follow a schedule: it can stay fixed, decay after a number of epochs or when the validation loss stops improving, or grow linearly at the start of training, a warm-up that large transformer models need. Momentum, described in 

Backpropagation and Gradient Descent, accelerates progress along consistent directions.

RMSprop adapts the learning rate for each parameter. It keeps a running average of the squared gradients and divides each step by its square root, so that parameters with consistently large gradients take smaller steps and parameters with small gradients larger ones. Adam combines this with momentum. It keeps running averages of the gradients, \mathbf{m}, and of their squares, \mathbf{v}, and corrects both for their initialization at zero:

Key Formula: Adam\mathbf{m} \leftarrow \beta_1 \mathbf{m} + (1 - \beta_1)\, \mathbf{g}, \qquad \mathbf{v} \leftarrow \beta_2 \mathbf{v} + (1 - \beta_2)\, \mathbf{g}^2, \qquad \mathbf{w} \leftarrow \mathbf{w} - \eta\, \frac{\hat{\mathbf{m}}}{\sqrt{\hat{\mathbf{v}}} + \varepsilon}

Here \mathbf{g} is the gradient of the current mini-batch, squares and roots are taken per component, and \hat{\mathbf{m}} = \mathbf{m} / (1 - \beta_1^t) and \hat{\mathbf{v}} = \mathbf{v} / (1 - \beta_2^t) correct the bias of the averages in step t. The step of each parameter is its average gradient divided by the typical size of its gradient.

Example: The first Adam step

With the usual settings \eta = 0.001, \beta_1 = 0.9, \beta_2 = 0.999, and \varepsilon = 10^{-8}, the first step has \hat{\mathbf{m}} = \mathbf{g} and \hat{\mathbf{v}} = \mathbf{g}^2, so every parameter moves by \eta \cdot g / |g| = 0.001 in the direction of descent. A parameter with the gradient g = 0.001, one with g = 1, and one with g = 1{,}000 all take a step of 0.001. Plain SGD with the same learning rate would move them by 

10-6, 0.001, and 1. Adam’s steps depend on the direction and the consistency of the gradients, not on their scale, which makes the learning rate much easier to choose.

Adam is the default optimizer for most networks today. For transformers, the variant AdamW applies the weight decay directly to the weights instead of adding it to the gradient, because Adam’s division by \sqrt{\hat{\mathbf{v}}} would otherwise weaken the decay for parameters with large gradients.

Where this is used

 shows that the first layer of a trained convolutional network learns filters that resemble the Sobel and Gabor kernels of 

, and it uses global average pooling to turn feature maps into an embedding; this section explains the layers behind both observations. 

Classifying Audio applies convolutional networks to spectrograms, which they treat like images. The receptive fields of the retina in 

The Human Visual System inspired the design, and 

CNN Architectures walks through the architectures built from these layers.

A fully connected layer connects every input to every neuron. For images, this is wasteful in two ways. It needs an enormous number of weights, and it ignores that pixels close to each other belong together and that a pattern means the same wherever it appears. Convolutional networks build these two assumptions into their layers. This section introduces the convolutional layer, the strides and padding that control its output size, pooling, the 1 \times 1 convolution, and the way a stack of these layers ends in a classifier.

hierarchy.lvl2: Local Receptive Fields and Shared Weights
Local Receptive Fields and Shared Weights

records.content:
Our eyes analyze a scene with receptive fields, small regions of the retina whose cells respond to local patterns, and the same kind of field works at every position of the visual field. A convolutional layer copies this design. Each neuron of the layer connects only to a small neighborhood of the input, for example 5 \times 5 pixels, as 

Figure 1 shows. The layer contains one such neuron for every position of the input, and all of them share the same weights and the same bias.



Figure 1:A hidden neuron connected to a small patch of the input, its local receptive field.

Earlier systems prepared images for learning with hand-designed filters, such as Gaussian smoothing, Sobel gradients, or HOG descriptors, and fed the results into a network. This limited what the network could learn, and filters chosen for one task did not necessarily transfer to the next. A convolutional layer learns its filters from the data instead.

Sharing the weights has three consequences. The layer computes the same feature at every position, so a pattern is detected wherever it appears. The number of parameters is small and independent of the image size. And every weight receives an update from every position in each backward pass, since the shared weights collect the deltas of all positions like the shared bias in 

Backpropagation and Gradient Descent. In a 1024 \times 1024 layer, a single example contributes more than a million terms to the gradient of each kernel weight.

An image has several input channels, three for an RGB image, and a layer computes several output features, the feature maps. 

Figure 2 shows the computation for one position: the kernel covers a neighborhood in all input channels, and each output feature has its own kernel and bias.

Key Formula: Convolutional Layero_{i,j,n} = \phi\Bigl(b_n + \sum_{k,l,m} w_{k,l,m,n}\; x_{i+k,\, j+l,\, m}\Bigr)

Output feature n at position (i, j) is the activation of a weighted sum over a neighborhood of all input channels m. The kernel weights w_{k,l,m,n} and the bias b_n are the same at every position.



Figure 2:A convolution over a multi-channel input: the kernel covers a local neighborhood in all channels and produces one value per output feature.

Strictly speaking, the formula computes a cross-correlation: a convolution in the mathematical sense would flip the kernel. Since the kernel is learned, the distinction does not matter, and deep learning libraries call the operation a convolution.

Example: A learned edge detector

A 5 \times 5 grayscale patch has the value 10 in its three left columns and 80 in its two right columns, a vertical edge. A 3 \times 3 kernel with the weights of the Sobel filter, (-1, 0, 1) in the top and bottom rows and (-2, 0, 2) in the middle row, slides over the nine positions where it fits. Where the window lies in the flat left region, the weighted sum is 0. Where it covers the edge, the left column contributes -4 \cdot 10 and the right column 4 \cdot 80, so the sum is 280. The result has the columns 0, 280, 280 in all three rows.

With the bias b = -100 and a ReLU, the neuron outputs 0 in the flat region and 180 along the edge: it responds only to edges strong enough to exceed the threshold that the bias sets. Training finds kernels and biases of this kind on its own; 

 shows that the first layer of a trained network contains many of them.

The savings are large. A 5 \times 5 convolution from 3 input channels to 20 output features has 5 \cdot 5 \cdot 3 \cdot 20 = 1{,}500 weights and 20 biases, for an image of any size. A fully connected layer that maps a 256 \times 256 \times 3 image to 256 \times 256 \times 20 outputs would need 196{,}608 \cdot 1{,}310{,}720 \approx 2.6 \cdot 10^{11} weights. The computing cost of a convolution still grows with the number of pixels, but the number of parameters does not.

The kernel slides over the input with a stride s, the distance between two consecutive window positions. A stride of 1 computes an output at every position; a stride of 2 skips every other position in both directions and produces a quarter of the outputs. Padding adds p rows and columns of zeros around the input, so that the kernel can also be centered on the border pixels. Kernels usually have an odd size k, so that they have a center.

Key Formula: Output Size of a Convolutionn_{\text{out}} = ⌊ \frac{n + 2p - k}{s} ⌋ + 1

An input of n positions along one dimension, a kernel of size k, padding p, and stride s give n_{\text{out}} output positions. With stride 1 and p = (k-1)/2, the output keeps the size of the input.

Example: Output sizes

A 32 \times 32 input with a 3 \times 3 kernel, stride 1, and padding 1 gives ⌊(32 + 2 - 3)/1 ⌋ + 1 = 32 outputs per dimension: the size is preserved. The same input with a 5 \times 5 kernel and no padding gives 28. The first layer of GoogLeNet in 

CNN Architectures applies a 7 \times 7 kernel with stride 2 and padding 3 to a 224 \times 224 image: ⌊(224 + 6 - 7)/2 ⌋ + 1 = 112, half the input size in each dimension.

Strides reduce the size of the network’s layers early and let later layers compute features at a coarser scale.

Convolutional layers are often followed by a pooling layer, which summarizes each small neighborhood of a feature map in a single value. Max pooling keeps the largest value of the neighborhood, as in 

Figure 3, and average pooling keeps the mean. Pooling has no parameters and no activation function, and it is applied to each feature map separately, so the number of features stays the same.



Figure 3:Max pooling: each output neuron takes the largest value of a 2 \times 2 neighborhood of the feature map.

Example: Pooling a feature map

A 4 \times 4 feature map has the rows (1, 3, 2, 0), (4, 6, 1, 1), (0, 2, 5, 7), and (1, 1, 3, 2). Max pooling over 2 \times 2 windows with stride 2 gives the 2 \times 2 output with the rows (6, 2) and (2, 7); average pooling gives (3.5, 1) and (1, 4.25). Each dimension is halved, so the map has four times fewer values. Max pooling also makes the output insensitive to small shifts: the 6 in the top left window could move to any of the four positions of its window without changing the result.

Pooling reduces the spatial size only with a stride larger than 1. Global pooling reduces each feature map of the last convolutional layer to a single value, its maximum or its average. Global average pooling turns the output of the last convolutional layer into a vector with one value per feature, the image embedding that 

 uses.

A convolution with a 1 \times 1 kernel looks at a single position. It does not combine neighboring pixels, but it combines the features at each position into new ones, like a fully connected layer applied to every pixel separately. Its main use is to reduce the number of features before an expensive convolution.

Example: Fewer parameters with a 1 × 1 convolution

A 5 \times 5 convolution from 20 input features to 20 output features needs 5 \cdot 5 \cdot 20 \cdot 20 = 10{,}000 weights and 20 biases, 10,020 parameters. A 1 \times 1 convolution can first reduce the 20 features to 3, with 20 \cdot 3 = 60 weights and 3 biases. The 5 \times 5 convolution from these 3 features to 20 outputs then needs 5 \cdot 5 \cdot 3 \cdot 20 = 1{,}500 weights and 20 biases. Together, the two layers have 1,583 parameters instead of 10,020, at the price of a compressed representation between them. The inception modules of GoogLeNet in 

CNN Architectures are built on this idea.

Figure 4 shows how the layers combine in an image classifier. Convolutional layers with activation functions alternate with pooling layers. With each stage, the feature maps become smaller and more numerous, and each neuron sees a larger part of the image: two stacked 3 \times 3 convolutions already cover a 5 \times 5 region of the input, so deep layers respond to object parts and whole objects instead of edges. At the end, a flattening layer turns the last feature maps into one long vector, and fully connected layers with a softmax output compute the class probabilities.



Figure 4:A convolutional network for image classification: convolution and pooling stages, a 1 \times 1 convolution, and flattening into a vector for the fully connected classifier.

Flattening ties the network to one input size, because the length of the vector depends on the size of the feature maps. Modern architectures replace it with global average pooling, which produces one value per feature map for any input size, followed by a single fully connected layer. 

CNN Architectures follows this development from LeNet to ResNet.

Where this is used

Automated Feature Extraction lists the milestones of neural image classification and links here for the architectures behind them. 

 uses a pretrained ResNet as a feature extractor, and 

 builds on the Vision Transformer described at the end of this section.

This section describes the architectures that lead from hand-designed pipelines to learned features: Rowley’s face detector, LeNet, AlexNet, VGG, GoogLeNet with its inception modules, ResNet, DenseNet, and the Vision Transformer. For each network, we look at its layer structure, the problem its design solved, its size, and its results on the benchmark of its time. 

Automated Feature Extraction tells the story of these milestones, and 

 shows how a trained network serves as an image feature extractor, what its first-layer filters look like, and how it transfers to new tasks. The building blocks used below, such as convolution, strides, padding, pooling, and 1 \times 1 convolutions, are introduced in the previous subsection.

In 1998, Henry Rowley, Shumeet Baluja, and Takeo Kanade at Carnegie Mellon University published a neural face detector that worked on cluttered photos. Its design keeps the network small and moves most of the work into fixed processing steps around it. 

Figure 1 shows the version that also finds rotated faces.



Figure 1:Rowley’s rotation-invariant face detector: image pyramid, router network, preprocessing, and detection network.

The detector examines windows of 20 by 20 pixels. To find faces larger than the window, it builds an image pyramid: it reduces the image repeatedly by a factor of 1.2 and applies the network at every pixel position of every level. Each window passes two preprocessing steps. First, a linear brightness function fitted to an oval face region is subtracted to compensate for uneven lighting. Second, histogram equalization stretches the contrast.

The detection network receives the 400 preprocessed pixel values, but its hidden units do not see the whole window. Four hidden units look at 10 by 10 subregions, 16 at 5 by 5 subregions, and 6 at overlapping horizontal stripes of 20 by 5 pixels. The stripes can detect a pair of eyes or a mouth, and the square fields can detect single eyes, the nose, or the corners of the mouth. The final systems replicate these hidden units two or three times. A single output unit makes the decision: it is trained to produce 1 for a face and -1 for anything else. The local fields resemble the receptive fields of a convolutional layer, but they are fixed by hand, and their weights are not shared across positions.

Face examples are easy to collect: the authors gathered about 1050 of them from face databases. Examples of nonfaces are harder, because almost any image region is a nonface. A bootstrap procedure solves this. The network is trained, applied to 120 scenery images that contain no faces, and every false detection is added to the training set as a negative example; then the network is trained again. A typical run selected about 8000 nonface windows out of 146 million available subimages. At detection time, overlapping detections are merged, and several networks vote. The upright detector found 90.5% of the faces in a test set of 130 complex images.

The rotation-invariant version adds a router network in front of the detector. It has 400 inputs, 15 hidden units, and 36 outputs. Output unit i stands for an angle of i \cdot 10^\circ, and to signal a face at angle \theta, unit i is trained to produce \cos(\theta - i \cdot 10^\circ). The window is rotated upright by the estimated angle before it enters preprocessing and detection. This system found 79.6% of the faces in 180 test images, with few false detections. 

Figure 2 shows results. The label in the upper left corner of each image gives the number of detected faces, the number of faces in the image, and the number of false detections; the label in the lower right gives the image size in pixels. The eye marks inside the boxes only indicate the estimated orientation; the detector does not locate the eyes.



Figure 2:Results of the rotation-invariant detector. Upper left: detected faces, faces present, false detections.

Every step except the final decision was designed by hand: the window size, the lighting correction, the histogram equalization, the derotation, and the sliding-window search. This made the method hard to reuse. A detector for cats or dogs would need its own preprocessing, its own receptive fields, and its own training set. Neural classifiers of this generation were optimized for one task and did not adapt to a new one without human work.

Yann LeCun and colleagues at AT&T Bell Labs developed LeNet in several versions between 1989 and 1998, first to read zip codes and later bank checks. LeNet-5, described in full by LeCun and colleagues in 1998, is the version usually meant. Its test bed was the MNIST database with 60,000 training and 10,000 test images of handwritten digits. The digits come from NIST collections written by Census Bureau employees and high school students on forms like the one in 

Figure 3. Each digit was scaled to fit into a 20 by 20 pixel box while keeping its aspect ratio, which introduced gray levels through anti-aliasing, and then placed into a 28 by 28 image with its center of mass in the center.



Figure 3:A NIST handwriting sample form from 1989. Forms of this kind provided the digits of MNIST.

LeNet-5 alternates convolution and subsampling and ends with dense layers. 

Figure 4 shows the layers:

C1 applies six 5 \times 5 convolution kernels and produces six feature maps of 28 \times 28.

S2 subsamples each map by combining 2 \times 2 neighborhoods, which gives six maps of 14 \times 14.

C3 applies sixteen 5 \times 5 kernels and produces sixteen maps of 10 \times 10. In the original network, each C3 map is connected to only a subset of the six S2 maps.

S4 subsamples to sixteen maps of 5 \times 5, 400 values in total.

Three dense layers with 120, 84, and 10 units produce the class scores.



Figure 4:LeNet-5: two convolution and pooling stages followed by three dense layers.

The original network takes a 32 \times 32 input, the 28 \times 28 digit surrounded by a border, and uses sigmoid-shaped activation functions. The figure shows the variant of the book Dive into Deep Learning, which takes the 28 \times 28 image directly and pads it by two pixels in C1. Weight sharing keeps the network small. Counting the layers of LeNet-5 gives 60,000 trainable parameters: 156 in C1, 12 in S2, 1,516 in C3, 32 in S4, 48,120 in the layer with 120 units, and 10,164 in the layer with 84 units. Four fifths of them sit in the first dense layer, which connects all 400 values of S4 to 120 units. The original output layer, which compares the 84 values with hand-chosen prototypes of the ten digits, is not counted. The fully connected variant in the figure has 61,706 parameters.

LeNet-5 reached a test error of 0.95% on MNIST, about 99% accuracy, and 0.8% when the training set was enlarged with distorted copies of the digits. The network learned its features from the pixels; apart from the size normalization of the digits, nobody designed a feature. Yet a support vector machine reached a comparable 0.8% in the same comparison, and convolutional networks remained a specialist tool for more than a decade. Today, ensembles of convolutional networks with data augmentation reach error rates below 0.1% on MNIST. The 

ConvNetJS MNIST demo trains a small convolutional network in the browser and visualizes the network while it learns.

AlexNet, by Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, and Geoffrey Hinton, won the ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge (ILSVRC) of 2012. The challenge asks for one of 1000 classes per image, a large step from the ten classes of digit recognition, and provides about 1.2 million training images, 50,000 validation images, and 150,000 test images. AlexNet follows LeNet’s pattern of convolution, pooling, and dense layers, but at a much larger scale: it has eight layers with parameters, five convolutional and three dense, and it processes images of 224 \times 224 pixels instead of 28 \times 28. The left column of 

Figure 5 shows its layers:

The first convolution applies 96 kernels of 11 \times 11 \times 3 with stride 4 to the 224 \times 224 \times 3 input.

The second convolution applies 256 kernels of 5 \times 5.

The third and fourth convolutions apply 384 kernels of 3 \times 3 each, the fifth 256 kernels of 3 \times 3.

Max pooling with 3 \times 3 windows and stride 2 follows the first, second, and fifth convolution.

Two dense layers with 4096 units each and a dense output layer with 1000 units and softmax classify the image.



Figure 5:AlexNet (left) and VGG-11 (right): large early kernels against stacked 3 \times 3 convolutions.

Several design choices made the training of such a network possible. The ReLU activation replaced the saturating tanh: a four-layer network with ReLUs reached a training error of 25% on CIFAR-10 six times faster than the same network with tanh units. A single GTX 580 GPU with 3 GB of memory limited the size of the network, so the authors split it across two GPUs. The second, fourth, and fifth convolutions connect only to the feature maps on the same GPU, and training took five to six days. Overlapping pooling, with windows of 3 and stride 2, reduced the top-1 and top-5 error rates by 0.4% and 0.3% compared with non-overlapping pooling. Local response normalization follows the first two convolutions. Against overfitting, the authors used data augmentation, with random 224 \times 224 crops, horizontal reflections, and color changes along the principal components of the RGB values, and dropout in the first two dense layers. Without dropout, the network overfitted substantially.

AlexNet has about 60 million parameters and 650,000 neurons. Counting the layers gives 60,965,224 parameters. Of these, 58.6 million, or 96%, belong to the three dense layers; the first dense layer alone connects 6 \times 6 \times 256 = 9216 values to 4096 units. In 32-bit floating point, the dense layers take about 235 MB; some descriptions quote nearly 1 GB for them, about four times too much. The figure shows the single-stream variant of Dive into Deep Learning, whose first convolution uses padding 1 and produces 54 \times 54 maps, and whose last pooling layer outputs 5 \times 5 \times 256 = 6400 values; this variant has 50.8 million parameters.

A single AlexNet reached a top-5 error of 18.2% on the validation data, and the average of five networks 16.4%. The winning entry averaged seven networks, two of which had been pretrained on the full ImageNet release of fall 2011 with 15 million images in 22,000 categories, and reached a top-5 test error of 15.3%. The second-best entry, which classified Fisher vectors of hand-crafted features, reached 26.2%.

Karen Simonyan and Andrew Zisserman of the Visual Geometry Group (VGG) at Oxford asked how depth alone affects accuracy. Their networks use only 3 \times 3 convolutions with stride 1 and padding 1, which keep the spatial size, and 2 \times 2 max pooling with stride 2, which halves it. A VGG block is a sequence of 3 \times 3 convolutions followed by one pooling layer. Five blocks with 64, 128, 256, 512, and 512 channels are followed by the same three dense layers as in AlexNet. VGG-11, on the right of 

Figure 5, has one convolution in each of the first two blocks and two in each of the last three: 8 convolutions plus 3 dense layers make 11 weight layers. VGG-16 has 2, 2, 3, 3, and 3 convolutions per block, 13 in total.

Small kernels lose nothing in reach. Two stacked 3 \times 3 convolutions see a 5 \times 5 region of their input, and three see a 7 \times 7 region. A stack of three 3 \times 3 layers with C input and output channels has 3 \cdot 3^2 C^2 = 27C^2 weights, a single 7 \times 7 layer 49C^2, which is 81% more. For C = 256, these are 1,769,472 against 3,211,264 weights. The stack also applies three ReLUs instead of one, which makes the function more expressive.

The paper reports 133 million parameters for VGG-11, 138 million for VGG-16, and 144 million for VGG-19. Counting the layers of VGG-16 gives 138,357,544 parameters. Of these, 123.6 million, or 89%, sit in the dense layers, and 102.8 million in the first dense layer alone, which connects 7 \times 7 \times 512 = 25{,}088 values to 4096 units. Training one network took two to three weeks on four GPUs. VGG placed second in the classification task of ILSVRC 2014, with a top-5 test error of 7.3% for an ensemble of seven networks, and first in localization. After the competition, an ensemble of two networks reached 6.8%, and the best single network 7.0%. The simple, uniform design made VGG a popular feature extractor for years.

GoogLeNet, by Christian Szegedy and colleagues at Google, won the classification task of ILSVRC 2014. Its name is a homage to LeNet. The task had the same format as in 2012: 1000 classes, about 1.2 million training images, 50,000 validation images, and 100,000 test images. The challenge with 200 object classes is the separate detection task. GoogLeNet was designed for efficiency, with a budget of 1.5 billion multiply-adds per image at inference.

Its building block is the inception module in 

Figure 6. It applies four branches in parallel to the same input: a 1 \times 1 convolution; a 1 \times 1 convolution followed by a 3 \times 3 convolution; a 1 \times 1 convolution followed by a 5 \times 5 convolution; and 3 \times 3 max pooling followed by a 1 \times 1 convolution. The outputs are concatenated along the channel dimension. The module looks at its input at several scales at once, and the following layers learn which scale matters, so the designer no longer has to choose one kernel size per layer. Stacking the module repeatedly creates many paths through different sequences of these basic convolutions. The 1 \times 1 convolutions in front of the 3 \times 3 and 5 \times 5 convolutions reduce the number of channels and with it the cost, the same idea as in the 1 \times 1 convolution example of the previous subsection.



Figure 6:The inception module: four parallel branches with 1 \times 1 reductions, concatenated along the channels.

Example

The first inception module of GoogLeNet receives 28 \times 28 \times 192 values, and its 5 \times 5 branch produces 32 channels. Applied directly, the 5 \times 5 convolution needs 5 \cdot 5 \cdot 192 \cdot 32 = 153{,}600 weights and 153{,}600 \cdot 28 \cdot 28 = 120.4 million multiply-adds. With a 1 \times 1 reduction to 16 channels first, it needs 192 \cdot 16 + 5 \cdot 5 \cdot 16 \cdot 32 = 15{,}872 weights and 12.4 million multiply-adds, almost ten times less.

The full network in 

Figure 7 has three parts. The stem takes the 224 \times 224 \times 3 image and applies a 7 \times 7 convolution with stride 2, max pooling, a 1 \times 1 and a 3 \times 3 convolution, and max pooling again, and delivers 28 \times 28 \times 192 values. The body stacks nine inception modules, with max pooling between groups of modules. The head averages each of the final 7 \times 7 maps into one value, which gives 1024 values, applies dropout of 40%, and classifies with one linear layer and softmax. Replacing dense layers by this average pooling improved the top-1 accuracy by about 0.6%. The network is 22 layers deep when counting layers with parameters, and 27 layers deep when counting pooling as well. The layer table of the paper adds up to about 6.8 million parameters, roughly a ninth of AlexNet; the text of the paper speaks of twelve times fewer.



Figure 7:GoogLeNet with its stem, nine inception modules, and two auxiliary classifiers.

Two auxiliary classifiers sit on top of intermediate modules, the third and the sixth of the nine. Each is a small network with average pooling, a 1 \times 1 convolution with 128 filters, a dense layer with 1024 units, dropout of 70%, and a softmax over the 1000 classes. During training, their losses are added to the total loss with a weight of 0.3, to strengthen the gradient signal that reaches the lower layers and to regularize the network. At inference, they are discarded. Later networks with batch normalization and residual connections train without them. An ensemble of seven GoogLeNets, each evaluated on 144 crops per image, reached a top-5 error of 6.67%; a single network on a single crop reached 10.07%.

Kaiming He, Xiangyu Zhang, Shaoqing Ren, and Jian Sun at Microsoft Research addressed a puzzle. On CIFAR-10, a plain network with 56 layers had a higher training error, and thus a higher test error, than a network with 20 layers. This degradation is not overfitting, since the training error itself gets worse. A deeper network could in principle copy the shallower one and turn its extra layers into the identity, but the training procedure does not find this solution.

The residual block makes the identity easy. Instead of learning the desired mapping H(\mathbf{x}) directly, the block learns the residual F(\mathbf{x}) = H(\mathbf{x}) - \mathbf{x} and adds its input back:\mathbf{y} = F(\mathbf{x}) + \mathbf{x}

If the identity is the best mapping, the block only has to push F toward zero. The shortcut adds neither parameters nor computation, and during backpropagation the gradient flows back through the addition unchanged, so the early layers keep receiving a useful signal.



Figure 8:Residual blocks with identity and 1 \times 1 projection shortcuts (left) and the ResNet-18 layout (right).

The basic block on the left of 

Figure 8 has two 3 \times 3 convolutions, each followed by batch normalization, a ReLU between them, and a final ReLU after the addition. The addition requires that F(\mathbf{x}) and \mathbf{x} have the same shape. When a block halves the resolution with stride 2 and doubles the number of channels, the shortcut applies a 1 \times 1 convolution with stride 2, shown in the middle, to bring \mathbf{x} to the new shape. The right part shows ResNet-18 as drawn in Dive into Deep Learning: a 7 \times 7 convolution with stride 2, batch normalization, 3 \times 3 max pooling, four modules of two basic blocks each, global average pooling, and one dense layer, 11.7 million parameters in total.

Deeper ResNets use bottleneck blocks: a 1 \times 1 convolution reduces the channels, for example from 256 to 64, a 3 \times 3 convolution works on the reduced channels, and a second 1 \times 1 convolution restores the 256 channels. ResNet-152 stacks 3, 8, 36, and 3 bottleneck blocks in four stages. Despite its 152 layers, it needs 11.3 billion multiply-adds per image, fewer than VGG-16 with 15.3 billion and VGG-19 with 19.6 billion. Counting its layers gives 60.2 million parameters; ResNet-50 has 25.6 million.

A single ResNet-152 reached a top-5 validation error of 4.49%, and an ensemble a top-5 test error of 3.57%, which won the classification task of ILSVRC 2015. ResNets also won ImageNet detection and localization and the COCO detection and segmentation tasks of that year. On CIFAR-10, the authors even trained a network with 1202 layers without optimization difficulty. Its test error of 7.93% was worse than the 6.43% of a 110-layer network, which the authors attribute to overfitting: 19.4 million parameters are too many for this small dataset.

Gao Huang, Zhuang Liu, Laurens van der Maaten, and Kilian Weinberger took shortcuts one step further. Inside a dense block, every layer receives the feature maps of all preceding layers, concatenated along the channel dimension, and passes its own maps to all following layers. A block with L layers thus has L(L+1)/2 direct connections instead of L. In a ResNet, layer \ell adds its input to its output; in a DenseNet, it concatenates all earlier outputs:\text{ResNet: } \mathbf{x}_\ell = H_\ell(\mathbf{x}_{\ell-1}) + \mathbf{x}_{\ell-1} \qquad \text{DenseNet: } \mathbf{x}_\ell = H_\ell\bigl([\mathbf{x}_0, \mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_{\ell-1}]\bigr)

Concatenation keeps the earlier features unchanged, so later layers can reuse them directly. Each layer adds only k new feature maps, the growth rate; the ImageNet models use k = 32. Layer \ell of a block therefore receives k_0 + k(\ell-1) maps, where k_0 is the number of channels entering the block. Because this number keeps growing, each layer first reduces its input with a 1 \times 1 convolution to 4k channels before its 3 \times 3 convolution. Between dense blocks, transition layers with batch normalization, a 1 \times 1 convolution, and 2 \times 2 average pooling with stride 2 halve the resolution and, with a compression factor of 0.5, also the number of channels.

Example

DenseNet-121 has four dense blocks with 6, 12, 24, and 16 layers. The first block starts with 64 channels and ends with 64 + 6 \cdot 32 = 256, which the transition halves to 128. The second block grows them to 128 + 12 \cdot 32 = 512, halved to 256; the third to 256 + 24 \cdot 32 = 1024, halved to 512; and the fourth to 512 + 16 \cdot 32 = 1024. Global average pooling turns these 1024 maps into the input of the final dense layer. Counting all layers gives 8.0 million parameters.

DenseNets reach the accuracy of ResNets with fewer parameters: a DenseNet-201 with 20 million parameters has about the same validation error as a ResNet-101 with more than 40 million.

Alexey Dosovitskiy and colleagues at Google Research removed the convolutions altogether. 

Figure 9 shows their Vision Transformer (ViT). It cuts the image into square patches of P \times P pixels; with P = 16, a 224 \times 224 image yields 224^2 / 16^2 = 196 patches. Each patch is flattened into 16 \cdot 16 \cdot 3 = 768 values and mapped by a trainable linear projection to a patch embedding with D dimensions. As in BERT, a learnable [class] embedding is placed in front of the sequence, and learnable position embeddings are added so that the model knows where each patch came from. The sequence passes through L transformer encoder layers. Each layer applies layer normalization, multi-head self-attention, layer normalization again, and a two-layer MLP, with a residual connection around the attention and around the MLP. The output state of the [class] token represents the image, and a classification head on top of it predicts the class.

A convolution builds two assumptions about images into the network: nearby pixels belong together, and a pattern means the same wherever it appears. The Vision Transformer has far less of this image-specific bias. Apart from cutting the image into patches, it must learn spatial relations from data. Trained on ImageNet alone, with 1.3 million images, ViT models end a few percentage points below ResNets of comparable size. Pretrained on ImageNet-21k with 14 million images, or on Google’s internal JFT-300M with 303 million images, they match or beat the best convolutional networks: ViT-H/14 pretrained on JFT-300M reaches 88.55% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet, ViT-L/16 87.76%, and ViT-L/16 pretrained on ImageNet-21k 85.30%.

Where this is used

Transformer Embeddings explains why transformers replaced recurrent networks for text: a recurrent network processes a sequence one step at a time, and its hidden state degrades over long distances even with LSTM and GRU cells. This section describes these networks and cells. Before transformers, recurrent networks also turned sequences of acoustic features into phonemes in speech recognizers, the step that 

Transcription now assigns to transformer models.

Text, speech, and video are sequences, and their meaning depends on order and context. A fully connected or convolutional network expects an input of fixed size. A recurrent network instead processes a sequence one element at a time and carries a state from one step to the next, so that each output can depend on everything the network has seen before. This section describes the basic recurrent network, explains why it is hard to train, and introduces the gated cells that solved the problem and the attention mechanism that eventually replaced recurrence.

At each time step t, a recurrent network combines the current input \mathbf{x}_t with its previous hidden state \mathbf{h}_{t-1} into a new hidden state, from which it can compute an output \mathbf{y}_t:

Key Formula: Recurrent Network\mathbf{h}_t = \tanh\bigl(\mathbf{W}_h\, \mathbf{h}_{t-1} + \mathbf{W}_x\, \mathbf{x}_t + \mathbf{b}\bigr), \qquad \mathbf{y}_t = \mathbf{W}_y\, \mathbf{h}_t + \mathbf{c}

The hidden state summarizes the sequence up to step t. The same weights \mathbf{W}_h, \mathbf{W}_x, and \mathbf{W}_y are used at every step.

Figure 1 shows the network unrolled in time: a chain of copies of the same cell A, one per time step, each passing its hidden state to the next. Unrolled, a recurrent network is a deep feed-forward network with one layer per time step and with weights shared across all layers. It is trained like one, with backpropagation over the unrolled graph, which is called backpropagation through time. Since the weights are shared, their gradients add up the contributions of all time steps, like the shared bias of 

Backpropagation and Gradient Descent.



Figure 1:A recurrent network unrolled over five time steps: the same cell A receives the input i_t and the hidden state of the previous step and passes its new hidden state on.

A recurrent network can map a sequence to a single output, for example a sentiment label for a sentence; to a sequence of the same length, for example one phoneme per audio frame; or, as the encoder-decoder below shows, to a sequence of a different length. A bidirectional network runs one recurrent network forward and one backward over the sequence and combines their hidden states, so that each position sees the context on both sides.

The depth of an unrolled network equals the length of the sequence, and long sequences make the gradient problems of 

Training Deep Networks severe. In the backward pass, the gradient that reaches step t from step T has passed through T - t multiplications with the same matrix \mathbf{W}_h and with the derivatives of the activation function.

Example: A scalar recurrent network over 50 steps

Take a network with a single hidden unit, h_t = \tanh(w\, h_{t-1} + u\, x_t). The derivative of h_{50} with respect to h_0 is a product of 50 factors w \cdot \tanh'(\cdot), and since \tanh' \le 1, its size is at most |w|^{50} when the unit stays in the steep range of the tanh. With w = 0.9, this is at most 0.9^{50} = 0.005: what the network saw 50 steps ago has almost no influence on the gradient. With w = 1.1 and the unit in its linear range, the factor can reach 1.1^{50} = 117, and the gradient explodes.

Exploding gradients are easy to contain with gradient clipping, which rescales the gradient whenever its norm exceeds a threshold. Vanishing gradients are the harder problem, because they prevent the network from learning dependencies over long distances, such as the agreement between a subject and a verb many words later.

The long short-term memory (LSTM) cell of Hochreiter and Schmidhuber (1997) adds a second state, the cell state \mathbf{c}_t, and three gates that control it. Each gate is a layer of sigmoid neurons that computes values between 0 and 1 from the input and the previous hidden state, and it multiplies another vector component by component:

the forget gate \mathbf{f}_t decides how much of the old cell state to keep,

the input gate \mathbf{i}_t decides how much of a new candidate \tilde{\mathbf{c}}_t to add,

the output gate \mathbf{o}_t decides how much of the cell state appears in the hidden state.

Key Formula: LSTM Cell State\mathbf{c}_t = \mathbf{f}_t ⊙ \mathbf{c}_{t-1} + \mathbf{i}_t ⊙ \tilde{\mathbf{c}}_t, \qquad \mathbf{h}_t = \mathbf{o}_t ⊙ \tanh(\mathbf{c}_t)

The cell state is updated by addition instead of by a matrix product and a squashing function. Its gradient flows back through the forget gate alone, so information and gradients can travel over many steps when the forget gate stays close to 1.

With a forget gate of 0.99, the cell state keeps 0.99^{50} = 0.61 of its content after 50 steps, where the scalar recurrent network above kept at most 0.005 of its gradient. The network learns when to keep and when to forget: the gates are trained with the rest of the network. The gated recurrent unit (GRU) of Cho and colleagues (2014) simplifies the LSTM to two gates, an update gate and a reset gate, and merges the cell state into the hidden state. It has fewer parameters and often performs as well.

For translation, an encoder-decoder architecture uses two recurrent networks. The encoder reads the source sentence and summarizes it in its final hidden state; the decoder starts from this state and generates the target sentence one word at a time, each step taking the previous word as input. A single vector must then hold the whole sentence, and translations of long sentences degrade. Bahdanau, Cho, and Bengio (2015) let the decoder look back at all hidden states of the encoder: at each step, it computes a weighted average of them, with weights that indicate which source words matter for the next target word. This mechanism is called attention.

The transformer of 2017 kept attention and dropped recurrence. Its self-attention connects every position directly with every other one, so information no longer has to pass through a chain of hidden states, and all positions can be computed in parallel instead of one after the other. 

Transformer Embeddings explains the architecture. Recurrent networks remain useful where a sequence arrives step by step and memory is limited, for example in speech recognition on small devices, and the idea of a compact state updated at every step returns in recent state-space models such as Mamba, which process very long sequences in time linear in their length.

A neuron computes a weighted sum of its inputs and passes it through a nonlinear activation function. A single layer of perceptrons separates classes only with hyperplanes and cannot compute XOR; a hidden layer computes a new representation in which the classes become separable.

Neural network research came in three waves: perceptrons from 1958, backpropagation from 1986, and deep learning from 2006, which won with large datasets, graphics processors, and the training techniques of C.3.

Training minimizes a loss with stochastic gradient descent on mini-batches, usually with momentum. Backpropagation computes all partial derivatives in one backward pass: the delta of a neuron is the derivative of the loss with respect to its sum, hidden deltas come from the deltas of the next layer, and each weight’s gradient is its input times the delta it feeds.

Sigmoid derivatives of at most 1/4 make gradients vanish in deep networks, and large weights make them explode. ReLU-type activations, He initialization, normalization layers, and residual connections keep signals and gradients at a stable scale.

Regularization fights overfitting: more data through augmentation and self-supervised pretraining, early stopping, weight decay, and dropout. Adam adapts the step size of each parameter to the size of its gradients.

Convolutional layers connect each neuron to a local receptive field and share the kernel across all positions. Stride and padding set the output size, pooling summarizes neighborhoods, 1 \times 1 convolutions reduce the number of features, and global average pooling turns feature maps into an embedding.

The architectures from LeNet to ResNet made convolutional networks deeper and cheaper: small kernels, inception modules, residual connections, and dense connections. The Vision Transformer replaces convolutions with attention over image patches.

Recurrent networks process sequences with a hidden state and are trained with backpropagation through time, where gradients vanish over long distances. LSTM and GRU cells keep information with gated additive updates; attention, and finally the transformer, removed the need for recurrence.

Key Formula: Backpropagation\delta_k = \phi'(s_k) \sum_{l} w_{k,l}\, \delta_l, \qquad \frac{∂ J}{∂ w_{j,k}} = a_j\, \delta_k

The delta of a hidden neuron collects the deltas of the next layer through the connecting weights; the gradient of a weight is its input times the delta of the neuron it feeds.

Key Formula: Stochastic Gradient Descent with Momentum\Delta \leftarrow \gamma\, \Delta + \frac{\eta}{|\mathbb{B}|} \sum_{\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{B}} \nabla J(\mathbf{x}; \mathbf{w}), \qquad \mathbf{w} \leftarrow \mathbf{w} - \Delta

Each mini-batch step combines the average gradient with a fraction \gamma of the previous step.

Key Formula: Output Size of a Convolutionn_{\text{out}} = ⌊ \frac{n + 2p - k}{s} ⌋ + 1

A kernel of size k with padding p and stride s maps n input positions to n_{\text{out}} output positions along each dimension.

Transformers appear in most chapters of this book: they produce the embeddings of semantic search, write the answers of retrieval-augmented generation, align images and text, and transcribe speech. It describes the families of transformer models and how they are pretrained, how a pretrained model is fine-tuned for a task, how the classifiers compare on a real text classification task, and how a generative model produces text.

Hundreds of transformer models exist, but they fall into three families that differ in which tokens may attend to which, and they are pretrained with a handful of self-supervised objectives. This section describes the three families, the pretraining objectives, the most important models since BERT, and the changes to the architecture that today’s models share. Together, they explain why one model suits classification, another generation, and a third transcription.

The transformer of 2017 had two halves: an encoder that reads the input and a decoder that generates the output, as 

Transformer Embeddings shows. Later models use either half alone or both.

Encoder-only models, such as BERT, let every token attend to every other token in both directions. They compute one contextualized vector per input token and are suited to understanding tasks: classification, named entity recognition, and the embeddings of semantic search. They cannot generate text, since every position sees the whole input.

Decoder-only models, such as GPT, Llama, and Qwen, let each token attend only to itself and the tokens before it. This causal attention makes them generators: they predict the next token from the previous ones, append it, and repeat (

Generative Language Models). Today’s large language models are decoders, and decoders increasingly serve as embedding models too, using the vector of the last token instead of [CLS].

Encoder-decoder models, such as T5, BART, and Whisper, keep both halves. The encoder reads the whole input bidirectionally; the decoder generates the output causally and attends to the encoder’s vectors through cross-attention. They suit tasks that transform one sequence into another: translation, summarization, and speech recognition, where the input is audio and the output text.

The difference between the families is a mask in the attention. Attention computes scores between all pairs of positions and turns each row into weights with a softmax. A mask adds -\infty to the scores of the forbidden pairs, so that their weights become exactly zero:

Key Formula: Masked Self-Attention\text{Attention}(\mathbf{Q}, \mathbf{K}, \mathbf{V}) = \operatorname{softmax}\!\left(\frac{\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K}^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}} + \mathbf{M}\right) \mathbf{V}, \qquad M_{ij} = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if position } i \text{ may attend to } j \\ -\infty & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}

An encoder uses \mathbf{M} = \mathbf{0}, so every token sees every other. A decoder uses the causal mask with M_{ij} = -\infty for j > i, so each token sees only itself and the past.

Example: Causal attention over four tokens

For the input “the cat sat down”, an encoder computes attention weights for all 4 \cdot 4 = 16 pairs. A decoder computes them only for the pairs with j \le i: “the” attends to itself, “cat” to “the” and itself, “sat” to three tokens, “down” to all four, which makes 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10 pairs. The vector of “cat” therefore cannot depend on “sat” or “down”. This is what allows a decoder to be trained on predicting every next token of a text at once: each position computes its prediction without seeing the token it predicts.

All three families are first pretrained on large text collections with self-supervised objectives, which take their targets from the text itself (

Self-Supervised Learning), and only then adapted to a task.

Masked language modeling (MLM) trains encoders. BERT selects 15% of the tokens and predicts them from the context. To avoid a mismatch with fine-tuning, where no [MASK] tokens occur, it replaces 80% of the selected tokens with [MASK], 10% with a random token, and keeps 10% unchanged. RoBERTa (2019) showed that BERT was undertrained: dropping the next-sentence task, choosing new masks in every epoch, and training longer on ten times more data improved every benchmark. ELECTRA (2020) replaces masked prediction with replaced token detection: a small generator fills in masked tokens, and the encoder learns to tell for every token whether it is original or replaced, so it learns from all tokens instead of 15% of them.

Causal language modeling trains decoders. The model predicts each token from the tokens before it, and the loss is the cross-entropy of 

Cross-Entropy summed over all positions:

Key Formula: Causal Language ModelingJ = -\sum_{t=1}^{T} \log P(x_t ∣ x_1, \dots, x_{t-1})

The negative log probability of each actual next token, given everything before it. Thanks to the causal mask, one forward pass computes the predictions for all T positions of a training text at once.

For example, the small language model SmolLM2-135M assigns the probability 0.096 to " Bern" as the next token after “The capital of Switzerland is”, so this position contributes -\ln 0.096 = 2.34 to the loss. Training on trillions of tokens drives such probabilities up for the tokens that actually follow.

Span corruption trains the encoder-decoder T5 (2019). It replaces random spans of the input with sentinel tokens and lets the decoder generate the missing spans. T5 casts every task as text to text, so that translation, classification, and summarization share one model and one loss. Denoising trains BART (2019): the input is corrupted by masking, deleting, and permuting, and the decoder reconstructs the original. Contrastive objectives train embedding models and multimodal models: they pull matching pairs together and push the other pairs of a batch apart, as in the multiple negatives ranking loss of 

Semantic Similarity with Transformers and the image-text training of CLIP in 

Multimodal Transformers.

Distillation produces smaller models from larger ones. A small student model is trained to reproduce the output distributions of a large teacher instead of the hard labels. DistilBERT (2019) is 40% smaller than BERT and 60% faster while keeping 97% of its language understanding.
