Embedding models such as E5, BGE, GTE, and Qwen3-Embedding are built on these families: an encoder or a decoder, pretrained as above and then fine-tuned with contrastive losses on pairs of queries and documents (

Fine-Tuning).

The transformers of today differ from the original in several details that make them more stable, faster, and able to handle longer inputs. The small model SmolLM2-135M, with 30 layers, a vocabulary of 49,152 tokens, and a context of 8,192 tokens, uses all of the first four.

Pre-normalization. The original transformer normalized after each sublayer and its residual connection. Moving the layer normalization of 

Training Deep Networks before the sublayer keeps the residual path free of normalization and makes deep transformers train stably; most models also use the simpler RMSNorm, which rescales without subtracting the mean.

Rotary position embeddings (RoPE). Instead of adding a position vector to each token, RoPE rotates the query and key vectors by an angle that grows with the position. The dot product of a query and a key then depends on their distance, not on their absolute positions, which helps models generalize to sequences longer than those seen in training.

Gated feed-forward layers. The feed-forward layer between the attention layers uses a gated activation such as SwiGLU, which multiplies one linear projection component by component with the activation of another and works better than a plain ReLU or GELU layer at the same cost.

Grouped-query attention (GQA). During generation, a decoder stores the keys and values of all previous tokens, the KV cache of 

Generative Language Models, so that it does not recompute them for each new token. GQA lets several query heads share one key and value head, which shrinks the cache. SmolLM2-135M has 9 query heads that share 3 key and value heads.

Example: The size of the KV cache

An 8B model with 32 layers and attention heads of dimension 128 stores two vectors, a key and a value, per layer and key-value head for each token, in 16-bit numbers. With 32 key-value heads, one per query head, this is 2 \cdot 32 \cdot 32 \cdot 128 \cdot 2 bytes = 512 KiB per token, or 4 GiB for a context of 8,192 tokens. With grouped-query attention and 8 key-value heads, as in Llama 3 8B, it is 128 KiB per token and 1 GiB for the same context: four times more conversations fit into the memory of one graphics processor.

Efficient attention kernels. Attention over n tokens computes an n \times n matrix of scores. FlashAttention computes exact attention in tiles that fit into the fast on-chip memory of a graphics processor and never stores the full matrix, which makes the memory grow linearly with the sequence length and the computation several times faster.

Mixture of experts (MoE). A mixture-of-experts layer contains several feed-forward networks, the experts, and a small router that sends each token to a few of them. The model has many parameters, but each token uses only a fraction. Mixtral 8x7B has 47 billion parameters, but each token activates only 13 billion; several Qwen3 models use the same design.

Where this is used

Query Understanding recognizes named entities with a transformer fine-tuned for token classification, and 

Result Generation extracts answer spans with a model fine-tuned on SQuAD. 

Semantic Similarity with Transformers trains bi-encoders and cross-encoders, both fine-tuned transformers. 

 contrasts a frozen backbone with a linear probe and full fine-tuning for image networks, and 

Evaluating RAG discusses when fine-tuning is the right tool and when retrieval is.

Pretraining gives a transformer a general model of language, but it does not teach it a task. Fine-tuning adapts a pretrained model to a task with labeled examples: it adds a small task-specific layer, the head, and continues training. Because the pretrained layers already encode most of what the task needs, a few thousand labeled examples are often enough where training from scratch would need millions. This section describes the heads for the most common tasks, the choice between freezing and training the pretrained layers, the hyperparameters that matter, parameter-efficient methods such as LoRA, and a complete fine-tuning loop.

An encoder computes one contextualized vector \mathbf{h}_t per input token. A head turns these vectors into the output the task needs.

Sequence classification assigns a label to a whole text, for example a sentiment or an intent. The head takes a single vector for the sequence, the output at the [CLS] token or the mean over all token vectors, and maps it with one linear layer to K logits, followed by the softmax of 

Softmax:

Key Formula: Classification HeadP(y ∣ \text{text}) = \operatorname{softmax}(\mathbf{W}\, \mathbf{h}_{\text{[CLS]}} + \mathbf{b}), \qquad \mathbf{W} \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times d}

A single linear layer on top of the sequence vector. With d = 768 and K = 2 classes, the head has only 768 \cdot 2 + 2 = 1{,}538 parameters; everything else is pretrained.

Token classification assigns a label to every token, for example for named entity recognition. The labels follow the BIO scheme: B-PER marks the first token of a person’s name, I-PER a following token of the same name, and O a token outside any entity, so that “Ada Lovelace visited Basel” is tagged B-PER I-PER O B-LOC. The head applies one linear layer to each token vector. Since a word may be split into several sub-word tokens, only the first sub-word of each word usually carries a label during training. Datasets such as CoNLL-2003 provide the annotations.

Span extraction finds the answer to a question inside a passage. The question and the passage form one input, separated by [SEP]. The head learns two vectors, \mathbf{s} for the start and \mathbf{e} for the end of the answer, and scores every token of the passage with them:

Key Formula: Span Extraction HeadP_{\text{start}}(t) = \operatorname{softmax}_t(\mathbf{s}^\top \mathbf{h}_t), \qquad P_{\text{end}}(t) = \operatorname{softmax}_t(\mathbf{e}^\top \mathbf{h}_t)

The answer is the span from the most likely start to the most likely end, with the end not before the start and the span not longer than a limit.

Example: Extracting an answer

A DistilBERT model fine-tuned on the SQuAD question-answering dataset receives the question “When was the University of Basel founded?” and the passage “The University of Basel was founded in 1460 and is the oldest university in Switzerland. Its faculty of science offers a master program in computer science.” The tokenizer turns both into 40 tokens; the year becomes the two sub-word tokens 146 and ##0. The start head gives 146 the probability 0.990, the next candidate “in” only 0.008; the end head gives ##0 the probability 0.999. The answer is “1460”. For the question “Which country is the university in?”, the same model extracts “switzerland” from the same passage.

Sentence embeddings need no new head, but a different loss. A bi-encoder pools the token vectors into one vector per text and is trained so that matching query-document pairs are close and other pairs are far apart, with the contrastive losses of 

Semantic Similarity with Transformers. A cross-encoder puts the query and the document into one input and uses a classification head with a single output, the relevance score; it is the reranker of the same section.

How much of the pretrained model should change? Three strategies trade cost against accuracy.

A frozen encoder keeps all pretrained weights and trains the head alone. This is the linear probe of 

: it is fast, it needs few examples, and one encoder can serve many tasks at once, since the embeddings can be computed once and reused. Its accuracy is limited by how much of the task the pretrained representation already captures.

Full fine-tuning trains all weights together with the head. It reaches the best accuracy, because the representation itself adapts to the task, but it needs more labeled data and computation, and it produces a complete copy of the model for every task. With too much training, the model can also lose general abilities it had before, an effect called catastrophic forgetting. 

Text Classification compares a frozen and a fully fine-tuned encoder on the same sentiment task.

Partial fine-tuning trains only the top layers and freezes the lower ones, which hold the most general features. It sits between the two in cost and accuracy.

Fine-tuning uses much smaller learning rates than training from scratch, because the pretrained weights are already good and large steps would destroy them. The authors of BERT recommended learning rates of 5 \cdot 10^{-5}, 3 \cdot 10^{-5}, or 2 \cdot 10^{-5}, batch sizes of 16 or 32, and two to four epochs. The optimizer is usually AdamW (

Training Deep Networks) with a weight decay around 0.01. The learning rate rises linearly during a short warm-up, typically the first 6 to 10% of the steps, and then decays linearly to zero.

A few pitfalls are common. Small datasets make fine-tuning unstable: two runs with different random seeds can differ by several percentage points, so results should be averaged over several seeds and compared on a validation set (

Training and Model Selection). The model overfits within a few epochs, so the validation loss decides when to stop. Inputs longer than the maximum length are truncated, which may cut off the part that decides the label. And a text classifier trained on one kind of text, such as tweets, may transfer poorly to another, such as product reviews.

Full fine-tuning of a model with billions of parameters needs the memory for all weights, their gradients, and the optimizer state, and a full copy of the model for each task. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning freezes the pretrained weights and trains a small number of new parameters. Adapters insert small bottleneck layers into each transformer layer and train only those. LoRA (low-rank adaptation) adds to each frozen weight matrix \mathbf{W}_0 \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d} a trainable update of low rank r:

Key Formula: LoRA\mathbf{W} = \mathbf{W}_0 + \mathbf{B}\mathbf{A}, \qquad \mathbf{B} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times r}, \; \mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times d}, \; r \ll d

The pretrained matrix stays frozen; only the two thin matrices \mathbf{B} and \mathbf{A} are trained. After training, \mathbf{B}\mathbf{A} can be added to \mathbf{W}_0, so the adapted model runs as fast as the original.

Example: How few parameters LoRA trains

A projection matrix of BERT-base has 768 \cdot 768 = 589{,}824 weights. LoRA with rank r = 8 trains 2 \cdot 768 \cdot 8 = 12{,}288 parameters instead, 2.1% of the matrix. Applied to the query and value projections of all 12 layers, LoRA trains 294{,}912 parameters, 0.27% of the 109{,}482{,}240 parameters of BERT-base. For GPT-3, the authors of LoRA report 10,000 times fewer trainable parameters and a third of the memory of full fine-tuning, with similar accuracy.

Since every task only needs its own small pair of matrices, one base model can serve many tasks, with the matching adapter loaded per request. QLoRA goes one step further: it stores the frozen base model in 4-bit numbers and trains LoRA adapters on top, which fits the fine-tuning of a 65-billion-parameter model onto a single graphics processor with 48 GB of memory.

The following loop fine-tunes a small pretrained encoder for binary classification with the Hugging Face transformers library and plain PyTorch. AutoModelForSequenceClassification loads the pretrained encoder and adds a new, randomly initialized classification head; the model computes the cross-entropy loss itself when it receives the labels.import torch
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForSequenceClassification

name = "sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2"          # 22.7M parameters
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(name)
model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(name, num_labels=2)

optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=5e-5, weight_decay=0.01)
model.train()
for texts, labels in train_batches:                       # mini-batches of 32 examples
    enc = tokenizer(texts, padding=True, truncation=True,
                    max_length=64, return_tensors="pt")
    loss = model(**enc, labels=torch.tensor(labels)).loss  # cross-entropy
    loss.backward()                                       # backpropagation
    optimizer.step()
    optimizer.zero_grad()

Freezing the encoder and training only the head takes one more line before the loop, for p in model.base_model.parameters(): p.requires_grad = False. A learning-rate schedule with warm-up, an evaluation on validation data after each epoch, and several seeds complete a careful run. Higher-level tools, such as the Trainer of the same library or the training utilities of sentence-transformers for embedding models, wrap this loop.

Fine-tuning changes how a model behaves: the labels it assigns, the format and style of its outputs, the tasks it can perform. It is a poor way to give a model new facts. Facts learned into the weights cannot be updated without training again, cannot be cited, and mix with what the model already believed. Retrieval-augmented generation supplies facts at query time instead, as 

Evaluating RAG discusses: fine-tune for behavior, retrieve for knowledge.

Where this is used

Intent Routing and Classification routes queries with Naive Bayes classifiers over words and character n-grams. 

Automated Feature Extraction treats text labels such as sentiment, topic, and language as the cheapest structural metadata, and 

Multimodal Transformers shows that the same JSON prompt that describes an image can classify a text. 

Evaluating Text Classifiers evaluates text classifiers, and 

When Evaluation Misleads warns about benchmarks that measure something other than the task. This section compares the classifiers on one dataset.

Text classification assigns a label to a text: a sentiment to a product review, a topic to a news article, an intent to a query, a language to a document. The labels feed facets and filters, route requests, and summarize large collections, for example the share of negative comments under a video. This section follows one task, the sentiment of tweets, through four generations of classifiers: Naive Bayes, a convolutional network, a transformer with a classification head, and zero-shot classification by embeddings and prompts. On the way, it shows that the most important step comes before any classifier: checking what the labels mean.

The Natural Language Toolkit (NLTK) provides a sentiment dataset of 5,000 positive and 5,000 negative tweets. We split it into 8,000 training and 2,000 test tweets, stratified so that both classes keep their shares. A tweet tokenizer lowercases the text, removes user names and links, and shortens repeated characters such as “sooooo”. Since tweets are short and most words occur only once, each tweet becomes a set of words, and a Bernoulli Naive Bayes classifier (

Naive Bayes) with Laplace smoothing learns from the presence and absence of each of the 11,241 distinct tokens.

Example: Naive Bayes on 10,000 tweets

Training takes 64 milliseconds on a laptop, and classifying the 2,000 test tweets 13 milliseconds. The classifier is correct on 99.98% of the training tweets and on 99.85% of the test tweets: it makes 3 errors in 2,000. The most informative features for the positive class are “:)”, “:-)”, “:D”, and “:p”; for the negative class “:(”, “:-(”, and “>:(”.

Such an accuracy should make us suspicious. Sentiment is hard, and no classifier understands sarcasm from a bag of words. The informative features point to the explanation.

According to the documentation of the dataset, the tweets were collected in July 2015 by searching for emoticons: the positive tweets with strings such as “:)”, “:D”, and “<3”, the negative tweets with strings such as “:(”, “:/”, and “>:(”. The labels were never assigned by people; they are the emoticons. In the data, 99.0% of the positive tweets contain a smiling emoticon and 98.1% of the negative tweets a frowning one. The classifier has learned the rule by which the dataset was collected, not the sentiment of the text.

Removing all emoticons from the tweets turns the task into the one we actually care about: deciding the sentiment from the words. The same Naive Bayes classifier then reaches 79.0% on the test tweets, with 420 errors instead of 3. Many tweets without their emoticon are routine messages with little sentiment: 62 of the positive tweets thank someone for following, such as “Thanks for following! Do get in touch if you’d like any more info about our project”. The remaining errors include the hard cases above.

When a feature gives away the label

Labels derived automatically from a feature, here emoticons, are a cheap way to build large training sets, called distant supervision. They are also a trap: if the feature stays in the input, a classifier learns the labeling rule and reports an accuracy that new data, labeled by people, will never reach. Before trusting a high accuracy, check how the labels were made and which features the model relies on. This is a form of the leakage that 

Training and Model Selection and 

When Evaluation Misleads describe.

All results below use the tweets without emoticons, with the same split.

TextCNN (Kim 2014) was the first neural architecture to beat bag-of-words classifiers widely. It turns the tokens into word embeddings and slides one-dimensional convolutions of widths 2 to 5 over the sequence, each with several filters, so that every filter responds to a pattern of a few consecutive words, such as “not good”. Max pooling over the positions keeps the strongest response of each filter, which makes the output independent of the text length, and a fully connected layer with a softmax maps the pooled vector to the classes. TextCNN is a historical step: transformers replaced it for almost every task.

A transformer classifier puts the classification head of 

Fine-Tuning on top of a pretrained encoder. We use MiniLM, a distilled encoder with 6 layers, 384 dimensions, and 22.7 million parameters, in three ways. A frozen encoder with a logistic regression on top of its sentence embeddings, a linear probe, needs only the embeddings, which take 30 seconds for all 10,000 tweets on a laptop processor; it reaches 79.1%, the same as Naive Bayes. Fine-tuning all weights for one epoch over the 8,000 training tweets with the loop of 

Fine-Tuning takes 189 seconds and reaches 82.8%, because the encoder can now adapt its representation to the sentiment of tweets.

A model fine-tuned by others can be used without any training. The RoBERTa model of the TweetEval benchmark was fine-tuned on tweets labeled by people with three classes, negative, neutral, and positive. Applied to our test tweets and forced to choose between positive and negative, it reaches 74.4%. It predicts “neutral” as its top label for 40% of the tweets without emoticons, an honest assessment for many of them, but our two labels do not allow it. A model from elsewhere brings its own definition of the classes.

Zero-shot classifiers need no labeled examples at all. The first approach uses label prototypes: we embed a short description of each class, “This tweet is positive and happy.” and “This tweet is negative and sad.”, and assign each tweet the class whose description is most similar to its embedding, as in the zero-shot classification of CLIP in 

Multimodal Transformers. With MiniLM, this reaches 67.5%: better than chance, but well below the trained classifiers. Adding a class only means adding a description.

The second approach uses a prompt to a generative language model (

Generative Language Models). The prompt describes the task and the classes and asks for the answer in a fixed format, typically JSON:Classify the sentiment of the following tweet as "positive", "negative", or "neutral".
Answer only with JSON of the form {"label": "...", "reason": "..."}.
Tweet: "Waiting at the airport for three hours now, just lovely."

A capable model can recognize the sarcasm in this example, which no bag-of-words classifier can. Prompts handle new classes and new tasks immediately and can explain their decisions. Their costs are the opposite of Naive Bayes: every classification is a full generation, which takes seconds instead of microseconds and costs money with a hosted model, and the results vary with the wording of the prompt and between model versions. Confidence values that the model writes into its JSON are not calibrated probabilities (

Generative Language Models).

Example: Two hosted models on the tweets

We sent the prompt for each of the 2,000 test tweets without emoticons to Claude Haiku 5.5, a small and fast model, and to Claude Sonnet 5.5, a larger one, on Amazon Bedrock. With the three classes of the prompt above, the models answer “neutral” for 39% and 33% of the tweets, which the dataset counts as errors, because every tweet is labeled positive or negative. On the remaining tweets, they reach 81.1% and 83.3%. With a prompt that allows only “positive” or “negative”, Haiku reaches 75.1% and Sonnet 79.1%.

The two models agree with each other on 88% of the tweets, and on 17% both give the same answer against the label. Many of these tweets carried their sentiment only in the removed emoticon: “same” is labeled positive, “i hope so” negative. Of Sonnet’s errors, 48% are tweets it had called neutral when allowed to. The prompt matches Naive Bayes without a single labeled example, but not the fine-tuned encoder, which has learned from 8,000 examples which words come with which label. A model can only be as accurate as the labels allow, and these labels say how the author decorated the tweet, not what the text says.

The comparison is above all a lesson in Occam’s razor (

Over- and Underfitting): among methods of similar accuracy, choose the simplest. Naive Bayes, the frozen encoder, and the prompt to Sonnet all reach 79%. The fine-tuned encoder is only four points ahead, a gap that can shrink or grow on other tweets and with labels that people assigned instead of emoticons. The costs, however, differ by orders of magnitude. Naive Bayes trains in 64 milliseconds and classifies a tweet in about 7 microseconds on a laptop. Fine-tuning takes about 3,000 times longer to train, and a prompt to Sonnet takes about 2 seconds per tweet, some 300,000 times longer, and costs about $1,100 per million tweets. A method that costs this much more has to earn its place with a clear gain on the task at hand.

This suggests an order of work. Start with a fast baseline such as Naive Bayes or logistic regression, and look at its most informative features to check the labels. Use embeddings with a linear probe when one encoder should serve several tasks. Fine-tune when the extra accuracy matters and labeled data exists. Use zero-shot prototypes or prompts when there are no labels, when the classes change often, or when the hard cases need an understanding of context that only a large model brings. And whichever method wins, the accuracy is only as meaningful as the labels it is measured against.

Where this is used

The retrieval-augmented generation of 

7 - Retrieval Augmented Generation and the agents of 

Agentic RAG are built around generative language models, and 

Multimodal Transformers uses them to describe images and names hallucination as the eighth obstacle of content analysis. 

Text Classification classifies text with a prompt that asks for JSON output. This section explains how these models produce text, why they sometimes produce wrong text fluently, and what the context window and the KV cache cost.

A generative language model is a decoder (

Model Families and Pretraining) pretrained to predict the next token. Generating text is nothing more than repeating this prediction: the model computes a probability distribution over its vocabulary, one token is chosen, it is appended to the input, and the model predicts again. How the token is chosen matters a great deal. The same model can be deterministic or creative, repetitive or varied, depending on its decoding strategy. This section follows the loop with a small open model, SmolLM2-135M-Instruct, whose 135 million parameters run on a laptop processor at about 26 tokens per second.

For a given input, the model outputs one logit per token of its vocabulary, 49,152 for SmolLM2, and the softmax of 

Softmax turns them into probabilities. For the input “The capital of Switzerland is”, the five most probable next tokens are:

Next token

" Geneva"

" Bern"

" called"

The model does not look up a fact. It has learned which continuations are likely after such a sentence, and many continuations are: “the city of ...”, a city name, “located in ...”. The correct answer, Bern, has slightly less probability than Geneva, which is wrong. A larger model trained on more data concentrates more probability on Bern, but the principle stays the same: the output is drawn from a distribution over plausible text.

Greedy decoding always chooses the most probable token. It is deterministic, but it tends to produce bland and repetitive text, and a locally best token can lead into a poor continuation. Beam search keeps the k most probable partial sequences instead of one and chooses the best complete sequence; it is common in translation and speech recognition, where one correct output is expected.

Sampling draws the next token at random from the distribution, so the same input can produce different outputs. Two parameters shape the distribution before sampling. The temperature \tau of 

Softmax divides the logits: a temperature below 1 sharpens the distribution toward the most probable tokens, a temperature above 1 flattens it. Top-p sampling, also called nucleus sampling, keeps only the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add up to at least p and samples from them after renormalizing, which cuts off the long tail of implausible tokens. Top-k sampling keeps the k most probable tokens instead.

Key Formula: Temperature and Nucleus SamplingP_\tau(w) = \frac{\exp(z_w / \tau)}{\sum_{v} \exp(z_v / \tau)}, \qquad V_p = \text{smallest set } V \text{ with } \sum_{w \in V} P_\tau(w) \ge p

The temperature \tau rescales the logits z_w before the softmax; the next token is then sampled from the nucleus V_p, the most probable tokens that together cover the probability p.

Example: Temperature and nucleus for one prediction

For the input “The capital of Switzerland is”, the entropy of the next-token distribution is 5.44 bits at \tau = 1, and the nucleus for p = 0.9 contains 110 tokens. At \tau = 0.5, the probability of " the" rises from 0.243 to 0.637, the entropy falls to 1.84 bits, and the nucleus shrinks to 4 tokens. At \tau = 2, the distribution is almost flat: the entropy is 12.38 bits, " the" keeps only 0.018, and the nucleus needs 10,840 tokens.

Greedy decoding continues with " the city of Bern, which is located in the northern part". Three samples with \tau = 1 and p = 0.9 continue with " the city of Basel.“, " the city of Zurich, known for its rich history, culture”, and " the largest city and cultural center in the country." All four continuations are fluent; three name the wrong city, and the greedy one places Bern in the wrong part of the country.

Such fluent but false statements are called hallucinations. They are not a malfunction but a consequence of the mechanism: the model produces likely text, and likely text is not always true. Larger models hallucinate less on common facts, but they still do so on rare facts, recent events, and questions outside their training data. This is the main reason why retrieval-augmented generation (

7 - Retrieval Augmented Generation) gives the model the relevant documents and asks it to answer from them.

A model pretrained on next-token prediction continues text; it does not follow instructions. Asked a question, it may continue with more questions. Turning it into an assistant takes two further training stages. Instruction tuning, a supervised fine-tuning on pairs of instructions and good responses, teaches the model to answer. Preference alignment then teaches it which of several possible answers people prefer. Reinforcement learning from human feedback (

Tasks and Experience) trains a reward model on human rankings of answers and tunes the language model to maximize the reward; direct preference optimization (DPO) reaches a similar result with a simple classification loss on pairs of preferred and rejected answers, without a separate reward model.

An instruction-tuned model expects its input in a fixed chat template, a serialization of the conversation with special tokens that mark the roles. For SmolLM2, a request to classify the sentiment of “The battery died after two days.” becomes the text<|im_start|>system
You are a helpful AI assistant named SmolLM, trained by Hugging Face<|im_end|>
<|im_start|>user
Classify the sentiment of this review as positive or negative: "The battery died after two days."<|im_end|>
<|im_start|>assistant

and the model continues after the last line with “The sentiment of this review is negative.” The template is part of what the model learned during instruction tuning; libraries apply it automatically, and a wrong template degrades the answers noticeably.

hierarchy.lvl2: The Context Window and the KV Cache
The Context Window and the KV Cache

records.content:
The context window is the maximum number of tokens the model can attend to: 8,192 for SmolLM2, and between 128,000 and a million tokens for current large models. Everything the model should consider must fit into it: the system instructions, the conversation so far, retrieved documents, and the answer being generated. Longer contexts are not used uniformly. Liu and colleagues showed that models use information at the beginning and the end of a long context much better than information in the middle, a reason why 

Chunking Strategies cares about which passages enter the prompt and where.

Generation runs in two phases. In the prefill phase, the model processes the whole prompt in one parallel pass, like an encoder. In the decode phase, it generates one token at a time. To avoid recomputing the keys and values of all previous tokens at every step, it stores them in the KV cache and only computes the new token’s query, key, and value. The cache grows with every token, and for long contexts it, not the model weights, fills the memory of the graphics processor: 

Model Families and Pretraining computes 1 GiB per 8,192 tokens for an 8B model with grouped-query attention. Serving systems such as vLLM therefore manage the cache in fixed-size blocks, like the pages of an operating system, to fit more requests into memory.

Large language models can learn a task from the prompt alone, without any change to their weights. A zero-shot prompt describes the task. A few-shot prompt adds a few solved examples, from which the model infers the pattern; GPT-3 showed in 2020 that this ability emerges with scale. Chain-of-thought prompting asks the model to write intermediate reasoning steps before the answer, which improves its accuracy on problems that need several steps, such as arithmetic word problems. Recent reasoning models are trained to produce such steps on their own.

Prompting has costs. A prompt adds tokens, and every token costs time and money. The output can vary from run to run, and small changes to the wording can change the result. For tasks with a fixed set of labels and enough training data, a fine-tuned classifier is often faster, cheaper, and more accurate (

Text Classification).

Many applications need machine-readable output instead of prose, for example a JSON object with a label and extracted fields. A prompt can ask for JSON and describe its fields, but a model may still produce invalid JSON or invent fields. Constrained decoding guarantees the format: at each step, it sets the probability of every token to zero that would violate a grammar or a JSON schema, so the model can only generate valid output. Most serving systems and model APIs offer such structured output modes.

Confidence values in generated text are not probabilities

A model asked to output a confidence for each label writes numbers that look like probabilities but are just more generated text. In an earlier version of this material, a model classified the opening of Arthur Conan Doyle’s novel A Study in Scarlet as song lyrics with a confidence of 0.7 and justified this with a “repetitive, rhythmic structure” that the prose does not have. When calibrated scores are needed, the probabilities that the model assigns to the label tokens are a better basis, and they must still be checked on validation data, as 

Scores, Thresholds, and ROC Curves describes.

Transformers come in three families that differ in their attention mask: encoders see the whole input and suit classification and embeddings, decoders see only the past and generate text, and encoder-decoders transform one sequence into another, as in translation and speech recognition.

Encoders are pretrained with masked language modeling, decoders with causal language modeling, encoder-decoders with span corruption or denoising, and embedding models with contrastive objectives. Distillation produces small models from large ones.

Today’s transformers share pre-normalization, rotary position embeddings, gated feed-forward layers, and grouped-query attention, and large models increasingly use mixtures of experts.

Fine-tuning adds a small head, for sequence classification, token classification, or span extraction, and continues training with small learning rates. A frozen encoder is cheap and shareable; full fine-tuning is more accurate; LoRA trains a fraction of a percent of the parameters with similar results.

On the NLTK tweets, Naive Bayes reaches 99.85% because the labels are the emoticons by which the tweets were collected. Without emoticons, Naive Bayes and a frozen encoder reach 79%, a fine-tuned encoder 83%, zero-shot prototypes 68%, and a prompt to Claude Sonnet 79% (Haiku 75%) without any labeled example; on 17% of the tweets, both language models disagree with the label, because the sentiment was in the removed emoticon. The most important check comes before any classifier: how were the labels made?

Among methods of similar accuracy, choose the simplest (Occam’s razor). Naive Bayes trains in milliseconds and classifies a tweet in microseconds, about 300,000 times faster than a prompt to a large model, and the four points of the fine-tuned encoder may not survive other data.

A generative model produces text by repeatedly sampling the next token. Temperature and top-p sampling shape the distribution; greedy decoding is deterministic. Fluent but false continuations, hallucinations, follow from the mechanism.

Instruction tuning and preference alignment turn a language model into an assistant, which expects its input in a chat template. The KV cache stores the keys and values of past tokens and dominates the memory for long contexts.

Prompts classify and extract without training, can follow new instructions immediately, and can be forced into valid JSON by constrained decoding, but they are slow and costly per request, and the confidences they write are not probabilities.

hierarchy.lvl1: E - Human Vision and Image Features
E - Human Vision and Image Features

records.content:
keeps the classical image features short. Human vision gets two paragraphs: three cone types, metamerism, and an illusion that shows that perception is not measurement. Lab and HSV appear as a choice of color space, without their conversion formulas. Gabor filters appear as a concept, without the computation behind them. This chapter supplies what the main text leaves out, for readers who want to know where the three numbers per pixel come from and how the features built on them are computed.

The details matter when a feature behaves unexpectedly: when two colors that look alike lie far apart in RGB, when a color moment computed in a single pass loses its precision, or when a filter bank is faster in Fourier space than as a convolution.

Where this is used

 keeps three cone types, metamerism, and the checker-shadow illusion from 

The Human Visual System, and it uses Lab and HSV, whose formulas are in 

Color Systems.

 introduces Gabor filters as a concept; 

Extended Image Features computes them in Fourier space and adds gradient moments and Laws’ texture energy.

 builds on the receptive fields and the orientation-selective cells of the visual cortex.

Distance and Similarity Measures treats the quadratic distance, which 

Extended Image Features turns into a Euclidean distance.

Prerequisites

Color histograms, color moments, and the quadratic distance: 

.

Gradients and Gabor filters: 

.

For the last section, eigenvectors of a symmetric matrix and the discrete Fourier transform.

The Human Visual System follows the light from a surface through the eye and the retina into the visual cortex. 

Color Systems turns the three cone signals into the color spaces that image features compute with, CIE XYZ, xyY, sRGB, Lab, HSL, and HSV, and follows one color through all of them. 

Extended Image Features shows how moments are computed in one pass, how the quadratic distance becomes a Euclidean distance, two further texture features, and how Gabor filters work in Fourier space.

Where this is used

 keeps the core of this section: three cone types, metamerism, and the checker-shadow illusion, which shows that perception is not measurement. 

 builds on the receptive fields and the orientation-selective cells of the visual cortex described below, because they inspired convolutional networks. The invariances that 

Automated Feature Extraction asks of perceptual features, such as stability under a change of light, are invariances the visual system already has. 

Color Systems turns the three cone signals into the color spaces that image features compute with.

This section follows the path of light from a surface to the cortex. We start with the physical signal, then look at how the eye samples it, how fine these samples are compared with other species, and how the retina and the brain process them.

Every image starts with light that falls on a surface and leaves it toward a viewer. Two quantities describe this interaction. The illumination l(x,y,z) is the amount of light that arrives at a point in space. We measure it in lux, a unit that weights the power at each wavelength by the sensitivity of the human eye. The reflectance r(x,y,z) is the fraction of that light that the surface at this point sends back. It lies between 0 for a surface that absorbs all light and 1 for a surface that reflects all of it.

Figure 1 shows both sides of the interaction. On the left, light from a source with color R_s G_s B_s hits a small surface fragment whose material has the reflectance R_m G_m B_m. Part of the light is reflected as in a mirror, at the same angle \theta to the surface normal at which it arrived. The rest is scattered diffusely in all directions. The viewer sees only the light that leaves the fragment toward the eye. A small change in the direction, the intensity, or the color of the light source therefore changes how the same surface looks.



Figure 1:Light-surface interaction (left) and spectral reflectance of natural surfaces (right).

The right side of the figure shows the reflectance of natural surfaces for wavelengths from 0.4 to 2.0 micrometers. Snow reflects about 80 to 90 percent of the visible light. Water reflects only a few percent at all wavelengths. Vegetation reflects little visible light, has a small peak in the green near 550 nm, and reflects strongly in the near infrared above 700 nm, which we cannot see. Leaves look green because chlorophyll absorbs mainly blue light (around 430 to 455 nm) and red light (around 640 to 665 nm). Green light is absorbed less, and the cell structures of the leaf scatter it back toward the viewer.

These curves show that the physical signal is a rich, continuous function of the wavelength. Human vision and camera sensors reduce it to three numbers per point. 

Color Systems describes this reduction in detail.

Key Formula: Image Formationf(x,y,z) = l(x,y,z) \cdot r(x,y,z), \qquad 0 < l(x,y,z) < \infty, \quad 0 < r(x,y,z) < 1

In the simplest model, the light f that a point sends toward the viewer is the product of illumination and reflectance. The same product holds for each wavelength separately: f(\lambda) = l(\lambda) \cdot r(\lambda).

The two factors vary on very different scales. Direct sunlight delivers 32,000 to 100,000 lux, an overcast day about 1,000 lux, office lighting 320 to 500 lux, and a full moon on a clear night only 0.05 to 0.3 lux. Reflectance, in contrast, spans from about 1 percent for a black fabric to about 90 percent for fresh snow. The illumination thus changes by a factor of 100,000 and more between day and night, the reflectance only by a factor of about one hundred.

Example

Consider a piece of black velvet with r = 0.01 in direct sunlight with l = 100{,}000 lux, and a sheet of white paper with r = 0.8 under office lighting with l = 500 lux:f_{\text{velvet}} = 100{,}000 \cdot 0.01 = 1{,}000, \qquad f_{\text{paper}} = 500 \cdot 0.8 = 400

The velvet sends 2.5 times more light into the eye than the paper. Still, we see the velvet as black and the paper as white. The visual system does not report the product f. It estimates the reflectance r and discounts the illumination, an ability called lightness constancy. A feature extractor that only sees pixel values, which are proportional to f, would call the velvet the brighter surface.

Lightness constancy also explains the checker-shadow illusion in 

: two squares that send the same light to the eye look different, because the visual system attributes the darkness of one of them to a shadow. For feature design, the formula suggests a remedy. Two neighboring points under the same light have the ratio f_1 / f_2 = (l \cdot r_1)/(l \cdot r_2) = r_1 / r_2, so the illumination cancels. Features that compare neighboring pixels, such as edges and gradients, are therefore more robust to lighting than features that use absolute brightness. The retina, as we will see below, works with exactly such comparisons.

The eye converts light into electrochemical signals that the brain can interpret. 

Figure 2 shows its structure. Light enters through the cornea, passes the pupil, and goes through the lens. Together, the cornea and the lens focus the image of an object onto the retina at the back of the eye. The lens changes its shape to focus on objects at different distances, and the iris changes the size of the pupil to adapt to the light level. A camera does the same with its focus and its aperture. The image on the retina is upside down, and the brain interprets it correctly.



Figure 2:The human eye, the layers of the retina, and the normalized absorbance of the three cone types and the rods.

The magnified part of the figure shows a surprising detail of the retina. Light passes through several layers of nerve cells before it reaches the photoreceptors, which point away from the light toward the pigment epithelium. There are two kinds of photoreceptors, rods and cones, and they serve different purposes.

Cones provide sharp, detailed, and colored vision in daylight. They are concentrated in the macula and in its center, the fovea, which is the part of the retina we point at whatever we look at. There are three types of cones with different sensitivity curves, shown on the right of the figure:

S cones (short wavelengths) peak near 420 nm, in the violet-blue.

M cones (medium wavelengths) peak near 534 nm, in the green.

L cones (long wavelengths) peak near 564 nm, in the yellow-green.

The common names “blue”, “green”, and “red” cones are convenient but misleading for the L cones. Their peak is not in the red. They earn their name because their sensitivity reaches furthest into the long wavelengths, so red light excites them much more than the M cones. The M and L curves overlap strongly. A single wavelength therefore excites two or three cone types at once, and the brain derives color from the comparison of their responses.

Rods dominate the periphery of the retina and work best in low light. They are essential for night vision and for noticing movement at the edge of the visual field. All rods share one pigment with a peak near 498 nm. With only one type of receptor, the rods cannot distinguish colors, which is why we see shades of gray at night.

The numbers of photoreceptors are large and vary between people. Curcio et al. (1990) counted an average of 4.6 million cones (4.1 to 5.3 million) and 92 million rods (78 to 107 million) per retina, with up to 199,000 cones per square millimeter in the center of the fovea. Many textbooks quote rounded values of 6 million cones and 120 million rods; the measured averages are lower.

The three cone types are far from equally frequent. S cones make up only about 7 percent of the cones near the fovea (Curcio et al., 1991). They are irregularly spaced, missing entirely in a small zone of about 0.35 degrees at the center of the fovea, and most dense in a ring just outside it. The ratio of L to M cones varies even more. In eight men with normal color vision, Hofer et al. (2005) measured ratios from 1.1:1 to 16.5:1. Fixed percentages for the three cone types should therefore be read as one example, not as a constant of human vision.

These variations do not cause color blindness: all the men in the study above saw colors normally. Color blindness arises when one cone type is missing or when its pigment is shifted to a different wavelength. The most common forms affect the L or the M cones and make red and green hard to tell apart.

Visual acuity measures how fine a detail the eye can resolve. The standard test is the Snellen chart: rows of letters of decreasing size, read from a distance of 20 feet (6 meters). A result of 20/20, written 6/6 in metric units, means that the eye resolves the critical details of a letter, such as the gap in a “C” or the width of a stroke, when they cover a visual angle of 1 arcminute (1/60 of a degree). The whole letter is five times larger and covers 5 arcminutes. At 20 feet, 1 arcminute corresponds to20 \text{ ft} \cdot \tan\!\left(\tfrac{1}{60}^\circ\right) = 6.096 \text{ m} \cdot 0.000291 = 1.77 \text{ mm},

so a person with 20/20 vision separates two contours about 1.77 mm apart at that distance, and the letters of that row are about 8.9 mm tall. A result of 20/40 means that the person must stand at 20 feet to read what a person with normal vision reads at 40 feet. The details must be twice as large, 2 arcminutes instead of 1.

Clinical practice also expresses acuity as a decimal number, the reciprocal of the minimum angle of resolution (MAR) in arcminutes:V = \frac{1}{\text{MAR}}

A result of 20/20 gives V = 1.0, and 20/40 gives \text{MAR} = 2 and V = 0.5. Vision science often uses a third unit, the number of grating cycles per degree that the eye can still resolve. One cycle consists of one dark and one bright bar. If each bar covers 1 arcminute, one degree holds 30 cycles, so 20/20 corresponds to 30 cycles per degree, and 20/40 to 15. In general, a Snellen fraction 20/D corresponds to 600/D cycles per degree. We use this conversion in the comparison of species below.

The value 20/20 is the lower limit of normal vision, not the average. Healthy young adults typically reach 20/16 to 20/12 (6/5 to 6/4), and the limit of the unaided human eye lies around 20/10 to 20/8, or about 60 cycles per degree. Driving licences set minimum values. In the European Union, a car driver needs a binocular acuity of at least 0.5 with both eyes, which is a MAR of 2 arcminutes or 20/40. The German screening test for a car licence is stricter and asks for 0.7, a MAR of about 1.4 arcminutes.

Animals perceive the world very differently. 

Figure 3 shows on the left the same farmhouse scene as a human sees it and as a cat sees it: the cat’s version has fewer colors and much less detail. The right side shows the four cone types of goldfish and zebrafish, which reach into the ultraviolet.



Figure 3:The same scene for human and cat vision (left) and the four cone types of goldfish and zebrafish (right).

The following table compares the acuity of several species. The Snellen equivalents use the conversion 600/D from the previous subsection, and all values are approximate.
