Curcio, C. A., & Allen, K. A. (1990). Topography of ganglion cells in human retina. Journal of Comparative Neurology, 300(1), 5-25. 

PubMed. Counts 0.7 to 1.5 million ganglion cells per retina and links cortical magnification to ganglion cell density.

Hofer, H., Carroll, J., Neitz, J., Neitz, M., & Williams, D. R. (2005). Organization of the human trichromatic cone mosaic. The Journal of Neuroscience, 25(42), 9669-9679. 

PubMed Central. Images of the cone mosaic in living eyes, with L:M ratios from 1.1:1 to 16.5:1 among people with normal color vision.

Goodale, M. A., & Milner, A. D. (1992). Separate visual pathways for perception and action. Trends in Neurosciences, 15(1), 20-25. 

PubMed. The proposal of the ventral stream for recognition and the dorsal stream for visually guided action.

Caves, E. M., Brandley, N. C., & Johnsen, S. (2018). Visual acuity and the evolution of signals. Trends in Ecology & Evolution, 33(5), 358-372. 

DOI. A survey of acuity across animals in cycles per degree, showing that most species see far less detail than humans.

Reymond, L. (1985). Spatial visual acuity of the eagle Aquila audax: A behavioural, optical and anatomical investigation. Vision Research, 25(10), 1477-1491. 

PubMed. The measurement behind the eagle’s acuity of about 140 cycles per degree, twice the human limit.

Allison, W. T., Haimberger, T. J., Hawryshyn, C. W., & Temple, S. E. (2004). Visual pigment composition in zebrafish: Evidence for a rhodopsin-porphyropsin interchange system. Visual Neuroscience, 21(6), 945-952. 

PubMed. Microspectrophotometry of zebrafish photoreceptors, the source of the four measured cone peaks from 361 to 565 nm.

Kolb, H., et al. Webvision: The organization of the retina and visual system. Online textbook. 

webvision.pitt.edu. A free, detailed reference on the cell types and circuits of the retina, including bipolar, ganglion, horizontal, and amacrine cells.

Smith, T., & Guild, J. (1931). The C.I.E. colorimetric standards and their use. Transactions of the Optical Society, 33(3), 73-134. 

IOP Science. The original description of the 1931 standard observer and of the XYZ system that every later CIE space builds on.

CIE (2018). Colorimetry (4th ed., CIE 015:2018). International Commission on Illumination. 

CIE. The current standard for XYZ, xyY, and Lab, including the official tables; not free of charge.

Colour & Vision Research Laboratory. CVRL database: Colour matching functions. University College London. 

cvrl.ucl.ac.uk. Free tables of the CIE 1931 color matching functions in 1 nm steps, the data behind the metamer example in E.2.

Stokes, M., Anderson, M., Chandrasekar, S., & Motta, R. (1996). A standard default color space for the Internet: sRGB (Version 1.10). W3C. 

w3.org. The original proposal by HP and Microsoft that became IEC 61966-2-1, with the primaries and the transfer function.

ITU-R (2015). Recommendation BT.2020-2: Parameter values for ultra-high definition television systems for production and international programme exchange. International Telecommunication Union. 

ITU. Defines the wide-gamut Rec. 2020 primaries used in E.2.

Smith, A. R. (1978). Color gamut transform pairs. Computer Graphics (SIGGRAPH '78 Proceedings), 12(3), 12-19. 

PDF. Introduces the HSV hexcone model and the fast conversion between RGB and HSV.

Sharma, G., Wu, W., & Dalal, E. N. (2005). The CIEDE2000 color-difference formula: Implementation notes, supplementary test data, and mathematical observations. Color Research & Application, 30(1), 21-30. 

PDF. The reference implementation of CIEDE2000, the corrected successor of the Euclidean distance in Lab.

Laws, K. I. (1980). Rapid texture identification. Proceedings of SPIE, 238, 376-381. 

SPIE Digital Library. Describes texture energy measures computed with small convolution masks, the basis of the method in E.3.

Stricker, M. A., & Orengo, M. (1995). Similarity of color images. Storage and Retrieval for Image and Video Databases III, Proceedings of SPIE, 2420. 

SPIE Digital Library. Introduces color moments as a compact alternative to color histograms, the features whose one-pass computation E.3 derives.

Hafner, J., Sawhney, H. S., Equitz, W., Flickner, M., & Niblack, W. (1995). Efficient color histogram indexing for quadratic form distance functions. IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence, 17(7), 729-736. 

IEEE Xplore. Shows how cheap lower bounds of the quadratic histogram distance prefilter a large image collection before the exact distance is computed.

Manjunath, B. S., & Ma, W. Y. (1996). Texture features for browsing and retrieval of image data. IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence, 18(8), 837-842. 

IEEE Xplore. The standard reference for Gabor texture features in image retrieval, with a comparison against other multiresolution texture features.

Frigo, M., & Johnson, S. G. (2005). The design and implementation of FFTW3. Proceedings of the IEEE, 93(2), 216-231. 

PDF. Explains how a modern FFT library computes transforms of any size, including primes, in O(n \log n) time.

Pébay, P. P. (2008). Formulas for robust, one-pass parallel computation of covariances and arbitrary-order statistical moments (Report SAND2008-6212). Sandia National Laboratories. 

OSTI. Update formulas for central moments that avoid the cancellation of the raw-sum approach and merge results computed in parallel.

hierarchy.lvl1: F - Human Hearing and Audio Features
F - Human Hearing and Audio Features

records.content:
11 - Audio Features keeps the physics and the physiology of hearing to a few sentences: decibels, a cochlea that analyzes frequencies, and a frequency resolution that decreases with frequency. It introduces the extended musical features, such as several simultaneous pitches and beat tracking, by their idea only, and it summarizes the classical speech recognizer in one paragraph. This chapter supplies what the main text leaves out, for readers who want to know why the mel scale has its shape, how a beat tracker decides where the beats are, and how hidden Markov models turned speech into text before transformers did.

The details matter when an audio feature behaves unexpectedly: when a pitch estimate jumps down an octave, when a tempo estimate doubles, or when a recognizer fails on a new microphone or a fast speaker.

Where this is used

From Sound to Spectrogram keeps decibels and the cochlea as a frequency analyzer; 

Human Hearing and Sound Physics adds the physics of sound waves, the anatomy of the ear, the cochlear frequency map, and the auditory pathway.

Perceptual Features builds the mel scale and the MFCC features on the frequency resolution of the ear and mentions the entropy of energy, which 

Extended Audio and Music Features defines.

Musical Features introduces pitch, chroma, and tempo; 

Extended Audio and Music Features adds the harmonic sum, the estimation of several simultaneous pitches, the tempo prior, and beat tracking by dynamic programming.

Transcription summarizes the classical speech recognizer; 

Speech Recognition with HMMs describes its phoneme models, its decoding, and how it copes with speaking rate, speakers, and microphones.

Prerequisites

The spectrogram, decibels, and the mel scale: 

From Sound to Spectrogram and 

Perceptual Features.

Pitch, chroma, and the onset strength: 

Musical Features.

For the last section, hidden Markov models with the forward and the Viterbi algorithm: 

Hidden Markov Models.

Human Hearing and Sound Physics follows a sound from the vibrating source through the air into the ear, along the cochlea, and up the auditory pathway to the cortex. 

Extended Audio and Music Features defines the entropy of energy, maps spectrum bins to chroma, estimates one or several fundamental frequencies, and estimates the tempo and the beats of music. 

Speech Recognition with HMMs builds a speech recognizer from hidden Markov models and follows its replacement by neural networks.

Where this is used

From Sound to Spectrogram keeps decibels and one paragraph on the cochlea, which analyzes a sound by frequency before the brain sees it. 

Perceptual Features builds the mel scale and the MFCC features on two properties of the ear described below: a frequency resolution that decreases with frequency and a roughly logarithmic perception of energy. The onset strength of 

Musical Features counts only increases of energy, as the adapting hair cells of the cochlea do. 

Speech Recognition with HMMs relies on the same front end.

Sound has two meanings. In physics, it is a mechanical wave that travels through a medium. In perception, it is the sensation that this wave creates in a listener. This section follows a sound from the vibrating source through the air into the ear, along the cochlea, and up the auditory pathway to the cortex. On the way, we meet the properties that audio features imitate.

Sound begins when something vibrates and disturbs the medium around it. A loudspeaker membrane pushes the air molecules in front of it together and pulls them apart, creating alternating regions of compression and rarefaction. These regions travel outward as a wave. The molecules themselves only oscillate around their resting positions; what travels is the pattern of pressure. Because sound passes from molecule to molecule, it needs a medium and cannot travel through empty space.

The speed of the wave depends on the medium. In air, it grows with the temperature T in degrees Celsius, approximately as v = 331 + 0.6 \cdot T m/s, which gives 343 m/s at 20 °C. Sound travels faster in liquids, about 1,482 m/s in water at 20 °C, and faster still in solids, around 4,000 m/s in wood and about 12,000 m/s in diamond, where the stiff structure passes vibrations on quickly. The speed links the frequency f of a wave to its wavelength \lambda.

Key Formula: Wavelength and Frequency\lambda \cdot f = v, \qquad v \approx 331 + 0.6 \cdot T \ \text{m/s in air}

The wavelength \lambda is the distance between two neighboring compressions. T is the air temperature in degrees Celsius.

Example: Wavelengths of audible sound

At 20 °C, the lowest audible frequency of 20 Hz has a wavelength of 343 / 20 = 17.1 m, a tone of 1 kHz has 34.3 cm, and the highest audible frequency of 20 kHz has 17.1 mm. Audible sound therefore spans wavelengths from the size of a building to the width of a fingertip. In water, the same 1 kHz tone has a wavelength of 1.48 m, more than four times as long as in air, because the frequency stays the same and the speed changes.

The wavelength decides how sound interacts with objects. Waves bounce off surfaces that are large compared with their wavelength and bend around smaller obstacles. A wall reflects a high tone and lets a low one bend around its edge, which is why we hear the bass of music from the next room better than the voices. At the boundary between two media, part of the wave is reflected and part continues in a new direction. On its way, the wave spreads over a growing area and loses energy to the medium, and high frequencies lose it faster than low ones, which is why distant thunder rumbles instead of cracking.

The pressure of the wave varies over an enormous range, from 20 µPa at the threshold of hearing to about 20 Pa near the threshold of pain, a factor of a million. 

From Sound to Spectrogram therefore measures sound pressure on the logarithmic decibel scale, with 0 dB at the threshold of hearing and 120 dB near the threshold of pain. Hearing damage depends on the level and the duration: long exposure to levels above about 85 dB damages the hair cells of the cochlea, and since these cells do not regrow in humans, the loss is permanent.

Humans hear frequencies from about 20 Hz to 20 kHz, and the upper limit falls with age. Other species hear different parts of the spectrum; Heffner and Heffner (2007) give an overview for laboratory animals. Cats hear tones well above our upper limit, and bats hear far into the ultrasound, which they use to navigate and to hunt by echolocation: they emit calls and locate obstacles and prey from the echoes.

Within the human range, the physical properties of a sound do not map one to one onto what we perceive. The following table lists six perceptual attributes, the physical property behind each, and how the two differ.

Perceptual attributes of sound and their physical correlates.

Attribute

Physical correlate

How perception differs

Pitch

Fundamental frequency

Needs a periodic sound that stands out from noise. The ear infers the pitch from the harmonics even when the fundamental is missing: a telephone line passes only 300 to 3,400 Hz, and a voice with a fundamental of 100 Hz still sounds as low as it is.

Loudness

Sound pressure level

Depends on the frequency: at the same level, tones near 3 kHz sound louder than low or very high tones. The ear also integrates energy over a few hundred milliseconds, so a short click sounds quieter than a long tone of the same level.

Duration

Length of the signal

Perception fills short gaps. A voice on a radio with brief dropouts is heard as one continuous message.

Timbre

Spectrum and its change over time

Distinguishes a guitar from a flute at the same pitch and loudness, and a falling rock from the wind. The attack at the start of a note matters as much as the steady part.

Sonic texture

Mixture of many sources

Describes the whole scene, such as a quiet market, a busy party, or an orchestra, rather than one source.

Spatial location

Differences between the two ears

Gives the direction from which a sound appears to come, which is not always where the source is, because reflections arrive from other directions. Together with timbre, it lets us follow one voice at a party.

The ear does not pass raw pressure changes to the brain. 

Figure 1 shows its three parts. The outer ear collects and filters the sound, the middle ear transfers it from the air into a fluid, and the inner ear breaks it down by frequency and converts it into nerve signals.



Figure 1:Anatomy of the human ear with the outer ear (pinna and ear canal), the middle ear (eardrum and the three ossicles), and the inner ear (cochlea and semicircular canals), after Chittka and Brockmann (2005).

The pinna, the visible part of the ear, reflects sound into the ear canal. Its folds reflect sounds from different directions differently, so the spectrum that arrives at the eardrum carries a direction-dependent coloring. The brain learns these colorings and uses them to tell whether a sound comes from above or below, and from the front or the back, which the differences between the two ears alone cannot decide.

The ear canal is a tube of about 2.5 cm, open to the outside and closed by the eardrum. Like an organ pipe closed at one end, it resonates at the frequency whose quarter wavelength equals its length: 343 / (4 \cdot 0.025) \approx 3.4 kHz. Around this resonance, the canal raises the sound pressure at the eardrum by about 10 to 20 dB. The boost falls into the range in which consonants such as “s” and “f” differ, and it is one reason why the ear is most sensitive between 2 and 5 kHz.

The middle ear solves a mismatch. The cochlea is filled with fluid, and a sound wave that hits a fluid surface from the air is almost completely reflected, because the fluid resists motion far more than the air does. The acoustic impedance, the product of density and speed of sound, measures this resistance: about 413 Pa·s/m for air and 1.48 \times 10^6 Pa·s/m for water. For a wave that hits the boundary head-on, the transmitted fraction of the energy is 4 Z_1 Z_2 / (Z_1 + Z_2)^2 = 0.0011, about 0.1 percent or a loss of 30 dB.

The middle ear recovers most of this loss. The sound moves the eardrum, which passes the vibration through three small bones, the ossicles: the hammer (malleus), the anvil (incus), and the stirrup (stapes). The footplate of the stapes sits in the oval window, the entrance to the cochlea. The eardrum is much larger than the footplate, so the force collected over a large area acts on a small one, and the ossicles add a lever. Both raise the pressure at the oval window. The round window below it bulges outward when the oval window moves inward, because the fluid cannot be compressed. The Eustachian tube connects the middle ear to the throat and equalizes the air pressure on both sides of the eardrum, which we notice in an airplane or a tunnel.

Two small muscles stiffen the chain of ossicles when a loud sound arrives, the acoustic reflex. It attenuates loud low-frequency sounds, but it needs a few tens of milliseconds to respond and therefore cannot protect the ear against sudden bangs.

hierarchy.lvl3: Inner Ear and the Cochlear Frequency Map
Inner Ear and the Cochlear Frequency Map

records.content:
The inner ear consists of the vestibular system, whose semicircular canals sense balance and the motion of the head, and the cochlea, a fluid-filled tube coiled two and a half times like a snail shell. Uncoiled, the cochlea is about 35 mm long. The basilar membrane runs along it and divides it lengthwise. Near the oval window, at the base, the membrane is narrow and stiff; toward the tip, the apex, it becomes wider and more flexible.

A vibration of the stapes sets the fluid in motion and launches a wave along the basilar membrane. Because the stiffness changes along the way, the wave of each frequency grows to a maximum at one place and dies out beyond it: high frequencies peak near the base, low frequencies near the apex. Each place on the membrane responds to its own frequency band, so the cochlea works as a bank of band-pass filters, and the nerve receives a time-frequency representation, something like a spectrogram, rather than a waveform. This arrangement by frequency is called tonotopy, and it continues all the way to the cortex.

Greenwood (1990) fitted a single function to the frequency at each place for humans and many other species.

Key Formula: Cochlear Frequency Map (Greenwood)f(x) = A \cdot \left(10^{a x} - k\right), \qquad A = 165.4 \ \text{Hz}, \quad a = 2.1, \quad k = 0.88 \ \text{for humans}

x is the position along the basilar membrane as a fraction of its length, from x = 0 at the apex to x = 1 at the base, and f(x) is the frequency to which this position responds best.

Example: Where the frequencies lie

The map gives 165.4 \cdot (1 - 0.88) = 20 Hz at the apex and 165.4 \cdot (10^{2.1} - 0.88) = 20{,}677 Hz at the base, which matches the range of human hearing. The middle of the membrane, x = 0.5, responds to 1,710 Hz, and x = 0.25 to 408 Hz. Inverting the map, 1 kHz lies at x = 0.400, which is 14.0 mm from the apex of a 35 mm cochlea, and 4 kHz at 23.3 mm.

The length per octave is not constant. The octave from 100 to 200 Hz occupies 2.5 mm, the octave from 1 to 2 kHz 4.5 mm, and every octave above that about 5 mm. Per hertz, the difference is far larger: the 100 Hz from 100 to 200 Hz occupy 2.5 mm, the 100 Hz from 10,000 to 10,100 Hz only 0.07 mm. The ear therefore resolves low frequencies finely and high frequencies coarsely in hertz, as 

From Sound to Spectrogram states.

The shape of the map explains the shape of the mel scale. Factoring out k turns the inverted map intox = \frac{1}{a}\left(\log_{10} k + \log_{10}\left(1 + \frac{f}{A k}\right)\right), \qquad A k = 145.6 \ \text{Hz}

The position grows with \log(1 + f / 145.6\,\text{Hz}). Below the knee at about 150 Hz, the logarithm is nearly linear in f, so equal steps in hertz occupy equal lengths; far above it, the position grows with \log f, so every octave occupies the same length. The mel scale m(f) = 2595 \log_{10}(1 + f / 700\,\text{Hz}) of 

Perceptual Features has exactly this form, with the knee at 700 Hz. The knees differ because the mel scale was fitted to listeners’ judgments of equal pitch distances rather than to the anatomy, but both describe a resolution that is roughly constant in hertz at low frequencies and constant per octave at high frequencies. MFCC features inherit this resolution from the mel filter bank.

The organ of Corti sits on the basilar membrane and converts its motion into nerve signals. It holds two kinds of hair cells: one row of about 3,500 inner hair cells and three rows of about 12,000 outer hair cells. Their hair bundles bend when the membrane moves.

The outer hair cells act as amplifiers. They change their length in step with the vibration and push against the membrane, which strengthens and sharpens its motion at the place of the current frequency. This makes the ear sensitive to quiet sounds and lets it separate frequencies that lie close together. The amplification is strongest for quiet sounds and weak for loud ones, which compresses a range of input levels of a factor of a million in pressure into a much smaller range of motion. Loud noise damages the outer hair cells first, and the ear then loses both its sensitivity and its sharp frequency tuning.

The inner hair cells are the actual sensors. When their bundles bend, they release a neurotransmitter onto the fibers of the auditory nerve. Their response is not proportional to the motion: it grows strongly for small movements and saturates for large ones. The cochlear nerve contains about 30,000 fibers, most of them connected to inner hair cells, and each fiber responds best to one frequency, the frequency of its place, within a range of levels. Fibers with different thresholds cover different parts of the loudness range together. This compressive, roughly logarithmic response is why decibels describe loudness well and why audio features take the logarithm of energies.

The cochlea also adapts. When a tone stays constant, the response of the fibers declines within a few tens of milliseconds, while a new or changing sound produces a strong response at its onset. Changes stand out against a steady background. The onset strength of 

Musical Features, which counts only increases of energy, imitates this emphasis on onsets. Together, amplification, compression, and adaptation make the ear both highly sensitive and highly selective, and features that mimic perception must reflect these non-linear and adaptive properties.

The cochlear nerve joins the vestibular nerve, which carries the signals for balance, to form the eighth cranial nerve. From there, sound information reaches the brain on two routes. The reticular pathway merges the input of all senses and decides which events deserve attention, for example whether a noise should wake us up. The primary auditory pathway analyzes the sound itself. 

Figure 2 shows its stations in sections of the brain stem, the midbrain, and the forebrain.



Figure 2:The primary auditory pathway: from the cochlear nerve through the cochlear nuclei and the superior olive in the brain stem, the inferior colliculus in the midbrain, and the thalamus to the auditory cortex.

The cochlear nuclei in the brain stem receive the fibers of the cochlear nerve. They are the first stage that analyzes the frequency, intensity, and duration of the signal, and some of their cells respond mainly to onsets.

The superior olivary complex, or superior olive, is the first stage that receives input from both ears. It compares the arrival times and the levels of a sound at the two ears, the two main cues for its direction.

The inferior colliculus in the midbrain integrates the direction cues with the frequency analysis and triggers fast reflexes, such as turning the head toward a sudden sound.

The medial geniculate body of the thalamus relays the information to the auditory cortex.

The auditory cortex in the temporal lobe handles both basic and advanced aspects of hearing. Its neurons are arranged in tonotopic maps that help identify sound sources and suppress the distortions caused by reflections. It also processes the fine timing of sounds, which speech and music depend on.

Example: How the brain locates a sound

A sound from the right reaches the right ear first. For a head with a radius of 8.75 cm, the delay is at most 0.0875 \cdot (\pi/2 + 1) / 343 = 0.66 ms, for a source directly to the side, and the superior olive detects differences of a few tens of microseconds. For high frequencies, whose wavelengths are shorter than the head (17 cm at 2 kHz), the head also casts an acoustic shadow, and the sound is louder at the near ear. The brain therefore uses mainly time differences for low frequencies and level differences for high frequencies. Neither cue tells front from back, since a source in front and its mirror image behind produce the same differences; the direction-dependent coloring by the pinna resolves this.

The ear thus passes on an organized description of the sound, not the raw signal: separated by frequency with a resolution that decreases with frequency, compressed in level, emphasizing changes, and compared between the two ears. Audio features copy the first three properties. The mel scale and the logarithm of the MFCC features model the cochlear map and the compression, and the onset strength models the adaptation. Classical features rarely use the fourth, since most collections store sound in mono or as stereo without the geometry of a head.

Where this is used

Perceptual Features mentions the entropy of energy as a third time-domain feature next to the short-time energy and the zero-crossing rate; the first section below defines it. 

Musical Features introduces chroma, the fundamental frequency, the onset strength, and the tempo from its autocorrelation, and it names three methods without their details: the harmonic sum, the estimation of several simultaneous pitches, and beat tracking by dynamic programming. The sections below supply these details. All methods work on the frames and the spectrum of 

From Sound to Spectrogram.

Each method answers a question that the basic features leave open. How abrupt is the energy change within a frame? Which pitch class does a spectrum bin belong to? Which fundamental explains a set of harmonics, and which several fundamentals explain a chord? Which of the many periodicities of an onset pattern is the tempo, and where exactly are the beats?

The short-time energy of 

Perceptual Features says how loud a frame is, but not how the energy is distributed within it. A frame with a steady tone and a frame that is quiet except for a short click can have the same energy. The entropy of energy distinguishes them. It splits frame t of N samples into L sub-frames of N_\text{sub} samples each, with N = L \cdot N_\text{sub}, computes the energy E_j of each sub-frame, and normalizes these energies by their sum, so that they add up to 1 like a probability distribution.

Key Formula: Entropy of Energye_j = \frac{E_j}{\sum_{l=1}^{L} E_l}, \qquad E_j = \sum_{n=(j-1) N_\text{sub}}^{j N_\text{sub} - 1} x_t(n)^2, \qquad H(t) = -\sum_{j=1}^{L} e_j \log_2 e_j

H(t) is largest, \log_2 L, when the energy is spread evenly over the sub-frames, and small when it is concentrated in a few of them.

The entropy is the information-theoretic entropy of 

Information Theory applied to the distribution of energy over time. A low value signals an abrupt change, such as the onset of a note, a plosive sound in speech, or a gunshot. The analogous spectral entropy applies the same formula to the energies of frequency bands instead of sub-frames; it is high for noise, whose energy spreads over all bands, and low for a tone.

Example: A tone and a click

A frame of 40 ms at 16 kHz has 640 samples. With L = 10 sub-frames of 4 ms, a steady 440 Hz tone gives H = 3.320 bits, almost the maximum of \log_2 10 = 3.322 bits. A click of 2 ms that falls into two neighboring sub-frames, over a quiet tone of one percent of its amplitude, gives H = 0.547 bits.

In silent frames, all E_j are zero and the normalization divides by zero. Implementations such as pyAudioAnalysis (Giannakopoulos, 2015), which uses ten sub-frames by default, add a small constant to the denominator and inside the logarithm.

Musical Features assigns a frequency to its pitch class by rounding its note number m(f) = 69 + 12 \log_2(f / 440). A chroma vector needs this assignment for every bin k of the spectrum, whose frequency is \omega(k) = k \cdot f_s / N for a frame of N samples at the sampling rate f_s. Written for the bin directly, the pitch class p(k) and the octave o(k) arep(k) = ⌊ 9.5 + 12 \log_2\left(\frac{\omega(k)}{440}\right) ⌋ \text{ mod } 12, \qquad o(k) = 4 + ⌊ \frac{1}{12}\left(9.5 + 12 \log_2\left(\frac{\omega(k)}{440}\right)\right) ⌋

The constant 9.5 combines two steps. A has the pitch class 9, and adding 0.5 before rounding down rounds to the nearest semitone. The formula therefore gives the same result as rounding m(f), because 69.5 = 60 + 9.5 and 60 is a multiple of 12. The 4 is the octave of the reference A4. A frequency of 440 Hz maps to A4, 261.63 Hz to C4, 246.94 Hz to B3, and 1,000 Hz to B5, since its note number 69 + 14.21 = 83.21 rounds to 83.

Bin 0, the constant component at 0 Hz, has no place on the logarithmic scale and is skipped, and so are the bins outside the range of musical notes. Summing |X(t,k)|^2 over all bins with the same pitch class and octave gives a pitch histogram with 12 values per octave; summing it over the octaves gives the chroma vector of 

Musical Features. The bin spacing f_s / N limits which notes the histogram separates. Neighboring semitones at the frequency f lie f \cdot (2^{1/12} - 1) \approx 0.0595 f apart, so a spacing of \Delta f separates them only above \Delta f / 0.0595 \approx 16.8 \, \Delta f. Frames of 40 ms with a spacing of 25 Hz therefore separate notes above about 420 Hz, and frames of 372 ms with a spacing of 2.7 Hz separate notes above about 45 Hz.

A harmonic tone with the fundamental f_0 has peaks in its spectrum at f_0, 2 f_0, 3 f_0, \dots. The harmonic sum turns this into an estimator: for every candidate f_0, add up the magnitudes at its first M harmonics, and choose the candidate with the largest sum, its salience. Summing with equal weights fails, because a candidate at half the true fundamental collects the same peaks: every harmonic of 220 Hz is also an even harmonic of 110 Hz. Klapuri (2006) therefore weights the harmonics.

Key Formula: Harmonic Sums(f_0) = \sum_{m=1}^{M} g(f_0, m) \cdot \max_{k \approx m f_0 N / f_s} |X(k)|, \qquad g(f_0, m) = \frac{f_0 + 27}{m f_0 + 320}, \qquad \hat{f}_0 = \arg\max_{f_0} s(f_0)

Frequencies are in hertz. The maximum takes the largest magnitude in a few bins around the expected harmonic, because the harmonic rarely falls exactly on a bin. M is limited by the highest frequency of the spectrum, M f_0 < f_s / 2.

The weight decreases with the harmonic number m, so a candidate whose evidence lies in its higher harmonics scores less. Since a candidate at f_0 / 2 explains the true harmonics only as its harmonics 2, 4, 6, \dots, it collects lower weights than the true fundamental, which explains them as harmonics 1, 2, 3, \dots. A candidate at 2 f_0 keeps high weights but finds only every second peak.

Example: A harmonic tone at 220 Hz

A tone at 220 Hz has five harmonics with the amplitudes 1, 0.6, 0.4, 0.3, and 0.2. We analyze 4,096 samples at 16 kHz with a Hann window, a bin spacing of 3.9 Hz, and search the candidates from 60 to 1,000 Hz in steps of 1 Hz with M = 10. Without the weights, 110 Hz and 220 Hz collect the same five peaks, and 110 Hz wins narrowly (2,408.1 against 2,408.0), an octave error. With the weights g(220, m) = 0.457, 0.325, 0.252, 0.206, 0.174 for m = 1, \dots, 5, the salience is 816.9 at 220 Hz, 453.1 at 110 Hz, and 460.5 at 440 Hz. The maximum lies at 222 Hz, within one bin of the true fundamental.

A chord contains several fundamentals, each with its own harmonics. The harmonic sum finds the strongest one; the others follow by iteration.

Compute the magnitude spectrum |X^{(0)}(k)| of the frame, the starting point of the iteration.

Estimate \hat{f}_0 on the current spectrum |X^{(i)}(k)| with the harmonic sum. The weighting is the same in every iteration.

Subtract the magnitudes at the harmonics of \hat{f}_0 to obtain |X^{(i+1)}(k)|, so that the next estimate cannot find the same note again.

Repeat from step 2 as long as the remaining magnitude \sum_k |X^{(i)}(k)| exceeds a threshold \varepsilon, or until a given number of notes is found. The threshold, or the number of notes, decides how many pitches the method reports.

Example: A fifth

A chord of 220 Hz (five harmonics as above) and 330 Hz (four harmonics with the amplitudes 0.8, 0.5, 0.3, and 0.2) gives 221 Hz in the first iteration. After its harmonics are removed, the second iteration gives 332 Hz. The partial at 660 Hz is the third harmonic of 220 Hz and the second of 330 Hz, and it disappears with the first note; the second estimate rests on the remaining harmonics of 330 Hz. Practical estimators therefore subtract less than the full peak at each harmonic.

The time domain offers an alternative. A periodic signal resembles itself when shifted by one period, so the autocorrelation of the frame is large at the lag of one period. With a search range from f_\text{min} to f_\text{max} for the fundamental, the lags m in samples are limited to f_s / f_\text{max} \le m \le f_s / f_\text{min}, and the lag m_0 with the largest autocorrelation gives the fundamental:R(m) = \sum_{n=m}^{N-1} x(n) \cdot x(n - m), \qquad m_0 = \arg\max_{m} R(m), \qquad \hat{f}_0 = \frac{f_s}{m_0}

For the tone at 220 Hz with a search range from 60 to 1,000 Hz at 16 kHz, the lags run from 16 to 266 samples. The maximum lies at m_0 = 73, which gives 16{,}000 / 73 = 219.2 Hz. The true period is 72.7 samples, and the neighboring lags 72 and 74 would give 222.2 Hz and 216.2 Hz, so the resolution of the estimate is limited by the integer lags; interpolating between neighboring lags refines it. The autocorrelation is also large at twice the period, since a signal shifted by two periods matches itself as well. Because the sum has fewer terms at larger lags, the true period usually wins, but the margin can be small.

Musical Features estimates the tempo from the autocorrelation of the onset strength o(t). With a hop of H samples, the onset strength has f_r = f_s / H frames per second, and a lag of l frames corresponds to 60 \cdot f_r / l beats per minute. The conversion uses the frame rate of the onset strength, not the sampling rate of the audio. The autocorrelation has peaks at the beat period and at its multiples and fractions, and the highest of them is not always the one a listener would tap.

Ellis (2007) therefore weights the autocorrelation with a tempo prior, a Gaussian on a logarithmic time axis around a preferred period \tau_0. On the training data of a beat-tracking evaluation, the best agreement with the tempos chosen by listeners, 77 percent, was reached with \tau_0 = 0.5 s, which corresponds to 120 bpm, and a width of \sigma_\tau = 1.4 octaves.

Key Formula: Tempo PriorW(\tau) = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\log_2(\tau / \tau_0)}{\sigma_\tau}\right)^2\right), \qquad \hat{\tau} = \arg\max_{\tau} \ W(\tau) \sum_t o(t) \, o(t - \tau)

\tau is the lag in seconds. Because the Gaussian lies on a \log_2 axis, \sigma_\tau is measured in octaves: halving and doubling the period are penalized equally.

Figure 1 shows the three steps on four seconds of music. The raw autocorrelation of the onset strength has peaks at regular lags with similar heights. The prior, the red curve, peaks at 0.5 s and lowers the peaks far from it. The highest weighted peak lies at about 0.36 s, a tempo of about 168 bpm; the second, at twice the lag, corresponds to 84 bpm.



Figure 1:Tempo estimation (Ellis, 2007): part of the onset strength (top), its raw autocorrelation (middle), and the autocorrelation weighted by the tempo prior around 0.5 s (bottom, red), with the primary tempo period at about 168 bpm and the secondary at 84 bpm.

Example: A rhythm with off-beats and accents

A synthetic onset strength of 6 seconds at f_r = 100 frames per second has onsets of strength 1 on every beat at 0.25, 0.75, 1.25, ... s, a tempo of 120 bpm. An off-beat onset of strength 0.7 follows every second beat after 0.12 s (at 0.62, 1.62, ... s), a syncopated accent of strength 1.5 follows every fourth beat after 0.2 s (at 0.95, 2.95, and 4.95 s), and all frames carry random noise up to 0.2. The off-beats repeat every second, so they add to the autocorrelation at 100 frames, and its highest peak lies there, R(100) = 20.05, at 60 bpm, slightly above R(50) = 19.37. The prior gives W(1.0\,\text{s}) = 0.775 and W(0.5\,\text{s}) = 1, so the weighted values are 15.53 and 19.37, and the estimate is \hat{\tau} = 50 frames, 120 bpm.

Peaks at \{\frac{1}{3}, \frac{1}{2}, 2, 3\} times the chosen lag indicate secondary tempos, the metrical levels above and below the beat. Whether a piece moves at 84 or at 168 bpm is often a matter of taste, and listeners disagree as well.

A single autocorrelation over the whole piece assumes a constant tempo. The tempogram computes it in a sliding window w(j) of W frames instead, one column per frame i:a(i, l) = \sum_{j=0}^{W} w(j) \cdot o(i + j) \cdot o(i + j + l)

Displayed as an image over the time i and the lag l, or the tempo 60 f_r / l, it shows how the tempo changes within a piece, as in classical music with an accelerando or a ritardando. Its column maxima, weighted by the prior, give a local tempo per frame.

The tempo gives the period, not the position of the beats. A beat tracker chooses beat times t_1, \dots, t_n that coincide with strong onsets and follow each other at intervals close to the period \tau_p. The two goals conflict: onsets alone would place beats on every accent and off-beat, and the period alone would tick like a metronome that ignores the music. Ellis (2007) combined both in one objective with a balance factor \alpha.

Key Formula: Beat Tracking Objective (Ellis)C(\{t_i\}) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} o(t_i) + \alpha \sum_{i=2}^{n} F(t_i - t_{i-1}, \tau_p), \qquad F(\Delta t, \tau_p) = -\left(\log \frac{\Delta t}{\tau_p}\right)^2

The penalty F is 0 for an interval equal to the period and symmetric on a logarithmic axis, so an interval of twice the period costs as much as one of half the period. The tracker maximizes C over the number and the positions of the beats.

The objective decomposes into a sum over consecutive beats, which allows dynamic programming. The best score C^*(t) of all beat sequences that end with a beat at time t is the onset strength at t plus the best combination of a predecessor \tau and its own best score:C^*(t) = o(t) + \max_{\tau = t - 2\tau_p}^{t - \tau_p / 2} \bigl(\alpha F(t - \tau, \tau_p) + C^*(\tau)\bigr), \qquad P^*(t) = \arg\max_{\tau} \bigl(\alpha F(t - \tau, \tau_p) + C^*(\tau)\bigr)

The search covers predecessors from 2 \tau_p to \tau_p / 2 before t, since the penalty makes more distant ones unlikely. The algorithm computes C^* and the backpointer P^* for every frame from the start, takes the frame with the largest C^* near the end as the last beat, and follows the backpointers to the first. This is the structure of the Viterbi algorithm of 

Hidden Markov Models: one best path per end point, and the decision at the end. Ellis’s Matlab version of both loops has ten lines, and the cost grows linearly with the length of the piece, with 1.5 \, \tau_p predecessors per frame.

Example: Choosing α

We track the beats of the synthetic rhythm of the tempo example with \tau_p = 50 frames. With \alpha = 2 or less, the tracker returns 15 beats: the nine beats at 0.25, 1.25, 1.75, 2.25, 3.25, 3.75, 4.25, 5.25, and 5.75 s, and around every accent a detour over the off-beat, 0.62 and 0.95 s instead of the beat at 0.75 s, and likewise near 2.95 and 4.95 s. Each detour replaces two intervals of 0.5 s by three intervals of 0.37, 0.33, and 0.30 s, which costs (0.091 + 0.173 + 0.261) \cdot \alpha = 0.52 \cdot \alpha, and gains between 1.2 and 1.4 in onset strength, since it collects 0.7 and 1.5 instead of 1. Above \alpha \approx 2.6, every detour costs more than it gains. With \alpha = 5 or more, the tracker returns the 12 beats at 0.25, 0.75, ..., 5.75 s, all on the beat.

The value of \alpha depends on the scale of the onset strength. Ellis used 400 by default and found 680 best on the evaluation data. With a fixed \tau_p, the tracker follows tempo changes of about 10 percent; larger changes require a local period from the tempogram, at the price of losing the guarantee that dynamic programming finds the best sequence. The librosa library (McFee et al., 2015) implements the onset strength, the tempogram, the tempo prior, and this beat tracker.

Where this is used

Transcription summarizes the classical speech recognizer in one paragraph, with MFCC features, phoneme models, a pronunciation dictionary, and a language model, before it turns to Whisper. This section describes how these components work together. It builds on the hidden Markov models of 

Hidden Markov Models, uses the k-means clustering and the Gaussian mixtures of 

Clustering and the decision trees of 

Decision Trees and Gradient Boosting, and ends with the neural networks of 

Recurrent Networks and the encoder-decoder transformers of 

Model Families and Pretraining.

For three decades, from the 1980s to the 2010s, speech recognizers were built from hidden Markov models. Their components are still visible in today’s systems: the MFCC or mel features, the 10 ms frames, the phonemes as units, the language model, and the search for the most probable transcript. We first state the problem, then build the recognizer from the phoneme upward, look at how it copes with speaking rate, speakers, and microphones, and finally follow its replacement by neural networks.

A recognizer receives a sequence of feature vectors O = o_1, \dots, o_T, one every 10 ms, and looks for the word sequence W that is most probable given these observations. Bayes’ rule splits this probability into two models that can be trained separately.

Key Formula: Speech Recognition as Bayes Decision\hat{W} = \arg\max_{W} P(W ∣ O) = \arg\max_{W} \ p(O ∣ W) \cdot P(W)

The acoustic model p(O ∣ W) says how well a word sequence explains the sound. The language model P(W) says how likely the word sequence is in the language. p(O) is the same for all W and drops out.

The acoustic model is trained on transcribed speech, the language model on text alone, of which far more exists. The language model resolves what the sound leaves open: “recognize speech” and “wreck a nice beach” sound almost the same, and the language model prefers the first.

The observations are the MFCC vectors of 

Perceptual Features: 13 coefficients from frames of 25 ms with a hop of 10 ms, extended by their first and second differences over time to 39 values. MFCCs describe the spectral envelope, the resonances of the vocal tract that distinguish one sound from another, and discard the fine structure of the harmonics. The features therefore depend little on the pitch of the speaker, which carries intonation but not the phoneme in most languages. They do not remove noise, and they do not compensate for the speaking rate; the model has to handle both.

The acoustic model is assembled from phonemes, the smallest sound units that distinguish words in a language, such as /p/ and /b/ in “pin” and “bin”. English has about 40 of them. Each phoneme has its own HMM with a left-to-right topology, shown in 

Figure 1.



Figure 1:A left-to-right HMM for one phoneme: a non-emitting entry state s_0 and three emitting states with self-loops a_{ii} and forward transitions a_{i,i+1}; b_{j,i} is the probability of emitting the observation o_i in state s_j.

The three emitting states stand for the beginning, the middle, and the end of the sound, which differ: the transition from the previous sound, the steady part, and the transition to the next. Each state either stays, with the self-loop probability a_{ii}, or moves on to the next state; it never goes back, because speech moves forward in time. The self-loops absorb the variation of the duration: a slowly spoken vowel stays longer in each state, a fast one passes in a few frames. The entry state s_0 emits nothing and connects the model to the end of the previous phoneme.

Each emitting state needs an emission probability b_j(o_t) for a 39-dimensional vector. Early systems used a discrete HMM: vector quantization with k-means (

Clustering) clusters the MFCC vectors of the training data into a codebook of, for example, 256 centroids, and each frame is replaced by the index of its nearest centroid. The clusters become the observation symbols of the HMM, not its states, and the emission probabilities are tables over the 256 symbols. Quantization discards the information within a cluster, so later systems modeled the vectors directly with a Gaussian mixture per state, trained with the expectation maximization of 

Clustering.

The sound of a phoneme depends on its neighbors: the /k/ in “key” is formed further forward in the mouth than the /k/ in “coo”. Recognizers therefore use triphones, phoneme models that depend on the previous and the next phoneme. With 40 phonemes, there are up to 40^3 = 64{,}000 triphones, most of which occur rarely or never in the training data. State tying groups similar states and trains them together: a decision tree (

Decision Trees and Gradient Boosting) asks questions about the neighbors, such as “is the left neighbor a nasal?”, and each leaf becomes one shared state. Large systems typically end up with a few thousand tied states.

A pronunciation dictionary lists the phonemes of every word: “speech” is /s p iː tʃ/. Concatenating the phoneme HMMs of a word gives a word HMM, and connecting the end of every word with the start of every other word gives one large HMM for all utterances. The language model contributes the transitions between words. An n-gram model estimates the probability of a word from its n - 1 predecessors, counted in a large text corpus and smoothed for unseen combinations (

Naive Bayes):P(W) = \prod_{i} P(w_i ∣ w_{i-2}, w_{i-1})

for a trigram model. Decoding finds the most probable path through the composite HMM with the Viterbi algorithm of 

Hidden Markov Models, which yields the phonemes, the words, and their time stamps at once. The composite HMM has millions of states, so decoders keep only the paths whose score lies within a beam of the best one at each frame, which makes the search fast but no longer guarantees the best path. In practice, the language model score is also raised to a power, a scale factor tuned on held-out data, because the acoustic probabilities of 100 frames per second overwhelm the few word probabilities otherwise.

Training needs no time alignment. Each training utterance comes with its transcript, the dictionary turns the transcript into a chain of phoneme HMMs, and the Baum-Welch algorithm of 

Hidden Markov Models estimates where each phoneme starts and ends while it estimates the parameters. The dictionary also sets the limit of the vocabulary: a word that is not in it cannot be recognized at all, which hits names, new terms, and words from other languages, exactly the words that searches often contain.

People speak at different speeds, and the same speaker stretches some words and swallows others. A left-to-right HMM handles this with its self-loops, but the self-loops imply a particular distribution of durations. A state with the self-loop probability a stays for d frames if it loops d - 1 times and then leaves.

Key Formula: State DurationP(d) = a^{d-1} (1 - a), \qquad E[d] = \frac{1}{1 - a}

The duration of a state follows a geometric distribution. Its most likely value is always one frame, whatever a is.

A larger self-loop raises the mean, but one frame remains the most likely duration. Three states in a row, each with a = 0.8, behave differently. Their total duration is at least 3 frames, has a mean of 15 frames (150 ms), and is most likely 10 or 11 frames, each with a probability of 0.060. The sum of three geometric durations has a peak away from its minimum, which is closer to how long phonemes actually last.

This is one reason why phoneme models have three states rather than one. Recognizers combine three measures against variation in the speaking rate:

Self-loops and several states per phoneme, as above, let a phoneme cover a variable number of frames. The topology is fixed; the training estimates the self-loop probabilities.

Explicit duration models replace the geometric distribution with a distribution estimated from data, in hidden semi-Markov models. They describe durations better, at the price of a more expensive decoding, since the Viterbi recursion must consider every possible duration of a state.

Training data with varied rates lets the models learn the variation. A common augmentation adds copies of the training recordings played about 10 percent slower and faster, so the same words appear at three rates.

Two further sources of variation do not concern the rate but the voice and the recording, and two normalizations remove much of them.

A microphone, a telephone line, or a room acts as a filter: it multiplies the spectrum of the speech S(f) with a fixed transfer function H(f). The logarithm of the mel energies turns this product into a sum, and the discrete cosine transform of the MFCC computation keeps it a sum, so every cepstral vector becomes c_t = s_t + h, the speech plus a constant vector of the channel. Cepstral mean normalization subtracts the mean over the utterance.

Key Formula: Cepstral Mean Normalization\hat{c}_t = c_t - \frac{1}{T} \sum_{\tau=1}^{T} c_\tau = s_t - \frac{1}{T} \sum_{\tau=1}^{T} s_\tau

The constant channel vector h cancels, whatever the microphone or the line was. Live systems use a running mean over the last few seconds instead.

The normalization also removes the long-term average of the speech itself, which carries little information about the phonemes. It cannot remove additive noise, which does not become a constant in the cepstrum.

Speakers differ in the length of their vocal tract. A shorter vocal tract, as in children and in most women, shifts the resonances that distinguish vowels, the formants, to higher frequencies. Vocal tract length normalization compensates for this by warping the frequency axis before the mel filter bank, f' = \alpha f, with a warping factor \alpha per speaker. The factor is chosen from a small grid, typically between 0.88 and 1.12, as the one under which the speaker’s speech is most likely for the acoustic model. Neither normalization concerns the speaking rate; both make the features of different speakers and recordings comparable.

The Gaussian mixtures were the first component to be replaced. In a hybrid HMM-DNN recognizer, a deep network receives a window of several frames and outputs a probability for each tied state, P(s ∣ o_t). The HMM needs the likelihood p(o_t ∣ s) instead, and Bayes’ rule provides it up to a constant: p(o_t ∣ s) \propto P(s ∣ o_t) / P(s), where P(s) is the frequency of the state in the training alignment. The rest of the recognizer, the HMM topology, the dictionary, the language model, and the decoder, stays as it was. Hinton et al. (2012) summarized the results of four research groups, in which such networks outperformed Gaussian mixtures on a variety of benchmarks, sometimes by a large margin. Within a few years, hybrid systems had replaced Gaussian mixtures in most recognizers.

The next step removed the HMM and the alignment. Connectionist temporal classification (CTC, Graves et al., 2006) trains a recurrent network (

Recurrent Networks) to output one symbol per frame, letters or phonemes, plus a blank symbol for “nothing new”. A frame sequence maps to a label sequence by merging repeated symbols and then deleting the blanks: “h h _ e l l _ l o” becomes “hello”, where the blank between the two l’s keeps them apart. The training objective sums the probabilities of all frame sequences that map to the transcript, with a forward-backward recursion like that of 

Hidden Markov Models. No phoneme boundaries are needed, and a network that outputs letters needs no pronunciation dictionary.

Encoder-decoder transformers (

Model Families and Pretraining) finally map the whole spectrogram to a sequence of text tokens. Whisper, described in 

Transcription, is the prominent example. It produces subword tokens, so it can write words that no dictionary listed, although it may misspell a rare name. The elements of the classical pipeline remain inside: log mel features with 10 ms hops, and a decoder that acts as a language model.

Once speech is text, it enters the inverted index of 

Inverted Files like any document, with time stamps that let a search jump to the moment a word was spoken. Recognition errors become retrieval errors, however: a word that was misrecognized cannot be found, and a word that was inserted produces false matches. Systems mitigate this by indexing alternatives, such as the several best transcripts or a lattice of competing words with their probabilities, so that a query can match a word that was not the top choice.

Phonetic search skips the words. It indexes the recognized phoneme sequence with overlapping phoneme n-grams, like the word n-grams of 

Phrases and Compounds, translates the query into phonemes with the pronunciation dictionary or a grapheme-to-phoneme model, and ranks passages by the n-grams they share with the query. This finds words that the vocabulary did not contain, and it tolerates partial errors. A query for “Basel” /b ɑː z ə l/ and a transcript that heard “basil” /b æ z ə l/ share one of three phoneme trigrams and two of four bigrams, while the two words share nothing.

Sound is a pressure wave that needs a medium. Its speed is about 343 m/s in air at 20 °C, 1,482 m/s in water, and higher in solids, and \lambda \cdot f = v gives wavelengths from 17.1 m at 20 Hz to 17.1 mm at 20 kHz.

Pitch, loudness, duration, timbre, sonic texture, and spatial location are perceptions with physical correlates, not measurements: the ear hears a missing fundamental, fills short gaps, and finds tones near 3 kHz louder than others of the same level.

The ear canal resonates near 3.4 kHz and boosts it by about 10 to 20 dB. The middle ear passes the sound from the air into the fluid of the cochlea, where a direct transition would transmit only about 0.1 percent of the energy.

The basilar membrane analyzes frequencies by place, high frequencies at the base and low ones at the apex. The Greenwood map grows with \log(1 + f / 146\,\text{Hz}), nearly linear at low and logarithmic at high frequencies, the same form as the mel scale with its knee at 700 Hz.

Outer hair cells amplify quiet sounds more than loud ones, inner hair cells transduce with a saturating response, and the nerve fibers adapt to constant sounds. Compression and adaptation are why audio features take logarithms of energies and why the onset strength counts only increases.

The primary auditory pathway runs from the cochlear nuclei through the superior olive, which compares the two ears, the inferior colliculus, and the thalamus to the tonotopic auditory cortex. Time differences of at most about 0.66 ms locate low frequencies, level differences caused by the head shadow locate high ones.

The entropy of energy splits a frame into sub-frames and computes the entropy of their normalized energies. It is close to \log_2 L for steady sounds and low for abrupt events.

A spectrum bin maps to its pitch class with ⌊ 9.5 + 12 \log_2(\omega(k)/440) ⌋ \text{ mod } 12, which rounds the note number, and to its octave with an offset of 4. A bin spacing \Delta f separates semitones only above about 16.8 \, \Delta f.

The harmonic sum estimates the fundamental as the candidate whose harmonics collect the largest weighted magnitude. Without weights, half the true fundamental collects the same peaks; the weights of Klapuri (2006) prevent this octave error.

Several simultaneous pitches follow by iteration: estimate the strongest fundamental, subtract its harmonics, and repeat. Shared partials are the difficulty.

The autocorrelation estimates the fundamental as f_s / m_0 for the lag m_0 with the highest correlation; its resolution is limited by integer lags.

The autocorrelation of the onset strength has peaks at the beat period and its multiples. A log-Gaussian tempo prior around 0.5 s (120 bpm) with a width of 1.4 octaves selects the period a listener would most likely tap. The tempogram computes the autocorrelation in a sliding window and shows tempo changes.

Ellis’s beat tracker maximizes the onset strength at the beats plus \alpha times a log-ratio penalty on the intervals, by dynamic programming in linear time. Too small an \alpha follows accents and off-beats; a larger one keeps the beats regular.

A classical recognizer chooses the word sequence that maximizes p(O ∣ W) \cdot P(W): an acoustic model trained on transcribed speech times a language model trained on text.

Each phoneme has a left-to-right HMM with three emitting states. Emissions were first discrete symbols from a k-means codebook, then Gaussian mixtures; triphones with decision-tree state tying model the influence of the neighbors.

A pronunciation dictionary and an n-gram language model connect the phoneme models into one large HMM, which Viterbi decoding with a beam searches. Training needs only transcripts, no time alignment, but the dictionary limits the vocabulary.

A self-loop gives a geometric duration whose most likely value is one frame. Several states per phoneme, explicit duration models, and training data at varied rates handle the speaking rate.

Cepstral mean normalization removes the constant effect of a microphone or a line, and vocal tract length normalization warps the frequency axis per speaker. Neither addresses the speaking rate.

Hybrid HMM-DNN systems replaced the Gaussian mixtures with networks whose state posteriors, divided by the state priors, act as likelihoods. CTC removed the alignment, and encoder-decoder transformers such as Whisper replaced the whole chain.

Spoken content becomes searchable through its transcript or through phoneme n-grams; the latter finds words outside the vocabulary and tolerates partial recognition errors.

Key Formula: Cochlear Frequency Map (Greenwood)f(x) = 165.4 \cdot \left(10^{2.1 x} - 0.88\right) \ \text{Hz}

The best frequency at the position x along the human basilar membrane, from x = 0 at the apex (20 Hz) to x = 1 at the base (20,677 Hz).

Key Formula: Entropy of EnergyH(t) = -\sum_{j=1}^{L} e_j \log_2 e_j, \qquad e_j = \frac{E_j}{\sum_{l=1}^{L} E_l}

The entropy of the normalized energies of L sub-frames is low for abrupt changes and close to \log_2 L for steady sounds.

Key Formula: Harmonic Sums(f_0) = \sum_{m=1}^{M} \frac{f_0 + 27}{m f_0 + 320} \cdot |X(m f_0)|, \qquad \hat{f}_0 = \arg\max_{f_0} s(f_0)

The weights decrease with the harmonic number m and prevent the estimate from jumping to half the true fundamental.

Key Formula: Beat Tracking Objective (Ellis)C(\{t_i\}) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} o(t_i) - \alpha \sum_{i=2}^{n} \left(\log \frac{t_i - t_{i-1}}{\tau_p}\right)^2

Strong onsets at the beats, intervals close to the period \tau_p, balanced by \alpha, maximized by dynamic programming.

Key Formula: Speech Recognition and State Duration\hat{W} = \arg\max_{W} \ p(O ∣ W) \cdot P(W), \qquad P(d) = a^{d-1} (1 - a)

Acoustic model times language model; a state with the self-loop probability a lasts d frames with a geometric distribution of mean 1 / (1 - a).

The chapters use a small set of mathematical tools again and again. 

Latent Semantic Indexing truncates a singular value decomposition and calls the result the best rank-k approximation. 

Approximate Nearest-Neighbor Search shrinks vectors with principal component analysis. 

From Sound to Spectrogram and 

Extended Image Features move signals and images into Fourier space and back. Decision trees, classifiers, and language models measure uncertainty with entropy and train with the cross-entropy. The chapters apply these tools and state their results. This chapter explains why the tools work and what exactly they optimize, without repeating how the chapters apply them.

The details matter when a tool is used outside its assumptions: when PCA runs on features with different units, when a convolution in Fourier space wraps around the border, when a spectrum shows frequencies that are not in the signal, or when a loss compares two distributions in the wrong direction.

Prerequisites

Eigenvectors, SVD, and PCA starts with the eigenvectors of symmetric matrices and the one inequality behind both the SVD and PCA, then shows why the truncated SVD minimizes the reconstruction error and why maximal variance and minimal reconstruction error are the same goal. 

Fourier Transform and Convolution treats the discrete Fourier transform as a change of basis, explains why the FFT is fast and why convolutions become products, and shows where leakage comes from and why the cosine transform of MFCC and JPEG approximates PCA. 

Information Theory defines entropy, cross-entropy, the Kullback-Leibler divergence, and mutual information, and shows why the cross-entropy is the standard loss.

Where this is used

Latent Semantic Indexing truncates the singular value decomposition of a term-document matrix and states that the result is the best rank-k approximation under the Frobenius norm; this section shows why, and what the statement leaves out. 

Word Embeddings projects embeddings onto two principal components for a plot, and 

Approximate Nearest-Neighbor Search shrinks vectors with principal component analysis before the search. 

Extended Image Features diagonalizes the matrix of the quadratic distance with its eigenvectors. 

Losses and Performance Measures measures dimensionality reduction by the reconstruction error, which PCA minimizes. 

Fourier Transform and Convolution shows that the cosine transform of MFCC and JPEG approximates PCA.

The SVD and PCA answer one question: which few directions describe a set of vectors best? Both answers rest on a single property of symmetric matrices. We first derive this property, then show what the SVD optimizes and why the truncated SVD is optimal, and finally show that PCA’s two goals, maximal variance and minimal reconstruction error, are the same goal.

A vector \mathbf{u} \neq \mathbf{0} is an eigenvector of a square matrix \mathbf{C} if the matrix only stretches it, \mathbf{C}\mathbf{u} = \lambda \mathbf{u}, with the eigenvalue \lambda as the stretch factor. For a symmetric matrix, \mathbf{C} = \mathbf{C}^\top, the spectral theorem guarantees real eigenvalues \lambda_1 \ge \lambda_2 \ge \dots \ge \lambda_d and an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors \mathbf{u}_1, \dots, \mathbf{u}_d. Collected as the columns of an orthogonal matrix \mathbf{U}:\mathbf{C} = \mathbf{U} \boldsymbol{\Lambda} \mathbf{U}^\top = \sum_{i=1}^{d} \lambda_i \mathbf{u}_i \mathbf{u}_i^\top

Applied to a vector, the decomposition reads from right to left: rotate the vector into the eigenvector axes, stretch each axis by its eigenvalue, and rotate back. The matrices that the chapters decompose are of this kind: covariance matrices, the co-occurrence matrices \mathbf{A}\mathbf{A}^\top and \mathbf{A}^\top\mathbf{A} of a term-document matrix, and the similarity matrix of the quadratic distance. The first two are also positive semidefinite, \mathbf{x}^\top \mathbf{C} \mathbf{x} \ge 0 for every \mathbf{x}, so their eigenvalues are nonnegative.

The property behind both the SVD and PCA concerns the quadratic form \mathbf{u}^\top \mathbf{C} \mathbf{u} of a unit vector \mathbf{u}. We write \mathbf{u} in the eigenvector basis, \mathbf{u} = \sum_i c_i \mathbf{u}_i with \sum_i c_i^2 = 1. Because the eigenvectors are orthonormal, the quadratic form becomes\mathbf{u}^\top \mathbf{C} \mathbf{u} = \sum_{i=1}^{d} \lambda_i c_i^2

This is a weighted average of the eigenvalues with the weights c_i^2. A weighted average cannot exceed its largest term, so the maximum is \lambda_1, reached when all weight lies on \mathbf{u}_1.

Key Formula: Rayleigh Quotient and Its Maximum\max_{\lVert \mathbf{u} \rVert = 1} \mathbf{u}^\top \mathbf{C} \mathbf{u} = \lambda_1, \qquad \max_{\mathbf{Q}^\top \mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{I}_k} \sum_{j=1}^{k} \mathbf{q}_j^\top \mathbf{C} \mathbf{q}_j = \lambda_1 + \dots + \lambda_k

For a symmetric \mathbf{C}, the first maximum is reached by the top eigenvector \mathbf{u}_1. The second, over k orthonormal directions \mathbf{q}_1, \dots, \mathbf{q}_k, is reached by the top k eigenvectors (Ky Fan’s theorem).

The second statement follows from the same argument. Each eigenvector \mathbf{u}_i receives a total weight of at most 1 from the k directions, and the total weight over all eigenvectors is k. The sum is therefore largest when the weight sits on the k largest eigenvalues, one unit each. The top k eigenvectors are the best k directions, and they are nested: the best direction is part of the best pair, which is part of the best triple.

A term-document matrix \mathbf{A} of size m \times n is neither square nor symmetric, but two symmetric matrices come with it. \mathbf{A}^\top\mathbf{A} of size n \times n holds the dot products between documents, and \mathbf{A}\mathbf{A}^\top of size m \times m holds the dot products between terms, a weighted count of how often two terms occur in the same documents. Both are positive semidefinite.

Let \mathbf{v}_i be the orthonormal eigenvectors of \mathbf{A}^\top\mathbf{A} with the eigenvalues \sigma_i^2, and define \mathbf{u}_i = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}_i / \sigma_i for every \sigma_i > 0. These vectors are orthonormal as well:\mathbf{u}_i^\top \mathbf{u}_j = \frac{\mathbf{v}_i^\top \mathbf{A}^\top \mathbf{A} \mathbf{v}_j}{\sigma_i \sigma_j} = \frac{\sigma_j^2 \, \mathbf{v}_i^\top \mathbf{v}_j}{\sigma_i \sigma_j} = \begin{cases} 1 & i = j \\ 0 & i \neq j \end{cases}

Rewriting \mathbf{A}\mathbf{v}_i = \sigma_i \mathbf{u}_i for all i at once gives \mathbf{A}\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{U}\mathbf{S}, and since \mathbf{V} is orthogonal, the singular value decomposition \mathbf{A} = \mathbf{U}\mathbf{S}\mathbf{V}^\top of 

Latent Semantic Indexing. The SVD exists for every matrix. The right singular vectors \mathbf{v}_i are the eigenvectors of \mathbf{A}^\top\mathbf{A}, the left singular vectors \mathbf{u}_i are the eigenvectors of \mathbf{A}\mathbf{A}^\top, and the singular values are the square roots of their common eigenvalues. The latent topics of LSI are therefore the eigenvectors of the term co-occurrence matrix: terms that occur in the same documents load on the same directions, which is why LSI places them close together.

Written as a sum, the SVD decomposes \mathbf{A} into rank-1 layers of decreasing weight:\mathbf{A} = \sum_{i=1}^{r} \sigma_i \mathbf{u}_i \mathbf{v}_i^\top, \qquad \lVert \mathbf{A} \rVert_F^2 = \sum_{j,l} a_{jl}^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{r} \sigma_i^2

The layers are orthogonal to each other, and each layer \mathbf{u}_i \mathbf{v}_i^\top has a Frobenius norm of 1, so the squared entries of \mathbf{A} add up to the sum of the squared singular values. The singular values say how much of the “energy” of the matrix each layer carries.

Latent Semantic Indexing keeps the first k layers, \mathbf{A}_k = \mathbf{U}_k \mathbf{S}_k \mathbf{V}_k^\top. The Eckart-Young theorem states that no matrix of rank k comes closer to \mathbf{A}.

Key Formula: Eckart-Young Theorem\min_{\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{B}) \le k} \lVert \mathbf{A} - \mathbf{B} \rVert_F^2 = \lVert \mathbf{A} - \mathbf{A}_k \rVert_F^2 = \sum_{i > k} \sigma_i^2

The truncated SVD minimizes the sum of the squared differences over all entries. The error is the energy of the discarded layers.

The proof needs two steps. First, a matrix \mathbf{B} of rank k has its columns in a k-dimensional subspace. For a fixed subspace with an orthonormal basis \mathbf{Q} of k columns, the closest \mathbf{B} projects every column of \mathbf{A} onto the subspace, \mathbf{B} = \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{Q}^\top\mathbf{A}, since the orthogonal projection is the closest point of a subspace. Second, the projection and the residual are orthogonal, so by Pythagoras\lVert \mathbf{A} - \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{Q}^\top\mathbf{A} \rVert_F^2 = \lVert \mathbf{A} \rVert_F^2 - \lVert \mathbf{Q}^\top \mathbf{A} \rVert_F^2 = \lVert \mathbf{A} \rVert_F^2 - \sum_{j=1}^{k} \mathbf{q}_j^\top \mathbf{A}\mathbf{A}^\top \mathbf{q}_j

\lVert \mathbf{A} \rVert_F^2 is fixed, so minimizing the error means maximizing the energy that the subspace captures. By the Rayleigh argument applied to \mathbf{A}\mathbf{A}^\top, this energy is at most \sigma_1^2 + \dots + \sigma_k^2, reached by the top k left singular vectors. The error is then \sum_{i > k} \sigma_i^2. The same matrix \mathbf{A}_k is also optimal in the spectral norm, the largest stretch of \mathbf{A} - \mathbf{B}, with the error \sigma_{k+1}.

Example: A small term-document matrix

Five terms (car, auto, engine, flower, garden) and four documents: d_1 contains car and engine, d_2 auto and engine, d_3 car, auto, engine, and flower, and d_4 flower and garden, each once. The matrix has \lVert \mathbf{A} \rVert_F^2 = 10 and the singular values 2.550, 1.461, 1.000, and 0.600, whose squares add up to 10. The rank-1 approximation keeps 2.550^2 / 10 = 65 percent of the energy and has the error \sqrt{1.461^2 + 1^2 + 0.6^2} = 1.870; the rank-2 approximation keeps 86 percent and has the error 1.166.

Other rank-1 approximations do worse. Projecting all documents onto the direction of a single document vector, the best choice d_3 gives the error 1.937, the others 2.345 and more. In the rank-2 space, the rows of \mathbf{U}_2 \mathbf{S}_2 for car and auto become identical (a cosine of 1.000, against 0.500 in \mathbf{A}), because d_1 and d_2 differ only in car versus auto, and the two leading dimensions do not distinguish them.

The theorem also says what the truncated SVD does not optimize. It minimizes the squared error over all entries, each entry weighted equally. Large entries dominate the error, so frequent terms and long documents shape the leading dimensions unless TF-IDF weighting and normalization tame them first. The objective knows nothing about queries or relevance: LSI finds the directions that reconstruct the matrix best, and the improvement in retrieval is a consequence that experiments confirm, not a guarantee.

The folding-in formula of 

Latent Semantic Indexing follows from the decomposition. Multiplying \mathbf{A} = \mathbf{U}\mathbf{S}\mathbf{V}^\top from the left with \mathbf{U}_k^\top and \mathbf{S}_k^{-1} gives \mathbf{V}_k^\top = \mathbf{S}_k^{-1} \mathbf{U}_k^\top \mathbf{A}, so every document \mathbf{d} of the collection maps to its row of \mathbf{V}_k by \mathbf{d}^\top \mathbf{U}_k \mathbf{S}_k^{-1}. A new document or a query receives the same map. It is placed where it would lie if it had been part of the collection, provided that it does not change the directions \mathbf{U}_k.

PCA asks the same question for a cloud of n points in d dimensions. We collect the points as the rows of a matrix and subtract their mean, so that the rows \mathbf{x}_i of \mathbf{X} are centered. The covariance matrix \mathbf{C} = \mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X} / (n - 1) is symmetric and positive semidefinite. The variance of the points along a unit direction \mathbf{u} is the mean squared length of their projections:\frac{1}{n - 1} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (\mathbf{u}^\top \mathbf{x}_i)^2 = \mathbf{u}^\top \mathbf{C} \mathbf{u}

By the Rayleigh argument, the direction of maximal variance is the top eigenvector of \mathbf{C}, the first principal component, and its variance is \lambda_1. The next components are the next eigenvectors, each orthogonal to the previous ones and each of maximal remaining variance.

The second view of PCA asks for the direction whose projections reconstruct the points best. Each point splits into its projection onto \mathbf{u} and a residual perpendicular to it, and by Pythagoras\lVert \mathbf{x}_i \rVert^2 = (\mathbf{u}^\top \mathbf{x}_i)^2 + \lVert \mathbf{x}_i - (\mathbf{u}^\top \mathbf{x}_i)\, \mathbf{u} \rVert^2

Summed over all points, the left side is the total squared distance from the mean, which does not depend on \mathbf{u}.

Key Formula: Variance and Reconstruction Error\underbrace{\sum_{i} \lVert \mathbf{x}_i \rVert^2}_{\text{total, fixed}} = \underbrace{\sum_{i} (\mathbf{u}^\top \mathbf{x}_i)^2}_{\text{captured variance} \,\times\, (n - 1)} + \underbrace{\sum_{i} \lVert \mathbf{x}_i - (\mathbf{u}^\top \mathbf{x}_i)\, \mathbf{u} \rVert^2}_{\text{reconstruction error}}

With a fixed total, maximizing the captured variance and minimizing the reconstruction error are the same goal. For k components, the error is (n - 1)(\lambda_{k+1} + \dots + \lambda_d).

Example: Five points in the plane

The points (2, 1), (3, 3), (4, 3), (5, 5), and (6, 3) have the mean (4, 3) and the covariance matrix with the entries 2.5 and 2 on the diagonal and 1.5 off it. Its eigenvalues are \lambda_1 = 3.771 and \lambda_2 = 0.729, and the first principal component points at 40.3°. The total squared distance from the mean is 4 \cdot (3.771 + 0.729) = 18. The table splits it for several directions:
