With a fixed-size sub-word vocabulary, we can map each token to a one-hot vector of manageable size (30k-50k dimensions). But one-hot vectors are still sparse and high-dimensional. The next step is to learn a dense, lower-dimensional representation, exactly as Word2Vec does.

An embedding layer is a weight matrix \mathbf{E} \in \mathbb{R}^{|\mathbb{T}| \times d} where row j is the d-dimensional embedding for token j. Multiplying a one-hot vector by \mathbf{E} simply selects the corresponding row, which is a fast lookup operation. The embedding dimensionality d (typically 768 for BERT-Base) is independent of the vocabulary size.

The key difference from Word2Vec: these embeddings are not trained separately. They are initialized randomly and refined during the training of the full model. The embedding layer is the first component of the transformer architecture; its weights are updated by the same gradient descent that trains the attention layers, so the embeddings co-adapt with the rest of the model.

This solves the variable-vocabulary problem: the embedding matrix is the only component whose size depends on |\mathbb{T}|. Everything downstream operates in d dimensions regardless of vocabulary size.

The remaining challenge is context. Word embeddings are context-free. To understand “bank” in “The bank approved the loan”, the model needs to attend to “approved” and “loan”. Earlier neural approaches tried to solve this:

Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) process tokens one at a time, carrying an internal hidden state that accumulates context from previous tokens. After reading “The”, the state captures some information about the first word. After “The bank”, it captures both. By the end of the sentence, the hidden state theoretically encodes the full context. LSTMs and GRUs improved on vanilla RNNs by better preserving long-range information.

RNNs had two critical limitations. First, they are inherently sequential: token i cannot be processed until token i-1 is finished. This prevents parallelization and makes training on long sequences very slow. Second, despite LSTM improvements, the hidden state still degrades over long distances. In a 500-word document, information from the first sentence is heavily diluted by the time the model reaches the last sentence.

The 2017 paper “Attention Is All You Need” (Vaswani et al.) introduced the transformer, arguably the most consequential architecture in modern AI. Every large language model (GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama), every modern embedding model (SBERT, GTE, Nomic), and every state-of-the-art retrieval system is built on transformers. The core innovation is self-attention: instead of processing tokens sequentially, every token directly attends to every other token in parallel.

Self-attention solves both RNN limitations at once. It processes all positions in parallel (enabling GPU acceleration over long sequences), and every token can directly access every other token regardless of distance (no information degradation over long sequences). The model itself learns which tokens are relevant to which other tokens, rather than relying on a fixed context window or a sequential accumulation of state.

Concretely, self-attention transforms each token embedding \mathbf{x}_i \in \mathbb{R}^d into a new, context-aware representation \mathbf{z}_i \in \mathbb{R}^d. The output has the same dimensionality as the input, but now “bank” at position 2 will have a different \mathbf{z}_2 depending on whether the surrounding words are about finance or rivers.

How self-attention works: Q/K/V mechanism (optional reading)

Self-attention computes context-aware representations through three steps: project, score, and aggregate.

1. Project each token embedding \mathbf{x}_i \in \mathbb{R}^d into three vectors using learned linear mappings \mathbf{W}_Q \in \mathbb{R}^{d_k \times d}, \mathbf{W}_K \in \mathbb{R}^{d_k \times d}, \mathbf{W}_V \in \mathbb{R}^{d_v \times d}:\mathbf{q}_i = \mathbf{W}_Q \mathbf{x}_i \in \mathbb{R}^{d_k}, \quad \mathbf{k}_i = \mathbf{W}_K \mathbf{x}_i \in \mathbb{R}^{d_k}, \quad \mathbf{v}_i = \mathbf{W}_V \mathbf{x}_i \in \mathbb{R}^{d_v}

The query \mathbf{q}_i is used to compare (via dot product) against the keys \mathbf{k}_j of all other tokens: a high dot product \mathbf{q}_i^\top \mathbf{k}_j means token j is relevant to token i. The value \mathbf{v}_j is the contribution that token j makes to the new representation of token i when the attention weight is high. Queries and keys must share the same dimensionality d_k (so the dot product is defined). In practice, d_k = d_v = d / h where h is the number of attention heads. For BERT-Base: d = 768, h = 12, so each head operates in d_k = 64 dimensions.

2. Compute attention weights for token i over all positions j. The raw compatibility between query i and key j is their scaled dot product \mathbf{q}_i^\top \mathbf{k}_j / \sqrt{d_k}. To convert these into a probability distribution, we apply the softmax function, which exponentiates each score and normalizes by the sum:\alpha_{ij} = \text{softmax}_j\!\left(\frac{\mathbf{q}_i^\top \mathbf{k}_j}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) = \frac{\exp\!\left(\mathbf{q}_i^\top \mathbf{k}_j / \sqrt{d_k}\right)}{\sum_{l=1}^{n} \exp\!\left(\mathbf{q}_i^\top \mathbf{k}_l / \sqrt{d_k}\right)}

The exponential ensures all weights are positive, and dividing by the sum ensures \sum_j \alpha_{ij} = 1. A high \alpha_{ij} means token i attends strongly to token j.

3. Aggregate by attention pooling: each token j contributes its value \mathbf{v}_j proportionally to its attention weight, producing the context-aware representation:\mathbf{z}_i = \sum_{j=1}^{n} \alpha_{ij} \mathbf{v}_j

Matrix form. All three steps can be computed in one expression using matrices \mathbf{Q}, \mathbf{K}, \mathbf{V} (whose rows are the individual query, key, and value vectors):\text{Attention}(\mathbf{Q}, \mathbf{K}, \mathbf{V}) = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K}^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) \mathbf{V}

Here \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K}^\top is an n \times n matrix of all pairwise dot products. The softmax is applied to each row independently (normalizing across columns). Multiplying by \mathbf{V} computes all weighted sums in parallel. The division by \sqrt{d_k} prevents dot products from growing too large with increasing dimension, which would push the softmax into near-zero gradients and slow training.

Figure 1 illustrates this process for computing \mathbf{z}_2 (“bank”) in “The bank approved the loan”. The query for “bank” is compared against all keys; “approved” and “loan” receive the highest attention weights because their keys are most compatible with “bank” in a financial context.



Figure 1:Self-attention computing z₂ for “bank”. The query q₂ is compared against all keys to produce attention weights. “Approved” (0.52) and “loan” (0.36) dominate, so z₂ is primarily a blend of their values, making “bank” context-aware as a financial institution.

Multi-head attention runs h parallel attention operations with different projection matrices, allowing the model to attend to different types of relationships simultaneously. The outputs are concatenated and projected back to d dimensions:\text{MultiHead}(\mathbf{Q}, \mathbf{K}, \mathbf{V}) = \text{Concat}(\text{head}_1, \ldots, \text{head}_h) \mathbf{W}_O

Each head operates in d/h dimensions; concatenating h heads recovers the full d-dimensional output. 

Figure 2 shows how multi-head attention works within one layer: h parallel heads each run self-attention in d/h dimensions with independent projections, then their outputs are concatenated and projected back to d dimensions.



Figure 2:Multi-head attention: h parallel heads each run self-attention in d/h dimensions with independent projections. Concatenating all heads recovers the full d-dimensional output.

Self-attention is permutation-invariant: the formula \mathbf{z}_i = \sum_j \alpha_{ij} \mathbf{v}_j depends on token content but not on position. “Dog bites man” and “man bites dog” would produce identical representations without additional information. To preserve sequence order, a positional encoding \mathbf{p}_i \in \mathbb{R}^d is added to each token embedding before the first attention layer:\mathbf{x}_i = \mathbf{E}[\text{token}_i] + \mathbf{p}_i

The original transformer uses fixed sinusoidal functions at different frequencies for each dimension. BERT uses learned position vectors (one per position up to 512). Both approaches add position information without increasing the embedding dimensionality.

A single self-attention layer produces one round of contextualization, but it has a fundamental limitation: the aggregation \mathbf{z}_i = \sum_j \alpha_{ij} \mathbf{v}_j is a weighted sum, linear in the value vectors. While the attention weights themselves are non-linear (due to softmax), stacking multiple attention layers alone would still produce representations that are largely linear combinations of the inputs. To model complex, non-linear relationships between tokens, two additional components are needed.

The feed-forward network (FFN) applies a non-linear transformation to each token independently: \text{FFN}(\mathbf{z}) = \text{ReLU}(\mathbf{z}\mathbf{W}_1 + \mathbf{b}_1)\mathbf{W}_2 + \mathbf{b}_2. The ReLU (or GELU in newer models) is where the non-linearity enters the transformer. Without it, the model could not learn complex token interactions regardless of depth.

Residual connections add the input of each sub-layer directly to its output (\mathbf{x} + \text{SubLayer}(\mathbf{x})), creating shortcut paths through the network. During backpropagation, gradients flow through these shortcuts without passing through the attention or FFN computations, which prevents vanishing gradients and allows transformers to be stacked 12 to 96 layers deep (this idea originates from ResNets in computer vision). Layer normalization normalizes the activations at each layer, stabilizing training and reducing sensitivity to weight initialization.

Together, one transformer layer consists of: multi-head self-attention → Add & Norm → feed-forward network → Add & Norm. 

Figure 3 shows the full architecture with these components stacked into an encoder and a decoder.

The left side is the encoder: it processes the full input sequence bidirectionally (each token attends to all others) and produces contextualized representations. The right side is the decoder: it generates output tokens one at a time, using masked self-attention (each token can only attend to previous positions) plus cross-attention to the encoder output. For embedding and retrieval, we use only the encoder side.



Figure 3:The transformer architecture (Vaswani et al., 2017). Left: the encoder processes input bidirectionally through stacked layers of multi-head self-attention and feed-forward networks. Right: the decoder generates output auto-regressively with masked attention. For text embeddings, only the encoder is used.

BERT (Devlin et al., 2019) applies the transformer encoder to produce contextualized token representations. Unlike GPT, which processes text left-to-right (suitable for generation), BERT attends to context from both directions simultaneously, making it better suited for understanding and representation tasks.

BERT uses WordPiece tokenization, learned positional encodings, and adds one BERT-specific element: segment encodings that mark whether a token belongs to sentence A or sentence B when processing sentence pairs. Two special tokens frame the input: [CLS] at the start (whose final hidden state serves as a sequence-level representation) and [SEP] separating segments. The maximum sequence length is 512 tokens; shorter sequences are padded, longer ones truncated.

Figure 4 shows the complete input construction for an example sentence. The three embeddings (token, position, segment) are summed element-wise to form the input to the first encoder layer. BERT-Base stacks 12 encoder layers with 12 attention heads per layer; BERT-Large uses 24 layers with 16 heads.



Figure 4:BERT input construction for “the cat that chased the mouse was black”. Token embeddings, positional encodings, and segment encodings are summed to produce the encoder input. After 12/24 layers, each token has a contextualized output vector. Option 1: use the [CLS] encoding as the sequence embedding. Option 2: pool over all non-masked token encodings.

BERT is pre-trained on two self-supervised tasks:

Masked Language Modeling (MLM): randomly mask 15% of input tokens and predict them from context.

Next Sentence Prediction (NSP): given two sentences, predict whether the second follows the first in the original text.

After pre-training on large corpora (Wikipedia + BookCorpus), BERT’s encoder produces 768-dimensional (Base) or 1024-dimensional (Large) contextualized vectors for each token. The same word receives different representations depending on its surrounding context.

What carries over from the previous section

Contextual embeddings: transformers such as BERT produce context-dependent token vectors, so the same word gets a different vector depending on its surrounding words. This is why static word embeddings are not enough for semantic search.

One vector per passage: a transformer yields a sequence-level embedding via the [CLS] token or by pooling over the token outputs. That single vector is the input to the retrieval architectures in this section.

Sub-word tokenization: text is split into sub-word units from a fixed-size vocabulary (BPE, WordPiece, or SentencePiece), which handles out-of-vocabulary words and many languages.

For the full background, see 

Transformer Embeddings.

Those contextual token representations are the starting point here. Turning them into a single comparable vector for retrieval, and comparing two passages accurately, is a separate problem. This section covers the three architectures that solve it: bi-encoders, cross-encoders, and late interaction models.

BERT produces rich contextualized token representations, but these are internal states optimized for the pre-training objectives (predicting masked tokens and sentence adjacency), not for representing the overall meaning of a passage. The [CLS] token’s hidden state encodes whatever information the Next Sentence Prediction task required, which is not the same as a general semantic summary. Using it directly as a sentence embedding for retrieval produces results worse than simple Word2Vec averaging. Mean pooling over all token outputs is marginally better but still underperforms static embeddings on semantic similarity benchmarks. Extracting useful sentence-level representations from BERT required a different training approach: Sentence-BERT.

Sentence-BERT (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019) restructures BERT into a bi-encoder (also called dual-encoder or siamese network): two sentences are encoded independently by the same transformer, then compared via dot product (equivalent to cosine similarity because the embeddings are normalized to unit length). 

Figure 1 contrasts this with the simpler approaches discussed earlier in this chapter.



Figure 1:Four architectures for sentence similarity, progressing from simple to powerful: (1) pooling static word embeddings, (2) pooling BERT token outputs, (3) bi-encoder with independently encoded sentences compared via learned similarity, (4) cross-encoder that jointly processes both sentences for maximum accuracy.

Which similarity measure for learned sentence embeddings

For static word embeddings the frequency argument settles the question in favor of cosine. For learned sentence embeddings the rule is different: match the measure the model was trained with. Some models are trained with a normalized cosine objective, so their output is unit length and cosine equals dot product. Others are trained for dot-product retrieval, where the vector norm carries meaning and normalizing it away would discard signal. The model card states which objective the model was trained with, and this is the case where “use the measure the model was trained with” is the correct rule.

The bi-encoder produces fixed-size sentence embeddings:

Pass a sentence through BERT (or any transformer encoder).

Apply mean pooling over the non-masked token outputs to produce a single d-dimensional vector.

Normalize the vector to unit length.

Training uses similarity-based losses on labeled sentence pairs:

Contrastive loss: pulls similar pairs close, pushes dissimilar pairs apart with a margin.

Triplet loss: given an anchor, a positive, and a negative, ensures \text{sim}(a, p) > \text{sim}(a, n) + \epsilon.

Multiple negatives ranking loss (MNRL): treats all other examples in the batch as negatives, maximizing efficiency of each training step.

Hard negative mining (selecting negatives that are challenging but incorrect) is critical for training high-quality bi-encoders.

The bi-encoder’s key advantage for retrieval: documents are encoded once during indexing. At query time, only the query needs encoding. Comparison is a dot product (equivalent to cosine similarity for normalized vectors), enabling sub-millisecond ranking over millions of pre-computed embeddings.

Since SBERT, the field has advanced significantly:

Instruction-tuned embeddings: models like E5-Mistral, GTE-Qwen2, and Nomic Embed accept a task instruction prefix (e.g., “Represent this document for retrieval:”) that adapts the embedding to the downstream task without retraining.

Decoder-based encoders: Qwen3-Embedding and similar models build on decoder transformers (using the final [EOS] token representation instead of [CLS]), achieving state-of-the-art quality at the cost of larger models (0.6B to 8B parameters).

Extended context: modern embedding models support 8k-32k token inputs, enabling direct encoding of longer passages without chunking. However, longer context does not come for free: compressing 30k tokens into a single d-dimensional vector loses more information than compressing 512 tokens into the same space. Research on long-context LLMs shows that attention disproportionately favors tokens near the beginning and end of the sequence, losing information from the middle. In practice, chunking a long document into shorter passages and retrieving at chunk level often outperforms encoding the full document as one vector. We return to this tradeoff in the next section.

A cross-encoder processes the query and document together as a single input sequence, separated by [SEP]:[CLS] query [SEP] document [SEP]

The [CLS] token’s final hidden state passes through a classification layer to produce a relevance score between 0 and 1. Because all tokens from both query and document attend to each other through every transformer layer, the cross-encoder captures fine-grained token-level interactions that bi-encoders miss.

Cross-encoders are too expensive for exhaustive search over large collections. The standard deployment pattern is:

Retrieve: a bi-encoder (or BM25) selects the top-k candidates (typically k = 100\text{-}1000).

Rerank: a cross-encoder scores each candidate with full token interaction and reorders the list.

This hybrid approach achieves near cross-encoder quality at near bi-encoder speed. The 

hands-on notebook for this section measures this tradeoff directly: it scores the same challenging sentence pairs with both a bi-encoder and a cross-encoder and compares the wall-clock cost of each.
ColBERT (Khattab and Zaharia, 2020) occupies the middle ground between bi-encoders and cross-encoders by computing interaction at the token level while still allowing document pre-computation.

Unlike bi-encoders (which compress each text into a single vector) or cross-encoders (which process both texts jointly), ColBERT (

Figure 2):

Encodes query and document independently through a transformer, retaining all token-level embeddings (not pooling to a single vector).

Interacts via late interaction: each query token computes maximum similarity against all document tokens.

Scores by summing these maximum similarities across query tokens:

Key Formula: ColBERT MaxSim Scoring\text{score}(q, d) = \sum_{i=1}^{|q|} \max_{j=1}^{|d|} \mathbf{q}_i^\top \mathbf{d}_j

Each query token finds its best-matching document token (MaxSim), and the total score sums these per-token matches. This captures fine-grained term-level alignment without requiring joint encoding.



Figure 2:ColBERT architecture: query and document are encoded independently (allowing document pre-computation), but scoring uses token-level MaxSim interaction rather than a single-vector dot product.

As with SBERT, raw BERT token outputs are not directly useful for MaxSim comparison. ColBERT uses a shared BERT encoder for both queries and documents, followed by a small linear projection that reduces each token embedding from 768 to 128 dimensions (reducing storage and comparison cost). The full system is trained end-to-end on triples of (query, relevant document, irrelevant document) with a ranking loss that maximizes the MaxSim score for the relevant document and minimizes it for the irrelevant one. Because the MaxSim scoring function is differentiable, gradients flow through it back into the encoder, teaching the model to produce token embeddings where semantically matching query-document token pairs have high dot products.

At first glance, ColBERT’s per-token matching looks similar to comparing word embeddings. The critical difference is that each token vector is a BERT output, not a static word embedding. Each \mathbf{q}_i and \mathbf{d}_j has been contextualized by self-attention over the entire query or document. The token “bank” in the document already encodes whether it means a financial institution or a riverbank, based on its surrounding context. When a query token matches a document token via dot product, it is comparing two context-aware representations, not two static word vectors.

This means the MaxSim operation captures phenomena that neither static word embeddings nor single-vector bi-encoders can:

Context-sensitive matching: a query token “treatment” will match strongly with “treatment” in a medical document but weakly with “treatment” in a document about surface treatment of metals, because the BERT outputs differ despite the word being the same.

Semantic matching: a query token “automobile” will have high similarity with the document token “car” because the ranking loss during training explicitly pushed embeddings of semantically related tokens closer together.

Partial matching: not every query token needs to match strongly; the sum allows documents to score well by matching the most important query aspects.

Unlike bi-encoders, ColBERT does not suffer from the compression problem discussed earlier. Each token retains its own vector, so no information is lost by squeezing an entire passage into a single representation. This is why ColBERT can use much lower-dimensional embeddings (128 dimensions per token, projected down from BERT’s 768) than bi-encoders (which typically need 768-4096 dimensions per passage): representing one contextualized token requires far fewer dimensions than representing an entire document.

The tradeoff is storage and search cost. A 500-token document produces 500 vectors instead of one. Searching requires computing |q| \times 500 dot products per document instead of a single one. Chunking remains useful not for avoiding information compression, but for limiting the number of vectors per unit and keeping semantically related tokens together for more focused matching. ColBERT v2 (Santhanam et al., 2022) addresses the storage cost of retaining per-token embeddings for every document through residual compression: token embeddings are quantized by storing only the residual from the nearest centroid, reducing storage by 6-10x while maintaining quality.

The previous sections traced a progression from BM25 through LSI and word embeddings to transformer-based models. At each step, we reduced the independence assumption between tokens, gaining recall: documents that share no surface terms with the query can now be retrieved through semantic similarity. But this gain comes at three costs that classical retrieval did not face:

Search is expensive. Dense vectors cannot use inverted indices. Comparing a query against one million document embeddings requires one million dot products. We examine vector search acceleration in the next chapter, but no method matches the pruning efficiency of inverted files for sparse vectors.

Precision drops. Casting a wider semantic net retrieves more relevant documents, but also more noise. A query for “training large language models” will match papers about “optimizing neural networks” (relevant) and “training dogs with reinforcement signals” (not relevant). Cross-encoders (see 

Semantic Similarity with Transformers) address this through reranking, but at the cost of a full transformer forward pass per candidate.

Compression loses information. Encoding a multi-page document into a single 768-dimensional vector discards detail. Chunking the document into shorter passages mitigates this, but multiplies the number of vectors to store and search.

Every design decision in a semantic search pipeline is a tradeoff among three dimensions: compute cost (encoding, storage, infrastructure), latency (how fast results arrive), and retrieval quality (precision and recall for the use case). There is no single optimal pipeline. A factual search engine serving millions of short queries per second operates in a different region of this space than a patent lawyer who needs exhaustive recall and is willing to wait for a thorough assessment.

This section shows how to navigate these tradeoffs through pipeline design, model selection, and efficiency techniques.

Before designing a pipeline, we need to choose the embedding model that will produce the dense vectors. The 

Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB) provides a standardized evaluation framework comparing embedding models across retrieval, semantic textual similarity, classification, and clustering tasks. Retrieval-specific metrics (nDCG@10) are most relevant for search.

The 

chapter introduction presented the retriever-ranker blueprint and five pipeline variants (A through E). Here we examine why each exists and when it fails, following the natural progression as requirements grow.

Pipeline A (BM25 only) is the baseline from classical retrieval: an inverted index with BM25 scoring, no semantic component. It is fast, well-understood, and sufficient when queries and documents share vocabulary. The subsequent pipelines add semantic components to address its limitations.

The simplest semantic search system adds a cross-encoder reranker on top of existing BM25 infrastructure (

Figure 1). BM25 retrieves the top-k candidates (typically k = 100\text{-}1000), and the cross-encoder reorders them by semantic relevance.

This works well when BM25 recall is sufficient: if the relevant documents contain at least some of the query terms, BM25 will find them, and the cross-encoder improves the ordering. It fails when the vocabulary mismatch is severe. A search for “efficient training of large language models” will miss a paper titled “Scaling Laws for Neural Network Optimization” because BM25 cannot connect these terms.

To overcome the recall ceiling of BM25, we replace it with a bi-encoder that retrieves candidates from a vector index (

Figure 2). The “Scaling Laws” paper is now retrieved because its embedding is semantically close to the query.

Dense retrieval finds documents that BM25 misses, but it has the opposite weakness: exact-match queries fail. A search for error code “NullReferenceException” or product ID “A1B2C3” depends on exact string matching; the bi-encoder may return semantically similar but wrong results.



Figure 2:Pipeline C: a bi-encoder retrieves candidates from a vector index by semantic similarity, with an optional cross-encoder for reranking.

The most robust approach runs both retrievers in parallel and fuses the results (

Figure 3):

BM25 retrieves top-k_1 candidates (handles exact matches, rare terms, proper nouns).

Dense retrieval retrieves top-k_2 candidates (handles semantic matches, paraphrases).

Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) merges both result lists.

A cross-encoder reranks the merged top-k for final ordering.

RRF assigns each document a fused score based on its rank in each result list:\text{RRF}(d) = \sum_{r \in R} \frac{1}{k + \text{rank}_r(d)}

where R is the set of result lists and k is a constant (typically 60) that dampens the influence of high ranks. Documents appearing in both lists receive contributions from both, naturally boosting results that both methods agree on.



Figure 3:Pipeline D: BM25 and dense retrieval run in parallel on the same query. Their candidate lists are fused, then a cross-encoder reranks the merged results.

All three pipelines require splitting long documents into shorter passages. The optimal chunk size differs by component:

BM25 tolerates large chunks (full sections, even full documents). It scores individual terms within the chunk; surrounding irrelevant text does not affect the score of matching terms. Traditional retrieval systems typically chunk at the page or section level.

Bi-encoders need shorter chunks (256-1024 tokens). The entire chunk is compressed into a single vector, so irrelevant content dilutes the embedding. Paragraph-level or sliding-window chunking with overlap produces the best results.

Cross-encoders can handle longer inputs (up to their context window) because they read query and document jointly with full token interaction. They are typically applied to the chunks retrieved by the earlier stages.

In hybrid systems, a common approach is to chunk at a granularity that works for the bi-encoder (the most sensitive component) and use the same chunks for BM25. The result metadata links chunks back to their source documents so that the final output can present either chunk-level or document-level results. We discuss chunking strategies (fixed-size, recursive, semantic, hierarchical) in detail in the RAG chapter, where the interaction between chunk design and generation quality adds further constraints.

records.content: As collections grow from thousands to millions of documents, the cost of encoding, storing, and searching becomes the dominant concern. Pipeline E addresses this with multi-stage retrieval: a cheap first stage scans the full collection for fast filtering, then a precise full-precision second stage reranks the surviving candidates. The two subsections below are variants of this pipeline. They differ only in how the cheap first stage is built: Matryoshka embeddings truncate the vector to a low dimension, while binary or scalar quantization compress each dimension into fewer bits.

Traditional embeddings use a fixed number of dimensions. Matryoshka embeddings (Kusupati et al., 2022) train the model so that truncated prefixes of the embedding remain useful: the first 64 dimensions capture coarse semantics, the first 128 add detail, and the full vector provides maximum precision. The training objective adds loss terms at multiple truncation levels:\mathcal{L}_{\text{MRL}} = \sum_{d \in \mathcal{D}} \mathcal{L}_d(\mathbf{x}_{[:d]}, \mathbf{y}_{[:d]})

where \mathcal{D} is a set of target dimensions (e.g., {64, 128, 256, 512, 1024}) and \mathbf{x}_{[:d]} denotes the first d components of the embedding.

This gives the first variant of Pipeline E, built entirely within a single model (

Figure 4). The truncated prefix serves as the cheap first stage:

Use truncated embeddings (e.g., 128 dimensions) for fast coarse retrieval over the full collection.

Use full embeddings (e.g., 1024 dimensions) to rerank the top candidates with higher precision.

A cross-encoder can still be appended as a final stage, but the two embedding stages already share one model, so no additional index or encoder is needed.



Figure 4:Multi-stage retrieval with Matryoshka embeddings: fast initial retrieval using small (truncated) embeddings narrows candidates, then full-dimension embeddings rerank with higher precision. A single model serves both stages.

The second variant of Pipeline E builds the cheap first stage through quantization rather than truncation. A compressed (quantized) index handles the fast filtering over the full collection, then the surviving candidates are rescored with the full-precision embeddings. Storage and comparison costs can be further reduced through quantization:

Binary quantization: replace each float dimension with a single bit (positive to 1, negative to 0). Reduces storage by 32x and enables fast Hamming distance computation. Quality loss is typically 5-10% on retrieval benchmarks.

Scalar quantization (int8): map each float to an 8-bit integer. Reduces storage by 4x with minimal quality loss (typically less than 2%).

Quantization is most effective as a first-stage filter: use quantized embeddings for coarse candidate retrieval, then rescore with full-precision embeddings.
There is no single best pipeline. The right design depends on where your application sits in the cost-latency-quality space. The following recommendations serve as starting points, not prescriptions.

The field has converged on hybrid pipelines: BM25 for exact match and fast candidate retrieval, bi-encoders for semantic recall, and cross-encoders for precision-critical reranking. ColBERT offers a middle path when single-vector bi-encoders lack sufficient quality but cross-encoder latency is unacceptable. 

Building Semantic Search organizes these components into five reference pipelines (A through E), from a pure BM25 baseline to multi-stage retrieval that pairs a cheap first stage with a precise rerank.

The vocabulary mismatch problem is the fundamental motivation for semantic search: related terms that share no surface forms cannot be matched by keyword methods alone.

Dimensionality reduction discovers latent structure: whether via SVD (LSI) or neural training (embeddings), mapping text to a compact space forces the model to group co-occurring patterns into latent topics or semantic directions.

Word embeddings learn meaning from context: the distributional hypothesis drives Word2Vec (Skip-Gram, CBOW) and GloVe, while fastText adds sub-word composition for morphology and out-of-vocabulary words. Transformer-era sub-word tokenizers (BPE, WordPiece, SentencePiece) extend the same idea with a fixed-size vocabulary; their internals are optional background.

Static embeddings cannot handle polysemy, and pooling is not enough: one vector per word gives “bank” a single representation regardless of context, and averaging or max-pooling word vectors into a passage vector dilutes long documents and discards word order. This is the bridge problem that motivates contextual encoders.

Context transforms meaning: transformer encoders produce a different vector for the same word depending on its neighbours, solving the multiple-meanings problem that static embeddings cannot. The internal mechanism (self-attention) is optional background; what carries forward to retrieval is the contextual token vectors and the single passage vector obtained by pooling them or reading the [CLS] token.

Bi-encoders enable scalable retrieval: encoding documents once and comparing via dot product achieves sub-millisecond search over millions of documents. Choose the similarity measure deliberately: cosine for static word embeddings (the vector norm tracks frequency and polysemy), and the measure the model was trained with for learned sentence embeddings (cosine when the output is normalized, dot product when the norm carries signal).

Cross-encoders provide precision: joint encoding of query and document captures fine-grained token interactions, producing the highest quality relevance scores at the cost of a full transformer pass per candidate.

Late interaction (ColBERT) preserves token-level detail while keeping documents pre-computable. Each token retains its own 128-dimensional vector, avoiding the compression problem of single-vector bi-encoders.

Hybrid retrieval is robust: combining BM25 (exact match, rare terms) with dense retrieval (semantic matching) via Reciprocal Rank Fusion covers failure modes of either method alone.

Every pipeline is a tradeoff among compute cost, latency, and retrieval quality. The five reference pipelines (A through E) span this space, from a pure BM25 baseline (A) to multi-stage retrieval (E) that pairs a cheap first stage (Matryoshka truncation or quantization) with a precise full-precision rerank. There is no single best pipeline; collection size and use case decide.

Key Formula: LSI Projection\bar{\mathbf{d}}^\top = \mathbf{d}^\top \mathbf{U}_k \mathbf{S}_k^{-1}

Maps a term-frequency vector into the k-dimensional latent topic space.

Key Formula: Skip-Gram ProbabilityP(w_s ∣ w_c) = \frac{\exp(\mathbf{u}_s^\top \mathbf{v}_c)}{\sum_{i \in \mathbb{T}} \exp(\mathbf{u}_i^\top \mathbf{v}_c)}

Probability of context word w_s given center word w_c, parameterized by embedding vectors.

Key Formula: ColBERT MaxSim Scoring\text{score}(q, d) = \sum_{i=1}^{|q|} \max_{j=1}^{|d|} \mathbf{q}_i^\top \mathbf{d}_j

Each query token’s best document-token match is summed for the final relevance score.

Key Formula: Reciprocal Rank Fusion\text{RRF}(d) = \sum_{r \in R} \frac{1}{k + \text{rank}_r(d)}

Fuses ranked lists from multiple retrievers; documents ranked highly by both methods receive the highest fused scores.

A user searching for “heart disease” expects to find documents about myocardial infarction, coronary artery conditions, and cardiology treatment, even when those documents share no keywords with the query. Classical retrieval models based on BM25 or the vector space model treat terms as independent symbols: they can match “heart” to “heart” but not to “cardiac”. Stemming and lemmatization help at the surface level, and hand-curated ontologies can map synonyms, but these approaches are labor-intensive, language-specific, and break down quickly when facing the full diversity of natural language expression.

Semantic search solves this problem by representing text as dense vectors in a continuous space where geometric proximity encodes meaning. Two words that never co-occur in a query-document pair can still be recognized as related if their embeddings point in similar directions. This shift from discrete term matching to continuous meaning matching (

Figure 1) is the central theme of this chapter.



Figure 1:Keyword matching operates on exact surface forms (left). Semantic matching maps terms into a continuous embedding space where conceptually related terms cluster together (right), enabling retrieval even when query and document share no words.

The path from keyword retrieval to modern semantic search spans three decades and three paradigm shifts:

Latent Semantic Indexing (Deerwester et al., 1988) applied Singular Value Decomposition to the term-document matrix, discovering latent topics that link related terms. LSI proved that dimensionality reduction could capture semantic relationships, but its computational cost and inability to use inverted indices limited practical adoption.

Static word embeddings (Mikolov et al., 2013; Pennington et al., 2014) learned dense vector representations from local context windows. Word2Vec and GloVe showed that simple neural architectures trained on large corpora produce vectors where semantic similarity corresponds to geometric proximity. However, each word receives a single vector regardless of context: “bank” has the same representation whether it refers to a financial institution or a riverbank.

Contextual embeddings and transformers (Vaswani et al., 2017; Devlin et al., 2019; Reimers and Gurevych, 2019) introduced attention mechanisms that produce different representations for the same word depending on its surrounding context. Sentence-BERT restructured transformers into efficient bi-encoders suitable for large-scale retrieval. Subsequent work refined this paradigm: ColBERT (Khattab and Zaharia, 2020) introduced token-level late interaction for higher quality, and Matryoshka embeddings (Kusupati et al., 2022) enabled multi-resolution search. Production systems today typically combine sparse and dense retrieval in hybrid pipelines.

Semantic search primarily improves recall: it expands the pool of candidate documents by finding matches that keyword methods miss. This comes at a cost. Dense embeddings lack efficient retrieval structures like inverted indices, so searching through millions of vectors requires approximate methods (covered in the next chapter). And because semantic retrieval casts a wider net, precision often drops; a reranker is typically needed to refine the ordering.

In practice, BM25 is not replaced by vector search. Instead, production systems combine both in hybrid pipelines. The blueprint is always the same two-component structure shown in 

Figure 2: a retriever that efficiently selects candidates (optimized for recall), followed by a ranker that reorders them (optimized for precision). What changes across pipelines is how each component is implemented.

The previous chapter turned text into embeddings: dense vectors whose geometry captures meaning, so that “heart disease” and “cardiology treatment” land close together even though they share no words. Images, audio, and video can be encoded the same way. Once every document and every query is a point in the same space, retrieval becomes a geometric question: which stored points lie closest to the query point? 

Figure 1 makes this concrete, showing a 2D projection of a word-embedding space in which related terms fall into the same neighborhood, so that proximity stands in for similarity in meaning.

That question is easy to state and expensive to answer. A collection may hold millions or billions of vectors, each with hundreds or thousands of dimensions. Comparing the query against every stored vector is correct but slow, and the classical spatial indexes that accelerate low-dimensional search collapse as the number of dimensions grows. That leaves a gap between the only method guaranteed to be correct, the full scan, and the speed a real system needs. This chapter is about closing it: how to measure closeness, why exact search becomes hopeless in high dimensions, and how approximate methods recover speed by giving up a little accuracy that the application never needed.



Figure 1:A 2D projection of a word-embedding space; semantically related terms form visible clusters.

The vectors themselves arrive from more than one source. We already have embeddings from learned models, built in the previous chapter; other applications extract vectors straight from the media, such as a color histogram of an image. Whatever their origin, the question this chapter asks is how to compare them, and there are two ways to do it. A similarity score, most often the dot product or cosine, rewards a close match with a larger value. A distance, such as Euclidean distance, marks a close match with a smaller value. The two are two sides of the same coin: a simple normalization turns one into the other, so the engineering problem, finding the closest points quickly, is the same whichever we use.

What you’ll learn

Explain how dot product, cosine similarity, and distance measures express closeness, and convert between them.

Describe how classical spatial indexes (Voronoi diagrams, grid files, R-trees) answer nearest-neighbor queries.

Explain the curse of dimensionality and why it forces exact search back to a full scan.

Compare approximate nearest-neighbor methods (IVF, HNSW, LSH, product quantization) and their recall-speed trade-off.

Choose a vector-search framework and combine similarity search with metadata filters.

Performance Evaluation: recall, which reappears here as the quality axis of approximate search.

Basic linear algebra: vectors, dot products, norms, and eigenvectors.

Consider again the query “heart disease”. In 

Vector Space Retrieval, the query and every document became TF-IDF vectors. These vectors are sparse: the query vector has only two non-zero components, one for “heart” and one for “disease”. An inverted file therefore reads just two posting lists, and a document that contains neither term is never touched. The embeddings of 

Building Semantic Search represent the same query as a dense vector with typically 768 components, all of them non-zero. Components can be positive or negative, so a document may gain score in one dimension and lose it in another, and even a small query component q_k matters when the matching document component d_{i,k} is large. No document can be skipped because it lacks a query term. So far we have answered dense queries with a linear scan over all document vectors. Can we do better?

Text is not the only source of vectors. Later chapters on visual, audio, and video features describe images, sounds, and video shots by vectors of low-level perceptual features, such as the distribution of colors in an image. These features differ from embeddings in how they are obtained: a hand-designed extraction rule computes them directly from the signal. They also differ in how they are compared. Perceptual features usually come with a distance, such as Euclidean distance, where a smaller value means a better match. As with embeddings, the comparison function belongs to the feature. It follows from how the feature was defined or learned, and we cannot simply replace it with another one.

For both approaches, the search task is the same. A linear scan compares the query with every stored vector and returns the best matches. A better approach organizes the vectors in advance, as the inverted file does for sparse vectors, so that a query visits only a small part of the collection. This task is the nearest-neighbor problem. It is well understood in two and three dimensions, where geographic information systems and computer graphics have solved it for decades. With embeddings of hundreds or thousands of dimensions, it has gained new interest. This section formalizes what a best match is, first under a similarity score and then under a distance. The rest of the chapter asks how to find the best matches without a full scan.

Embeddings are compared with the dot product or with cosine similarity, the two measures of the vector space model in 

Vector Space Retrieval. Writing the query vector as \mathbf{q} and a document vector as \mathbf{d}_i, the dot product sums the products of matching components, while cosine similarity divides that sum by the two vector lengths so that only direction matters.

Key Formula: Dot Product and Cosine Similarity\text{sim}_{\text{dot}}(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{d}_i) = \mathbf{q} \cdot \mathbf{d}_i = \sum_{k=1}^{M} q_k\, d_{i,k}\text{sim}_{\text{cos}}(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{d}_i) = \frac{\mathbf{q} \cdot \mathbf{d}_i}{\lVert \mathbf{q} \rVert \, \lVert \mathbf{d}_i \rVert}

The dot product rewards vectors that are both aligned and long; cosine similarity divides out the lengths and rewards alignment alone.

Figure 1 contrasts the geometry of the two measures. For cosine similarity (left), the best matches lie inside a cone around the query, and the length of a document vector plays no role. For the dot product (right), a hyperplane orthogonal to the query separates the best matches from the rest. Documents farther out along the query direction score higher, so the dot product favors long vectors. A document in the half-space opposite the query scores negatively under both measures.



Figure 1:Cosine similarity (left) selects the documents inside a cone around \mathbf{q}; the dot product (right) selects the documents beyond a hyperplane orthogonal to \mathbf{q}.

With a comparison function in place, we can state the search problem. Given a query embedding \mathbf{q} and a set \mathbb{P} of stored document embeddings, we look for the documents that maximize the score.

Key Formula: Best-Match Search\mathbf{d}^{*} = \arg\max_{\mathbf{d}_i \in \mathbb{P}} \text{sim}(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{d}_i), \qquad \text{sim} \in \{\text{sim}_{\text{dot}}, \text{sim}_{\text{cos}}\}

More generally, the top-k result consists of the k documents with the highest scores. The definition says nothing about how to find them; a linear scan computes all scores and keeps the best.

In practice, the choice between the two measures is often made once, when the index is built. Most embedding models output vectors of unit length, and otherwise we normalize every document vector once before indexing, \hat{\mathbf{d}}_i = \mathbf{d}_i / \lVert \mathbf{d}_i \rVert. On the unit sphere, cosine similarity and dot product coincide, so the index only needs to compute dot products. The query needs no normalization at all:\text{sim}_{\text{cos}}(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{d}_i) = \frac{1}{\lVert \mathbf{q} \rVert}\; \mathbf{q} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{d}}_i

The factor 1/\lVert \mathbf{q} \rVert is the same for every document. It scales all scores of a query equally and leaves the ranking unchanged. Normalizing the query does no harm, and it is useful when scores must be comparable across queries, for example against a fixed similarity threshold. For ranking alone, it is not required.

To see how a perceptual feature turns media into a vector, consider the color content of an image. 

Figure 2 splits a photograph into its red, green, and blue channels and summarizes each channel by a histogram over its 256 intensity values. To build the histograms, we visit every pixel and increase three bins by one: the bin for the pixel’s red intensity in the red histogram, and likewise for green and blue. The three histograms together hold 3 \times 256 = 768 counts, which we read as a 768-dimensional feature vector of the image.



Figure 2:A color image split into its red, green, and blue channels, each summarized by an intensity histogram.

Exact intensities are too fine-grained for comparing images. Two photographs of the same pasta under slightly different light would share hardly any bins. We therefore quantize each histogram into fewer, wider bins, for example 16 bins per channel that each cover 16 intensity values. Similar shades now fall into the same bin, and the feature vector shrinks to 3 \times 16 = 48 values, each counting the pixels in one bin.

To compare two images by their colors, we sum the absolute differences of their counts over all 48 bins. Two images with similar color distributions differ little in every bin and receive a small sum. A photograph of a blue sky differs strongly from the red pasta in many bins and receives a large sum. This sum is the Manhattan distance between the two feature vectors. The color histogram is deliberately simple: it only shows how image content is reduced to a vector. Later chapters introduce more expressive perceptual features.

A distance \delta(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{p}_i) between the query \mathbf{q} and a stored vector \mathbf{p}_i reverses the direction of comparison: a smaller value means a better match, and identical vectors have distance zero. Most distances used in retrieval are metrics, which means they are non-negative, symmetric, and satisfy the triangle inequality. Each distance induces a different notion of a neighborhood, that is, a different shape for the set of points within a fixed distance of a center. 

Figure 3 shows these shapes in 2D.

Euclidean distance (L2) measures straight-line distance and gives a round neighborhood. It is the default for continuous features.

Manhattan distance (L1) sums the absolute differences per dimension and gives a diamond neighborhood. It emphasizes many small differences.

Maximum distance (L-infinity) takes the single largest component difference and gives a square neighborhood. It lets the worst dimension dominate.

Quadratic distance weights and correlates the dimensions through a matrix, giving a tilted-ellipse neighborhood.



Figure 3:Neighborhood shapes of four distance measures in 2D: Euclidean (round), Manhattan (diamond), maximum (square), and quadratic (tilted ellipse).

Distances and similarity scores are two views of the same comparison. On the unit sphere the link is exact. For normalized vectors, the squared Euclidean distance is a linear function of the dot product:\lVert \hat{\mathbf{q}} - \hat{\mathbf{d}}_i \rVert^2 = 2 - 2\, \hat{\mathbf{q}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{d}}_i

Ranking normalized vectors by increasing Euclidean distance therefore returns the same order as ranking them by decreasing cosine similarity. In general, any distance can be turned into a similarity score with a decreasing function, such as 1/(1 + \delta), without changing the ranking. Such a conversion keeps the comparison and changes only the scale of the values. Replacing the comparison is a different matter. Using cosine similarity instead of the Manhattan distance on color histograms changes the ranking, and only the design of the feature can justify that change.

One awkward property of distances is that they are hard to read on their own. A cosine of 0.9 clearly signals a strong match, but a distance of 32.8 says nothing until it is compared with other distances. This is one reason why normalized similarity scores are convenient when a human or a downstream system needs to interpret the score.

With a distance, the search problem keeps its form. We minimize instead of maximize, and the best match becomes the nearest neighbor.

Key Formula: Nearest-Neighbor Search\text{NN}(\mathbf{q}) = \arg\min_{\mathbf{p}_i \in \mathbb{P}} \delta(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{p}_i)

The k nearest neighbors are the k stored vectors with the smallest distances. This is best-match search with the direction of comparison reversed; for normalized vectors under Euclidean distance, both return the same result.

Embeddings rarely need further adjustment, because every dimension comes from the same learned space and lives on a comparable scale. Perceptual features are different. A feature vector often combines values that were measured independently, and the color histogram shows two forms of the resulting problem.

The first is scale. Bin counts depend on the size of the image: a photograph with four times as many pixels has four times larger counts, so the Manhattan distance between a small and a large image of the same scene is large. This is the same problem the dot product has with long documents in 

Vector Space Retrieval, and the fix is similar. We divide every count by the number of pixels. Each channel’s histogram then holds fractions that sum to 1, independent of the image size.

The second is mixing features. Suppose we append the image’s average brightness, measured on a scale from 0 to 255, to the 48 normalized bins. The bins of each channel sum to 1, so the Manhattan distance over all 48 bins can never exceed 6. A brightness difference of 50 alone outweighs any possible color difference, and the distance effectively compares brightness only. To give each dimension a fair share, we rescale it by its spread over the collection. For each dimension j, we subtract the mean \mu_j and divide by the standard deviation \sigma_j of that dimension, both estimated once from the collection or from a representative sample.\hat{v}_j = \frac{v_j - \mu_j}{\sigma_j}

After this Gaussian normalization, every dimension has mean 0 and unit variance. A difference of one unit then means the same in every dimension: one standard deviation of the typical variation. Equivalently, the distance weights each dimension’s difference by 1/\sigma_j, so each dimension contributes in proportion to how much it actually varies.

Normalize on statistics, not on a single query

Gaussian normalization uses the mean and standard deviation of the whole collection, not of one query or one result set. Estimate \mu_j and \sigma_j once from a representative sample and keep them fixed, so that the same vector always maps to the same normalized point regardless of which query retrieves it.

Gaussian normalization treats the dimensions as independent, but the bins of a color histogram are not. The bin for red is related to the bin for orange, because the two colors are perceptually close, while red and blue are not. The quadratic distance captures such relationships through a positive semi-definite matrix \mathbf{A}, whose eigenvectors define the main axes of the data and whose eigenvalues scale them.

Computing (\mathbf{q} - \mathbf{p}_i)^\top \mathbf{A} (\mathbf{q} - \mathbf{p}_i) for every candidate is expensive, but an eigenvalue decomposition avoids it. Rotating and scaling the space along the eigenvectors of \mathbf{A}, shown in 

Figure 4, maps the quadratic distance in the original space onto a plain Euclidean distance in the transformed space. We transform all vectors once when building the index and then compare them with ordinary Euclidean distance at query time.



Figure 4:Whitening: rotating along the eigenvectors of the weighting matrix and scaling by the square roots of its eigenvalues turns a correlated distribution into an isotropic one.

Whether we maximize a similarity score or minimize a distance, we now have a precise definition of the best matches. The rest of the chapter answers a single question about these definitions: how do we compute the arg-max or arg-min without comparing the query to every stored vector? For a few thousand vectors a full scan is fine. For millions or billions it is not, and the structures that speed up the search behave very differently depending on how many dimensions the vectors have.

Hands-on: Distance measures and normalization

Compute dot product, cosine, and Euclidean and Manhattan distances on the same vectors, watch length normalization make cosine and dot product agree, and see Gaussian normalization rebalance dimensions on different scales.

A city has a few dozen post offices, and a resident wants to know which one is closest to home. This is the nearest-neighbor problem of the previous section in two dimensions, and Donald Knuth used exactly this scenario to name it: the post-office problem. In two dimensions the problem is easy, and its solution has been known for a long time. This section follows how the solutions for two and three dimensions grew from a precomputed map of all answers into tree structures, and why the hope of searching in logarithmic time, as a B-tree does for one-dimensional keys, was never quite fulfilled.

For the post-office problem, we can draw a map that answers every possible query in advance. Around each post office, we mark the region of all locations that are closer to this office than to any other. The result is a Voronoi diagram: a partition of the space into one cell per stored point, as shown in 

Figure 1. To answer a query, we locate the cell that contains the resident’s home and return the post office of that cell.



Figure 1:A Voronoi diagram: every location inside a cell is closer to the cell’s seed point than to any other seed point.

The Voronoi diagram inverts the search problem. Instead of searching for the nearest neighbor of one query, it computes the nearest neighbor of all possible queries at once and stores the answers as regions. This is the geometric analogue of the inverted file. An inverted file precomputes the result of every single-term query; a Voronoi diagram precomputes the result of every nearest-neighbor query. The idea is not tied to Euclidean distance: Voronoi diagrams exist for other distance measures as well.

The difficulty lies in building and storing the cells. In two dimensions, the diagram of n points has a size proportional to n. In d dimensions, its worst-case size grows like n^{⌈d/2⌉}, so already in three dimensions it can grow quadratically, and finding the cell that contains a query becomes as hard as the search it was meant to replace. A common workaround approximates each cell by its minimum bounding rectangle, but the rectangles of neighboring cells overlap, so a query must check several candidates instead of one. Insertions and deletions are awkward too, since one new point reshapes all neighboring cells. Voronoi diagrams remain the clearest mental model of exact nearest-neighbor search, but not a practical index beyond a few dimensions.

Spatial search is much older than embeddings. Geographic information systems, computer-aided design, and image databases needed it from the 1970s onward, and the research followed a familiar path. It started with simple partitions of space and moved on to tree structures, in the hope of repeating for two and three dimensions what the B-tree achieves for one-dimensional keys: finding any entry in a logarithmic number of steps.

These structures were designed for range search first. A range query asks for all points within a region, for example all points within distance r of the query \mathbf{q}, as in 

Figure 2, or all points inside a map window. The region is known before the search starts, so the index only needs to identify the parts of the space that overlap it.



Figure 2:A range query returns all points within radius r of the query \mathbf{q}.

The grid file is the simplest such structure. It lays a grid over the space, chooses the grid lines so that each cell holds roughly the same number of points, and stores the points of each cell on a disk page, as shown in 

Figure 3. A directory maps every cell to its page. A range query reads only the pages of the cells that overlap the query region. In two dimensions, a small query window needs only a few page reads, however large the collection is.



Figure 3:A grid file partitions the space into cells (left) and maps each cell through a directory to a disk page holding its points (right).

How a grid file grows (optional reading)

The grid lines of a grid file are not equally spaced. They are placed so that the resulting disk pages hold roughly the same number of points, which keeps the cost of reading a page predictable.

The directory associates each grid cell with the disk page that holds its points. Many cells stay empty or nearly empty when the data is unevenly distributed, so several cells may share one disk page. This keeps the number of pages close to the minimum needed for the data.

When an insertion fills a page that serves several cells, the grid file creates a new page and distributes the cells evenly between the two pages. Only the directory entries of these cells change. When a single cell grows too large for one page, the grid file adds a new partition line along a chosen dimension. This splits every cell that the line crosses and enlarges the directory, but again only the points of the overflowing cell move to new pages.

The directory is also the grid file’s weakness. Splitting each of d dimensions only once already produces 2^{d} cells. For the 48-dimensional color histograms of the previous section this is 2^{48} \approx 2.8 \times 10^{14} cells, almost all of them empty, and the directory no longer fits in memory.

hierarchy.lvl2: R-trees and the problem of overlap
R-trees and the problem of overlap

records.content:
The R-tree carries the idea of the B-tree directly into the multi-dimensional space. It groups nearby points into a minimum bounding rectangle (MBR), groups nearby rectangles into larger rectangles, and continues up to a single root. 

Figure 4 shows a small R-tree. Like a B-tree, it is balanced: all leaves are at the same depth, and every node holds between a minimum and a maximum number of entries. When a node overflows, it is split into two nodes, and the split may propagate up to the root. R-trees index points, rectangles, and polygons, and they are a mainstay of spatial databases to this day.



Figure 4:An R-tree groups points into nested minimum bounding rectangles (left) that form a balanced tree (right).

Splitting a leaf is easy. We divide its points at the median of one dimension, and the two new rectangles do not overlap. Splitting an inner node is harder, because its entries are rectangles, not points, and two groups of rectangles often cannot be separated cleanly. 

Figure 5 shows the possible outcomes: a clean split, a split whose rectangles overlap, and a split where one rectangle lies completely inside the other.



Figure 5:Splitting an inner node: a clean split (left), overlapping rectangles (middle), and one rectangle contained in the other (right).

Overlap also grows over time. When a new point falls into the overlap of two rectangles, as in 

Figure 6, the insertion must choose a path. The usual heuristic follows the child whose rectangle needs the least enlargement. A poor choice inflates a rectangle, which then overlaps its neighbors even more and makes the next decision harder. Every query that reaches an overlapping region must follow several branches, and the tree loses the single root-to-leaf path that makes a B-tree fast.



Figure 6:Inserting a point into overlapping rectangles: the blue path keeps the rectangles tight, the green path enlarges them.

A second problem is less visible but more fundamental: nearest-neighbor search is not a range search. A range query knows its region in advance. A nearest-neighbor query does not know how far away its answer lies. It must find a candidate and then prove that no other point is closer. If the query lies near the border of a leaf, the closest point may well sit in a neighboring leaf, possibly in a different subtree, and the search has to look there before it can stop. Even without any overlap, a nearest-neighbor search therefore tends to visit more than one path from the root to the leaves.

Hjaltason and Samet proposed a nearest-neighbor algorithm that works for any structure that divides the space into nested regions: grid files, R-trees, and their many variants. It is optimal in a precise sense. It finds the nearest neighbor and proves that no other point is closer, and no correct algorithm can do this with fewer node inspections.

The algorithm keeps a priority queue of nodes and points, ordered by their distance to the query \mathbf{q}. For a point, this is the exact distance. For a node, it is a lower bound: the smallest distance that any point inside the node’s region could have.insert the root into the queue with its lower bound
while the queue is not empty:
    remove the entry e with the smallest distance
    if e is a data point:   return e as the nearest neighbor
    if e is a leaf:         insert every point of e with its distance to q
    if e is an inner node:  insert every child of e with its lower bound

The algorithm only needs two primitives: the distance between the query and a point, and a lower bound for the distance between the query and a region. For a rectangle and Euclidean distance, the lower bound is the distance to the closest point of the rectangle.

Key Formula: Lower Bound to a Bounding Rectangle

For a rectangle with per-dimension bounds [l_j, u_j], the smallest possible L2 distance from the query \mathbf{q} is\text{lBnd}(\mathbf{q}, \text{MBR}) = \sqrt{\sum_{j} \begin{cases} (l_j - q_j)^2 & q_j < l_j \\ (q_j - u_j)^2 & q_j > u_j \\ 0 & l_j \le q_j \le u_j \end{cases}}

Dimensions in which the query lies inside the rectangle contribute nothing; the others contribute the gap to the nearer edge.

To find the k nearest neighbors, the algorithm continues until k data points have been removed from the queue. The following example shows what the search costs even in two dimensions.

Example

An R-tree stores twelve points in four leaves. The inner node A holds the leaves L1 and L2, and the inner node B holds L3 and L4. The query is \mathbf{q} = (4.6, 4.6), which lies in the gap between the two subtrees. For leaf L1 with rectangle [1, 3.8] \times [1, 3.4], the query lies to the right of and above the rectangle, so \text{lBnd} = \sqrt{(4.6 - 3.8)^2 + (4.6 - 3.4)^2} = \sqrt{2.08} = 1.44. For L3 with rectangle [5.2, 8] \times [5.4, 9], it is \sqrt{0.6^2 + 0.8^2} = 1.00.

The leaf L3 looked most promising, but its closest point is 2.06 away. The nearest neighbor (3.8, 3.4) lies in the other subtree. The search followed two paths from the root to the leaves, root-B-L3 and root-A-L1, and opened two of the four leaves. L2 and L4 were never opened, because their lower bounds exceed the distance 1.44 of the nearest neighbor.

The example shows the cost structure of every tree-based nearest-neighbor search. The search visited both inner nodes and two leaves, twice as many as a single root-to-leaf path. Because the algorithm is optimal, nothing can be done about this: any correct algorithm must open L3, since a point within distance 1.00 of the query could have been there. The extra paths are the price of proving the answer, not a weakness of the algorithm.

Why the algorithm is correct and optimal (optional reading)

Correctness. The queue orders its entries by increasing distance. Every child of a node lies inside the node’s region, so its lower bound is at least as large as the node’s lower bound, and every point inside a region is at least as far away as the region’s lower bound. When a data point reaches the front of the queue, every entry still in the queue, and every descendant of these entries, is at least as far from the query as this point. No closer point can remain hidden, so the point at the front is the nearest neighbor.

Optimality. Suppose we already knew the nearest neighbor of \mathbf{q}. The NN-sphere is the sphere centered at \mathbf{q} that passes through this nearest neighbor, drawn in 

Figure 7. Any node whose region intersects the NN-sphere might contain a closer point, so any correct algorithm must inspect it; skipping it would leave the answer unproven. A node whose region lies entirely outside the NN-sphere cannot contain a closer point and need not be inspected.

The algorithm inspects nodes in increasing order of their lower bounds and stops as soon as the nearest neighbor reaches the front of the queue. At that moment, it has inspected exactly the nodes whose lower bound is at most the nearest-neighbor distance, which are the nodes whose regions intersect the NN-sphere. It therefore inspects no node that a correct algorithm could skip. In the example above, the NN-sphere has radius 1.44 and intersects A, B, L1, and L3, which are exactly the nodes the search opened.



Figure 7:The NN-sphere around \mathbf{q}: regions that intersect it must be inspected, regions outside it can be skipped.

The same argument extends to the k nearest neighbors, with the sphere passing through the k-th nearest neighbor.

hierarchy.lvl2: Beyond Euclidean distance: dot product and cosine
Beyond Euclidean distance: dot product and cosine

records.content:
The algorithm never looks inside the distance function. It needs a bound for each region that is optimistic, meaning it never promises less than the region could deliver. For a distance, this is a lower bound; for a similarity score, it is an upper bound, and the queue is ordered by decreasing score instead of increasing distance. 

Figure 8 shows both cases.



Figure 8:Bounding a region: for L2 distance (left), the nearest and farthest points of the region bound the distance; for the dot product (right), two hyperplanes orthogonal to \mathbf{q} bound the similarity.

For the dot product, the bounds follow from the fact that the score is a sum of component-wise products. Each product q_j p_j is largest at the upper edge u_j if q_j is positive and at the lower edge l_j if q_j is negative:\text{uBnd}(\mathbf{q}, \text{MBR}) = \sum_j \begin{cases} q_j\, u_j & q_j \ge 0 \\ q_j\, l_j & q_j < 0 \end{cases}

For a spherical region with center \mathbf{c} and radius r, the bound is \mathbf{q} \cdot \mathbf{c} + r \lVert \mathbf{q} \rVert, attained by the point of the sphere that lies farthest in the direction of \mathbf{q}. Ram and Gray used this bound to run exact maximum-inner-product search on ball trees.

So do these structures work with dot product and cosine out of the box? Largely yes, with a few caveats.

Grid files and R-trees work with the dot product as soon as the bound function is replaced. Nested rectangles keep the property the algorithm relies on: a child’s bound never exceeds its parent’s bound. Correctness is therefore guaranteed. Efficiency is not, because the split and insertion heuristics were designed to keep rectangles small under Euclidean distance, not to group vectors that score similarly.

Cosine similarity needs no special treatment. After normalizing the stored vectors, ranking by cosine equals ranking by Euclidean distance, as the previous section showed. Any Euclidean index can be used unchanged.

Metric trees such as the M-tree prune with the triangle inequality. The dot product is not a metric, so these structures cannot use it directly. With cosine, they can again work on the Euclidean distance between normalized vectors.

Voronoi diagrams change their character. Under the dot product, a point is not necessarily its own best match: for \mathbf{p} = (1, 1), the longer vector (2, 2) scores 4 against \mathbf{p}, while \mathbf{p} scores only 2 against itself. Only the vertices of the convex hull of the collection can be the best match of any query; all other points have empty cells.

There is also a general trick that turns maximum-inner-product search into nearest-neighbor search. Let M be the largest vector length in the collection. Appending the component \sqrt{M^2 - \lVert \mathbf{p}_i \rVert^2} to every stored vector and 0 to the query gives all stored vectors the same length M. The squared Euclidean distance between the extended vectors is then \lVert \mathbf{q} \rVert^2 + M^2 - 2\, \mathbf{q} \cdot \mathbf{p}_i, so the nearest neighbor is exactly the vector with the largest dot product, and any Euclidean index can answer the query.

In two and three dimensions, the extra paths are a small price. A nearest-neighbor search opens a few more leaves than a range search would, and the structures easily beat a full scan. Research in the 1990s, however, showed that the price grows with the number of dimensions. Rectangles overlap more, the nearest neighbor lies farther away, and the NN-sphere intersects more and more leaves, until the optimal algorithm visits almost all of them.

The research community responded with a long series of new structures. They changed the shape of the bounding regions to spheres or combinations of spheres and rectangles, introduced split strategies that reduce overlap, enlarged nodes when splitting did not pay off, or replaced the data-space metric by an object metric such as edit distance. Notable examples include the R+-tree (1987), R*-tree (1990), TV-tree (1994), vp-tree (1993), GiST (1995), X-tree (1996), SS-tree (1996), SR-tree (1997), M-tree (1997), and Pyramid-tree (1998), and many more followed. Each improved on its predecessors for some data and some dimensions. None of them restored logarithmic search in high dimensions.

That so many clever designs failed in the same way suggests that the problem lies not in any single structure but in high-dimensional space itself. The effect is known as the curse of dimensionality, a term originally coined by Richard Bellman. The next section explains what makes high-dimensional spaces so hostile to search.

Optional Background Reading

This section explains why exact nearest-neighbor search fails in high dimensions, with the geometry and statistics behind it, and it is here as background. The next section only needs its conclusions, so a reader focused on the search methods can skim or skip it. The next section opens with a short recap of what carries forward.

All the structures of the previous section were developed with two or three dimensions in mind. Their inventors argued with drawings in the plane: rectangles that enclose points, spheres that touch rectangles, regions that can be skipped. When feature vectors with dozens or hundreds of dimensions arrived, the natural expectation was that these arguments would carry over, and that an index would prune the search in 100 dimensions much as it does in 2. This intuition turned out to be wrong. This section shows why, first for distances and then for the dot product, and draws a conclusion that shapes the rest of the chapter: in high dimensions, the exact nearest neighbor is not worth chasing.

Take the unit square and two points that are clearly close: the center \mathbf{c} = (0.5, 0.5) and a point \mathbf{p} = (0.4, 0.4) slightly off-center. Around \mathbf{p} we draw a circle of radius r = 3, shown in 

Figure 1. The farthest corner of the square is only 0.85 away from \mathbf{p}, so the circle covers the whole square many times over. A radius of 3 looks absurdly large.



Figure 1:A circle of radius r around \mathbf{p}, close to the center \mathbf{c} of the unit square.

Now we add dimensions, keeping the same pattern: \mathbf{c} has the value 0.5 and \mathbf{p} the value 0.4 in every dimension. The two points differ by 0.1 in each of d dimensions, so their Euclidean distance is 0.1\sqrt{d}. The farthest corner of the unit cube lies at distance 0.6\sqrt{d} from \mathbf{p}. Both distances grow with \sqrt{d}, while the radius stays fixed:

Up to d = 25, the sphere of radius 3 still contains the whole unit cube, because 0.6\sqrt{25} = 3.

Beyond d = 25, corners of the cube start to fall outside the sphere, and their number grows quickly.

Beyond d = 900, even the center \mathbf{c} falls outside, because 0.1\sqrt{900} = 3.

Nine hundred dimensions are common for features extracted from media. In such a space, a point we would call “close” by any 2D standard lies outside a radius that covers the entire square in 2D. Distances simply grow with the dimension, and they grow for all pairs of points alike.

Growing distances alone would only change the scale. The real problem is that the distances of all points to a query grow at the same pace, so they become ever more similar. A simple measure for this is the contrast between the farthest and the nearest point.

Key Formula: Loss of Contrast

For a query and a fixed set of data points, let \delta_{\max} and \delta_{\min} be the distances to the farthest and the nearest point. For independent random data, as d \to \infty:\frac{\delta_{\max} - \delta_{\min}}{\delta_{\min}} \to 0

The farthest point is barely farther away than the nearest one; “nearest” loses its distinction.

Example

We place 10,000 random points uniformly in the unit cube and measure the contrast from random queries, averaged over 50 queries:

In 2D, the farthest point is hundreds of times farther away than the nearest one. At d = 1000, it is only 17 percent (L1) or 14 percent (L2) farther. The last two columns show why: the mean distance grows like \sqrt{d}, but the spread around it stays at about 0.23. The same spread on top of an ever larger distance means ever less contrast. The Manhattan distance keeps a little more contrast than the Euclidean distance, but both collapse.

Figure 2 shows the same effect as distributions. In two dimensions, distances spread over a wide range; at d = 8192, they pile up around a mean of about 36.9 with a standard deviation near 0.24, so that 99 percent of all pairs fall into a band barely more than one unit wide.



Figure 2:Distributions of Euclidean distances between random points in the unit cube, from d = 2 to d = 8192.

The loss of contrast has two consequences. The first concerns the index structures of the previous section; the second concerns the meaning of the nearest neighbor itself.
