records.content:
The optimal algorithm of the previous section must inspect every node whose region intersects the NN-sphere, the sphere around the query that passes through the nearest neighbor. If the nearest neighbor is far away, this sphere is large, and few regions can be skipped. To estimate the cost, we use a simple model: the data space is the unit cube, the dimensions are independent and uniformly distributed, and we use Euclidean distance. In this model, the probability that a point falls into a region equals the region’s volume.

Two quantities compete, shown side by side in 

Figure 3. The first is the expected nearest-neighbor distance, which grows with the dimension (left). For one million points, it is 0.24 at d = 10, 1.37 at d = 40, 2.03 at d = 60, and 2.97 at d = 100.

The second is the size of a leaf (right). A tree cannot split every dimension. Each split in the middle of a dimension halves the number of points in a region, so one million points support only about 14 splits: after that, a leaf holds 10^6 / 2^{14} \approx 61 points, about one disk page. A leaf is therefore split along d' \approx 14 dimensions and spans the full range in all others. The largest distance from any query to such a leaf is l_{\max} = 0.5\sqrt{d'} \approx 1.87, no matter how many dimensions the space has.



Figure 3:Left: the expected nearest-neighbor distance grows roughly like \sqrt{d}. Right: a leaf split along d' dimensions; no query in the unit cube is farther than l_{\max} = 0.5\sqrt{d'} from it.

Once the expected nearest-neighbor distance exceeds l_{\max}, every leaf lies closer to the query than the query’s own nearest neighbor. Every leaf intersects the NN-sphere, and even the optimal algorithm must visit all of them. For one million points, this happens between d = 40 and d = 60. Beyond that point, the hierarchy only adds overhead: why build a tree if every leaf must be read anyway? In practice the index loses even earlier. A full scan reads the data sequentially, while a tree reads its leaves one by one; once a tree must visit a sizeable fraction of its leaves, the scan is faster. Weber, Schek, and Blott showed that for uniform data this happens beyond roughly ten dimensions (see the Further Reading section of the chapter summary).

Two more surprises of high-dimensional space (optional reading)

The growth of distances is one of several ways in which high-dimensional space defies intuition. Two further puzzles make the point. Each one ends with a question: try to answer it before you open the resolution.

The escaping sphere. Place a square of side 2 with a circle of radius 1 at each corner, so that the circles cover all edges of the square. A further circle at the center just touches the four corner circles, as in 

Figure 4.



Figure 4:The escaping-sphere puzzle in 2D: four corner circles of radius 1 and a central circle that touches all of them.

What is the radius r of the central circle? Now repeat the construction in d dimensions, with a hypersphere at each corner of the hypercube and a central hypersphere that touches all of them. Does the central sphere stay inside the cube?

Resolution

The distance from the center of the square to a corner is \sqrt{2}, so the central circle has radius r = \sqrt{2} - 1 \approx 0.41. In d dimensions, the distance from the center of the hypercube to a corner is \sqrt{d}, so r = \sqrt{d} - 1. At d = 4 the radius is exactly 1, and the central sphere touches the faces of the cube. At d = 100 it is 9, and the “inner” sphere reaches far outside the cube that supposedly contains it.

The reason is that the corner spheres cover less and less of each face as the dimension grows. Already in 3D, the center of each face is left uncovered, and in higher dimensions the central sphere escapes through these gaps.

Where have all the points gone? Place a smaller square of side s = 0.99 at the center of the unit square, as in 

Figure 5, and distribute points uniformly over the unit square. The inner square seems to cover almost everything.



Figure 5:An inner square of side s centered in the unit square.

What fraction of the points lies inside the inner square? How does this fraction change in d dimensions, and where are the points that are not inside?

Resolution

The fraction equals the volume of the inner square. In 2D it is 0.99^2 \approx 98 percent. In d dimensions it is 0.99^{d}: about 37 percent at d = 100 and only 4.3 \times 10^{-5} at d = 1000. Of one million uniformly distributed points, only about 43 lie inside the inner cube.

In each single dimension, a point lies inside the inner range with probability 0.99. But with 1000 dimensions, the probability that it lies outside in at least one of them is 1 - 0.99^{1000} = 0.99996. Almost every point lies within 0.005 of one of the 2d faces of the cube. The center of a high-dimensional space is empty, and any partition of the space into regions produces regions that almost certainly contain no data.

The second consequence is more fundamental. If all points are almost equally far from the query, the nearest neighbor is only marginally nearer than the rest. Proximity stops expressing similarity: a point that is 14 percent farther away than the nearest neighbor is not meaningfully less similar.

Real data is kinder than this model. The analysis above assumes uniformly distributed, independent dimensions, and real feature vectors and embeddings are neither. They form clusters: images of sunsets lie closer to each other than to images of forests, and documents about cardiology lie closer to each other than to documents about tax law. Relative to the uniform background, in which everything appears equally far away, the members of a cluster stand out as outliers with clearly smaller distances. This is why vector search works at all in high dimensions, and why the approximate methods of the next section can exploit the structure of the data.

Within such a cluster, however, the loss of contrast remains. The nearest neighbor and the next few points lie at almost the same distance from the query. The exact nearest neighbor is not necessarily the best match in the sense the user cares about; it is one good match among several that are about equally close. Spending a full scan, or a visit to every leaf, to determine which of them is nearest buys a distinction that carries little meaning.

Embeddings are usually compared with the dot product or cosine, so we repeat the argument for similarity scores. In 2D, it seems reasonable to assume that a query and its best matches lie in the same quadrant. In 

Figure 6, the query \mathbf{q} points to the upper right. Under cosine similarity, \mathbf{d} has the highest score because it has the smallest angle to \mathbf{q}. Under the dot product, \mathbf{e} wins, because no other point lies beyond the hyperplane through \mathbf{e} orthogonal to \mathbf{q}. Both best matches lie in the query’s quadrant.



Figure 6:A query \mathbf{q} and candidate points in 2D: the best matches under cosine (\mathbf{d}) and dot product (\mathbf{e}) lie in the query’s quadrant.

The high-dimensional counterpart of a quadrant is an orthant: the region in which every component has a fixed sign. Two dimensions have 4 quadrants; d dimensions have 2^{d} orthants. Two vectors share an orthant if their components agree in sign in every dimension. For random vectors, each sign agrees with probability 1/2, so two vectors share an orthant with probability 2^{-d}.

The number of orthants soon outgrows any collection. With one billion vectors, there are on average about one million vectors per orthant at d = 10, but fewer than one at d = 30, and about 8 \times 10^{-22} at d = 100. Most orthants are empty, and almost no two vectors share one. “The same direction as the query” no longer describes any stored vector.

Conceptually, this is not yet a problem. Each dimension of an embedding can be read as a latent concept, and two vectors that agree on most concepts are similar even if they disagree on a few. Agreement in many dimensions is good enough. The trouble lies in how much “many” still stands out.

Figure 7 shows the dot product between pairs of random unit vectors. At d = 2, the values spread over the full range from -1 to 1. As the dimension grows, they concentrate around 0, and at d = 8192 they form a narrow spike: two random vectors in high dimensions are almost orthogonal.



Figure 7:Dot products between random unit vectors, from d = 2 to d = 8192.

A short statistical argument explains the spike. Draw the components x_k and y_k of two vectors independently and uniformly from [-1, 1]. Each product x_k y_k has expected value 0 and variance 1/9. The dot product is the sum of d such products, so it has expected value 0 in any dimension, and its standard deviation grows like \sqrt{d}/3. The lengths of the two vectors, however, grow faster: each is about \sqrt{d/3}, so their product is about d/3. Dividing the two gives the cosine, whose spread shrinks with the dimension.

Key Formula: Concentration of Cosine Similarity

For two independent random vectors in d dimensions, the cosine similarity has expected value 0 and a standard deviation of about\sigma_{\cos} \approx \frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}

The positive and negative products cancel out more and more completely; random vectors become almost orthogonal.

What does this mean for the dot product? For unit vectors, which most embedding models produce and which 

Figure 7 uses, the dot product is the cosine, and nothing changes. For vectors that are not normalized, the spread of the dot product grows like \sqrt{d}/3, so in absolute numbers it does not shrink. But it must be read against the scale of the vectors: the largest possible dot product of two vectors is the product of their lengths, about d/3. Relative to this scale, the spread is (\sqrt{d}/3) / (d/3) = 1/\sqrt{d}, exactly as for the cosine.

The lengths themselves concentrate as well. In our example, the length of a random vector is about \sqrt{d/3} with a spread of about 0.26 in every dimension, so its relative variation shrinks like 1/\sqrt{d}: about 4.5 percent at d = 100 and 1.6 percent at d = 768. The dot product is the cosine multiplied by two almost equal lengths, and it ranks random vectors almost exactly like the cosine. In a simulation with 20,000 pairs, the correlation between the two measures is 0.88 at d = 2, 0.998 at d = 100, and 0.9997 at d = 768. The length effect that separates the dot product from the cosine in 2D fades, and the concentration applies to both measures. Learned embeddings may still carry some information in their lengths, but the random background against which a good match must stand out concentrates in the same way.

For the 768-dimensional embeddings of the previous chapter, \sigma_{\cos} \approx 1/\sqrt{768} = 0.036; at d = 8192, it is 0.011, and the values that separate good from bad matches differ in the third decimal. Even the best of one million random vectors reaches a cosine of only about 0.17 at d = 768.

The discussion now runs parallel to the one for distances. Vectors that live alone in their orthants are hard to group, because no two of them agree in all signs, and the loss of contrast again weakens the meaning of similarity. Real data again saves the method. The embeddings of related documents form clusters, and their cosine values stand far above the narrow band around zero that random pairs occupy. A relevant document is an outlier in the distribution of scores. But among these outliers, the top few scores lie close together, and the document with the highest score is not necessarily the best semantic match. Any of the top-k results may be an equally good, or even better, answer.

records.content:
High-dimensional space does not behave like the plane on which our intuition was trained. Distances grow, their contrast fades, and directions become meaningless; index structures that prune well in 2D end up visiting every leaf. At the same time, the loss of contrast questions the goal itself. When the nearest neighbor is only marginally nearer than its competitors, chasing the exact nearest neighbor is wasted effort. What matters is to find good matches: points that clearly stand out from the uniform background, even if they are not provably the nearest.

The retrieval pipelines of 

Building Semantic Search relax the requirement further. A fast retriever based on embeddings collects candidates, and a reranker reorders them with a more precise but more expensive model. The retriever does not need to deliver the exact top-k in the exact order, as long as the good hits are among its candidates; the reranker restores the precision. Exact nearest-neighbor search is therefore rarely needed. Giving up exactness on purpose, and searching approximately for good matches, buys back the speed that the curse of dimensionality took away. This is the subject of the next section.

Hands-on: The curse of dimensionality

Watch distance distributions collapse in a Monte Carlo experiment, measure how the contrast between the nearest and the farthest point shrinks with the dimension, and explore the escaping-sphere puzzle and the thin outer shell of high-dimensional space.


Open notebook ->

Includes pre-run results: you can read through or download and experiment.

A retrieval system rarely shows the raw output of a vector search to its users. In 

Semantic Similarity with Transformers, embeddings served as a first stage: a bi-encoder retrieves a few hundred candidates, and a cross-encoder reorders them with a stronger and more expensive model. Media retrieval follows the same pattern. A compact color feature finds candidate images, and a more detailed comparison puts them in their final order. For such a first stage, the exact nearest neighbor has no special value. What matters is that the good matches are among the candidates, because the second stage decides their order.

Even without a second stage, users want to see good matches, not necessarily the single best one. The previous section showed that high dimensions reduce contrast: the nearest neighbor is only marginally closer than the next few points, and all of them stand out clearly from the background. Returning the third-best match instead of the best one hardly changes what the user sees. This opens the door to a trade: we give up exactness and gain speed.

What carries over from the previous section

High dimensions defy 2D intuition: distances grow like \sqrt{d}, while their spread stays the same. The contrast between the nearest and the farthest point vanishes, (\delta_{\max} - \delta_{\min}) / \delta_{\min} \to 0, and dot products of random vectors concentrate around zero. This holds for Euclidean distance, dot product, and cosine alike.

Trees can no longer prune: beyond a few dozen dimensions, the sphere around the query that passes through its nearest neighbor intersects every leaf, so even the optimal search algorithm reads all the data. In practice, a full scan is faster than a tree index beyond roughly ten dimensions.

Real data still works: related items form clusters, and good matches stand out clearly from a background in which everything else appears equally far away.

For the full background, see 

The Curse of Dimensionality.

How can we accelerate the search? A full scan reads every vector, so its cost is the number of vectors times the size of each vector. A concrete collection makes this tangible. One billion embeddings with 768 dimensions, stored as 4-byte floats, occupy 10^9 \times 768 \times 4 bytes, about 3 TB. A full scan reads all 3 TB for every query. There are three levers to reduce this volume, and this section treats them in turn:

Fewer dimensions: map the vectors into a lower-dimensional space.

Fewer bits per vector: store each vector as a compact code.

Fewer vectors read: visit only the part of the collection near the query.

Each lever trades a little accuracy for speed. Combined, they reduce the work per query by two to three orders of magnitude.

The first lever shrinks every vector before the search starts. Principal component analysis (PCA) finds the directions along which the data varies most and projects every vector onto the leading ones. It works well when the original dimensions are not independent. The color histogram of 

Distance and Similarity Measures is a good case. Neighboring bins cover similar intensities, so a slightly brighter photograph moves pixels from one bin into the next. Correlated dimensions carry overlapping information, and a few principal components capture most of it. Distances in the reduced space then approximate the distances in the original space well.

Embeddings can be trained for this purpose. The Matryoshka embeddings of 

Building Semantic Search arrange their information so that the leading dimensions carry the most significant part, and a prefix of the vector is itself a usable embedding. Truncation needs no projection at all, only a shorter read.

Dimensionality reduction is a modest lever. Depending on the features, it removes roughly 20 to 60 percent of the data without changing the results much. Reducing our example collection from 768 to 384 dimensions halves 3 TB to 1.5 TB. Every vector must still be read, so the search remains a full scan, only a cheaper one.

The second lever keeps the dimensions but stores each vector with fewer bits. A float uses 32 bits per component, far more precision than a similarity comparison needs. The errors that compression introduces are small compared to the gap between good matches and the background, so they rarely change which matches stand out.

The simplest form replaces each float with a small integer. We divide the value range of each dimension into 2^b intervals and store only the number of the interval that contains the value. With b = 8, every component becomes one byte, and the vector shrinks by a factor of 4. With b = 4, as in the FAISS index type SQ4, it shrinks by a factor of 8. Distances computed on the interval numbers are approximations of the true distances.

Quantization does not have to give up exactness. The vector approximation file (VA-file) of Weber, Schek, and Blott (1998) accepts the conclusion of the previous section: if every leaf must be read anyway, make reading cheaper. The interval numbers of a vector describe a cell of a grid, and from the cell we can compute a lower and an upper bound on the distance between the query and any vector inside it. The search first scans the compact approximations and discards every vector whose lower bound exceeds the k-th smallest upper bound. Only the few remaining candidates are read in full and compared exactly. The result is exact, while the scan reads only a fraction of the data. Skipping the exact comparisons turns the same codes into an approximate method. Scalar quantization is therefore the bridge between exact and approximate search.

How the VA-file stays exact (optional reading)

Consider two dimensions with values in [0, 1] and b = 2 bits per dimension. Each dimension splits into four intervals of width 0.25, and every vector is stored as two 2-bit numbers. The vector \mathbf{p} = (0.62, 0.10) lies in interval 2 of the first dimension, [0.50, 0.75], and in interval 0 of the second, [0, 0.25], so its approximation is the code (10, 00).

For the query \mathbf{q} = (0.20, 0.55), the code alone bounds the distance. In the first dimension, any value in [0.50, 0.75] lies at least 0.50 - 0.20 = 0.30 and at most 0.75 - 0.20 = 0.55 from q_1. In the second dimension, any value in [0, 0.25] lies at least 0.55 - 0.25 = 0.30 and at most 0.55 - 0 = 0.55 from q_2. Combining the two dimensions gives \sqrt{0.30^2 + 0.30^2} \approx 0.42 as the lower bound and \sqrt{0.55^2 + 0.55^2} \approx 0.78 as the upper bound. The exact distance, \sqrt{0.42^2 + 0.45^2} \approx 0.62, lies between them.

The search runs in two phases. The filtering phase scans all approximations, computes both bounds for each, and keeps track of the k smallest upper bounds. A vector whose lower bound exceeds the k-th smallest upper bound cannot be among the k nearest neighbors and is discarded. The refinement phase visits the remaining candidates in order of increasing lower bound, reads their exact vectors, and computes their true distances. It stops as soon as the next lower bound exceeds the k-th smallest true distance found so far, because no later candidate can be closer.

Both phases are exact, so the result is exact. The gain comes from the size of the approximations: with 4 to 8 bits per dimension, the filtering phase reads 4 to 8 times less data than a full scan, and only a small number of exact vectors is read in the refinement phase. Because the scan is sequential, it also avoids the random disk accesses of a tree index.

Scalar quantization treats every dimension separately and needs at least one bit per dimension. Product quantization (PQ), introduced by Jégou, Douze, and Schmid (2011), quantizes groups of dimensions together. 

Figure 1 shows the idea for the eight-dimensional vector (0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.2, 0.6, 0.4, 0.9, 0.8). We split it into m = 4 sub-vectors of two components each: (0.1, 0.3), (0.5, 0.2), (0.6, 0.4), and (0.9, 0.8). Each sub-space has its own codebook of 2^b representative sub-vectors, found by running k-means on the sub-vectors of the collection. With b = 2, each codebook holds four centers, and each sub-vector is replaced by the 2-bit number of its nearest center: 00, 10, 01, and 10. The code 10 appears twice but refers to different centers, because sub-spaces 2 and 4 have different codebooks. Instead of eight floats with 256 bits, the vector is stored in 8 bits, a compression of 1:32.



Figure 1:Product quantization of an eight-dimensional vector. The vector is split into four sub-vectors, and each sub-vector is replaced by the 2-bit number of its nearest center in its own codebook. Eight floats become 8 bits.

The search uses lookup tables. We split the query \mathbf{q} in the same way into \mathbf{q}_1, \dots, \mathbf{q}_m and compute, for every sub-space j and every center of its codebook, the squared distance between \mathbf{q}_j and that center. This fills m tables with 2^b entries each, once per query. The approximate distance to a stored vector is then a sum of m table look-ups, one per code.

Key Formula: Product Quantization Distance\tilde{\delta}(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{p})^2 = \sum_{j=1}^{m} \lVert \mathbf{q}_j - \mathbf{c}_j(\mathbf{p}) \rVert^2

Here \mathbf{c}_j(\mathbf{p}) is the center of codebook j that represents the j-th sub-vector of \mathbf{p}. The query stays exact; only the stored vector is replaced by its centers, so each term is read from a table computed once per query.

Example

For our collection of one billion 768-dimensional vectors, we choose m = 96 sub-vectors of 8 dimensions each and b = 8 bits per code. Every vector becomes 96 bytes instead of 3,072, a compression of 1:32, and the whole collection needs 96 GB instead of 3 TB. Per query, the lookup tables hold 96 \times 256 entries, each a distance over 8 dimensions: 96 \times 256 \times 8 \approx 197{,}000 multiply-adds, as much as comparing the query with 256 full vectors. Against a billion stored vectors, this cost is negligible. Each stored vector then costs 96 look-ups and additions instead of 768 multiply-adds, and 96 bytes read instead of 3,072.

The standard choice is b = 8: each code is one byte, and each table of 256 entries fits into the processor cache. The sub-vector length then sets the compression. Sub-vectors of 4 to 16 dimensions give ratios between 16 and 64 times over 4-byte floats. Jégou and colleagues stored 128-dimensional SIFT image descriptors in 8 bytes, a ratio of 64. Longer sub-vectors compress more but approximate the distance more coarsely, which a final reranking step on the exact vectors compensates. At 96 bytes for 768 dimensions, PQ uses exactly one bit per dimension, and at 48 bytes only half a bit, a rate that scalar quantization cannot reach.

Locality-sensitive hashing (LSH), one of the first approximate methods from the late 1990s, maps vectors to bit strings. It chooses h hyperplanes and records for each one on which side a vector lies: bit j is 1 if the vector lies on the positive side of hyperplane j and 0 otherwise. In 

Figure 2, three hyperplanes divide the plane into seven regions. One of the eight possible 3-bit codes does not occur, because three lines cannot create more than seven regions in the plane. The query \mathbf{q} lies on the positive side of hyperplane 1 only, so its code is 100. Points in the same region share the query’s code, and points in a neighboring region differ from it in one bit.



Figure 2:Locality-sensitive hashing with three hyperplanes. Each point receives one bit per hyperplane, set to 1 on the positive side. The query \mathbf{q} lies on the positive side of hyperplane 1 only and receives the code 100.

The obvious way to use the codes is as hash buckets: return the points that share the query’s code. This fails as soon as h grows. With 64 hyperplanes there are 

264 possible codes, far more than stored vectors, so most buckets are empty, and the query’s bucket is likely empty as well. LSH therefore ranks all stored codes by their Hamming distance to the query’s code, the number of bits in which they differ, and returns the vectors with the smallest Hamming distance. Comparing bit strings is extremely cheap: an exclusive-or followed by a count of the set bits. With h = 256 hyperplanes, a 768-dimensional vector shrinks from 3,072 bytes to 32 bytes, a factor of 96. Since the Hamming distance takes only h + 1 different values, many vectors tie, and an exact reranking of the best candidates resolves the ties.

The Hamming distance is a good proxy because it tracks the angle between vectors. For random hyperplanes through the origin, the probability that a hyperplane separates two vectors equals \theta / \pi, where \theta is the angle between them, so the expected Hamming distance is h \cdot \theta / \pi. The hyperplanes in the figure are drawn freely to make the regions visible; the analysis assumes hyperplanes through the origin, the common choice in practice. Because LSH approximates the angle, it serves cosine similarity directly. For the dot product, the extension trick of 

Low-Dimensional Search Structures first gives all stored vectors the same length, after which ranking by angle equals ranking by dot product.

Why the Hamming distance tracks the angle (optional reading)

Consider two vectors \mathbf{x} and \mathbf{y} with angle \theta between them, and a random hyperplane through the origin. The hyperplane separates the two vectors if they fall on different sides, which gives them different bits. Only the plane spanned by \mathbf{x} and \mathbf{y} matters for this question. The hyperplane cuts this plane along a line through the origin, and for a random hyperplane the direction of this line is uniformly distributed.

The line separates \mathbf{x} from \mathbf{y} exactly if it passes through the angle between them. A line through the origin covers two opposite directions, so it falls into the angle \theta or into its mirror image on the other side of the origin. Both together cover 2\theta of the full circle of 2\pi, and the probability of a separating hyperplane is 2\theta / 2\pi = \theta / \pi. This argument is due to Charikar (2002), who introduced hyperplane hashing for the cosine.

With h independent hyperplanes, the Hamming distance is a count of h independent events with probability \theta / \pi each. Its expected value is h \cdot \theta / \pi, and its standard deviation is \sqrt{h \cdot (\theta / \pi)(1 - \theta / \pi)}. For h = 256 and \theta = \pi / 4, the expected Hamming distance is 64 with a standard deviation of about 6.9. The estimate of \theta / \pi is therefore accurate to about \pm 0.03, and more bits make it more accurate.

The same reasoning explains the limits of LSH. Two vectors at angles of 0.24\pi and 0.26\pi to the query are hard to tell apart with 256 bits, which is exactly the situation inside a cluster, where the nearest neighbors are almost equally close. LSH finds the cluster reliably but not the order within it. This is why LSH results are usually reranked with exact vectors.

The second lever gains between a factor of 4 for 8-bit scalar quantization and roughly a factor of 100 for short LSH codes, with product quantization typically in between at 16 to 64. Every vector is still read, but each one costs only a fraction of a full comparison.

The third lever reduces the number of vectors read. This was the idea behind the tree structures in 

Low-Dimensional Search Structures: skip regions that cannot contain the answer. The previous section showed that exact pruning fails in high dimensions, because the sphere around the query intersects every region. Approximate methods relax the requirement. They visit only the regions most likely to contain good matches and accept that a neighbor just across a boundary may be missed. 

Figure 3 contrasts the two approaches.



Figure 3:Exact search compares the query to every vector (left). An approximate method partitions the space into clusters and searches only those near the query (right), trading a little recall for a large speed-up.

The inverted file (IVF) borrows the inverted index from text retrieval. A clustering algorithm, usually k-means, chooses n_{\text{list}} centers and assigns every vector to its nearest center, as in 

Figure 4. The index is a dictionary that maps each center to the list of its vectors, just as an inverted index maps each term to its posting list. A query is first compared with all centers, and the search then scans only the lists of the n_{\text{probe}} nearest centers. The share of the collection read is n_{\text{probe}} / n_{\text{list}}. For our billion vectors with n_{\text{list}} = 4{,}096, each list holds about 244,000 vectors, and probing 16 lists reads 1/256 of the collection.



Figure 4:An inverted file clusters the data around centers. The query is routed to its nearest center \mathbf{c}_2, and only that cluster’s list is scanned; probing more clusters trades speed for recall.

The parameter n_{\text{probe}} is the tuning knob. A neighbor that sits just across a cluster boundary is missed if its list is not probed, and each additional list recovers some of these misses. The cost grows linearly with the number of probed lists, while the gain in recall shrinks. The following measurements from the ann-benchmarks project, discussed below, use FAISS with 4,096 lists on 1.2 million GloVe word vectors with 100 dimensions:

Doubling the probes from 100 to 200 almost halves the throughput but adds only 4 points of recall. Even at 200 probes, the search is 18 times faster than the full scan, which manages 16.5 queries per second on the same hardware.

A different approach navigates a graph. A navigable small-world (NSW) graph turns every vector into a node and links it to a fixed number of its nearest neighbors, its “friends”, plus some long-range links that act as shortcuts across the space. The graph has two key properties. It is navigable: from any node, a step to the neighbor closest to the query makes progress toward the query. And it is a small world: any two nodes are connected by a short path, whose length grows only poly-logarithmically with the number of nodes.

Search starts at an entry point and greedily moves to whichever neighbor is closest to the query, as traced in 

Figure 5. It stops when no neighbor is closer than the current node. This node is a local minimum of the distance on the graph, not necessarily the global one, which is why the result is approximate. To reduce the risk of stopping early, the search keeps a list of the best ef_{\text{search}} candidates instead of a single node and expands all of them. A longer list costs more steps and finds better neighbors.



Figure 5:Greedy search on a navigable small-world graph. From the entry point, each step moves to the neighbor closest to the query \mathbf{q} until no neighbor is closer.

The hierarchical version, HNSW (Malkov and Yashunin, 2016), stacks several such graphs. The base layer contains all vectors. Each higher layer contains a random subset of the layer below, with fewer and fewer nodes toward the top. The search starts at the top, where few nodes and long links cover large distances in few steps. It then descends layer by layer, using the best node of each layer as the entry point for the next one, and refines the result on the base layer. Two parameters control the index: M, the number of links per node, and ef_{\text{search}}, the length of the candidate list. HNSW is among the fastest ANN methods and is included in most vector databases.

The speed has a price. The links need memory: with M = 32, the base layer stores about 64 links of 4 bytes per node, roughly 256 bytes per vector. Greedy steps jump to arbitrary nodes, so the vectors must reside in main memory. For our billion vectors, this means 3 TB of vectors plus 256 GB of links in memory. Building the graph is also slow, because every insertion runs a search to find the new node’s friends.

The graph and the inverted file combine well. Instead of single vectors, the base layer can hold clusters: the graph is built over the IVF centers, and each center points to its list. This matters when the number of lists is large. With n_{\text{list}} = 65{,}536 lists for a billion vectors, comparing the query with every center already becomes noticeable, while a graph over the centers finds the nearest ones in a few steps. The search then scans the lists of the n_{\text{probe}} nearest centers, and its cost again grows linearly with the number of lists visited. In FAISS, the coarse quantizer IVF65536_HNSW32 implements this design. It also suits collections larger than main memory: the graph over the centers stays in memory, while the lists reside on disk.

No single lever wins on its own, so production libraries combine all three. Facebook AI Similarity Search (FAISS) is the standard example. It organizes an index into four stages, which map directly onto the levers:

Vector transformers prepare vectors: PCA to reduce dimensions (lever 1), or L2-normalization for cosine search.

Coarse quantizers select the vectors to read, for example with IVF or HNSW (lever 3).

Fine quantizers encode the selected vectors compactly, for example with scalar quantization, PQ, or LSH (lever 2).

Refiners rerank the best k' candidates with exact distances on the original vectors, or apply metadata filters.

A FAISS index type names its stages in this order. For our billion vectors, PCA384,IVF4096,PQ48,RFlat reduces the vectors to 384 dimensions, clusters them into 4,096 lists, encodes each vector into 48 bytes, and reranks the best candidates exactly. The codes of the whole collection take 48 GB and fit into main memory. Probing 16 lists reads 10^9 / 256 \approx 3.9 million codes of 48 bytes each, about 190 MB per query. Reranking k' = 100 candidates reads another 300 KB of exact vectors from disk. Compared with the 3 TB of a full scan, the data read per query shrinks by a factor of about 16,000. The actual speed-up is smaller, because table look-ups, center comparisons, and random reads also cost time.

The levers compound their errors as well as their gains. PCA loses some information, PQ distorts the distances, and IVF misses neighbors in unprobed lists. Each error alone is harmless, but stacking several approximations can reduce result quality quickly. The parameters, here the target dimension, the code length, n_{\text{list}}, n_{\text{probe}}, and k', must therefore be tuned together, by measuring the result quality on a sample of queries, ideally against relevance judgments rather than only against exact search.

Every ANN method exposes parameters that trade recall for speed: the number of probed lists in IVF, the candidate list length in HNSW, the code length in PQ and LSH. To compare methods fairly, we measure both axes at once. The quality axis is recall against the exact result.

Key Formula: Recall@k for Approximate Search\text{recall@}k = \frac{\lvert \text{approximate top-}k ∩ \text{exact top-}k \rvert}{k}

The fraction of the true k nearest neighbors that the approximate search also returned; 1.0 means the approximation matched exact search on this query.

The speed axis is throughput, in queries per second. Plotting throughput against recall traces a curve for each method, and the public benchmark at 

ann-benchmarks.com collects these curves for many libraries on standard datasets. 

Figure 6 shows the comparison on GloVe-100: 1.2 million word vectors with 100 dimensions, compared by cosine, with k = 10. Reading it is straightforward: fix the recall you need, then pick the method with the highest throughput at that recall. A method whose curve lies above another one dominates it.



Figure 6:Recall versus queries per second for about 30 ANN methods on GloVe-100 (k = 10, cosine), from ann-benchmarks. Up and to the right is better; at a chosen recall, the highest curve is the fastest method.

The plot quantifies the trade. The full scan reaches 16.5 queries per second at a recall of 1.0. The fastest method at each recall level does far better:

Approximation buys two to three orders of magnitude, and the last few points of recall are the most expensive. The plot does not show everything, though. Memory use and build time appear in separate plots on the benchmark site, and they are where methods differ most: HNSW needs its graph and the full vectors in memory, while PQ needs a fraction of the memory and builds quickly.

The ann-benchmarks view makes approximation look costly. The last points of recall are expensive, and many cheap configurations return only a third of the exact top 10. But recall against exact search compares one retriever with another. A user never sees the exact top 10. The user sees the final result of a pipeline, and its quality is measured against relevance judgments with nDCG, as in 

Evaluating Graded Relevance.

We test this on TREC-COVID: 171,332 abstracts of COVID-19 research papers, 50 topics, and graded relevance judgments. The retrievers combine the three levers. Matryoshka embeddings from Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B are truncated to between 1024 and 64 dimensions. A full scan, IVF, or HNSW selects the vectors, and exact floats, PQ codes, or LSH bits compare them. This gives 140 retrievers. Each returns its top 50, and the cross-encoder Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B reorders them into the final top 10. TREC judged only the documents that the systems of 2020 retrieved, so the pool from 

Designing a Retrieval Benchmark misses documents that only an approximate retriever surfaces. An LLM judge graded these missing pairs. Otherwise they would count as not relevant and penalize exactly the retrievers we want to evaluate.

Figure 7 measures every retriever in three ways. We focus on the 126 retrievers that read at least 100 times less data than a full scan. Against exact search (left), their median recall@10 is 0.24, so the typical cheap retriever returns only a quarter of the exact top 10. By this measure, approximate search fails. Judged for relevance (middle), the same top 10 reach a median nDCG@10 of 0.80, against 0.91 for exact search. The documents they return instead of the exact neighbors are often just as relevant. This is the loss of contrast from 

The Curse of Dimensionality at work: the exact neighbors are only marginally nearer than the next candidates, and many of those candidates are good matches too. After reranking (right), the median rises to 0.88, against 0.92 for exact search, and 44 percent of the cheap retrievers end within 0.03 of exact search.



Figure 7:Recall against exact search (left), nDCG@10 of the retriever alone (middle), and nDCG@10 after reranking its top 50 (right) for 140 retrievers on TREC-COVID. Each point is one retriever; the dashed line marks exact search.

Figure 8 follows five retrievers through the pipeline. One retriever uses 256 dimensions, 16 of 1,024 IVF lists, and 32-byte PQ codes. It reads 608 times less data than a full scan and returns only a third of the exact top 10, yet after reranking it reaches an nDCG@10 of 0.92, the same as exact search. HNSW on 64-dimensional embeddings reads 2,604 times less data with the same result. Once a reranker follows, even aggressive Matryoshka truncation costs almost nothing.



Figure 8:nDCG@10 of five retrievers alone and after reranking, annotated with recall@10 against exact search and the share of data read.

The two remaining retrievers show where this stops. PQ with 8 bytes per vector distorts the distances so strongly that only 6 percent of the exact top 10 survive, and on its own it reaches an nDCG@10 of 0.66. Many relevant documents are still among its 50 candidates, so the reranker lifts the result to 0.80 and repairs more than half of the gap. IVF with a single probed list fails differently. It never reads the clusters next to the query’s own cluster, so the reranker never sees their documents, and the result stays at 0.86 before and after reranking. Fine-filter errors are repairable; coarse-filter errors are not. Production systems therefore keep the coarse filter generous, with enough probed lists or a long candidate list, and let the fine filter be aggressive.

There is no single best method, only the best operating point for a given collection, memory budget, and quality target. Recall against exact search is a useful diagnostic for one index, but the operating point should be chosen on end-to-end quality: the cheapest retriever whose reranked result stays close to that of exact search. The benchmark above covers one collection and one embedding model, so the operating point must be measured again for each application. HNSW is a strong default as long as the vectors fit into main memory. Beyond that, IVF with product quantization and a final reranking step is the common choice.

The methods of the previous section rarely reach an application in raw form. They arrive packaged inside libraries, search engines, and databases that also handle storage, updates, and scale. This section follows one realistic query through four widely used systems: the FAISS library, the Lucene library, the OpenSearch engine, and the pgvector extension for PostgreSQL. We first look at how each system answers the vector part of the query, and then at how each one adds metadata filters and keyword search.

The movie table of 

Practical Frameworks stored a title, an overview, a rating, and a year for every movie. We extend it with two text fields, the main actors and the genres, and with an embedding of the overview, computed by an embedding model as in 

Building Semantic Search. With a model such as Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, every movie receives a vector with 1,024 dimensions. A user now types:

a mind-bending heist thriller with Leonardo DiCaprio, released after 2005, rated 7.5 or better

No single retrieval method covers this request. Each part of it asks for a different kind of match:

Part of the query

Kind of match

Handled by

“mind-bending heist”

meaning of the plot

vector search on the overview embedding

“with Leonardo DiCaprio”

exact name

BM25 on the actors field

“thriller”

category term

BM25 on the genres field

“released after 2005”, “rated 7.5 or better”

hard constraints

filters on year and rating

The overview of Inception describes a thief who steals secrets by entering the dreams of his targets. It contains neither “mind-bending” nor “heist”, so BM25 on the overview would miss it. An embedding does better, but not well enough on its own: among 10,000 movies embedded with Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, the vector search alone ranks Inception only 138th, behind movies whose overviews match “heist thriller” more literally. Names behave the other way round. An embedding blurs “Leonardo DiCaprio” into a region of similar actors, while BM25 matches the name exactly. The year and the rating are not matters of degree at all: a movie from 2001 must not appear, however similar it is. Each ingredient matters. The filters on year and rating lift Inception to second place among the 261 admitted movies, and fusing the vector ranking with BM25 on the actors puts it first. The rest of this section builds this query step by step: first the vector search, then the filters and the keyword search.

FAISS (Facebook AI Similarity Search), developed at Meta, is a C++ library with Python bindings that runs on CPUs and GPUs. It implements all methods of the previous section and lets us combine them freely through index type strings. FAISS stores only vectors and their integer identifiers. The titles, the actors, and the years stay in the application’s own data store, and the application maps the returned identifiers back to movies.import faiss
import numpy as np

# 1. Movie embeddings (one row per movie) and their movie ids
X = np.load("overview_embeddings.npy").astype("float32")   # shape (n, 1024)
ids = np.load("movie_ids.npy").astype("int64")
faiss.normalize_L2(X)               # unit length: inner product = cosine

# 2. Build an IVF index with PQ codes (lever 3 + lever 2)
index = faiss.index_factory(1024, "IVF256,PQ64", faiss.METRIC_INNER_PRODUCT)
index.train(X)                      # k-means for the centers and the codebooks
index.add_with_ids(X, ids)

# 3. Search: embed the query and probe 16 of the 256 lists
q = embed("a mind-bending heist thriller").reshape(1, -1)
faiss.normalize_L2(q)
index.nprobe = 16
scores, movie_ids = index.search(q, 10)

Step 1 normalizes the vectors, so that the inner product equals the cosine similarity. Step 2 builds the composite index of the previous section: train runs k-means to find the 256 centers of the inverted file and the codebooks of the product quantizer, and add_with_ids encodes every vector into 64 one-byte codes. Step 3 sets the tuning knob n_{\text{probe}} and returns the ten best movie ids with their approximate scores. Changing the index string, for example to HNSW32 or to IVF256,PQ64,RFlat with an exact refinement stage, changes the method without changing the rest of the code.

The pgvector extension adds a vector column type to PostgreSQL. We extend the movie table with a vector column and an HNSW index:-- 1. Enable the extension and add a vector column
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector;
ALTER TABLE movies ADD COLUMN embedding vector(1024);

-- 2. Approximate index: HNSW with cosine distance
CREATE INDEX ON movies USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops)
  WITH (m = 16, ef_construction = 64);

-- 3. k-NN query: order by cosine distance to the query embedding
SET hnsw.ef_search = 100;
SELECT title, year, embedding <=> '[0.021, -0.013, ...]' AS distance
FROM movies
ORDER BY embedding <=> '[0.021, -0.013, ...]'   -- 1,024 values
LIMIT 10;

pgvector works with distances: smaller is better. The operator <=> computes the cosine distance 1 - \cos, <-> the Euclidean distance, <+> the Manhattan distance, and <#> the negative dot product, negated to fit the same convention. Without an index, the query scans all rows and returns exact results. With the HNSW index of step 2, PostgreSQL’s planner uses the index for the ORDER BY ... LIMIT pattern. The index parameters are m (default 16) and ef_construction (default 64); the query parameter hnsw.ef_search (default 40) sets the candidate list length. The second index type, IVFFlat, is an inverted file with exact vectors in its lists, with lists centers and ivfflat.probes probed lists (default 1).

pgvector also exposes the other two levers. A halfvec column stores 16-bit floats. The function binary_quantize reduces every component to its sign bit, compared with the Hamming distance operator <~>. An index on subvector(embedding, 1, 256) searches only the leading 256 components of a Matryoshka embedding. The refine step is plain SQL: an inner query retrieves candidates through a compact index, and an outer query reorders them by the full vectors.-- Binary codes for the candidate search, full vectors for the final order
CREATE INDEX ON movies
  USING hnsw ((binary_quantize(embedding)::bit(1024)) bit_hamming_ops);

SELECT title FROM (
  SELECT title, embedding FROM movies
  ORDER BY binary_quantize(embedding)::bit(1024)
           <~> binary_quantize('[0.021, ...]'::vector)
  LIMIT 100                                     -- k' = 100 candidates
) AS candidates
ORDER BY embedding <=> '[0.021, ...]'
LIMIT 10;

The vector query finds movies with mind-bending heist plots, but it ignores the rest of the request. We now add the filters on year and rating and the keyword part for the actor and the genre.

Combining a filter with a vector search is harder than it looks, because the ANN index knows nothing about the metadata. There are three strategies.

Pre-filtering applies the metadata condition first and then compares the query exactly with the vectors that pass. The result is exact, and the cost depends on how many vectors pass. A selective filter makes this cheap: if a filter admits 0.01% of the billion vectors of the previous section, an exact scan over the 100,000 survivors reads only 300 MB. A mild filter makes it expensive, because the scan over the survivors approaches a full scan.

Post-filtering runs the ANN search first and discards the results that fail the filter. This keeps the index intact, but it can return too few results. With HNSW and the default hnsw.ef_search of 40, a pgvector index scan delivers about 40 candidates. If the filter matches 10% of the rows, only about 4 of them survive, even if the query asked for 10. A fixed over-fetch, retrieving more candidates than requested, helps only if we guess the selectivity right. The robust form treats the index as a stream of candidates in order of increasing distance, like the incremental nearest-neighbor algorithm of 

Low-Dimensional Search Structures: the filter consumes candidates from the stream until k of them pass. HNSW suits this form well. Its search already maintains a queue of candidates, and continuing the search simply extends the queue into regions further away from the query. pgvector’s iterative index scans work this way.

Post-filtering can silently return too few results

If a query asks for the ten nearest neighbors and then removes those failing a selective filter, the final list may contain far fewer than ten items, or be empty, even though many matching documents exist deeper in the ranking. Over-fetch a larger candidate set before filtering, and verify that enough results survive.

Filtering during the search evaluates the filter first, for example as a bitmap over all document ids, and passes it to the ANN search, which only accepts admitted documents as results. This fits the inverted file particularly well. An IVF search with PQ codes scans the lists of the probed centers entry by entry anyway; checking each entry against the bitmap costs one bit lookup and lets the scan skip the distance computation for every non-admitted vector. The search itself does not change, only its result is restricted. In the billion-vector example with 16 of 4,096 lists probed, the scan visits about 3.9 million codes. If the filter admits 1% of the collection, about 39,000 of these are admitted, far more than needed for a top 10.

The limit lies in very selective filters. If the filter admits only 0.001% of the collection, the probed lists contain about 39 admitted vectors, and the ten best of them may be poor matches, because the good admitted matches lie in lists that were not probed. Probing more lists helps, but at this selectivity the 10,000 admitted vectors fit into an exact scan of 30 MB, which is both cheaper and exact. Systems that filter during the search therefore choose per query: if only a few documents pass the filter, they skip the index and fall back to pre-filtering with an exact scan. Graph indexes can filter during the search as well, but they must still step through non-matching nodes, because these can lie on the path to a matching one. With a selective filter, most steps of the graph search are wasted.

Keyword search adds a second ranking. 

Building Semantic Search fused a BM25 ranking and a dense ranking with reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) in Pipeline D. RRF needs only ranks, so it fuses a cosine similarity and a BM25 score without calibrating them against each other. The four systems differ in which strategy they use for filters and in how much of the fusion they provide.

In SQL, the filter is an ordinary WHERE clause. With an approximate index, PostgreSQL applies it after the index scan, which is post-filtering with the risk described above. Since version 0.8, pgvector’s iterative index scans continue through the index until enough rows pass the filter. The keyword part uses PostgreSQL’s full-text search from 

Practical Frameworks, and the fusion is written in SQL:-- 1. Filtered vector search; continue the index scan until enough rows pass
SET hnsw.iterative_scan = relaxed_order;

-- 2. Hybrid search: dense and sparse rankings, fused with RRF (k = 60)
WITH dense AS (
  SELECT id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY embedding <=> '[0.021, ...]') AS r
  FROM movies
  WHERE year > 2005 AND rating >= 7.5
  ORDER BY embedding <=> '[0.021, ...]'
  LIMIT 50
),
sparse AS (
  SELECT id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY ts_rank(tsv, q) DESC) AS r
  FROM movies, to_tsquery('(leonardo <-> dicaprio) | thriller') AS q
  WHERE tsv @@ q AND year > 2005 AND rating >= 7.5
  ORDER BY ts_rank(tsv, q) DESC
  LIMIT 50
)
SELECT m.title,
       COALESCE(1.0 / (60 + d.r), 0) + COALESCE(1.0 / (60 + s.r), 0) AS rrf
FROM dense d
FULL OUTER JOIN sparse s ON d.id = s.id
JOIN movies m ON m.id = COALESCE(d.id, s.id)
ORDER BY rrf DESC
LIMIT 10;

Here the tsv column covers the actors and the genres in addition to the title and the overview. The dense part ranks the admitted movies by cosine distance, the sparse part ranks the movies that match the actor or the genre by ts_rank, and the final query adds the RRF contributions of both rankings. A movie found by only one of the two rankings receives a contribution of zero from the other. As noted in 

Practical Frameworks, ts_rank is not BM25, but RRF only uses the order of the sparse ranking, which makes the difference smaller.

The four systems implement the same methods but serve different settings. FAISS gives the most control over the index and the highest speed, including on GPUs, but it handles only vectors: filters, keyword search, storage, and updates remain the application’s job. Lucene keeps vectors, text, and metadata in one index and filters during the search, which suits Java applications that embed their search. OpenSearch adds distribution across many machines and a complete hybrid pipeline with filters and rank fusion, at the price of operating a cluster. pgvector keeps vectors next to the relational data, with SQL filters, joins, and transactions, and suits collections that fit on a single database server. Dedicated vector databases, such as Milvus, Qdrant, and Weaviate, follow the same patterns, and several of them appear in the benchmark of the previous section.

Whatever the system, the query of this section needs the same three ingredients: an approximate vector search for the meaning, a keyword search for names and terms, and filters for the hard constraints. What differs is how much of the combination the system does for us.

The levers are complementary rather than exclusive. A production index reduces the dimensions, selects a few lists or graph regions to read, encodes the vectors in those lists compactly, and reranks the best k' candidates with exact distances. For one billion 768-dimensional vectors, the stack PCA384,IVF4096,PQ48,RFlat reads about 190 MB per query instead of 3 TB. On the ann-benchmarks GloVe-100 dataset, the fastest methods answer 60 to 850 times more queries per second than a full scan, depending on the recall target. Recall against exact search is only part of the story: after reranking, retrievers with far lower recall reach almost the quality of exact search (see Key Takeaway 6).

Vectors come from learned embeddings or from perceptual features such as color histograms. They are compared either with a similarity score, where larger is better (dot product, cosine), or with a distance, where smaller is better (Euclidean, Manhattan). The comparison function belongs to the feature. Length normalization turns cosine similarity into a plain dot product, and on the unit sphere ranking by Euclidean distance equals ranking by cosine.

Classical spatial indexes (Voronoi diagram, grid file, R-tree) were built for two and three dimensions. The optimal algorithm of Hjaltason and Samet runs on all of them and needs only an optimistic bound per region, so it also works for the dot product. Even in 2D, a nearest-neighbor search follows several paths, because it must prove that no closer point exists.

The curse of dimensionality is quantifiable. Distances grow like \sqrt{d} while their spread stays constant, so the contrast between the nearest and the farthest point vanishes, and dot products of random vectors concentrate around zero. Once the expected nearest-neighbor distance exceeds the size of a leaf, even the optimal algorithm visits every leaf, and decades of R-tree variants did not change this.

Loss of contrast also weakens the meaning of “nearest”. Real data still works because related items form clusters that stand out from the background, but within a cluster the exact nearest neighbor is just one of several good matches. Vector search often serves as a first stage whose candidates a reranker reorders, and even without a reranker users want good matches rather than the single best one. Both arguments justify trading exactness for speed.

Approximate search pulls three levers. Fewer dimensions (PCA, Matryoshka) is a modest lever that still reads every vector. Fewer bits per vector (scalar quantization, product quantization, LSH) makes every comparison cheaper; the compression errors are small compared to the gap between good matches and the background, and the VA-file shows that bounds on the quantized cells even keep the search exact. Fewer vectors read (IVF, HNSW) visits only the regions near the query. Combined, the levers cut the work per query by two to three orders of magnitude, but their errors compound, so their parameters must be tuned together, on end-to-end quality rather than on recall alone.

Recall against exact search understates the quality of approximate search. On TREC-COVID, retrievers that read hundreds of times less data than a full scan return only a quarter of the exact top 10, yet after reranking many come within a few points of exact search, because the documents they return instead are often just as relevant. A reranker repairs fine-filter errors, such as coarse PQ codes, but not coarse-filter errors, such as unprobed IVF lists, so the coarse filter should stay generous.

In practice, vector search lives inside libraries (FAISS, Lucene), search engines (OpenSearch), and databases (pgvector). Realistic queries combine a vector search for meaning, a keyword search for names and terms, and filters for hard constraints. Filters are applied before, after, or during the search: pre-filtering suits selective filters, post-filtering suits graph indexes that deliver a stream of candidates, and filtering during the search suits the list scans of an inverted file. Dense and sparse rankings are fused with reciprocal rank fusion, as in 

Building Semantic Search.

Key Formula: Cosine Similarity and Normalization\text{sim}_{\text{cos}}(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{d}_i) = \frac{\mathbf{q} \cdot \mathbf{d}_i}{\lVert \mathbf{q} \rVert \, \lVert \mathbf{d}_i \rVert} = \hat{\mathbf{q}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{d}}

Normalize vectors once, then compare them with a dot product.

Key Formula: Product Quantization Distance\tilde{\delta}(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{p})^2 = \sum_{j=1}^{m} \lVert \mathbf{q}_j - \mathbf{c}_j(\mathbf{p}) \rVert^2

The exact query sub-vectors are compared with the codebook centers that represent the stored vector; each term is a look-up in a table computed once per query.

Key Formula: Recall@k\text{recall@}k = \frac{\lvert \text{approximate top-}k ∩ \text{exact top-}k \rvert}{k}

The ann-benchmarks quality axis: how well the approximate search reproduces exact search. It understates what the user sees, which is measured with nDCG against relevance judgments after reranking.

Reciprocal rank fusion, introduced in 

Building Semantic Search, remains the standard way to blend the dense and sparse rankings of a hybrid query.
