A generated answer can never be better than the evidence it is built from, so the retrieval metrics of 

Performance Evaluation still apply, recast to describe the retrieved context rather than a result list. Context recall asks whether everything needed to answer the question was retrieved. If a required fact never reaches the generator, no model and no prompt can recover it; the best it can do is admit the gap, and the worst is to invent the missing piece. Context precision asks how much of the retrieved context is actually relevant. Irrelevant passages are not harmless padding: they compete for the generator’s attention, and closely related but wrong evidence is the most dangerous kind.

Example: context recall and precision on the Nobel question

Recall the running question: “Who won the 2025 Nobel Prize in Physics, and which universities are they affiliated with?” A complete answer needs four pieces of evidence: one passage naming the three laureates and one affiliation for each of them.

A fixed pipeline that retrieves the top five chunks for the whole question returns the passage naming the winners, one laureate’s affiliation, two chunks about the 2025 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, and one about the award ceremony. Two of the four required pieces arrived, so context recall is 2/4 = 0.5; two of the five chunks are relevant, so context precision is 2/5 = 0.4. The answer will be missing two affiliations, and the Chemistry chunks invite the generator to attach a chemist’s university to a physicist.

The agent from 

Agentic RAG first retrieves the winners and then looks up each laureate in turn. It gathers all four pieces and nothing else: context recall and context precision are both 1.

Recall needs to know the full set of evidence an answer requires, so it depends on a labelled reference. Precision over the retrieved context can often be judged without one, by asking whether each passage bears on the question. Both trade off as they do in classical retrieval: retrieving more raises the chance of capturing every required passage but dilutes the context with noise.

A ranked list arrives in milliseconds and costs a fraction of a cent. A generated answer can take seconds, and every request consumes tokens that someone pays for. An agent multiplies both, since each pass through the loop is another model call and possibly another tool call. The bar is therefore higher than for classical search: a RAG answer must be clearly better for the user, not merely different, to justify the extra latency and cost.

Latency should be measured as a high percentile rather than an average. The 95th percentile, or p95, is the time within which 95 per cent of requests complete, and it reflects the slow cases users actually notice. Cost is best expressed per answered question, combining input tokens, output tokens, and tool charges.

For an agent, the path to the answer matters as well as the answer itself. A correct answer reached in two tool calls is better than the same answer reached in ten, even though both are equally correct. Evaluating the trajectory means recording how many iterations the loop took, which tools it called, whether each call was the right one, and whether it kept searching after it already had enough evidence.

The hardest dimension to measure is the quality of the answer itself, because it is free text rather than a ranked list. It is useful to separate four questions, which overlap but are not interchangeable.

Correctness: is the answer factually right? This is judged against a trusted reference answer or a list of expected facts.

Faithfulness: is every claim in the answer supported by the retrieved context? This measures grounding.

Relevance: does the answer address the question that was asked, rather than a neighbouring one?

Completeness: does the answer contain all the facts the question requires?

Faithfulness is the dimension specific to RAG, since it ties the answer to the evidence the system actually retrieved.

Key Formula: Faithfulness\text{faithfulness} = \frac{\lvert \{\text{claims in the answer supported by the context}\} \rvert}{\lvert \{\text{claims in the answer}\} \rvert}

The fraction of the answer’s claims that the retrieved passages support. A value of 1 means every claim is grounded; a lower value means the generator added content the evidence does not back.

Example

The answer reads: “The 2025 Nobel Prize in Physics went to Clarke, Devoret, and Martinis, who shared 11 million Swedish kronor.” The retrieved context names the three laureates but says nothing about the prize money. Of the two claims, one is supported, so faithfulness is 1/2 = 0.5. The prize amount happens to be correct, yet it still lowers faithfulness: the generator took it from its own memory rather than from the evidence, and a claim taken from memory can just as easily be wrong.

Faithful is not the same as correct

Faithfulness measures agreement with the retrieved context, not with the world. A true claim that the context does not support lowers faithfulness, as in the example above. And a perfectly faithful answer can be wrong if the retrieved documents are outdated or mistaken. Measure correctness separately, against a reference.

The four dimensions of answer quality, correctness, faithfulness, relevance, and completeness, are measured in two modes. Reference-based evaluation compares the answer with a trusted expected answer; it gives the strongest signal of correctness and completeness but requires someone to write the references. Reference-free evaluation judges faithfulness and relevance from the question, the answer, and the retrieved context alone, which scales to thousands of production requests where no reference exists. A sound evaluation uses both: a smaller reference set for correctness and a larger reference-free sweep for grounding.

Most of these judgements are made by another language model acting as an evaluator, an approach called LLM-as-a-judge. For faithfulness, the judge splits the answer into individual claims and checks each against the context. RAGAS packages the common metrics in this way: context precision and recall, faithfulness, and answer relevance, along with reference-based correctness.

Validate the judge before trusting it

An LLM judge is itself a model, with its own blind spots: it can miss subtle factual errors, favour longer answers, and change its verdicts when the evaluation prompt changes. Check its scores against a sample of human judgements before relying on them, and keep the judge model and prompt fixed while comparing systems. Where a rule can decide, such as a date, an amount, or whether a cited passage exists, use a deterministic check instead of a judge.

Measuring retrieval and answer quality separately also tells us where to look when something goes wrong.

Retrieval quality

Answer quality

Likely diagnosis

Low

Low

Fix retrieval: chunking, indexing, or query formulation.

High

Low

Fix generation: the prompt, the model, or how the context is used.

Low

High

Suspicious: the model may be answering from memory rather than evidence.

High

High

Working; look for savings in latency and cost.

These are heuristics rather than proofs, but they turn a single disappointing score into a direction to investigate.

The practical question is usually narrower than “which configuration is best”. We have a system A and a proposed change B, perhaps a new chunking strategy, a reranker, or an agent loop, and we want to know whether B is better. The method is a controlled experiment.

Start from a fixed benchmark: a set of representative questions, each with a reference answer and the evidence it requires, built the same way as the test collections of 

Designing a Retrieval Benchmark. Run A and B on exactly the same questions, changing only the one component under test, and record for every question the retrieved context, the answer, the latency, the tokens used, and for an agent the tool calls. Then compute every dimension for both systems. The sketch below shows the shape of such a harness; the judge_* functions stand for evaluators such as those RAGAS provides.def evaluate(system, benchmark):
    rows = []
    for item in benchmark:   # question, reference answer, required evidence
        start = time.perf_counter()
        run = system.answer(item.question)   # answer, retrieved, tool_calls, tokens
        latency = time.perf_counter() - start   # stop the clock before evaluating
        rows.append({
            "context_recall": recall(run.retrieved, item.evidence),
            "context_precision": precision(run.retrieved, item.evidence),
            "correct": judge_correct(run.answer, item.reference),
            "faithfulness": judge_faithful(run.answer, run.retrieved),
            "latency_s": latency,
            "tokens": run.tokens,
            "tool_calls": len(run.tool_calls),
        })
    return rows

results_a = evaluate(system_a, benchmark)
results_b = evaluate(system_b, benchmark)

A higher average for B is not yet proof that B is better. Benchmarks are small, and some questions are easy or hard for reasons unrelated to the change. Because both systems answered the same questions, the right comparison is paired: look at the questions where the two systems disagree, as in the paired tests of 

Evaluating Ranked Results.

Example: is B really better?

On a benchmark of 50 questions, system A answers 38 correctly (76 per cent) and system B answers 44 (88 per cent). Is B better, or did it get lucky? The test proceeds in four steps.

Keep only the disagreements. Both systems get 36 of the same questions right and 4 of the same questions wrong. These 40 questions say nothing about which system is better, so we set them aside. What remains are the 10 questions where the systems disagree: B is right and A wrong on 8, A is right and B wrong on 2.

Assume there is no difference. If B were no better than A, each disagreement would be equally likely to go either way, like the toss of a fair coin. The number of disagreements won by B would then follow a binomial distribution: the probability that B wins exactly k of the 10 is \binom{10}{k} / 2^{10}, where \binom{10}{k} counts the ways to choose which k of the 10 questions B wins.

Measure how extreme the observed split is. The probability of exactly 8 to 2 is 45/1024 \approx 0.044, but that number is misleading on its own. Every individual outcome is unlikely, even the most typical one: an even 5 to 5 split has probability 252/1024 \approx 0.25, and the probability of any single exact outcome shrinks further as the number of disagreements grows. The meaningful question is how often chance alone produces a result at least as one-sided as the one we saw, so we add up 8 to 2, 9 to 1, and 10 to 0: (45 + 10 + 1)/1024 \approx 0.055.

Count both directions. Before the experiment we did not know which system would come out ahead, and a 2 to 8 split in favour of A would have been just as surprising. Since the distribution is symmetric, we double the probability:p = 2 \cdot \frac{\binom{10}{8} + \binom{10}{9} + \binom{10}{10}}{2^{10}} = 2 \cdot \frac{45 + 10 + 1}{1024} \approx 0.11.

If A and B were truly equally good, a split at least this uneven would still occur about one time in nine. That is not rare enough to rule out chance, against the common threshold of 0.05, so the twelve-point gap is not conclusive. With the same pattern on a benchmark of 100 questions, B winning 16 of 20 disagreements, the same calculation gives p \approx 0.012, and the improvement becomes convincing. The ratio is unchanged; what changed is the amount of evidence behind it.

Quality is only half of the decision. If B is more accurate but doubles the p95 latency or the cost per answer, whether it is better depends on what the application can afford, and that is a product decision the measurements inform rather than settle. A good habit is to fix the acceptable latency and cost before running the experiment, so the result cannot quietly move the goalposts.

Tooling helps with the bookkeeping. Metric libraries such as RAGAS and DeepEval supply the judges and turn quality thresholds into regression tests, and tracing tools such as Phoenix and LangSmith record each run so that a surprising score can be traced to the step that caused it. Running such comparisons systematically over many parameters at once, known as hyperparameter search, builds on exactly this A-versus-B foundation and goes beyond the scope of this book.

The cost argument above cuts both ways. RAG is not the default answer to every question-answering problem, and reaching for it when a simpler tool fits adds cost and latency for no benefit. Four situations call for a different approach.

The knowledge is stable and general. The model already holds it. Asking a current model for a textbook definition or a historical fact gains nothing from retrieval and only adds a retrieval step that can fail.

The corpus fits in the context window. When the entire relevant collection is small enough, long-context prompting can be simpler and more reliable than retrieval, because there is no chance of retrieving the wrong passage. As context windows grow, the size threshold for this keeps rising.

The task is to change behaviour, not to supply facts. When the goal is a different style, tone, or output format, fine-tuning is the right tool, since RAG changes what the model reads, not how it writes.

The question maps onto structured data. For a query such as “how many orders shipped last week”, a direct database or API query, possibly generated by a text-to-SQL model, gives an exact answer where retrieval over unstructured text would only approximate one.

An agent softens the choice, because it can decide per query: it can answer a stable fact from memory, send a structured question to a database tool, and reserve document retrieval for the questions that need it. The question then shifts from “RAG or not” to “which tool for this query”.

Even where RAG is appropriate, it carries ongoing costs that the alternatives do not: an index to build and keep fresh, retrieval latency on every query, and a quality ceiling set by the corpus. If the document collection is noisy or out of date, retrieval faithfully supplies bad evidence, and the grounded answer is confidently wrong. RAG is the right choice when answers must draw on private, changing, or very specific knowledge and must be verifiable against sources, and the wrong choice when a cheaper tool already meets those needs.

Hands-on: Evaluating RAG

Compare a fixed pipeline with an agent on a small Nobel benchmark: context recall and precision, p95 latency and tokens per answer, correctness and faithfulness with an LLM judge checked against a rule, and a paired sign test on the questions where the two disagree.

The result-generation stage is the clearest fork in a RAG design, so it is worth seeing its three forms side by side.

Form

How it answers

Best for

Main risk

Reader

Marks and returns the answer span verbatim from one passage

Exact facts, short passages, high-stakes answers

Cannot combine or rephrase; fails if no single span holds the answer

Generator

Writes a new, direct answer from several passages with a language model

Open-ended questions, fluent answers across sources

Hallucination; must be grounded by prompt and guardrails

Synthesizer

Loops retrieval and reasoning over several documents, then summarizes

Deep research needing evidence gathered across sources

Latency and complexity; drift across hops

The progression is one of flexibility traded against faithfulness. The reader cannot say anything its source did not, which makes it safe but rigid; the synthesizer can assemble an answer no single source contains, which makes it powerful but the hardest to keep honest. The form is chosen per query by the context available, the question’s complexity, the user’s intent, and how costly a wrong answer would be. In an agentic system that choice moves into the loop itself.

A ranked list leaves the user to find the answer, and a language model alone cannot answer what it never saw. RAG combines the two: retrieval supplies the evidence, the generator turns it into a direct answer, and grounding ties the answer to sources a user can check.

A RAG system reuses the retrieval machinery of earlier chapters, BM25, embeddings, vector search, and cross-encoder reranking, and adds two parts that exist because a model, not a human, now consumes the results: two-level chunking and a result-generation stage.

Chunking balances sharp embeddings against enough context for the generator. Two-level chunking keeps both, small chunks for matching and larger parents for generation, and no strategy wins everywhere: the right one is the one that retrieves the answers to our own questions.

The result-generation stage comes in three forms, a reader that marks a span, a generator that writes a direct answer, and a synthesizer that summarizes across documents. For the generator, the prompt is a real lever on quality, not boilerplate.

Agentic RAG replaces one hand-wired pipeline per intent with a single reason-act-observe loop over declared tools. The loop detects the intent, rewrites the query for each tool, follows multi-hop chains no one coded in advance, and stops within a step budget, with guardrails at its input and output.

Evaluating RAG means more than precision and recall. Retrieval still sets the ceiling, but answer quality has four dimensions, correctness, faithfulness, relevance, and completeness, and latency and cost must justify the answer. Two configurations are compared on the same benchmark with a paired test over the questions where they disagree.

Key Formula: Faithfulness\text{faithfulness} = \frac{\lvert \{\text{claims in the answer supported by the context}\} \rvert}{\lvert \{\text{claims in the answer}\} \rvert}

The share of the answer’s claims that the retrieved passages support. It measures grounding, not truth: a correct claim the context does not back still lowers it, and a fully faithful answer can be wrong if the sources are.

Exam focus

Why a ranked list falls short for single-answer questions, why parametric knowledge fails on recent or private facts, and when RAG is not the right tool.

Two-level chunking, and why hybrid retrieval over two chunk levels must reconcile both rankings to a common unit before rank fusion.

Reader versus generator versus synthesizer: mechanism, strengths, and failure modes.

Fixed pipeline versus agent loop: what the loop takes over (intent, query transformation, multi-hop expansion, stopping) and where input and output guardrails apply.

Correctness versus faithfulness versus relevance, and why an LLM judge must be validated against human judgements.

Comparing two configurations: why only the disagreements count, and why the test asks for a result “at least as extreme” rather than the exact split.

(Understand) A user asks a plain language model about an event last week and gets a confident but wrong answer. Explain which limit of parametric knowledge this illustrates and how RAG would address it.

(Understand) Dense retrieval runs on small chunks and sparse retrieval on their larger parents. Explain why their result lists cannot be fused with reciprocal rank fusion directly, and what has to happen first.

(Analyze) A RAG system splits documents into 2000-token chunks and retrieval precision is high, but generated answers are vague and incomplete. Diagnose the likely cause and propose a chunking change.

(Analyze) An answer scores 0.9 on answer relevance but 0.4 on faithfulness. What does this combination tell you about the system, and where would you look first?

(Apply) On a benchmark of 50 questions, a new configuration B answers 41 correctly and the baseline A answers 38. They disagree on 5 questions, of which B wins 4. Compute the two-sided sign-test probability and decide whether B is convincingly better.

(Evaluate) You are asked to build a question-answering feature over a product catalogue whose prices and stock change hourly. Argue whether RAG, fine-tuning, or direct structured-data queries is the better fit, and justify the trade-offs.

(Evaluate) A support assistant scoped to one insurance product starts answering questions about competitors’ policies and sometimes states facts not found in its retrieved passages. Explain which guardrails are missing and where in the agent loop each one belongs.

Type “uni basel” into a search engine. Even two short words are a strong filter: of the hundreds of billions of pages in the index, almost all contain neither term and drop out. But a tiny fraction of the web is still thousands to millions of pages: the university’s home page, every course and news page, student blogs, a marathon result list with a runner from Basel. The ranking functions of the earlier chapters score these pages by how well their words match the query, and for a two-word query most of them match about equally well. Yet the user expects the home page at rank 1, and expects it within a fraction of a second. The words of the query cannot decide this ranking on their own.

Four problems make the web the hardest setting for retrieval in this book:

Too many equal matches. A short query discards almost the whole web but still leaves far more matching pages than anyone can read, with nearly equal term-based scores.

Different intents, one result list. Queries range from a site name such as “instagram”, typed instead of a URL, to a full question such as “Who was Albert Einstein?”. Each intent expects a different kind of result (

Intent Routing and Classification). With two or three words and no context, the engine cannot know what one particular user wants, so it serves what most users want. For “apple”, that is the home page of Apple, not an article about the fruit.

No editor. The collections of earlier chapters were curated: nobody adds hundreds of useless books to a university library catalogue to promote their own. The web has no such gatekeeper. Its content ranges from careful reference works to outdated or false information, clickbait, and scams, and much of it exists in many copies, such as mirrored manuals, the documentation of popular frameworks, and copied blog posts. The first web search engines learned the hard way that term matching ranks such pages high.

Adversarial ranking. A position on the first result page is worth money, because results on the second page are almost never clicked. Search engine optimization (SEO) is an industry that tunes pages to rank higher, from legitimate improvements to plain manipulation. Unlike in a library, no central authority decides which document deserves the top position, and every signal that rewards a page invites someone to fake it.

If the keywords cannot decide, the engine needs evidence from elsewhere. The web offers more of it than any curated collection:

The query intent. The engine detects the type of query and applies a strategy for it. A navigational query must lead to the official website every time; for frequent queries, this can come from a curated list, much like the entries of an FAQ service.

The page and what others say about it. Term positions, the HTML structure, and the anchor texts of the links that point to a page (

Ranking Signals Beyond Term Counts).

The link graph. Popular pages receive more links, so the link structure shows what people in general consider important (

Link Analysis: PageRank and HITS). The goal is not to optimize every single query, but to make the great majority of the queries people actually type work very well.

User behaviour. Clicks, the time users spend on a result, and reformulated queries show which results satisfy. Learning to rank combines hundreds of such signals into one model that keeps adapting as behaviour changes (

Learning to Rank).

The intent also decides what the result page looks like. Instead of one list of links, the engine sends the query to specialized searches and composes the page for it: a highlighted passage or a generated answer for a question, facts from a curated knowledge base for a known entity, a map for a place, a product list for a purchase, and related searches for the next step. All of this rests on a crawler that does more than copy the web: by following its links, it collects the evidence about each page that the page itself does not provide (

The Web Search Landscape).

The same machinery now works without a query at all. Social media feeds and video platforms decide, for every user and every scroll, which post to show next. They retrieve and rank candidates just like a search engine, but the user’s history plays the role of the query, and the reactions of communities and individual users train a ranking that is personalized for every user (

Ranking Without a Query: Feeds).

What you’ll learn

Explain why term-based ranking breaks down on the web (equal matches, diverse intents, uncurated quality, SEO), how the query intent shapes the result page, and what a crawler contributes beyond collecting pages.

Compute web-specific content signals: term proximity, BM25F field weighting, and per-domain anchor-text scores.

Compute PageRank by power iteration and HITS hub and authority values, and contrast global with query-specific link analysis.

Compare pointwise, pairwise, and listwise learning to rank, and explain how click data must be debiased before training.

Explain how a feed ranks content without a query, and why optimizing engagement differs from optimizing value.

Prerequisites

Classical Text Retrieval: the vector space model and BM25, which web signals extend (see 

BM25).

Performance Evaluation: graded relevance and nDCG, the target measure of learning to rank (see 

Evaluating Graded Relevance).

Index for Text Retrieval: inverted files and postings lists, which proximity scoring extends with term positions.

Semantic Search and 

Vector Search: embeddings, cross-encoders, and approximate nearest-neighbour search, reused for neural reranking and feed retrieval (see 

Semantic Similarity with Transformers).

Retrieval Augmented Generation: generated answers, which modern result pages show above the links.

The chapter opener named four problems: too many equal matches, diverse intents, no editor, and adversarial ranking. This section looks at them more closely and then at the two ends of a web search engine: the result page, which the engine composes for the intent of each query, and the crawler, which collects the pages and the evidence about them.

hierarchy.lvl2: How Web Search Differs from Classical Retrieval
How Web Search Differs from Classical Retrieval

records.content:
Five differences shape every design decision in web search:

aspect

classical retrieval

web search

collection

controlled and quality-assured, such as a product catalogue or a library

no quality control; ranges from reference works to errors, propaganda, and spam

documents

shared structure, rich metadata, structured or faceted search

heterogeneous formats (HTML, PDF, scripts); beyond title, URL, and text, little reliable structure

queries

narrow context, such as artists, albums, and songs in a music database

any topic, two or three words, no explicit context; the engine must infer the intent

results

manageable result sizes, filters, facets, sorting

billions of matching pages for a short query; ranking decides everything

relationships

curated relations with little extra information

a huge link graph whose topology reveals which pages people consider important

Classical retrieval assumes that every document in the collection deserves to be found and that its text describes it honestly. On the web, neither assumption holds.

Much low-quality content is not malicious. Pages that were correct when written become outdated, blogs are abandoned, and errors are never corrected. Other content is deliberately misleading: false information, scams that imitate banks or shops, and clickbait whose content does not deliver what its title promises. On top of this, much of the web exists in many copies. The manuals of popular products, the documentation of popular frameworks, and successful blog posts are mirrored and republished on many sites, and the same article is often reachable under several URLs. A ranking that only matches terms scores all copies equally, so the result list may show the same content ten times. In a library, a librarian filters all of this before a document enters the collection. On the web, the search engine must do it at ranking time, with the quality and spam signals of 

Ranking Signals Beyond Term Counts.

Ranking on the web is also adversarial, because visibility is worth money. In a 

backlinko.com analysis of 4 million Google search results, the first organic result received an average click-through rate of 27.6%, and only 0.63% of searchers clicked on anything on the second page. A page that is not on the first page is practically invisible. Search engine optimization (SEO) is the discipline of improving a page’s position in the results. Much of it is legitimate and welcome to search engines, which publish guidelines for it: descriptive titles, a clean HTML structure, fast pages, and good content that others link to. Its other side manipulates the ranking signals directly, with keyword stuffing, hidden text, link farms, and cloaking, which serves the crawler different content than the user. No central authority decides which page deserves the top position. The ranking itself is the only arbiter, and many of the signals in this chapter were designed to be hard to fake.

Together, these differences shift the weight of the ranking away from the page text. A two-word query matches millions of pages that all look equally similar to the query, and the page text is exactly what an SEO controls. Signals that do not come from the page text, such as links, anchors, and user behaviour, therefore carry much of the ranking.

Parts of the web are invisible to a search engine. Pages behind logins, results of database queries, and content that single-page applications assemble in the browser with JavaScript are publicly reachable but hard or impossible to crawl. This deep web is many times larger than the indexed web. A crawler can reach a deep page only if some other page links to it directly, a so-called deep link.

Andrei Broder classified web queries by the user’s goal into three types:

Navigational queries aim at one specific website or a section of it: “youtube”, “amazon prime”, “facebook login”. Bookmarks were designed for this need, but many users prefer to type the name into a search engine. There is usually exactly one correct result.

Transactional queries express the intent to do something, typically to buy, book, or download: “new coffee machine”, “trip to Hawaii”. The transactional intent is often implicit.

Informational queries seek knowledge about a topic: news, events, people, how-to instructions. Some are phrased as questions: “who won the 2025 Nobel Prize in Physics”, “how to make mac and cheese”, “where to swim near Basel”.

The intent changes what a good result looks like. A navigational query is answered by one link at rank 1. An informational question may be answered best by a sentence on the result page itself, and a transactional query by a list of products to compare. 

Chapter 3 shows how a system detects the intent of a query and routes it to a backend. Broder’s three types are a coarse version of the routing intents there. A navigational query stays in the web index, with the strong expectation of a single result. Informational and transactional queries are often routed further, for example “Who was Albert Einstein?” to a people search, “where to swim near Basel” to a map search, and “new coffee machine” to a product search.

Most queries do not state their intent, and many are ambiguous. “apple” can mean the company, the fruit, or the record label; “jaguar” can mean the car or the animal. The engine cannot ask back, so it ranks for the interpretation that most users mean, which it learns from the clicks of earlier users. For “apple”, the home page of Apple comes first. Rarer interpretations receive a few positions further down, so that a user with a less common intent still finds something on the first page. This mix of interpretations is called result diversification.

Frequent navigational queries need no ranking computation at all. The correct target of “instagram” or “uni basel” is known and stable, and the engine can serve it from a curated or learned table of query-target pairs, much like the entries of an FAQ service. Here, a single wrong result is a failure: if the official site is not at rank 1, the quality of the remaining ranks does not matter.

Web queries are short. 

Figure 1 shows the share of search volume by query length: most search volume comes from queries of one to three words and around ten to twenty characters. Longer queries are more frequent among the distinct query strings than in the volume, because each long query is typed by few users.



Figure 1:Share of search volume by query length in words (left) and characters (right). Source: 

backlinko.com.

Query frequencies follow Zipf’s law. A small set of queries, mostly navigational ones such as “amazon” or “netflix”, is repeated millions of times per month and forms the fat head of the search demand curve in 

Figure 2. In the chunky middle, queries reach thousands of searches per month. The long tail contains all the rest, each typed fewer than about a hundred times per month. In a 2020 analysis of 306 million keywords, 

backlinko.com found that 91.8% of all queries are long-tail queries with at most 100 searches per month, and that the median query is searched only 10 times per month. The head nevertheless carries a large share of the total volume: the 500 most popular queries alone account for 8.4% of all searches.



Figure 2:Share of searches by question word (left) and the search demand curve with its fat head, chunky middle, and long tail (right). Sources: 

backlinko.com, 

ahrefs.com.

The long tail is where search engines compete. Head queries are easy: any engine can learn the right answer for “youtube” from the clicks of millions of users, or simply store it. Tail queries have little or no click history, and many are entirely new. Google reports that about 15% of the queries it sees every day have never been seen before, driven by news, new products, and the endless variety of how people phrase a question. About 14% of queries are phrased as questions (

backlinko.com); “how” is the most common question word, followed by “what” and “where” (

Figure 2, left). Many queries without a question word are implicit questions too: a person’s name usually means “who is ...”, and a product name often means “what does it cost”.

Early search engines treated every query the same way. A single retriever over an inverted index returned a list of links with ads in between, the “ten blue links” (

Figure 3). For a question such as “who is the US president”, the user had to open a result, find the answer on the page, and leave the search engine, which could then no longer show them ads.



Figure 3:Early web search: a retriever over an inverted index returns a list of links.

A modern engine produces the result page in three steps. It detects the intent of the query, sends the query to one or several specialized searches, and generates the elements of the page from their results. Each step keeps more of the user’s journey on the result page.

Intent detection and specialized searches. Besides the web index, a search engine runs vertical searches over collections of its own: images, videos, news, maps with local businesses, products with prices, and flights. The intent classifier decides which verticals to query and how to mix their results into the web results. Some intents need no search at all: weather, calculations, unit conversions, and translations are answered directly, like the one-shot vertical intents of

With BERT-based passage ranking, launched in 2021, the engine scores individual passages within long pages. This is the retriever-reader architecture of

Most of these components appeared within the last fifteen years, on top of a ranking core that dates from the late 1990s.

How web search engines evolved (optional reading)

In the 1990s, the web was small enough to be organized by hand. Yahoo started as a human-edited directory, a hierarchical catalogue of websites sorted into topics, and added keyword search later. AltaVista, launched in 1995, was one of the first engines to index the full text of a large part of the web. Its ranking relied on classical term weighting with some tweaks such as boosts for terms in the title or domain name. With a few million pages, this was good enough: queries matched few pages, and the best ones usually contained the query terms prominently.

Google grew out of a research project by Larry Page and Sergey Brin at Stanford and launched as a company in 1998. Three ideas set it apart. It ranked pages with link analysis (PageRank) and anchor text, which were much harder to manipulate than the page text. It optimized its ranking for the most common types of web queries instead of generic relevance. And it ran on a distributed architecture of cheap commodity machines, which let it crawl more pages and answer more queries than its competitors. Within a few years, Google dominated web search.

The 2000s added machine learning to the ranking (learning to rank, 

Learning to Rank), universal search that mixes images, news, videos, and maps into the result list, and the Knowledge Graph in 2012. The late 2010s brought transformer models: BERT for understanding queries and ranking results in 2019, and the ranking of individual passages within pages in 2021.

The 2020s brought generated answers. Microsoft’s integration of GPT-4 into Bing in 2023, Google’s AI Overviews in 2024, and chat-first assistants such as ChatGPT search and Perplexity changed what users expect from a search engine: an answer, not a list. Classical ranking remains at the core of these systems, because the generated answer is only as good as the retrieved results it is based on.

The result page (SERP, search engine results page) combines the outputs of all these components. 

Figure 7 shows a schematic for “uni basel”. An AI overview with source links sits at the top. Ads follow, marked as sponsored and ranked by bid and predicted relevance. The organic results are the ranked list of web pages with title, URL, and snippet; this is what the ranking signals of this chapter decide. Related questions expand to a featured snippet each, a carousel shows images or videos, and the knowledge panel on the side shows facts about the university.



Figure 7:Schematic of a modern result page for “uni basel”: AI overview, ads, organic results, related questions, media carousel, and knowledge panel.

The search engine must decide for each query which elements to show and in which order. This is itself a ranking problem, with the additional constraint that the page must load in a fraction of a second.

Answers on the result page change the economics of the web. When the answer is on the result page, the user has no reason to click. A 2024 clickstream study by SparkToro found that 58.5% of Google searches in the US and 59.7% in the EU end without a click on any result, a share that has grown with every new answer feature. Publishers, who depend on search traffic, lose visitors, while the search engine keeps users on its own page. A new optimization industry has emerged as well: generative engine optimization (GEO) tries to make a page more likely to be cited in generated answers, for example by adding statistics, quotations, and authoritative sources. Aggarwal et al. reported that such changes can raise a page’s visibility in generated answers by up to 40%.

A search engine can only rank pages it has fetched. Collecting the pages, however, is the smaller part of what a crawl provides. Sites can already announce their content themselves: a sitemap lists the URLs of a site, and some engines accept notifications of changed pages through protocols such as IndexNow. But everything a site submits is the site’s own claim about itself, and the web has no editor and strong incentives to cheat. The crawler gives the engine an independent view of the web, and this view is what most ranking signals of this chapter are built on:

The view from outside. By following links, the crawler sees each page through the rest of the web: which pages link to it, and with which anchor texts. This evidence is written by others and is therefore much harder to fake than the page’s own text. It feeds the anchor index (

Ranking Signals Beyond Term Counts) and the link graph (

Link Analysis: PageRank and HITS). Global measures such as PageRank need the whole graph, which no single site can provide.

The content as delivered. The crawler fetches a page the way a browser does, so the engine judges the content that users actually receive, not the keywords and descriptions that a site declares about itself in its metadata.

Duplicates and change. Only a crawl across many sites reveals that a page is one of a hundred copies, and only repeated visits reveal how often a page changes, which the engine needs to keep its results fresh.

The basis for answers. Featured snippets, knowledge panels, and generated answers are only as good as the crawled pages behind them. The crawl is the corpus that the generated answers of 

Chapter 7 are grounded on.

The crawler (also called spider or bot) works in the loop shown in 

Figure 8:

The crawl starts from a set of seed URLs, for example well-known sites and previously crawled pages.

The URL frontier holds all URLs waiting to be fetched, ordered by priority. Important pages (high PageRank, frequent changes) are fetched first.

The fetcher downloads a page. Before fetching from a site, it reads the site’s robots.txt file, which lists the paths the site owner does not want crawled.

The parser extracts the text, the outgoing links, and their anchor texts. New URLs go back into the frontier; each link and its anchor text is stored under the target URL for the anchor index (

Ranking Signals Beyond Term Counts) and the link graph (

Link Analysis: PageRank and HITS).

Duplicate detection discards pages already seen. Exact duplicates are found by hashing the URL and the content; near-duplicates, such as the same article with different ads, by comparing compact fingerprints of the content such as SimHash.



Figure 8:The crawler loop: frontier, fetcher, parser, and duplicate detection feed the index and the link graph.

Three requirements make crawling at web scale hard. Politeness: a crawler must not overload a site, so it limits the request rate per host, typically by keeping one queue per host in the frontier and waiting between requests. Freshness: pages change at very different rates. A news front page changes every few minutes, a professor’s home page every few months. The crawler estimates the change rate of each page and schedules recrawls accordingly; the index is never a snapshot of the web, but a mix of pages crawled at different times. Robustness: the web contains spider traps, such as calendars with an endless sequence of “next month” links, and servers that respond slowly or with garbage.

The robots.txt convention dates from 1994 and was standardized only in 2022 (RFC 9309). It is a request, not an access control: well-behaved crawlers follow it, but nothing enforces it. It has gained new attention with language models. AI companies crawl the web to collect training data, and site owners increasingly use robots.txt to block crawlers such as OpenAI’s GPTBot while still allowing search engine crawlers.

Web search engines extend the document description with additional signals:

proximity of the query terms in the document (the closer, the better)

field weighting: occurrences in the title or a heading count more than occurrences in body text

anchor text: the words that other pages use when they link to this page

location of the user and the page

language of the user and the page

quality and trust: penalties for spam, thin content, and untrustworthy sites

The query “roger federer” is not a request for any page that contains “roger” and “federer”: a marathon result list with a Roger in row 12 and a Federer in row 4,000 matches both terms but answers nothing. In

That works for a fixed list of known phrases, but it cannot adapt to the new names and phrases that appear with every news event. Names matter a lot on the web, since people, places, and products are among the most frequent search topics. We therefore want a proximity measure that works for any combination of query terms and is computed at query time.

The index provides the raw material. Instead of storing only the term frequency in a posting, a positional index stores every position at which the term occurs in the document. This list is called a hit list. As document D, we take the lead section of the English Wikipedia article on Roger Federer (revision of 25 October 2026, CC BY-SA 4.0). We count positions in its plain text without the pronunciation guide; the lead is 626 words long. For the query “roger federer”, the hit lists are:

At query time, we pair up occurrences of the two terms. The full cross product would create 30 pairs, most of them meaningless: “roger” at position 1 and “federer” at position 619 are more than 600 words apart. Instead, we merge both hit lists into one list sorted by position and form a pair wherever two neighbouring entries belong to different terms (Büttcher, Clarke, and Lushman; see the Further Reading section of the chapter summary). The merged list starts with roger (1), federer (2), federer (57) and ends with federer (509), roger (532), federer (533), federer (560), federer (619).

The pair (509, 532) is in reversed order and links the end of one mention to the start of the next: “Federer played an instrumental role in the creation of the Laver Cup team competition. He is also an active philanthropist, having established the Roger”. The rule treats both query terms alike, needs no window size, and works unchanged for queries with more than two terms.

Next, we sort the pair distances into bins, an idea that goes back to the original Google design of Brin and Page. Bin i counts the pairs at distance i, for i = 1, \ldots, 10. Pairs that are farther apart are “not even close” and do not count. The distances are 1, 23, and 1, so bin 1 holds two pairs, and the reversed pair at distance 23 drops out. Finally, a weight vector that decreases with distance turns the bin counts into a score.

Now take a marathon result list of 5,000 runners: a long table of ranks, names, and finishing times. Production systems use more refined functions. They weight in-order pairs higher than reversed ones, treat a pair that crosses a sentence or paragraph boundary as weaker evidence, and often replace the bins by a smooth function of the distance d, such as 1/d^2 in the method of Büttcher et al. Our example treats both orders alike and ignores boundaries. Here this makes no difference: the only reversed pair, which also crosses a sentence boundary, is too far apart to count. The idea stays the same: the closer the query terms appear, the more likely the page is about the combination and not just about each term on its own. Proximity has a storage price. The postings lists of 

Inverted Files store only the documents that contain a term; a positional index adds every position of the term and is therefore considerably larger. Web search engines pay this price, because the same positions also answer phrase queries such as “new york city” without indexing every n-gram.

HTML gives us more than a sequence of words. A term in the was chosen by the author to describe the whole page. A term in an <h1> heading names a main topic, and a term in bold marks something the author wanted to stress. Classical retrieval counts all of these occurrences alike. Figure 2 shows the home page of the University of Basel with every occurrence of “university” and the tag that surrounds it. A natural first idea is to saturate the count in each tag separately, as BM25 does for the whole document, and then add up the weighted results. This idea is flawed. If every field saturates on its own, a spammer can repeat a keyword in the title, in every heading, in bold text, and in the body, and collect the full saturated score once per field. The combination grows almost linearly with the number of fields, and the protection that saturation was meant to provide is gone. BM25F (BM25 with fields) does it the other way around. It first combines the per-field counts into one weighted term frequency and only then applies the BM25 saturation: Key Formula: BM25F\widetilde{\text{tf}}(t, D) = \sum_{f} w_f \cdot \text{tf}_f(t, D)\text{sim}_{\text{BM25F}}(Q, D) = \sum_{t \in Q} \text{idf}(t) \cdot \frac{\widetilde{\text{tf}}(t, D) \cdot (k_1 + 1)}{\widetilde{\text{tf}}(t, D) + k_1 \cdot \left(1 - b + b \cdot \frac{|D|}{\text{avgdl}}\right)} Weight each occurrence by its field (w_f for title, heading, body, ...), add the weighted counts, then saturate once. A title occurrence counts like several body occurrences, but repetition in any field still runs into the same saturation limit. Saturation matters more on the web than in a curated collection, because keyword stuffing is a standard SEO technique ( The Web Search Landscape). Field weighting also extends beyond HTML tags: the URL, the domain name, and the anchor texts of incoming links (next subsection) are all fields with their own weights.

The anchor text of a link is the clickable text that leads to another page. It usually describes the target page in a few precise words, chosen not by the target’s author but by someone else. Generic anchors such as “click here” or “more” carry no information, but with thousands of links to a page the useful descriptions dominate. 

Figure 3 shows two pages that link to the University of Basel home page: a Wikipedia list of Swiss universities and an Erasmus exchange portal. Both describe the target as “University of Basel” or “Universität Basel”.



Figure 3:Two external pages (a Wikipedia list and an Erasmus portal) link to the University of Basel home page; their anchor texts describe the target.

Anchor text is valuable because it is hard to manipulate. A page author controls every word on their own page, but not the words that thousands of other sites use to link to it. Anchor text also describes pages that contain little text of their own, such as a home page made of images and navigation menus, and it can even describe pages the crawler has never fetched.

Using anchor text requires work at crawl time. When the crawler parses a page, it extracts each link together with its anchor text and stores the pair under the target URL (

Crawling the Web). After the crawl, the search engine builds a separate anchor index in which each target page is described by the concatenation of all anchor texts pointing to it. At query time, the anchor index contributes its own score, usually with a higher weight than the page’s own text.

The saturation for anchor counts must be gentler than BM25’s. Many independent pages voting for a description is exactly the evidence we want, so the score should keep growing with the number of votes, only more slowly. A logarithm such as \log(1 + n) for n anchor occurrences has this property.

An unbounded score invites manipulation. A Google bomb is a coordinated attempt to attach a keyword to a target page by placing that keyword in a very large number of links. The best-known example linked the phrase “miserable failure” to a biography of George W. Bush in 2003 and 2004 and pushed the page to the top for that query. The countermeasure is to count votes per domain: each domain has at most one vote for how well a term describes a target page.

Many queries have a local intent that the user does not spell out. Someone typing “best pizza” on a phone in Basel wants a restaurant within walking distance, not the best pizzeria in Naples. Google introduced a major local-search update, nicknamed Pigeon, in 2014, which tied local results more closely to the user’s location and to the distance to businesses. Today, location influences the ranking of restaurants, shops, services, events, and many general queries.

Location-aware ranking needs three pieces of information:

The location of a page. For businesses, the owners often maintain an entry with address and opening hours in a directory such as Google Maps, so the search engine knows the location exactly. For other pages, the crawler estimates a location from the address on the page, the country domain, or the server’s IP address.

The location of the user. The device may report its GPS position. Otherwise the search engine estimates the location from the IP address, which fails when the user connects through a VPN. If the query names a place, that place takes precedence: “best pizza in Paris” ranks Paris restaurants, even for a user in Basel. The query analyzer recognizes places as named entities (

Query Understanding) and maps them to coordinates. This works for landmarks too, as in “best pizza near the Golden Gate Bridge”.

How much location matters for this query. “best pizza” depends strongly on location. “Albert Einstein” is a global query, but a local museum with an Einstein exhibition can still receive a modest local boost.

A user who asks for a recipe in German does not want English pages, even if an English page matches the query terms well. Language is therefore a signal of its own. The search engine detects the language of each page at indexing time, with the same classifiers that detect the language of a query (

Chapter 3). On the user side, the language of the query, the interface language, the browser settings, and past queries indicate which languages the user reads.

The engine can use this signal in two ways. A classical filter restricts the results to pages in the user’s languages, like the language option of an advanced search form. A filter is simple, but it is all or nothing: it also removes an English page that would be the best result when no good German page exists. Learning to rank (

Learning to Rank) instead treats the language match as one feature among many and learns from user behaviour how strongly to prefer pages in the query language. A recipe query then shows German pages first, while a query for an error message of a programming framework may still rank English pages high, because that is where the answers are.

The Web Search Landscape described the kinds of low-quality content on the web, from outdated pages to scams and pages that exist only to rank. Search engines respond by estimating the quality of each page and the trustworthiness of its site. Typical measures include:

Penalties for low-quality pages: thin content that wraps a few sentences in ads, pages copied from elsewhere, aggressive keyword stuffing, and clickbait whose content does not deliver what the title promises.

Removal of entire sites from the results: link farms that exist only to create links, doorway pages that redirect users elsewhere, malware sites, and illegal content.

Site-level trust: signals such as the known ownership of a site, its age, its editorial quality, and its reputation in other sources. A registered news organization or a university earns more trust than an anonymous site created last week.

Quality updates can shift results on a large scale. Google’s 2011 Panda update, which targeted thin and low-quality content, noticeably affected about 12% of US English queries. Since then, quality assessment has moved to machine-learned classifiers. Google uses a spam detection system called SpamBrain, and its human quality raters judge pages by experience, expertise, authoritativeness, and trustworthiness (E-E-A-T); their judgments become training labels for the ranking models (

Learning to Rank). Since 2023, large amounts of cheap, machine-generated text have made this defence harder and more important.

Quality signals have a cost. A ranking that rewards established, trusted sites makes it harder for a new site to reach the top, even if its content is excellent. Search engines therefore balance trust against freshness and diversity, a trade-off we meet again in

Return to the two candidate pages for “uni basel” in 

Figure 1. Content signals and anchor texts already favour the home page, but there is a stronger and more general clue: the structure of the web itself. Thousands of pages link to the university home page, while only a handful link to a single course page. A hyperlink is an implicit recommendation: the author of the linking page considered the target worth visiting. The web is a directed graph with pages as nodes and links as edges, and its topology tells us which pages the web itself considers important.

This section develops two classic ways to read that graph. PageRank computes one global importance score for every page, independent of any query. It was the key innovation of Google in 1998 and is still the reference model for ranking nodes in a graph. HITS distinguishes two roles that a page can play for a topic, hub or authority, and computes them on a small, query-specific subgraph. Both turn out to be the same mathematical idea: an eigenvector of a link matrix, computed by repeated matrix-vector multiplication.

The simplest link-based score counts the incoming links of a page, its in-degree. 

Figure 1 shows a small web of seven pages. Page E receives six links and ranks first. B and G follow with four links each, C has two, A and D one each, and F none.



Figure 1:A seven-page web graph; the number below each page is its in-degree.

This ranking matches our first intuition: E is clearly the centre of this graph. But look at B and G, which tie with four incoming links. G receives a link from E, the most important page. B receives its links from A, C, D, and F, which are all minor pages themselves. G should rank above B, because a recommendation from an important page should count more than a recommendation from an unimportant one. The in-degree treats all links as equal votes.

There is a second, more practical problem. In-degree is easy to manipulate. Anyone can create a thousand pages that all link to a target page, a practice called link farming, and inflate its in-degree at almost no cost. We need a measure in which a link is worth only as much as the page it comes from. Then a thousand links from a thousand worthless pages add up to very little.

PageRank, developed by Larry Page and Sergey Brin at Stanford, defines importance through a thought experiment. A random surfer starts on some page and browses the web forever. On each page, the surfer does one of two things:

With probability \alpha, the surfer clicks one of the links on the page, choosing each link with equal probability.

With probability 1 - \alpha, the surfer gets bored and jumps to a random page, for example by typing a URL or opening a bookmark. Every page is equally likely as the jump target.

If a page has no outgoing links (a dangling node), the surfer always jumps to a random page. The PageRank of a page is the long-run fraction of time the surfer spends on it. In terms of probability theory, the surfer performs a Markov chain with pages as states, and PageRank is the stationary distribution of this chain. A page with high PageRank is a page that people browsing the web would visit often, which makes it a good candidate for the top of a result list.

To compute the PageRank of a page p, we ask how the surfer can arrive there. Either they follow a link from some page q that links to p (written q \rightarrow p), or they jump to p at random. Let L(q) denote the number of outgoing links of q, and let \mathbb{P} be the set of all pages with N = |\mathbb{P}|.

Key Formula: PageRank\text{PR}(p) = \frac{1 - \alpha}{N} + \alpha \cdot \sum_{q \rightarrow p} \frac{\text{PR}(q)}{L(q)} \qquad \forall p \in \mathbb{P}

A page is important if important pages link to it. Each page passes its PageRank in equal shares along its outgoing links; the random jump term \frac{1-\alpha}{N} gives every page a small base score. A common choice is \alpha = 0.85.

The formula captures both problems with in-degree. A link from q contributes \text{PR}(q), so links from important pages count more. And the contribution is divided by L(q), so a page that links to a thousand targets gives each of them only a thousandth of its vote. A link farm of a thousand pages that nobody links to has a combined PageRank of only about 1000 \cdot \frac{1-\alpha}{N}, a negligible amount on a web of billions of pages. To inflate a target’s PageRank, a spammer needs links from pages that already have a high PageRank, and those are much harder to get.

The random jump also matters. Without it, a group of pages that link only to each other, a rank sink, would absorb the surfer forever and collect all PageRank. The jump guarantees that the surfer can always leave, and it makes the Markov chain irreducible and aperiodic. These two properties guarantee that a unique stationary distribution exists.

The PageRank formula defines one equation per page, and each equation refers to the PageRank of other pages. We solve this system iteratively. Let \mathbf{r} \in \mathbb{R}^N be the vector of all PageRank values, and define the transition matrix \mathbf{M} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times N} asM_{i,j} = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{L(p_j)} & \text{if } p_j \rightarrow p_i \\ \frac{1}{N} & \text{if } p_j \text{ has no outgoing links} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}

Column j of \mathbf{M} describes where the surfer goes from page p_j; every column sums to 1. With this matrix, the PageRank formula for all pages becomes\mathbf{r} = \frac{1 - \alpha}{N} \cdot \mathbf{1} + \alpha \cdot \mathbf{M} \mathbf{r}

where \mathbf{1} is the column vector of N ones. Power iteration starts with the uniform distribution and applies the equation repeatedly:

Initialization: \mathbf{r}^{(0)} = \frac{1}{N} \cdot \mathbf{1}

Iteration: \mathbf{r}^{(t+1)} = \frac{1 - \alpha}{N} \cdot \mathbf{1} + \alpha \cdot \mathbf{M} \mathbf{r}^{(t)}

Stop when \lVert \mathbf{r}^{(t+1)} - \mathbf{r}^{(t)} \rVert_1 < \varepsilon

Each iteration is one multiplication of a sparse matrix with a vector. The web graph is extremely sparse: a page has a few dozen outgoing links, not billions. One iteration therefore costs time proportional to the number of links, and it parallelizes well across many machines. The number of iterations grows only slowly with the size of the graph. Page et al. reported that PageRank on a database of 322 million links converged in roughly 52 iterations, and on half of the data in roughly 45.

PageRank is not a relevance score

PageRank measures how often a random surfer visits a page. It does not know the query. A search engine computes PageRank once after each crawl and uses it as one feature among many, combined with content signals such as BM25F and proximity. Ranking by PageRank alone would return the same famous pages for every query. PageRank is therefore not “how relevant a page is”, but “how prominent a page is in the web graph”.

PageRank also favours old pages. A new page, however good, has not yet collected incoming links, and links from important pages take time to appear. This is one reason why search engines add freshness signals for news and events, where the best page may be only a few minutes old.

In 1998, Jon Kleinberg proposed a different reading of the link graph. He observed that pages play two distinct roles for a topic, shown in 

Figure 3:

An authority is a page that the community recognizes as a definitive source on a topic, such as Wikipedia, IMDb, or the official site of an organization. Good authorities receive many links.

A hub is a page that collects links to the authorities of a topic without providing much content itself, such as a curated list of resources or a directory. Good hubs have many outgoing links.



Figure 3:An authority receives links from many pages; a hub links to many pages.

The two roles reinforce each other. A good hub links to good authorities, and a good authority is linked from good hubs. Crucially, both are defined for a topic: a page that is a great authority on Basel is not an authority on jaguars. HITS (Hyperlink-Induced Topic Search) therefore does not run on the whole web, but on a small graph built for each query Q, as shown in 

Figure 4:

Root set: take the top results for Q from a text search engine, for example the top 200. This set already contains relevant pages, but not necessarily the best hubs and authorities.

Base set: extend the root set with all pages that a root page links to, and with pages that link to a root page (limited to, say, 50 per root page). Links within the same domain are usually dropped, since they are mostly navigation menus.



Figure 4:HITS expands the root set (the top text-search results) into the base set by following links in both directions.

The outgoing links of a root page are found by parsing it. The incoming links require a link index of the web, which a search engine builds during the crawl anyway. For each page p in the base set, HITS computes an authority value a(p) and a hub value h(p).

Key Formula: HITS Updatea^{(t+1)}(p) = \sum_{q \rightarrow p} h^{(t)}(q) \qquad h^{(t+1)}(p) = \sum_{p \rightarrow q} a^{(t)}(q)

followed by normalization, so that \sum_p a(p)^2 = \sum_p h(p)^2 = 1. The authority of a page is the sum of the hub values of the pages that link to it; the hub value of a page is the sum of the authority values of the pages it links to.

The iteration starts with a^{(0)}(p) = h^{(0)}(p) = \sqrt{1/N} for all N pages of the base set and stops when the values change by less than \varepsilon. In matrix notation, with the adjacency matrix A_{i,j} = 1 if p_i \rightarrow p_j and 0 otherwise, the updates are \mathbf{a}^{(t+1)} = \mathbf{A}^{\top} \mathbf{h}^{(t)} and \mathbf{h}^{(t+1)} = \mathbf{A} \mathbf{a}^{(t)}. Like PageRank, this is a power iteration: \mathbf{a} converges to the principal eigenvector of \mathbf{A}^{\top} \mathbf{A} and \mathbf{h} to the principal eigenvector of \mathbf{A} \mathbf{A}^{\top}.

Example: HITS on an eight-page base set

Figure 5 shows a base set of eight pages, its adjacency matrix, and the converged hub and authority values (as fractions of the unit-length vectors, rounded).

A is the best hub (h = 0.60): it links to D, G, and E, the three best authorities.

D is the best authority (a = 0.69), linked by six pages, followed by G (a = 0.54).

E (a = 0.31) is a slightly better authority than C (a = 0.29), even though E has two incoming links and C has three. E is linked by the two strong hubs A and F. C is linked by A, by the average hub G, and by the weak hub D.

Roles mix. B is a weak authority and an average hub; G is a top authority but also has some hub value. C and H are pure types: C has no outgoing links, and nobody links to H.



Figure 5:An eight-page base set, its adjacency matrix, and the converged hub (h) and authority (a) values.

PageRank and HITS answer different questions. PageRank is computed once, offline, for the whole web, and measures global prominence regardless of the query. HITS is computed at query time on a few thousand pages and finds the best sources for one topic. This is also HITS’s main weakness: building and iterating a base graph for every query is expensive, and the topic focus is fragile, since a few strongly linked off-topic pages in the base set can take over the result. Web search engines adopted PageRank-style global scores. The hub and authority idea survived elsewhere. SALSA, a random-walk variant of HITS by Lempel and Moran, powered Twitter’s “Who to Follow” service, where the accounts closest to a user act as hubs and the accounts they follow act as authorities (

Ranking Without a Query: Feeds).

SALSA: hubs and authorities as a random walk (optional reading)

HITS sums the hub values of all linking pages and then normalizes. A hub passes its full value to every page it links to, however many links it has, and the principal eigenvector concentrates on the most densely linked group of pages in the base set. Lempel and Moran called this the tightly knit community effect: a small group of pages that all link to each other can take over the result, even if the group is off topic. SALSA (Stochastic Approach for Link-Structure Analysis) replaces the sums with a random walk, in the spirit of PageRank.

The walk alternates between the two roles. From an authority p, the surfer follows one of the incoming links of p backwards to a hub, each with equal probability. From a hub q, the surfer follows one of the outgoing links of q forwards to an authority, again with equal probability. With \text{in}(p) the number of incoming and \text{out}(q) the number of outgoing links, the updates area^{(t+1)}(p) = \sum_{q \rightarrow p} \frac{h^{(t)}(q)}{\text{out}(q)} \qquad h^{(t+1)}(q) = \sum_{q \rightarrow p} \frac{a^{(t)}(p)}{\text{in}(p)}

Each hub splits its value among its outgoing links, and each authority splits its value among its incoming links. Both vectors remain probability distributions, so no normalization step is needed.

Lempel and Moran showed that the stationary distribution of this walk has a closed form. Within each connected component of the graph, the authority value of a page is proportional to its in-degree, and the hub value to its out-degree. A dense community therefore gains only as much as it has links, and the iteration is not even necessary. The price is the mutual reinforcement of HITS: within a component, a link from a strong hub counts as much as a link from a weak one. SALSA is in effect an in-degree count on the query-specific base set. Its topic focus comes from the base set, not from the link weights.

On the eight-page base set of 

Figure 5, all pages form one component with 17 links, so each authority value is its in-degree divided by 17: D 35%, G 24%, C 18%, E 12%, B and F 6% each. The hub values follow the out-degrees: A 29%, F and H 18% each, B and G 12% each, D and E 6% each. The top two authorities agree with HITS, but C and E swap places. HITS ranks E above C because the strong hubs A and F link to E. SALSA ignores hub strength and ranks C above E, since it has three incoming links and E only two.

Early experiments with HITS revealed three problems. An entire domain linking to one external page creates an overpowered authority. Automatically generated links, such as advertisements or “site by” credits, grant authority to off-topic pages. And for a query such as “jaguar car”, the more frequent term dominates, so the top authorities are about cars in general rather than about Jaguar.

Making HITS robust: the Bharat and Henzinger improvements (optional reading)

Krishna Bharat and Monika Henzinger proposed two refinements of HITS in 1998 that address these problems.

The first refinement fixes overpowered hubs and authorities by letting each domain cast one vote instead of each page. If k pages of one domain link to a page p, each of these links receives the weight aw(q, p) = \frac{1}{k} in the authority update of p. If a page p links to l pages of one domain, each of these links receives the weight hw(p, q) = \frac{1}{l} in the hub update of p. 

Figure 6 shows the case of three pages on the example domain a.com linking to one page, and of one page linking to four pages on b.com. The updates becomea^{(t+1)}(p) = \sum_{q \rightarrow p} aw(q, p) \cdot h^{(t)}(q) \qquad h^{(t+1)}(p) = \sum_{p \rightarrow q} hw(p, q) \cdot a^{(t)}(q)

The second refinement keeps the computation on topic. Bharat and Henzinger build a reference document C from the terms with the highest \text{tf} \cdot \text{idf} weights in the root set, so rare and specific terms such as “jaguar” are represented more strongly. For each page p in the base set, they compute the cosine similarity s(p) = \frac{\mathbf{c}^{\top} \mathbf{p}}{\lVert \mathbf{c} \rVert \cdot \lVert \mathbf{p} \rVert} between the \text{tf} \cdot \text{idf} vectors of C and p (

Vector Space Retrieval). Pages with a similarity below a threshold, for example the median of all s(p) values, are removed from the base set, which drops about half of the pages.

The remaining similarity values weight the propagation, so that relevant pages pass on more of their hub and authority value:a^{(t+1)}(p) = \sum_{q \rightarrow p} aw(q, p) \cdot s(q) \cdot h^{(t)}(q) \qquad h^{(t+1)}(p) = \sum_{p \rightarrow q} hw(p, q) \cdot s(q) \cdot a^{(t)}(q)

In their evaluation on 28 topics, the combination of both refinements improved the precision of the top ten results by at least 45% over the original HITS algorithm. The same two ideas, counting votes per domain and weighting links by topical similarity, reappear in many later link-analysis methods, including the per-domain anchor votes of 

Ranking Signals Beyond Term Counts.



Figure 6:Domain weights: three pages of a.com share one vote (\frac{1}{3} each); four linked pages of b.com share one vote (\frac{1}{4} each).

Hands-on: PageRank and HITS

Let a random surfer loose on the seven-page web, compute PageRank by power iteration, vary the damping factor \alpha, create a rank sink, and personalize the random jump. Then compute HITS hubs and authorities on the eight-page base set, check them against the eigenvectors, and compare with SALSA.

The previous two sections produced a long list of signals: BM25F over several fields, proximity, anchor text, PageRank, site quality, location, and language. A real search engine adds many more, such as freshness, the URL depth, the share of users who clicked a page for similar queries, or the score of a neural reranker. Google has long described its ranking as built from hundreds of signals. All of them must be combined into one score per page, and the combination decides what the user sees.

This section starts with an example that combines four signals by hand and asks how to find the best combination. It then formalizes the question as a machine learning problem with three parts: the training data, the scoring model, and the loss. Finally, it shows how the models are trained and how search engines keep collecting the labels for training, mainly from the clicks of their users. The section closes with feeds, which use the same machinery to rank content without any query.

No search engine applies its most expensive ranking function to billions of pages. Ranking happens in stages, and each stage hands a smaller candidate set to a more expensive model, as 

Figure 1 shows. The retriever uses the inverted index (

4 - Index for Text Retrieval) and a cheap score such as BM25F to select on the order of ten thousand candidates. For each candidate, the system computes the full feature vector. A learned ranker, typically an ensemble of gradient-boosted decision trees, orders the candidates. A neural reranker, such as a cross-encoder (

Semantic Similarity with Transformers), rescores the top hundred. Finally, the result page is composed from the ranked list and other elements such as ads and knowledge panels (

The Web Search Landscape).



Figure 1:The web ranking stack: each stage passes fewer candidates to a more expensive model.

This section is about the learned ranker in the middle of the stack. Its input is one feature vector per query-page pair, and its output is a score used for sorting.

Recall the query “uni basel” from the chapter opener. We take four candidate pages and four of the signals from the previous sections, already scaled to comparable ranges. Each page also has a relevance grade from 0 (irrelevant) to 3 (perfect), as in the graded benchmarks of
