Adding proximity does not help, since the three pages that matter score almost the same on it. Adding PageRank or anchor text fixes the ranking. But three quite different weight vectors are now perfect, including one that uses the anchor text alone. This query cannot tell them apart. Other queries can: anchor text alone fails for a new page that nobody links to yet, and a high PageRank weight pushes strong home pages to the top even for queries that they match only weakly.

A good weight vector must therefore work on average over thousands of queries at once. It must cover hundreds of signals, not four, and it must be chosen again whenever the signals or the web change. Tuning by hand does not scale to this. Instead, we collect queries with judged candidates and let an algorithm search for the weights that rank them best. Learning to Rank (LTR) treats the combination of signals as a supervised machine learning problem: given examples of queries, candidate pages, and their known relevance, learn a function that orders the candidates well.

Figure 2 shows the three parts of the problem. A scoring model s_\theta maps the feature vector \mathbf{x} of a query-page pair to a score s, and sorting by s gives the ranked list. The parameters \theta of the model are not set by hand. They are learned from training data, a set of queries with candidate pages and labels y. The loss \mathcal{L} compares the scores with the labels and measures how well the model ranks: the better the ranking, the smaller the loss. Training updates \theta until the loss is small, that is, until sorting by s orders the candidates like their labels.



Figure 2:The learning-to-rank problem: a scoring model maps features to a score, and training updates its parameters \theta from a loss on labeled data.

Since only the order of the candidates of one query matters, the loss is computed per query and summed over all training queries:

Key Formula: The Learning-to-Rank Objective\theta^* = \arg\min_{\theta} \sum_{Q} \mathcal{L}\big(\mathbf{s}_Q, \mathbf{y}_Q\big) \qquad \mathbf{s}_Q = \big(s_\theta(\mathbf{x}_{Q,D_1}), \dots, s_\theta(\mathbf{x}_{Q,D_n})\big)

Find the parameters whose scores order the candidates D_1, \dots, D_n of every training query Q as their labels \mathbf{y}_Q do. The loss \mathcal{L} measures, per query, how far the scores disagree with the labels.

In the running example, the training data holds one query with n = 4 candidates and \mathbf{y}_Q = (3, 1, 0, 2). The model is the weighted sum, its parameters \theta are the four weights \mathbf{w}, and every row of the table above is one candidate \theta. The three parts of the objective can be chosen independently, and the following subsections take them in turn.

Each training example is a pair (Q, D) of a query and a candidate page, described by a feature vector \mathbf{x}_{Q,D} and a label y_{Q,D}. The training set is \mathbb{T} = \{(Q, \mathbf{x}_{Q,D}, y_{Q,D})\} over many queries, each with tens to hundreds of judged candidates. Features fall into three groups:

Query-dependent features describe how well the page matches the query: BM25F per field, proximity, anchor-text score, cosine similarity of embeddings (

Building Semantic Search).

Query-independent features describe the page itself: PageRank, site quality, page length, URL depth, age.

Query features describe the query alone: its length, its intent class, whether it names a place. They do not separate the candidates of one query, but they let the model weight other features differently for different kinds of queries.

The label y_{Q,D} says how relevant D is for Q. The classic source is human judgment on a graded scale, as in our table. Search engines employ thousands of trained raters who judge pages according to detailed guidelines. The second source is user behaviour, mainly clicks. Both sources are discussed in 

Labels for Continuous Training.

The scoring model decides which combinations of signals the ranker can express at all. Three model families are common, shown in the middle of 

Figure 2.

A linear model computes the weighted sum of our hand-tuned attempts, s_\theta(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{w}^{\top} \mathbf{x} with \theta = \mathbf{w}. It has one weight per signal, is cheap to evaluate, and its weights are easy to read. But each signal adds its contribution regardless of the other signals. A linear model cannot express that a high PageRank should count only if the page also matches the query well. Without that condition, a strong home page outranks better pages for every query that it matches even weakly.

A regression tree captures such interactions. It asks a sequence of threshold questions about the features and returns the value stored in the leaf it reaches. A tree with three questions reproduces the grades of our four pages exactly. It first asks whether the anchor score exceeds 3. If so, it asks whether PageRank exceeds 0.8 and returns 3 (d_1) or 2 (d_4). If not, it asks whether proximity exceeds 0.5 and returns 1 (d_2) or 0 (d_3). PageRank is used only for pages with strong anchor text, which is an interaction that no single weight can express. A single tree is coarse, so rankers use a tree ensemble that adds up the outputs of hundreds of small trees, s_\theta(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{m=1}^{M} f_m(\mathbf{x}). In gradient-boosted decision trees (GBDT), each new tree f_m is trained to correct the remaining errors of the trees before it. Trees also handle features on different scales and missing values without manual feature engineering. They do need features that mean the same for every query, since one threshold such as “BM25F > 5” applies to all queries alike. A query with rare terms produces high BM25F scores because of their IDF, and a query with frequent terms produces low ones, so a score of 5 can be mediocre for the first and excellent for the second. Learning-to-rank benchmarks therefore scale each query-dependent feature to the range 0 to 1 within the candidates of each query.

A neural network learns the interactions in its hidden layers. A small multi-layer perceptron computes s_\theta(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{w}_2^{\top} \, \text{ReLU}(\mathbf{W}_1 \mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}_1), with all weight matrices and vectors in \theta. A cross-encoder (

Semantic Similarity with Transformers) goes one step further: it reads the text of the query and the page directly instead of a feature vector, and learns its own features.

The three families trade expressiveness against cost and transparency. Tree ensembles are the strongest choice for hand-crafted features such as those in our table, and they sit in the middle of the ranking stack. Cross-encoders are the most expressive, but also the most expensive, so they only rescore the top candidates.

The loss decides what the training optimizes. LTR methods differ in what they treat as one training example and in the loss they minimize. 

Figure 3 compares the three families on the same four documents.

records.content:
The pointwise approach ignores that we want a ranking. It treats each (Q, D) pair on its own and trains a regression model to predict the grade y, or a classifier to predict the grade class. Any standard learner works, for example least-squares regression with the loss \mathcal{L} = \sum_{D} \big(s_\theta(\mathbf{x}_{Q,D}) - y_{Q,D}\big)^2. On our four pages, a linear model reproduces the grades 3, 1, 0, 2 exactly, but with the weights (0.13, 0.65, 0.73, -3.16). A negative PageRank weight makes no sense: four examples and four free weights can fit any grades, so a perfect fit on so little data says nothing about which signals matter.

The pointwise view has two weaknesses. First, it spends effort on the wrong goal. Predicting 4.0 instead of 3 for d_1 costs a squared error of 1.0, but it is harmless, since d_1 stays on top. Predicting 1.6 for d_4 and 1.7 for d_2 costs only 0.16 + 0.49 = 0.65, yet it swaps two pages. Second, grades are not comparable across queries. For a query with one perfect page, a grade of 2 may be the second-best result. For a query with fifty perfect pages, the same grade lands on page three. Only the order within a query matters.

The Loss: Three Ways to Learn a Ranking

records.content:
The pairwise approach turns ranking into classification of pairs. For each query, every pair of documents with different grades becomes one example: d_i should rank above d_j, written d_i \succ d_j, if y_i > y_j. Our four pages yield six such pairs: d_1 \succ d_2, d_1 \succ d_3, d_1 \succ d_4, d_2 \succ d_3, d_4 \succ d_2, and d_4 \succ d_3. A model that orders every pair correctly produces the ideal ranking.

RankNet (Burges et al., 2005) is the classic pairwise method. It turns the score difference into a probability that d_i should rank above d_j, using the logistic function \sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}, and minimizes the cross-entropy loss on all pairs:

Key Formula: Pairwise Logistic Loss (RankNet)P(d_i \succ d_j) = \sigma\big(s_i - s_j\big) \qquad \mathcal{L} = \sum_{(i, j) : \, y_i > y_j} -\log \sigma\big(s_i - s_j\big)

A pair costs little if the better document scores clearly higher, and a lot if it scores lower. Training pushes the scores of each pair apart in the right direction.

Example: Pairwise loss of two scoring functions

With BM25F alone, the scores are s = (2.1, 2.3, 1.9, 2.0). Two of the six pairs are in the wrong order: d_1 \succ d_2 (2.1 < 2.3) and d_4 \succ d_2 (2.0 < 2.3). Because all scores lie close together, even the correct pairs have probabilities near 0.5. The total loss is \mathcal{L} = 4.052.

With the linear model \mathbf{w} = (1.0, 0.5, 0.3, 1.0), the scores are (5.49, 3.23, 2.05, 4.55). All six pairs are in the right order, and the loss drops to \mathcal{L} = 1.044. Training moves the weights from the first situation towards the second, as 

Training the Model shows.

The pairwise view is much closer to the ranking goal, and it produces many training examples from few judgments. Clicks also naturally produce pairs, as we will see. Its weakness is that every pair counts the same. Swapping the pages at ranks 1 and 2 hurts the user far more than swapping the pages at ranks 40 and 41, but both cost the same in \mathcal{L}.

records.content:
The listwise approach optimizes a measure of the whole ranked list, such as nDCG. The difficulty is that nDCG depends on the sorted order, so it changes in jumps when two scores cross and has no useful gradient. LambdaRank (listwise, built on RankNet’s pairs) solves this with a simple trick. It keeps the pairwise gradients of RankNet, but scales the gradient of each pair by how much nDCG would change if the two documents swapped positions in the current ranking:

Key Formula: LambdaRank Pair Weight\lambda_{ij} = \big|\Delta \text{nDCG}_{ij}\big| \cdot \sigma\big(-(s_i - s_j)\big)

The push on a pair grows with the damage a swap would do to nDCG and with how badly the pair is currently ordered. Pairs near the top of the list, where nDCG is most sensitive, get the strongest updates.

Pointwise, pairwise, listwise: what is the training example?

The three families are not model types. Any of the scoring models above (a linear function, trees, or a neural network) can be trained with any of the three losses. What differs is the unit of training and the loss: one document and its grade (pointwise), one pair and its order (pairwise), or one whole result list and its nDCG (listwise).

The formalization leaves two practical questions. How does an algorithm find the parameters \theta^* for a given model and loss? And where do the labels come from, not once, but continuously, as the web and its users change?

For a linear model or a neural network, training uses gradient descent, as for the word embeddings of 

Word Embeddings. For a linear model with the RankNet loss, each pair pulls the weights in the direction of the feature difference \mathbf{x}_i - \mathbf{x}_j between the better and the worse page. The pull is strong if the pair is currently mis-ordered and weak if it is already well separated:\frac{∂ \mathcal{L}}{∂ \mathbf{w}} = -\sum_{(i, j) : \, y_i > y_j} \sigma\big(-(s_i - s_j)\big) \, \big(\mathbf{x}_i - \mathbf{x}_j\big) \qquad \mathbf{w} \leftarrow \mathbf{w} - \eta \, \frac{∂ \mathcal{L}}{∂ \mathbf{w}}

Example: One gradient step from BM25F alone

We start with \mathbf{w} = (1, 0, 0, 0), the BM25F ranking with \mathcal{L} = 4.052. Summed over the six pairs, the gradient is (-0.06, -1.19, -11.82, -1.45). Its largest component is the anchor weight, because the anchor scores differ most between the better and the worse pages of each pair. One step with the learning rate \eta = 0.05 gives \mathbf{w} = (1.003, 0.060, 0.591, 0.073) and the scores (6.24, 3.02, 1.92, 4.78). The ranking is now ideal, and the loss drops to \mathcal{L} = 0.762. Further steps keep pushing the correct pairs apart: after 50 steps, the loss is 0.115, although the ranking no longer changes.

With thousands of queries, the gradient sums the pulls of all their pairs, and the weights settle on a compromise that ranks well on average. LambdaRank uses the same update, but multiplies the term of each pair by its \lvert \Delta \text{nDCG}_{ij} \rvert, which is exactly the lambda weight of the example above.

Trees cannot be trained by gradient descent on their parameters, since their thresholds and leaf values do not change smoothly. LambdaMART (LambdaRank trained with decision trees) combines the lambda weights with MART (multiple additive regression trees), a form of gradient-boosted decision trees. LambdaRank defines what to optimize: the lambdas. MART defines how the model grows: each new tree is fitted to the lambdas of the current ensemble, so the ensemble grows in the direction that improves nDCG most. LambdaMART won the Yahoo! Learning to Rank Challenge in 2010 and remains a strong baseline for ranking over many hand-crafted features. Libraries such as LightGBM and XGBoost implement it with a lambdarank objective.

Gradient-boosted trees over hand-crafted features dominated web ranking in the 2000s and early 2010s. Since 2019, transformer models have taken over a growing part of the stack. Google announced in 2019 that it uses BERT to understand queries and rank results, affecting about one in ten English queries in the US at launch. A cross-encoder reads query and page together and captures meaning that no feature vector expresses, for example that “can you get medicine for someone pharmacy” is about picking up a prescription for another person. Neural rankers have not replaced learning to rank; they have joined it. A neural reranker is trained with the same pointwise, pairwise, or listwise losses, often on the same mix of human labels and clicks. Its output can become one more feature for a tree ensemble, or the final stage of the stack in

A ranker is never trained only once. New pages appear, events create new queries, the meaning of queries shifts, and every new signal requires a new model. Search engines therefore retrain their rankers regularly, and they need a steady supply of fresh labels. Two sources provide them.

Human raters judge query-page pairs on a graded scale, following detailed guidelines. Their labels are precise and reflect the intended notion of quality, but they are slow and expensive. Search engines therefore spend them where precision matters most: on test sets that evaluate every new ranker offline with nDCG (

When Evaluation Misleads), and on hard or new kinds of queries.

User behaviour is the second source: which results users click, how long they stay on the clicked page, and whether they return to the result list to try another result. Clicks are abundant and free, and they reflect the needs of real users rather than the opinion of raters. Every day of traffic adds millions of new examples. They are also heavily biased.

The strongest bias is position bias. Users click the top results much more often, partly because they are better, but mostly because they are on top. In an eye-tracking study, Joachims et al. swapped the first two results without telling the users, and the result at rank 1 still received most clicks. A click on rank 1 is weak evidence of relevance; a click on rank 5 is strong evidence, since the user read past four other results to get there. Joachims’s early solution used clicks to create pairwise preferences: if the user skipped the result at rank 2 and clicked the one at rank 3, then d_3 \succ d_2 for this query. These pairs feed directly into a pairwise learner such as RankNet.

Modern unbiased learning to rank corrects position bias explicitly. It estimates the probability p_k that a user even looks at rank k, the propensity, for example through small randomized swaps in a fraction of the result pages. Each click at rank k is then weighted by \frac{1}{p_k} in the loss, so clicks at rarely viewed positions count more. Under the assumption that users click a result exactly when they see it and find it relevant, this inverse propensity weighting removes the position bias in expectation.

Clicks are not relevance

A click shows that a result looked promising in the result list, not that the page satisfied the user. Attractive titles and thumbnails earn clicks regardless of quality, which rewards clickbait. Search engines therefore use refined signals: long dwell time on the clicked page counts as success, while a quick return to the result list (a “pogo-stick” back to the results) counts as failure. Even so, a model trained on clicks optimizes what users click, which is not always what is good for them. We meet this tension again in 

Ranking Without a Query: Feeds.

Clicks also decide whether a new ranker goes live. Offline metrics on a judged test set cannot capture everything. Search engines therefore run online experiments: an A/B test shows the new ranker to a small fraction of users and compares click and satisfaction metrics with the current one. Interleaving mixes the results of both rankers into one list and checks which ranker’s results attract more clicks; it needs far fewer users than an A/B test to detect a difference.

Together, these steps form a loop. The deployed ranker produces result pages, the result pages produce clicks, the debiased clicks train the next ranker, and online experiments decide whether it replaces the current one. The loop has a blind spot: users can only click what the ranker shows, so a page that never reaches the first result page never collects the clicks it would need to get there. The randomized swaps that estimate propensities also help here, since they show some results at positions where the current ranker would not put them. The same staged design and the same loop also power recommendation feeds, which we turn to next.

Open TikTok, YouTube, Instagram, or X, and the app shows content before the user types anything. Every swipe asks the same question as a search engine: of the hundreds of millions of items available right now, which few should this user see next? The difference is where the information need comes from. In web search, the user pulls information with a query. In a feed, the system pushes content, and the user’s history, social connections, and context take the role of the query. For videos, music, and images, this has become the main way people discover content.

A feed reuses the machinery of this chapter and of earlier chapters almost unchanged, in the same staged design as the web ranking stack (

Figure 4):

Candidate generation takes the place of the retriever. One source is embedding retrieval: a two-tower model encodes the user and every item into one vector space. This is the bi-encoder of 

Semantic Similarity with Transformers with the user in the place of the query, and an approximate nearest-neighbour index (

Approximate Nearest-Neighbor Search) returns the closest items in milliseconds. Since the item vectors are computed from the content, a new video can be recommended before anyone has watched it; the multimedia features of later chapters feed exactly this step. A second source is the social graph: Personalized PageRank and SALSA (

Link Analysis: PageRank and HITS) find the accounts closest to a user, which yields “who to follow” suggestions and the posts that these accounts liked.

Ranking is learning to rank. A heavy ranker predicts, for each candidate, the probability of every possible reaction: like, reply, share, watch to the end, hide, or report. This is pointwise learning to rank with several labels at once, and the predictions are combined in a weighted sum.

Filters remove content the user has already seen or blocked, limit the number of posts per author, and mix in new creators and topics.



Figure 4:The recommendation funnel: candidate sources select about 1,500 posts, rankers order them, and filters shape the final feed.

The weights of the sum are a product decision, not a learned quantity, and they decide what the feed becomes. X, which published the source code of its home timeline in 2023, weighted a like with 0.5, a reply with 13.5, and a reply that the post’s author engages with 75. Such weights favour conversations; high weights on shares or watch time favour content that spreads. The warning about clicks applies here with full force. Replies, shares, and watch time correlate with interest, but outrage and sensational content produce them as well. A feed trained purely on engagement can amplify divisive content and narrow what a user sees into a filter bubble. Platforms counter this with negative feedback signals, quality classifiers, diversity rules, and surveys that ask users directly whether a post was worth their time.

Feeds also face sharper versions of the evaluation problems of web search. The log only shows reactions to what the current system chose to show, so a feed reserves part of its slots for exploration, such as new creators and new topics, to learn anything new about its users. And since there is no ground truth for which post a user should have seen, feeds are evaluated almost entirely online, with A/B tests that track long-term effects such as whether users return next week, not only short-term engagement. Search and feeds thus share the same end point: both learn to rank from user behaviour, and both must keep the measured behaviour from replacing the goal it stands for.

The link-analysis models all compute an eigenvector of a link matrix by power iteration; they differ in where the random walk restarts (everywhere, at a fixed set, or nowhere) and in which graph they walk (the whole web or a query-specific base set). The learning-to-rank families can use the same model and differ in the unit of training: one document, one pair, or one list. A modern search engine uses link analysis to produce features and learning to rank to combine them, and a recommendation feed reuses both: random walks and embeddings to generate candidates, and a learned multi-task ranker to order them.

Web search differs from classical retrieval in an uncurated, adversarial collection, short and ambiguous queries, huge result sets with nearly equal term scores, and a link graph that reveals which pages people consider important. The engine serves the intent most users mean, composes the result page for that intent, and relies on a crawler that collects the evidence about each page that the page itself does not provide.

Content signals go beyond term counts: proximity rewards query terms that appear close together, BM25F weights fields before a single saturation, anchor text describes a page in other people’s words, counted with one vote per domain, and location, language, and site quality adapt the ranking to the user and the source.

PageRank is the stationary distribution of a random surfer and measures global prominence, not relevance; HITS computes topic-specific hubs and authorities on a query-dependent subgraph.

Learning to rank combines hundreds of signals; pairwise and listwise objectives target the order of results, and LambdaRank weights each pair by its effect on nDCG. Clicks are abundant training labels but must be corrected for position bias.

Feeds rank without a query, with the same staged design: embeddings and the social graph supply candidates, a learned ranker predicts the user’s reactions, and the weights on these predictions decide what the platform optimizes.

The previous chapters built a complete toolkit for text. An inverted file finds every document that contains a query term, BM25 ranks them, embeddings match “heart disease” with “cardiology”, vector indexes search millions of embeddings in milliseconds, and a language model turns the top passages into an answer. Now point the same system at a photo archive, a music catalogue, or a video library. The query is still text, but the documents are pixels, audio samples, and video frames. Nothing in a JPEG file says “Taj Mahal”. Can we do for images, audio, and video what we did for text?

The answer comes in steps. The obvious fix is to describe every item with keywords and reuse text search. It works, and curated catalogues such as IMDb live on it, but human annotation does not scale and metadata from the wild cannot be trusted. The lasting answer is to extract descriptions from the content itself: perceptual features that describe what humans see and hear, classifiers that turn those features into labels, and multimodal transformers that either write a description for the text index or place images and text in one shared vector space. Audio and video add time as a new dimension, and some tasks, such as naming a song from a noisy phone recording, need solutions of their own. The chapters that follow open the toolbox for each modality; this chapter draws the map.

Consider a photo of the Taj Mahal in a large image collection. The Taj Mahal, located in Agra, India, is a mausoleum that Emperor Shah Jahan built in memory of his wife Mumtaz Mahal, who died in 1631. It is one of the most recognized buildings in the world and a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Users who look for such a picture type very different queries: “building, outdoor, sky”, “mausoleum, dome, minaret”, “Taj Mahal”, “UNESCO World Heritage Site”, or even “where is Mumtaz Mahal buried?”. A text retrieval system answers each of these queries by matching words. The photo contains no words.

Text carries its meaning on the surface. Words and sentences are symbols that people invented to express concepts, so a query and a document share the same symbol system. Even the vocabulary mismatch between “heart disease” and “cardiology treatment”, which defeated keyword search for decades, was largely closed by the embeddings of 

Semantic Similarity with Transformers: the model learned that both phrases mean similar things. In every case, the starting point was a sequence of words.

An image starts from a grid of light intensities. A photo of 1024 by 768 pixels with three color channels is a list of 1024 \cdot 768 \cdot 3 = 2{,}359{,}296 numbers between 0 and 255. None of these numbers is “dome”, “sky”, or “Taj Mahal”. 

Figure 1 contrasts the two views: what the machine processes is a patch of color values, and what the user enters is a list of concepts at very different levels of abstraction.



Figure 1:The semantic gap: the pixel values a machine processes versus the queries a user enters for the same photo.

The semantic gap is the distance between the low-level features that a system can compute from the signal and the high-level concepts that people use to describe and search for content. The term became standard with the survey by Smeulders et al. in 2000, listed in the Further Reading of the chapter summary, but the problem applies to every non-text medium.

The queries in 

Figure 1 reveal that the gap has two parts. Concepts such as “building”, “sky”, and “dome” are visible in the image: a system that interprets the pixels well enough can find them. Concepts such as “UNESCO World Heritage Site” or “where is Mumtaz Mahal buried?” are not in the pixels at all. They require knowledge about the world that the photo does not contain. A system can close the first part by analyzing the content; the second part needs context from outside the content. Such context comes from metadata, from the web page around the photo, or from the world knowledge that a large model absorbed during training, as 

Multimodal Transformers shows.

The semantic gap appears in every medium, but its shape differs:

Text: the gap is small because the symbols already carry meaning. Keyword search bridged it for decades, and embeddings closed most of the remaining vocabulary mismatch.

Images: a blue region can be sky, water, or fabric. Interpreting the pixels requires recognizing objects, scenes, and people, and relating them to each other.

Audio: a CD stores 44,100 samples per second and channel, so a three-minute stereo song is 44{,}100 \cdot 180 \cdot 2 = 15{,}876{,}000 amplitude values. A user asks for “a sad piano piece” or “the song that is playing right now”.

Video: frames, sound, and subtitles unfold together over time. At 25 frames per second, a one-hour film has 90,000 frames, and a user wants the one scene in which a character says a certain sentence.

For text, the meaning is in the data and needs to be matched. For the other media, the meaning must first be extracted from the data before anything can be matched. This extraction is called content analysis, and it is the subject of this chapter and the chapters that follow.

The semantic gap is not a vocabulary mismatch

It is tempting to equate the semantic gap with the vocabulary mismatch of text retrieval (“car” versus “automobile”). In text, query and document use the same kind of symbols, and the problem is that different words express the same concept. In images, audio, and video, the document contains no symbols at all. The system must first produce a description before it can face the vocabulary mismatch.

Three application areas show why content analysis has become essential.

Social media and content platforms. Users upload billions of images and videos every day. Early platforms recommended content mostly through collaborative filtering: users who liked the same items in the past get similar suggestions. A new clip has no viewing history yet, so behavioral signals cannot place it. Behavior alone cannot tell whether a clip shows playful kittens or a lion in a documentary. Feed algorithms such as the one behind TikTok combine behavioral signals with content signals: captions, hashtags, the sound track, and visual features of the video itself. The feeds subsection of 

Learning to Rank describes how such feeds are ranked; this chapter is about where the content signals come from.

Media archives and newsrooms. Broadcasters and news agencies hold millions of photos, video clips, audio recordings, and articles collected over decades. 

Figure 2 shows the tape archive of the Danish Broadcasting Corporation. When breaking news arrives, editors have minutes to assemble the material. Suppose Roger Federer announces the end of his career. The evening news wants the highlights of 24 years on tour, from the first Wimbledon title to the last match. A sports broadcaster holds millions of hours of video, and thousands of them show Federer playing tennis. Finding clips with Federer is not enough: the editors need the few that are worth showing.

Traditionally, archivists answered this question at filing time. For each new clip, they judged its value for future use, described it with keywords such as the names of the people, the event, and the date, and filed it into tagged folders. The folders worked like an inverted file: the folder “Federer” pointed to the clips worth keeping, so an editor could pull the material within minutes. This metadata was of high quality, but production volumes outgrew the cataloguers long ago, and a decision made at filing time cannot anticipate every future question. Modern archives use face recognition to identify people across thousands of hours of footage, scene detection to cut videos into segments, speech-to-text to make interviews searchable, and multimodal embeddings so that a query for “earthquake” finds relevant clips even without a matching keyword.



Figure 2:The tape archive of the Danish Broadcasting Corporation: when breaking news arrives, the right material must come out within minutes.

Music and audio services. Shazam names a song from a few seconds recorded in a noisy bar. Spotify recommends tracks that fit a mood, such as “music for a rainy afternoon”, or that sound like a given song. Both must connect acoustic patterns with what listeners mean, and both return in 

Time-Based Media and Specialized Solutions.

Several complementary strategies connect media content with the concepts of the user. They form the road map of this chapter. 

Figure 3 shows them side by side.



Figure 3:Three paths from media content to search: keywords, features, and transformers.

Keywords (metadata). Describe each item with text and search the text with the toolkit of the previous chapters. Humans write the descriptions, or the system harvests them from the context, such as the web page around an image. 

Metadata and Its Limits shows how far this path goes and where it breaks.

Features. Compute perceptual features that describe how the content looks or sounds, and compare items by feature similarity, for example “find images with similar colors”. Classifiers turn features into labels such as “person” or “outdoor”, which feed back into the keyword path. 

Automated Feature Extraction introduces this level.

Transformers. Multimodal transformers either generate a rich description of the content, which again feeds the keyword path, or map media and text into a shared embedding space, so that a text query can be compared directly with an image. 

Multimodal Transformers explains both options.

Audio and video add time, and some tasks need specialized solutions. 

Time-Based Media and Specialized Solutions covers both. The remaining chapters of this part then work out the perceptual features for images, audio, and video in detail.

The quickest way across the semantic gap avoids the content altogether. If the Taj Mahal photo comes with the description “Taj Mahal, mausoleum in Agra, India, built by Shah Jahan”, then the query “Taj Mahal” matches the description and the photo is found. Every tool from the previous chapters applies unchanged: tokenization, an inverted file, BM25, embeddings, and filters. This section follows this keyword path from its strengths to its two fundamental problems: someone has to write the descriptions, and the descriptions are not always true.

Metadata is additional information attached to a media item that describes its content, its context, or its technical properties. For retrieval, the important property of metadata is that it is text, or at least structured values such as dates and coordinates. Once each item has metadata, a multimedia search becomes a text search over the metadata, and the semantic gap is bridged by whoever wrote it.

Metadata comes from three sources. Humans can annotate each item manually. The system can capture or harvest metadata automatically: the camera writes the date and the GPS position into the file, and a web page provides captions and surrounding text. Finally, machine learning models can analyze the content and produce labels or descriptions. This section covers the first two sources; the third is the subject of 

Automated Feature Extraction and 

Multimodal Transformers.

Metadata values describe the content at three levels:

Generic metadata names general classes: “building”, “sky”, “outside”, “summer”.

Specific metadata names individual entities and facts: “Taj Mahal”, “Agra”, “2006”, “UNESCO World Heritage Site”.

Abstract metadata names subjective concepts and interpretations: “love”, “devotion”, “iconic”, “beautiful”.

Annotation schemas organize these values into facets, each describing one aspect of the item. 

Figure 1 annotates the Taj Mahal photo along five facets: objects (from “building, water, sky” to “Taj Mahal”), space (from “outside” to “India, Uttar Pradesh, Agra”), events (from “tourism” to a specific expert meeting in 2006), time (“summer, daytime” and “2006”), and context (topic, related persons, abstract concepts such as “love, death, devotion”, and the history of the building). Each facet holds generic and specific values side by side.



Figure 1:A faceted annotation of the Taj Mahal photo with generic, specific, and abstract values.

Some of these values can be read from the pixels: “outside”, “sky”, “daytime”, and “building” are visible to any careful observer, human or machine. Others, such as “UNESCO”, “Mumtaz Mahal”, or “completed 1648”, require an annotator who knows the context, because no analysis of the pixels can produce them. This is the second part of the semantic gap from 

The Semantic Gap, and it explains why metadata remains valuable even when automated content analysis becomes very good. Facets also map directly to the filters and facet counts of 

Filtering, Facets, and Compression: a user narrows the results to “location: Agra” or “year: 2006” with one click.

EXIF is the metadata that every digital camera and smartphone writes without being asked. It is generic but precise: a timestamp and a GPS position answer the query “photos taken in Paris in 2023” without any content analysis. Many social platforms strip EXIF data on upload, mainly to protect the privacy of the uploader, so this valuable source often disappears on the way to the web. IPTC fields carry the editorial metadata of the news industry. They are usually stored inside the image file in XMP, an extensible metadata format that photo management software reads and writes. Dublin Core is the common denominator of libraries and digital archives. ID3 tags travel inside MP3 files and are the reason a music player shows title and artist. Finally, 

schema.org markup tells search engines what an embedded image or video shows; a VideoObject can even list the key moments of a video with their timestamps.

The standards fix the names of the fields, not their values. Two photographers who both fill in the IPTC keyword field may write “Taj Mahal” and “religious building”. The standards solve the problem of where to find the description; they do not solve the problem of what the description says.

In some domains, metadata is excellent. IMDb holds records for millions of movies and episodes. Each record follows a fixed schema with cast, crew, release dates, genres, plot summaries, and user ratings, and links to related records. Volunteers, actors, crews, and studios maintain the content. MusicBrainz is a community-maintained open encyclopedia of music with artists, releases, recordings, and their relationships. 

Figure 2 shows its record for the song “Paparazzi” next to the lyrics of the song. Together, the two sources provide rich text features that cannot be derived from the video or audio signal alone.



Figure 2:The MusicBrainz record for “Paparazzi” by Lady Gaga, linked to the lyrics of the song.

With curated catalogues, the metadata alone often bridges the semantic gap. Searching for a movie by its director or a song by its lyrics never touches the video or audio. The content itself is only needed for special tasks, such as identifying the song that is currently playing. Curated catalogues exist where commercial or community interest pays for the effort: the revenue of streaming platforms and the enthusiasm of fans cover the cost of the annotation. For an arbitrary photo collection, no one pays.

Human annotation has become an industry because machine learning needs labeled training data, and these labels are metadata at the same time. Crowdsourcing platforms such as Amazon Mechanical Turk give access to over 500,000 independent workers who perform small, well-defined tasks for a fixed price. 

Figure 3 shows the setup of a labeling job in Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth. The requester chooses the task type (image classification, bounding boxes, semantic segmentation, or label verification), the workforce, and a price per task. The suggested price for a segmentation task that takes 90 seconds to 2 minutes is $0.84.



Figure 3:Configuring an image labeling job: task type, workforce, and price per task.

Example: The cost of annotating a photo archive

A media archive holds 1 million photos. At $0.84 per task, a single annotation pass costs 1{,}000{,}000 \cdot 0.84 = 840{,}000 dollars. At 2 minutes per photo, it takes 1{,}000{,}000 \cdot 2 / 60 \approx 33{,}333 hours of human work. Domain experts, such as archivists who recognize historical persons, cost far more than crowd workers. And the archive keeps growing every day.

Crowdsourcing scales the annotation to millions of items, but only for tasks that untrained workers can perform, and only for collections whose value justifies the cost. The fine-tuning of large language models relies on the same workforce: thousands of workers rated the quality of generated answers. Once a model is trained on such labels, it produces labels automatically, which is the step that 

Automated Feature Extraction takes.

Cost is not the only problem; consistency is another. Suppose two workers annotate the Taj Mahal photo. Worker A writes “Taj Mahal, India, iconic building, 17th century”. Worker B writes “religious building, great weather, few people outside, nice”. Both annotations are correct, but they sit at different levels. Worker A knows the building and uses specific terms; Worker B describes what any observer sees and uses generic terms. Similar relationships appear everywhere in language: horse and mammal, Matterhorn and mountain, Italy and Europe. The embeddings of 

Building Semantic Search can relate “Taj Mahal” to “religious building”, but only to a degree. Worker B’s “nice” is an abstract and subjective judgment: two people rarely agree on it, yet it may be exactly what a user means with “great architecture in India”.

The depth of the annotation varies as much as its level. 

Figure 4 contrasts a stock photo with a short list of keywords and an expert article that labels every architectural element of the building, from the finial on the dome to the calligraphy on the arches. The keyword list may be too thin to rank the photo for “Taj Mahal architecture”; the expert article is so detailed that most of its terms never appear in a query.



Figure 4:The same building annotated with stock photo keywords (left) and with an expert description (right).

Stock photo agencies and media archives therefore maintain concise keyword lists and add faceted navigation for the most requested facets: prominent persons, locations, brands, and decades. Annotators examine the photos of an event and tag only selected shots that show known persons. 

Figure 5 shows the benefit and the drawback. A journalist who needs a picture of the tennis player Darlene Hard for an obituary browses a curated folder instead of thousands of pictures. But a photo of children playing tennis today remains unannotated, because none of them is famous yet. If one of them becomes a champion in twenty years, the archive holds the early photos and cannot find them. The archivists of 

The Semantic Gap face the same limit: a clip that was not judged valuable when it was filed cannot be found when it is needed.



Figure 5:Faceted navigation by person finds annotated shots of known players, while photos of the not yet famous stay unfindable.

When images and videos are embedded in web pages, the page provides metadata at almost no cost. The HTML tags and carry attributes such as alt and title that describe the referenced object. Figure 6 shows a news article about the Taj Mahal next to its HTML source: the image has the title “Taj Mahal” and an alt text that repeats the headline, and a caption element below the image repeats the name. The headline, the article text, and the page title contain many more of the keywords a user would type. Figure 6:A news article and its HTML source: title, alt text, and caption describe the embedded image. The difficulty is to decide which text belongs to the image. On early web pages, the describing text sat next to the tag in the source, so a window of a few dozen tokens around the tag, plus the headers and the page title, captured most of the useful keywords. On modern pages, scripts and style sheets place elements on the screen independently of their position in the source. Extractors therefore judge proximity on the rendered page: text in the same visual zone as the image counts more than a sidebar with unrelated news, as Figure 7 shows. Web search engines add the anchor texts of links that point to an image, which describe it in the words of other authors, as Ranking Signals Beyond Term Counts explains. Figure 7:Visual zones of a news page: the article text near the image versus unrelated sidebars. Harvested image-text pairs have since gained a second role. Open datasets such as LAION-5B collected billions of images together with their alt texts from web pages, and contrastive models such as CLIP in Multimodal Transformers learn from such pairs. The cheap and noisy metadata of the web became the training signal for the models that now match images and text without any metadata.

Harvested metadata is cheap, but it is written by people who may have their own goals. In 2001, Cory Doctorow listed in his essay “Metacrap” (see the Further Reading of the chapter summary) “seven insurmountable obstacles” between the world and a “meta-utopia” in which all content is accurately described:

People lie. Content creators publish misleading metadata to attract traffic.

People are lazy. Many publishers do not bother to annotate their content at all.

People are stupid. Many publishers lack the skill to catalogue their content well.

Mission impossible: know thyself. Even honest creators describe their own content inaccurately.

Schemas aren’t neutral. Every classification scheme reflects the views and priorities of its designers.

Metrics influence results. Agreeing in advance on what to record and how to measure it decides what can be found later.

There’s more than one way to describe something. Description is subjective; different perspectives are all valid.

This does not make metadata worthless. Curated catalogues such as IMDb and MusicBrainz are highly reliable, because their maintainers have an interest in quality and control the content. Observational metadata, which describes an item in the words of others rather than its owner, is harder to manipulate. Web search engines trust the anchor texts of links from other pages more than the keywords the page owner chooses. Even this signal can be manipulated by coordinated campaigns, as the Google bombs described in 

Ranking Signals Beyond Term Counts showed. The lesson is to weigh each metadata source by how much it can be trusted, and to evaluate it before relying on it.

Metadata is a claim, not a fact

A keyword attached to an image states what somebody wanted the image to be found for. A common mistake is to treat metadata as ground truth when evaluating a retrieval system. Before using metadata as relevance labels or as filters, check who wrote it, what interest they had, and whether a second source agrees.

The keyword path thus fails in two ways. Manual annotation is too expensive for arbitrary collections, and harvested metadata cannot always be trusted. Both problems point in the same direction: describe the content from the content itself, automatically and consistently. The next section starts with the simplest form of such descriptions.

Send the Taj Mahal photo to a commercial image analysis service, and within a second it returns two kinds of results. 

Figure 1 shows them. The perception branch lists the dominant colors with their shares (steel blue 35%, a light beige 22%, gray 14%) and measures brightness, sharpness, and contrast. The recognition branch lists labels with confidence values: “Arch” 96.5%, “Architecture” 96.5%, “Person” 94.9%, “Tomb” 78.5%, “Fun” 72.9%, “Monument” 65.7%, “Dome” 57.5%. For a second image, the service detects a face and estimates attributes such as age range and glasses; for a third, it recognizes the actress Brie Larson with 99% confidence.



Figure 1:Automated analysis of images: perceptual features (dominant colors, quality) and recognition results (labels, face attributes, celebrity).

Nobody annotated these photos. The two branches correspond to two levels of automated content analysis. The colors describe how the image looks; the labels describe what it shows. This section walks up these levels, from features that describe perception to classifiers that produce labels, and ends with how neural networks took over the classification step.

Automated content analysis works in layers. Each layer transforms the output of the layer below into a more abstract representation and closes a part of the semantic gap. 

Figure 2 shows the layers for a photo of a coyote on a snowy road.



Figure 2:Five layers of content representation, from the raw file to semantic descriptions and metadata.

Raw level: the file as stored, such as JPEG, MP3, or MP4. It holds pixel intensities or amplitude samples. This level preserves the content for playback but helps little with search, because similar content rarely means similar raw data: two photos of the same building, taken a few steps apart, share almost no identical pixel values.

Perceptual level (low level): features that describe how the content looks or sounds, such as color histograms, textures, and edges for images, or the spectral properties of sound. They support comparisons such as “images with similar colors”, but they do not interpret the content. Perceptual features invert the argument of the raw level: they assume that similar statistics of the signal indicate similar content. This assumption often holds, but not always.

Structural level (mid level): patterns and categories recognized in the features, such as detected objects (“wolf”, “road”, “snow”), scene types, music genres, or shot boundaries in a video. Classifiers and learned embeddings work at this level.

Semantic level (high level): interpretable descriptions such as captions, keywords, transcribed speech, or recognized text. At this level, the content is described in concepts that people use.

Contextual level: information from outside the content, such as timestamps, locations, device data, user tags, and social context. Metadata from 

Metadata and Its Limits lives here, and the outputs of the higher levels are stored here as new metadata.

The layers show where each technique of this part of the book sits. The following subsections cover the perceptual and structural levels in general terms; the semantic level is the subject of 

Multimodal Transformers.

Perceptual features describe content the way humans perceive it. They do not attempt to recognize objects or interpret scenes. Instead, they measure properties of the signal that matter to human perception: the distribution of colors, the texture of surfaces, the shapes of edges, the pitch and timbre of a sound, the motion in a video. Each feature turns an item into a feature vector. A color histogram, for example, counts how many pixels fall into each of a fixed set of color bins, and the vector of counts describes the color impression of the image.

The idea is familiar from text retrieval. In 

Vector Space Retrieval, a document became a vector of term frequencies. A color histogram is the image counterpart of such a term vector: the bins play the role of terms, and the pixel counts play the role of term frequencies. The difference is that a term refers to a concept, while a color bin refers to a sensation. A red bin is high for a red car and for a sunset alike.

A system uses perceptual feature vectors in two ways:

Similarity search. The system compares feature vectors directly with a distance measure and returns the items closest to a query. This is content-based retrieval: the query is an example image, a sketch, a color palette, or a hummed melody instead of keywords. The distance measures and index structures of vector search apply directly. The comparison function belongs to the feature: color histograms, for example, come with their own distances, as 

Distance and Similarity Measures explains.

Classification. The system feeds the feature vectors into a classifier that predicts labels such as “outdoor”, “speech”, or “contains a face”. The labels are text, so they return to the keyword path of 

Metadata and Its Limits, but now the system writes them automatically.

Good perceptual features must be stable under the variations that human perception ignores. A photo of a cat is still a photo of a cat after small changes, and a song is still the same song when played a little louder. The most important invariances are:

Translation: an object shifted to a different position in the image is still the same object.

Rotation: a slightly rotated coffee mug does not lose its identity.

Scale and resolution: a tree in the background and the same tree close up, or a high-resolution photo and its thumbnail, show the same content.

Lighting and loudness: a face in harsh sunlight and in soft indoor light is the same face; a song at two volume levels is the same song.

Noise and distortion: sensor noise, compression artifacts, background noise in a recording, or a low-quality microphone should not change the feature much.

Each modality has its own perceptual features, and they are inspired by how human vision and hearing work. The following chapters develop them in detail: color, texture, and shape for images; time-domain, frequency-domain, and psychoacoustic features for audio; shot and motion features for video.

Perceptual similarity is not semantic similarity

A red car and a sunset have similar color histograms, while a black cat on a white carpet and a ginger cat on a green lawn have very different ones. It is tempting to expect perceptual features to find “similar content”. They find content that looks or sounds similar, which is useful for queries by example, near-duplicate detection, or “more like this”, but not for concept queries such as “pictures of cats”.

Classification moves from the perceptual to the structural level. A classifier learns from labeled examples how feature values relate to classes and then predicts the class of new items. For two decades, the standard approach combined hand-crafted perceptual features with a classical learning algorithm such as a decision tree or a support vector machine, both described in 

B - Classical Machine Learning Methods.

A classic example is separating speech from music in a radio stream. Speech alternates between voiced sounds and short pauses, so its energy drops frequently; music keeps a more continuous energy level. The signal of speech also crosses zero at a more irregular rate than the signal of most music. A few features computed over short time frames, such as the share of low-energy frames and the variation of the zero-crossing rate, are enough for a decision tree to separate the two classes with high accuracy. The predicted labels “speech” and “music” become metadata, and they decide which analysis follows: speech goes to transcription, music to genre classification.

How well such a classifier works is measured with the confusion matrix and the metrics derived from it: accuracy, precision, recall, specificity, and the ROC curve. They apply to image, audio, and video classifiers exactly as to the text classifiers of 

Evaluating Text Classifiers.

Automatically extracted labels are claims too. The classifier behind 

Figure 2 labeled the animal on the snowy road “wolf”. It is a coyote, as the metadata at the bottom of the figure states. The two species look alike, and the classifier confused them. Better models reduce such errors but do not remove them. A classifier knows only the classes it was trained on and tends to confuse similar ones. Even the multimodal transformers of 

Multimodal Transformers, which can name almost anything, still mistake similar species, buildings, or persons, and sometimes describe details that are not in the image. Like the human metadata of 

Metadata and Its Limits, automatically extracted metadata must be evaluated before it is trusted.

A confidence value is not a probability of being right

The service in 

Figure 1 labels the Taj Mahal as “Gothic Arch” with 89.4% confidence, although the building is Mughal, not Gothic. For the face in the car, it reports “not smiling” with 63.5% and “appears to be happy” with 70%. Confidence values express how strongly the model favors a label, not how often such labels are correct. Before turning predicted labels into metadata, choose a threshold per label based on an evaluation against ground truth, as in 

Scores, Thresholds, and ROC Curves.

The weak point of this approach is the hand-crafted feature. A human expert must decide which properties of the signal separate the classes. That works for speech versus music, but not for the thousands of object classes that users search for. No one can design a feature that separates “Taj Mahal” from “other white buildings with domes”. The breakthrough came when neural networks learned the features themselves.

Neural networks for image classification went through several generations. Each one solved a specific obstacle of its predecessors, and most of them have since been replaced. 

Figure 3 shows the milestones, and the dropdown below tells the story in more detail; 

CNN Architectures describes the architectures themselves.



Figure 3:Milestones of neural image classification and what each step solved.

Several advances worked together. The ReLU activation function reduced the vanishing gradient problem that had blocked the training of deep networks. Large labeled datasets such as ImageNet and fast GPUs made it possible to train millions of parameters. Regularization methods such as dropout and data augmentation reduced overfitting, and better optimizers such as Adam made training faster and more stable. Convolutional networks exploit the spatial structure of images: they share weights across positions, which gives them translation invariance by design. Residual connections let the gradient flow back to early layers, so depth stopped being a problem.

The layers of a trained convolutional network form their own abstraction ladder. Early layers respond to edges and color blobs, much like the perceptual features above. Middle layers respond to textures and parts, and the last layers respond to whole objects. The output of the second-to-last layer is a dense vector that describes the image, and these vectors became the first learned image embeddings. Two photos of mountains have close vectors even when their color histograms differ.

From hand-wired face detectors to residual networks (optional reading)

Rowley, Baluja, and Kanade at Carnegie Mellon University built one of the first practical neural face detectors in 1998. To keep the network small, they trained it on preprocessed 20 by 20 pixel windows: each window was corrected for lighting, its histogram was equalized, and a second “router” network first estimated the rotation of a potential face so that the window could be rotated upright. At detection time, the system slid the window over the image at many positions and over a pyramid of downscaled copies to find faces of different sizes. The method worked well, but every step except the final decision was designed by hand.

LeNet, developed by Yann LeCun and colleagues for reading handwritten digits, showed that a network could learn the features itself. Its convolution layers apply small learned filters across the whole image, and its pooling layers reduce the resolution step by step. On the MNIST digits it reached accuracies close to human performance without any manual feature design. Yet for more than a decade, convolutional networks remained a niche: the images were small, the datasets were small, and training deeper networks failed because the gradients vanished on their way back to the early layers.

AlexNet changed this in 2012. It won the ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge, which asks for one of 1,000 classes per image, with a top-5 error of 15.3%, against 26.2% for the best entry based on hand-crafted features. It was deeper than LeNet, processed 224 by 224 pixel images, used the ReLU activation instead of saturating functions such as tanh, and was trained on two GPUs. Its two large fully connected layers needed most of its 60 million parameters. The result convinced the computer vision community within a year.

The following years were a race for depth. VGG from Oxford built networks from repeated blocks of 3 by 3 convolutions. GoogLeNet won the 2014 challenge with inception modules that run convolutions of several sizes in parallel and concatenate the results. ResNet added a shortcut around every block. If f(\mathbf{x}) is the mapping that a block should compute, the block learns only the residual g(\mathbf{x}) = f(\mathbf{x}) - \mathbf{x} and adds it to its input, so the output is \mathbf{x} + g(\mathbf{x}). If a block is not needed, it can learn g = 0, and the gradient flows back through the shortcut unchanged. ResNet trained networks with 152 layers and became the standard backbone for years. DenseNet went one step further and connected every layer to all following layers.

The Vision Transformer of 2020 finally removed the convolutions. It cuts an image into patches of 16 by 16 pixels, embeds each patch like a token, and processes the sequence with the same transformer encoder that 

Transformer Embeddings describes for text. With enough training data, it matches or beats convolutional networks, and it opened the door to models that process text and images with one architecture.

Most of these networks are no longer trained for retrieval systems today. Each one learned a fixed set of classes from a labeled dataset, and adding a new class meant collecting new labels and training again. Two developments replaced them. Self-supervised learning trains models on huge unlabeled or weakly labeled collections, for example by predicting masked parts of the input, so manual labels are no longer the bottleneck. Contrastive learning aligns different modalities in one embedding space, so that a model learns from image-caption pairs found on the web instead of from fixed label sets. The ideas of the older networks survive: convolutions, residual connections, and patches are building blocks of current models. The next section shows what these models do for retrieval.

Show a photo of the Matterhorn to a current multimodal language model and ask for a description. The answer reads like the work of a careful human annotator: “The image centers on a single, dramatic mountain peak with a sharp, pyramid-like summit. Its steep faces are streaked with snow and dark gray rock. The peak looks like the Matterhorn in the Swiss Alps, a shape recognized around the world.” The model recognized a specific named entity, described the scene, the colors, and the lighting, and did so without any task-specific training.

Transformers process sequences of tokens. 

Transformer Embeddings applied them to text. The Vision Transformer applies them to images: it cuts an image into patches of 16 by 16 pixels and processes the patches like the tokens of a sentence. Multimodal transformers combine both: they encode images, audio, or video together with text. For retrieval, they offer two paths across the semantic gap. The first path generates text that describes the content and then searches the text. The second path maps content and text into one shared embedding space and compares them directly. This section covers both and compares them.

An image-to-text model has two parts. A visual encoder, usually a Vision Transformer, turns the image into a sequence of embeddings. A transformer decoder generates text token by token. Through cross-attention, each generated token looks at the image embeddings, so the words follow the visual content. Such models are trained on large collections of image-caption pairs. Current multimodal language models go one step further: the image embeddings enter a full language model together with a text prompt, so the user controls through the prompt what the model writes.

This control turns the model into a configurable metadata extractor. 

Figure 1 shows a two-step pipeline for the Matterhorn photo. The first prompt asks for a detailed description of the main subject, the setting, the colors, and the lighting. The second prompt asks for a JSON document with predefined fields: a headline, keywords, named entities, dominant colors and shapes, extracted text, and boolean flags such as people_present and is_outdoors.



Figure 1:Two-step metadata extraction with a multimodal language model: a free-text description and a structured JSON document.

Each field of the JSON document has a place in the index of 

4 - Index for Text Retrieval. The headline and the description become text fields for BM25 and for text embeddings. The keywords and named entities become fields for exact matching and facets. The boolean fields become filters: “outdoor photos without people” is a simple filter query. The prompt decides which metadata the archive gets, at which level, and in which format. Changing the schema means changing the prompt, not retraining a model. A good starting point for writing such prompts is to ask the model itself to draft a prompt from a short specification, a technique called meta-prompting.

The same path works for other media. A speech recognition model such as Whisper transcribes the spoken words of a podcast, an interview, or a video into text with timestamps. It is a transformer that encodes the audio signal and decodes text tokens, trained on 680,000 hours of weakly labeled audio from the web. Text recognition (OCR) extracts the words shown in images and videos, from street signs to presentation slides. For video, a multimodal model can describe the frames of each shot. In all cases, the output is text, and the complete text toolkit applies: BM25, embeddings, filters, and the retrieval-augmented generation of 

7 - Retrieval Augmented Generation.

The describe path has clear strengths. The metadata is readable, so an archivist can check and correct it. The search uses mature, cheap, and well-understood text indexes. Search results can be explained, because each hit matched specific words. But it also has a fundamental limit: the index contains only what the model chose to write at indexing time. If the description of a beach photo does not mention the red umbrella in the corner, the query “red umbrella” will not find the photo. Generating rich descriptions for every item is also expensive, because a large model must process each item once, and again whenever the prompt changes.

Doctorow’s seven obstacles in 

Metadata and Its Limits describe the weaknesses of human metadata, and 

Automated Feature Extraction showed that classifiers confuse similar classes. Generated metadata adds an eighth obstacle that is harder to spot: models hallucinate. A language model produces the most plausible continuation of its input, not a verified statement of fact. When the visual evidence is weak, it fills the gap with a plausible guess and states it with the same confidence as a correct observation. A mountain that resembles the Matterhorn may be labeled “Matterhorn”; a person in a suit at a lectern may be named after a well-known politician; text that is too small to read may be “extracted” anyway.

Hallucinations are especially harmful for specific metadata, such as names, places, and dates, because users trust exactly these fields. Several measures reduce the risk. The prompt can ask the model to mark uncertain values or to leave a field empty when the evidence is unclear. Generated values can be cross-checked against independent metadata: if the EXIF GPS coordinates place the photo in Canada, the label “Matterhorn” is wrong. Specific named entities can be restricted to a controlled list, such as the known persons of a news archive. For high-value collections, a human verifies the generated metadata, which is far cheaper than writing it from scratch.

Generated metadata looks better than it is

Generated descriptions are fluent, detailed, and consistent in style, so they look more reliable than the terse keywords of human annotators. It is tempting to judge the quality of generated metadata by reading a few examples. Evaluate it like any other classifier: sample items, compare the generated fields with ground truth, and measure precision and recall per field.

The second path avoids the detour through text. It rests on one idea: all modalities can be mapped into the same embedding space, so that one comparison works across text, images, audio, and video. Two kinds of models build such a space, and they use it in different ways.

Multimodal language models map an image into the embedding space of their text tokens. The open model LLaVA, for example, encodes the image with a Vision Transformer and multiplies each output vector by a learned projection matrix. The result is a sequence of image tokens with the same dimension as the word embeddings of the language model, which then reads the image tokens and the text prompt as one sequence. This is what the describe path above relies on. The shared space stays inside the model, however: an image becomes a sequence of tokens, not one vector that an index can store and compare.

Dual encoders train one encoder per modality and align their outputs, so that an image and its caption get nearby vectors. Every item becomes one vector, which a vector index can store and search. The best-known dual encoder is CLIP (Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training), published by OpenAI in 2021. Its text encoder is a transformer, and its image encoder is a Vision Transformer or a convolutional network; both map their input to a vector of the same dimension. CLIP learned from 400 million image-caption pairs collected from the web: training pulls the vectors of matching pairs together and pushes mismatched pairs apart, and the captions that people wrote for their images are the only supervision. After training, the shared space supports retrieval in every direction. For text-to-image search, the system encodes every image of the collection once and stores the vectors in a vector index from 

6 - Vector Search. A text query such as “a snow-covered mountain at sunrise” is encoded with the text encoder, and a nearest-neighbor search returns the closest images. No keyword was ever attached to them. For image-to-image search, the query is an image, and the same index returns visually and semantically similar images. For image-to-text search, the system finds the captions or documents closest to an image.

The shared space also turns CLIP into a classifier for any set of classes, without training. For zero-shot classification, the system writes a short text prompt for each class, such as “a photo of a mountain”, encodes the prompts, and assigns the image to the class whose prompt is closest. Text classifiers use the same idea with a short description of each class; 

Text Classification compares it with trained classifiers and with prompting a language model.

Key Formula: Zero-Shot Classification with CLIPp(c ∣ \text{image}) = \frac{e^{s_c}}{\sum_{c'} e^{s_{c'}}} = \frac{e^{s_c - s_{\max}}}{\sum_{c'} e^{s_{c'} - s_{\max}}} \quad \text{with} \quad s_c = \frac{\cos(\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{t}_c)}{\tau}

Encode the image as \mathbf{v} and the prompt of each class c as \mathbf{t}_c, divide the cosine similarities by the temperature \tau, and apply a softmax to the scores s_c. Subtracting the largest score s_{\max} does not change the result, because the factor e^{-s_{\max}} cancels in the numerator and the denominator, but it keeps every exponential between 0 and 1. The temperature is learned during training; for CLIP it is \tau = 0.01, so the scores are the similarities multiplied by 100.

Example: Classifying the Matterhorn photo

CLIP ViT-B/32 compares the Matterhorn photo on the right of 

Figure 2 with five prompts. The cosine similarities are 0.293 for “a photo of a mountain”, 0.221 for “a photo of a building”, 0.213 for “a photo of a tennis player”, 0.212 for “a photo of a city”, and 0.202 for “a photo of a dog”.

Dividing by \tau = 0.01 gives the scores s_c = 29.3, 22.1, 21.3, 21.2, and 20.2. Subtracting s_{\max} = 29.3 gives the exponents 0, -7.2, -8.0, -8.1, and -9.1. Their exponentials are 1, 0.00075, 0.00034, 0.00030, and 0.00011, which sum to 1.0015. The class “mountain” receives 1 / 1.0015 = 99.85\%, “building” 0.07%, and the other three classes 0.03% or less.

The same five prompts assign a photo of Roger Federer to “a photo of a tennis player” with 99.9998%: its similarity is 0.304, against 0.157 to 0.163 for the other prompts.

The absolute values are low: between an image and a text, cosine similarities typically lie between 0.1 and 0.4, and what carries the information is the difference between the candidates, which the temperature amplifies.

Dual encoders are not limited to images and text. CLAP (Contrastive Language-Audio Pre-training) applies the same idea to audio clips and their descriptions, so a query such as “dog barking in the rain” can retrieve sound recordings. Video models embed frames or short clips and align them with transcripts and captions. Newer models embed several modalities into one space.

The describe path excels at specific facts, filters, and explainable results: “photos of the Matterhorn taken in winter without people”. The embedding path excels at visual concepts that nobody thought to describe: “a lonely bench in the fog”. A hybrid system runs both and fuses the rankings with reciprocal rank fusion, which scores each item by summing 1/(k + \text{rank}) over the result lists, as 

Building Semantic Search does for sparse and dense text retrieval. The generated descriptions can also serve as passages in a multimodal retrieval-augmented generation pipeline, where a language model answers questions about an image archive.
